Window functions
Difference between ROW_NUMBER and RANK?
Key concepts: ROW_NUMBER; RANK; DENSE_RANK; ties; partition
ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequential number to each row in the partition, breaking ties arbitrarily (or by the ORDER BY). RANK gives tied rows the same number and then skips numbers (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same number without gaps (1, 2, 2, 3).

Partitioning and scaling
What is partitioning?
Key concepts: table partitioning; range and hash partitioning; partition pruning; partition key; vertical vs horizontal; sharding
Partitioning splits one large logical table (or index) into smaller physical pieces, partitions, inside the same database, while queries still see a single table. Horizontal partitioning divides rows by a partition key: range (e.g. by month), list (by region) or hash (even spread). Vertical partitioning splits columns, for example moving rarely used or large columns to another table. Benefits: partition pruning, where a query filtering on the partition key reads only the relevant partitions; cheap maintenance such as dropping or archiving an old partition instead of a huge DELETE; smaller indexes and per-partition operations; and sometimes parallelism. Costs: queries that do not filter on the partition key touch all partitions; a poor key creates skew or hot partitions; extra operational complexity; and in some systems (e.g. PostgreSQL) unique and primary keys must include the partition key. It differs from sharding, where pieces live on different servers. Support and syntax vary by database, and SQLite has no native partitioning.

Indexing and performance
What is a clustered index?
Key concepts: clustered index; one per table; leaf level holds rows; page splits; range scans; InnoDB primary key; heap
A clustered index defines how the table's rows themselves are organised: the leaf level of the index is the data, with rows kept in the order of the clustering key (physically approximately, as linked pages). Because the rows can be in only one order, a table has at most one clustered index. It makes range scans and ORDER BY on the key fast, and lookups by key need no extra step. Trade-offs: inserting keys out of order (random UUIDs) causes page splits and fragmentation, while an ever-increasing key appends efficiently; updating the key moves the row; and the clustering key is carried in every non-clustered index, so a wide key bloats them. Engine specifics: in SQL Server the primary key is clustered by default but you can choose another; in MySQL InnoDB the table is always clustered on the primary key (or a hidden row id); PostgreSQL has no maintained clustered index (the CLUSTER command reorders once and is not kept up). Tables without a clustered index in SQL Server are heaps.

Indexing and performance
What is a non-clustered index?
Key concepts: non-clustered index; row locator; key lookup; covering index; INCLUDE columns; write cost
A non-clustered (secondary) index is a separate structure, usually a B-tree, holding the indexed key columns in sorted order plus a row locator that points back to the table row. The locator is a row id (RID) when the table is a heap, or the clustering key when the table has a clustered index (as in SQL Server and InnoDB). A table can have many of them. A lookup finds the key in the index, then performs a lookup (key lookup / bookmark lookup) into the table to fetch other columns; this extra step is why the optimizer may ignore a non-clustered index when many rows match and a scan is cheaper. A covering index avoids the lookup by containing all columns the query needs, e.g. with INCLUDE columns in SQL Server or PostgreSQL. Trade-offs: each index costs storage and slows INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, so index the columns used in filters, joins and sorts, not everything.

Transactions and concurrency
What is a deadlock?
Key concepts: deadlock; lock cycle; wait-for graph; victim rollback; consistent lock ordering; retry logic; blocking vs deadlock
A deadlock is a cycle of transactions in which each holds a lock another needs and waits for it, so none can proceed. Example: T1 locks row A then requests row B, while T2 locks B then requests A. Unlike ordinary blocking, which ends when the holder commits, a deadlock cannot resolve itself. Databases detect it (typically with a wait-for graph, or via lock timeouts) and abort one transaction, the victim, with an error; its work is rolled back and the application must catch that error and retry. So they are not 'indefinite' in practice, but they cost latency and failed requests. Prevention and mitigation: access tables and rows in a consistent order, keep transactions short, avoid user interaction inside a transaction, acquire needed locks early (e.g. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), use appropriate indexes so fewer rows are locked, use a lower isolation level where acceptable, and implement retry with backoff. Deadlock logs or graphs show which statements collided.

Partitioning and scaling
What is sharding?
Key concepts: sharding; shard key; consistent hashing; cross-shard queries; hotspots; replication; horizontal scaling
Sharding is horizontal partitioning of data across multiple independent database servers (shards), each holding a subset of the rows, so storage and read/write load scale out beyond one machine. A shard key decides placement: range-based (simple, supports range queries, but can create hot shards), hash-based (even spread, poor range queries) or directory/lookup-based (flexible, extra lookup layer). Consistent hashing reduces data movement when shards are added. Trade-offs: queries must include the shard key to hit one shard, otherwise they fan out; cross-shard joins and transactions are hard or need distributed commit; rebalancing and resharding are operationally difficult; skewed keys create hotspots; and global unique ids and schema changes need coordination. It differs from replication (copies of the same data for availability and read scaling) and from partitioning within a single server. Prefer simpler options first (indexing, caching, read replicas, vertical scaling) and shard when one node cannot handle the data size or write throughput.

Indexing and performance
How do you improve a slow query?
Key concepts: execution plan; index design; sargable predicates; statistics; keyset pagination; N+1 queries; materialized view
Measure before changing anything. Capture the slow statement (slow query log or monitoring) and read its execution plan with actual row counts (EXPLAIN ANALYZE or equivalent) to see where time goes. Then work through the usual causes. Full scans on large tables: add or fix an index matching the filter, join and sort columns, with composite column order chosen for the query, and consider a covering index. Non-sargable predicates that cannot use an index: functions or casts on the indexed column, implicit type conversion, leading-wildcard LIKE; rewrite them (e.g. a date range instead of wrapping the column in a function). Doing too much work: select only needed columns, filter early, avoid SELECT *, avoid correlated subqueries that run per row if a join works, and replace deep OFFSET pagination with keyset pagination. Bad estimates: update statistics so the optimizer picks good join order and join type. Application patterns: remove N+1 queries and batch. If the query is inherently heavy, precompute (summary table, materialized view), cache, partition or denormalise. Re-measure after each change, since every index slows writes.

Indexing and performance
What are execution plans?
Key concepts: execution plan; query optimizer; cost estimation; table statistics; index seek vs scan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE; join algorithms
An execution plan is the optimizer's chosen strategy for running a query: a tree of operators such as table scan, index seek or scan, join (nested loop, hash, merge), sort and aggregate, showing the order and method for each step. The optimizer enumerates alternatives and picks the one with the lowest estimated cost, based on table statistics (row counts, value distributions) and available indexes. You view it with EXPLAIN (PostgreSQL, MySQL), EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (SQLite), or graphical plans in SQL Server. EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8) actually runs the query and adds real row counts and timings, so be careful with data-changing statements. What to look for: full scans where an index seek was expected, large gaps between estimated and actual rows (stale statistics), expensive sorts, spills to disk, and unsuitable join types. Plans can change with data size, parameters and statistics. SQLite example:

```sql
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;
```

How do you handle exceptions in Python?

Data structures and algorithms
Implement Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm.
Key concepts: Dijkstra's algorithm; shortest path; min-heap; Bellman-Ford; negative weights
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source to all nodes in a graph with non-negative edge weights. Use a min-heap keyed by distance; repeatedly pop the closest unfinalised node and relax its edges. With a binary heap it runs in O((V + E) log V). It fails with negative weights (use Bellman-Ford).

```python
import heapq

def dijkstra(graph, source):
    """graph: {node: [(neighbour, weight), ...]} with non-negative weights."""
    dist = {node: float("inf") for node in graph}
    dist[source] = 0
    heap = [(0, source)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue  # stale entry
        for v, w in graph[u]:
            nd = d + w
            if nd < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = nd
                heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, v))
    return dist
```

Data structures and algorithms
What is quicksort and how would you implement it in Python?
Key concepts: quicksort; pivot; divide-and-conquer; partition; worst case
Quicksort is a divide-and-conquer sort: choose a pivot, partition the items into smaller, equal and larger groups, and recursively sort the outer groups. Average time is O(n log n); the worst case is O(n^2) (for example consistently bad pivots), and the in-place version uses O(log n) extra stack space on average. The version below favours clarity (it allocates new lists):

```python
def quicksort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr
    pivot = arr[len(arr) // 2]
    left = [x for x in arr if x < pivot]
    mid = [x for x in arr if x == pivot]
    right = [x for x in arr if x > pivot]
    return quicksort(left) + mid + quicksort(right)
```

Data science libraries
Implement a simple linear regression from scratch using NumPy.
Key concepts: linear regression; NumPy; normal equation; sum of squared errors; gradient descent
Linear regression picks the parameters that minimise the sum of squared errors. With a design matrix Xb (including a column of ones), the closed-form (normal-equation) solution is theta = (Xb^T Xb)^-1 Xb^T y; gradient descent is the alternative for large or high-dimensional data. Implementation:

```python
import numpy as np

def fit_linear_regression(X, y):
    """Ordinary least squares via the normal equation; adds an intercept."""
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float).reshape(len(X), -1)
    Xb = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]
    theta = np.linalg.pinv(Xb.T @ Xb) @ Xb.T @ np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    return theta  # theta[0] = intercept, theta[1:] = coefficients

def predict(theta, X):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float).reshape(len(X), -1)
    return np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X] @ theta
```

Testing
How do you use mocking in unit tests with pytest?
Key concepts: unittest.mock.patch; monkeypatch fixture; return_value and side_effect; autospec; assert_called_once_with; patch where it is used; test isolation
Mocking replaces a dependency of the code under test (network call, database, clock, environment) with a controllable fake, so the unit test is fast, deterministic and checks only your logic. In pytest you use the standard library's unittest.mock together with pytest's built-in monkeypatch fixture (pytest does not ship its own mock objects; the pytest-mock plugin adds a 'mocker' fixture that wraps unittest.mock, but is not needed).

```python
import sys
from unittest.mock import patch, create_autospec
import pytest


def fetch_json(url):
    raise RuntimeError("real network call - must be mocked in unit tests")


def get_username(user_id):
    data = fetch_json(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}")
    return data["name"].title()


THIS = sys.modules[__name__]


def test_with_unittest_mock_patch():
    with patch.object(THIS, "fetch_json", return_value={"name": "ada lovelace"}) as m:
        assert get_username(7) == "Ada Lovelace"
        m.assert_called_once_with("https://api.example.com/users/7")


def test_with_monkeypatch(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(THIS, "fetch_json", lambda url: {"name": "alan turing"})
    assert get_username(1) == "Alan Turing"


def test_error_path():
    with patch.object(THIS, "fetch_json", side_effect=TimeoutError("slow")):
        with pytest.raises(TimeoutError):
            get_username(2)


def test_autospec_rejects_wrong_signature():
    m = create_autospec(fetch_json, return_value={"name": "x"})
    m("url")
    with pytest.raises(TypeError):
        m("url", "extra")


def test_unpatched_call_hits_real_function():
    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError):
        get_username(3)
```

This file was run with pytest: 5 tests pass. Key points: return_value fixes the result and side_effect makes the mock raise or return a sequence, which lets you test error handling; assert_called_once_with checks how the dependency was called; create_autospec (or patch(..., autospec=True)) makes the mock follow the real function's signature so wrong calls fail; patch and monkeypatch undo the change automatically when the test or block ends.

The most common pitfall is patching the wrong name: patch where the object is looked up (the module that uses it, e.g. 'myapp.service.fetch_json'), not where it was defined. Also avoid over-mocking, which couples tests to implementation details, and keep a few integration tests that exercise the real dependency.

Tokenisation and vocabulary
You are building a ticket classifier for a support inbox whose text contains typos ('refundd'), SKU codes ('XJ-2200B') and newly coined words. A teammate wants a 500k-entry word-level vocabulary; you prefer a 32k BPE vocabulary. How does each handle an unseen word such as 'unrefundable', and what changes if you move the BPE vocabulary from 8k to 128k entries?
Key concepts: byte pair encoding; WordPiece; out-of-vocabulary; unknown token; byte-level base vocabulary; vocabulary size trade-off; sequence length
The BPE vocabulary handles unseen words; the word-level one cannot. A word-level vocabulary maps 'unrefundable' to <unk> (or to a hashed/rare bucket), so the model loses all information about it, and it still needs a huge embedding table in which most rows are rare and poorly trained. BPE starts from characters (or bytes) and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair until the target vocabulary size is reached. An unseen word is then segmented into known pieces (a typo such as 'refundd' similarly falls back to smaller pieces, with the exact split depending on the learned merges), for example something like un + refund + able, though the actual split depends on the learned merges. With a byte-level base vocabulary no input is truly out of vocabulary. WordPiece is similar but chooses merges by a likelihood-style score instead of raw pair frequency.
Vocabulary-size trade-off: a larger vocabulary gives shorter token sequences (cheaper attention, more text per context window) but a larger embedding/output matrix, and many rare tokens that see few updates. A smaller vocabulary gives longer sequences and less meaningful pieces but compact, well-trained embeddings. Tune on a validation metric, and check how SKUs and numbers are split, since subwords are not guaranteed to be semantically aligned.

Text preprocessing and representation
Without calling scikit-learn in your solution, implement tfidf(docs) that returns (vocab, rows) reproducing TfidfVectorizer's default output (lowercasing, default token pattern, smooth idf, l2-normalised rows). Then explain why a word that appears in every document does not get weight zero, and how you would verify your implementation against sklearn on a tiny corpus.
Key concepts: smooth idf; l2 normalisation; term frequency; document frequency; token pattern; TfidfVectorizer
Smoothed idf is idf(t) = ln((1+n)/(1+df(t))) + 1, tf is the raw count, tf-idf = tf*idf, and each row is then l2-normalised (sklearn defaults). A term in every document gets idf = 1, not 0, so it is down-weighted but never discarded; the textbook ln(n/df) would zero it. Default tokenisation is lowercase with tokens of 2+ word characters.
```python
import math
from collections import Counter

def tfidf(docs, token_pattern=r"(?u)\b\w\w+\b"):
    """sklearn-style: lowercase, tokens of 2+ word chars, smooth idf, l2 norm.
    Returns (vocab, matrix) with vocab sorted alphabetically."""
    import re
    toks = [re.findall(token_pattern, d.lower()) for d in docs]
    vocab = sorted({t for ts in toks for t in ts})
    n = len(docs)
    df = Counter(t for ts in toks for t in set(ts))
    idf = {t: math.log((1 + n) / (1 + df[t])) + 1 for t in vocab}
    rows = []
    for ts in toks:
        c = Counter(ts)
        row = [c[t] * idf[t] for t in vocab]
        norm = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in row))
        rows.append([x / norm if norm else 0.0 for x in row])
    return vocab, rows
```

Note the sort order: sklearn sorts the vocabulary alphabetically, so columns line up only if you do too.

A support-ticket router (TF-IDF + logistic regression over 12 queues) scored 0.96 macro-F1 in offline random-split cross-validation, but a week-one spot check of production predictions shows roughly 60% agreement with agents. The offline pipeline fitted the vectorizer on the full labelled dataset, then split it; labels are the queue the ticket was finally resolved in. List the most likely causes in the order you would check them, with a concrete diagnostic for each.
Key concepts: data leakage; train/serve skew; near-duplicate leakage; group split; time-based split; feature leakage; vectorizer fit inside fold; preprocessing parity
Check in this order, cheapest first.
1) Duplicates and threads: random splits put near-identical tickets (reply chains, templated emails) in both train and test. Diagnose by deduplicating/near-dup hashing and re-evaluating with a group split by thread/customer and a time-based split.
2) Label leakage via artefacts: signatures, 'Category: Billing' headers, queue footers, or ticket-ID prefixes that exist only after routing. Inspect the top-weighted features, ablate suspicious fields, and check that every input field is available at prediction time. Labels set after resolution also differ from what the router sees at arrival.
3) Preprocessing mismatch: production may lowercase, strip HTML, normalise Unicode or truncate differently. Replay the same raw tickets through both paths and diff the cleaned text and feature vectors; ship one serialised Pipeline (preprocessing + vectorizer + model).
4) Vectorizer fitted on all data: for unsupervised TF-IDF this leaks only vocabulary/idf, which is usually a small inflation, but it is wrong in principle and severe if any supervised selection (chi2, top-k by label) was done before splitting. Refit inside each fold.
5) Drift and metric mismatch: new products and vocabulary, and check that the production check measures the same thing (agents' initial routing versus the final resolved queue, accuracy versus macro-F1, and a large enough sample); compare OOV rate and length distributions, and evaluate on the most recent weeks.

Word embeddings
In word2vec skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS), write the loss for one (centre, context) pair, explain why it is used instead of a full softmax and what the noise distribution and k control, and explain why 'bank' in 'river bank' and 'bank account' ends up with a single vector.
Key concepts: skip-gram; negative sampling; noise distribution; softmax normalisation cost; polysemy; distributional hypothesis; subsampling frequent words
For centre word w and observed context c, SGNS maximises log σ(u_c·v_w) + Σ_{i=1..k} E_{n~P_n}[log σ(−u_n·v_w)], with separate input vectors v and output vectors u. It is a binary task: real pairs against k sampled fake pairs. A full softmax needs a normaliser over the whole vocabulary V for every pair, cost O(|V|·d); negative sampling touches only k+1 output vectors, O(k·d). The noise distribution is the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power (it works better than plain unigram or uniform, per the original paper), which boosts rarer words relative to frequent ones. The paper suggests k of 5-20 for small corpora and 2-5 for large ones; more negatives give a stronger signal per pair at higher cost. Frequent-word subsampling is a separate speed/quality trick.
Vectors capture distributional similarity: words used in similar contexts get similar vectors. The model is type-level and context-independent, so 'bank' gets one vector that is a blend of its senses, weighted by corpus frequency. Contextual encoders (ELMo, BERT) assign token-level vectors instead.

Write perplexity(token_probs) that returns the perplexity of a language model on one sequence from its per-token probabilities. A colleague then reports 'our new subword model has perplexity 2.2 on the validation set, much better than the old word-level model's 10, so we are shipping it'. Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-probability per token: PPL = exp(−(1/N) Σ ln p(token_i | context)). Lower is better; it is the weighted effective branching factor (a uniform model over V tokens has PPL = V). A zero-probability token makes perplexity infinite (this code raises ValueError from math.log(0)), so smoothing is needed.
```python
import math

def perplexity(token_probs):
    """exp of the mean negative natural-log probability per token."""
    if not token_probs:
        raise ValueError("empty sequence")
    nll = -sum(math.log(p) for p in token_probs)
    return math.exp(nll / len(token_probs))

def per_unit_perplexity(token_probs, n_units):
    """Same total log-likelihood, normalised by a tokeniser-independent unit
    (words, characters or bytes of the original text)."""
    nll = -sum(math.log(p) for p in token_probs)
    return math.exp(nll / n_units)
```
Why the comparison is invalid: the average is over tokens, and the number of tokens depends on the tokeniser. Test case: a sentence of 4 words with total probability 1e-4 has PPL 10 when the model scores 4 word tokens, but the same joint probability scored as 12 subword tokens gives PPL about 2.15. Same text, same information, very different numbers. To compare models with different vocabularies, normalise the same total log-likelihood by a tokeniser-independent unit (per word, per character or bits-per-byte) on identical text, as per_unit_perplexity does.

Transformers and attention
Implement single-head scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask in NumPy for one sequence: Q and K of shape (T, d_k), V of shape (T, d_v), returning the outputs and the (T, T) weight matrix. Explain why scores are divided by sqrt(d_k), and list the properties you would assert in tests.
Key concepts: scaled dot-product attention; sqrt(d_k) scaling; causal mask; softmax saturation; numerically stable softmax; autoregressive property
Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the score variance near 1. If query and key components are independent with zero mean and unit variance, q·k has variance d_k, so scores grow in magnitude with d_k, the softmax saturates to near one-hot, and gradients through it become tiny. A quick simulation confirms variance about 4, 64 and 1024 unscaled for d_k = 4, 64, 1024, and about 1 after scaling. The causal mask sets future positions (above the diagonal) to −inf before the softmax so they get exactly zero weight.
```python
import numpy as np

def causal_attention(Q, K, V):
    """Q, K: (T, d_k); V: (T, d_v). Returns (output (T, d_v), weights (T, T))."""
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)
    T = scores.shape[0]
    mask = np.triu(np.ones((T, T), dtype=bool), k=1)   # True above the diagonal = future
    scores = np.where(mask, -np.inf, scores)
    scores = scores - scores.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)  # stability
    w = np.exp(scores)
    w = w / w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return w @ V, w
```
The test checks output/weight shapes, that each weight row sums to 1, that the upper triangle is exactly zero, that token 0 attends only to itself, that perturbing future keys/values leaves earlier outputs unchanged, and that very large scores stay finite thanks to the max-subtraction. Pitfalls: masking after the softmax without renormalising, masking with 0 instead of −inf, and scaling by sqrt(T) instead of sqrt(d_k).

Information extraction
A NER model outputs BIO tags and reports 90% token accuracy, yet users say it misses most organisations. Write extract_entities(tags) that turns a BIO sequence into (type, start, end) spans, and entity_prf(gold_seqs, pred_seqs) that returns entity-level micro precision, recall and F1. Explain why token accuracy misleads, and say how your code treats an I- tag that does not follow a matching B-/I- tag.
Key concepts: BIO tagging; entity-level F1; exact span match; token accuracy; class imbalance; micro-averaging; invalid tag sequences
Entity-level evaluation counts an entity as correct only if both its type and its exact span match. Token accuracy rewards the dominant 'O' class and partial matches: in the test example (20 tokens, 3 gold entities) the prediction truncates the ORG span and misses the LOC, yet token accuracy is 0.90, and an all-'O' predictor gets 0.70 while finding nothing. Entity-level scores for the same example are precision 0.5, recall 1/3, F1 0.4. A boundary error counts as one false positive and one false negative.
```python
def extract_entities(tags):
    """BIO tags -> set of (type, start, end_exclusive).
    An I-X that does not continue an open entity of type X starts a new entity
    (conlleval-style leniency)."""
    ents, start, etype = set(), None, None
    for i, tag in enumerate(list(tags) + ["O"]):      # sentinel closes the last span
        if tag == "O":
            prefix, typ = "O", None
        else:
            prefix, typ = tag.split("-", 1)
        if etype is not None and (prefix in ("O", "B") or typ != etype):
            ents.add((etype, start, i))
            etype = None
        if prefix == "B" or (prefix == "I" and etype is None):
            start, etype = i, typ
    return ents

def entity_prf(gold_seqs, pred_seqs):
    tp = fp = fn = 0
    for g, p in zip(gold_seqs, pred_seqs):
        assert len(g) == len(p)
        G, P = extract_entities(g), extract_entities(p)
        tp += len(G & P); fp += len(P - G); fn += len(G - P)
    prec = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    rec = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec) if prec + rec else 0.0
    return prec, rec, f1
```
Design choices: a stray I-X (after O, or after a different type) starts a new entity here, which is the lenient convention used by the CoNLL evaluation script; a strict evaluator could instead drop or penalise invalid sequences, so state which you use. Counts are pooled across sentences (micro-averaged); report per-type scores as well when classes are imbalanced.

Semantic search and LLM applications
Design semantic search over a company's help-centre (about 8,000 articles, edited daily, several locales). Cover how you chunk and embed, how you index and retrieve, whether and where to re-rank, how you evaluate offline and online, and how you keep the index fresh. State the trade-offs of each choice.
Key concepts: chunking; bi-encoder; approximate nearest neighbour; hybrid retrieval; cross-encoder re-ranking; recall@k; MRR; incremental indexing
Ingestion: split articles on their heading structure into chunks of a few hundred tokens with small overlap (smaller chunks match more precisely but lose surrounding context and grow the index; larger chunks keep context but blur the embedding; overlap adds redundancy and storage; tune on the eval set), prepend the title/section, and store metadata: article ID, URL, locale, updated_at, content hash.
Retrieval: a bi-encoder embeds chunks offline and queries online with the same model (respect any query/document prefix the model needs); use normalised vectors with cosine/inner product. At this scale (roughly 8,000 articles at ~5-10 chunks each is tens of thousands of chunks, more if 8,000 is per locale) exact search may already meet latency; use an ANN index (e.g. HNSW or IVF) when it does not, trading recall, memory and build time. Add BM25 and fuse the rankings (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion) because dense models can miss exact error codes and product names, at the cost of a second index and fusion parameters to tune. Filter by locale/permissions as metadata, and use a multilingual embedding model plus per-locale BM25 analysers (stemming/tokenisation) if users may search across or within several languages; collapse chunks to unique articles.
Re-ranking: a cross-encoder scores the query with each top-50 candidate jointly, which is more accurate but costs per-query compute and latency; apply it only to the shortlist.
Evaluation: build labelled query-to-article judgments (from search logs plus reviewer labels); measure recall@k for the retriever, and MRR/nDCG for the final ranking; ablate chunk size, hybrid and re-ranker. Online: click-through, reformulation rate, zero-result rate, 'was this helpful'.
Freshness: on each edit re-chunk and re-embed only changed articles (content hash), delete removed chunks, and re-embed everything if the embedding model changes (build the new index alongside the old one and switch over). Trade-off: event-driven updates keep search minutes-fresh but need a queue and idempotent upserts, whereas a nightly batch is simpler but leaves edits unsearchable for up to a day.

Plain prompting only works if the whole corpus (or a small relevant slice) fits in context and is cheap to resend; 20,000 pages does not, and long contexts raise cost and latency and models can use them unevenly.
Fine-tuning is poor for facts that change weekly: it is slow to refresh, unreliable at recall of specific passages, cannot cite, and cannot easily unlearn removed or restricted documents. It suits style, format, terminology and behaviours (e.g. answering only from context, abstaining).

Topic modelling
You fit LDA with 20 topics on 50k news articles. Many topics are dominated by words like 'said' and 'would', and rerunning with another random seed gives noticeably different topics. Explain the generative model, what the inputs and outputs are, why you see this behaviour, and how you would choose the number of topics and make the results more reliable.
Key concepts: generative model; Dirichlet prior; bag of words; topic coherence; held-out perplexity; local optima; document-frequency pruning
LDA's generative story: for each topic k draw a word distribution φ_k ~ Dirichlet(β); for each document draw topic proportions θ_d ~ Dirichlet(α); for each word position draw a topic z ~ Categorical(θ_d), then the word w ~ Categorical(φ_z). Input is a document-term count matrix (word order ignored). Outputs are θ (document-topic) and φ (topic-word), found by posterior inference such as variational Bayes or collapsed Gibbs sampling.
Frequent function-like words ('said', 'would') appear in nearly every document, so they carry a lot of probability mass in some topics; remove stop words and use document-frequency pruning (min_df/max_df), lemmatisation and corpus-specific stop lists. The seed dependence arises because the posterior is non-convex, so inference lands in different local optima. Run several seeds and compare or align topics, use more iterations, and keep topics that recur.
Choosing K: scan several values and combine a topic coherence measure (e.g. NPMI) with held-out likelihood or perplexity on unseen documents, plus manual inspection of top words. Held-out likelihood does not always track human-judged interpretability. Priors matter: smaller α gives sparser document-topic mixtures (scikit-learn defaults both priors to 1/n_components).

Text preprocessing and representation
Your sentiment classifier (CountVectorizer + logistic regression) mislabels reviews like 'not good' and 'not bad'. The vectorizer is CountVectorizer(stop_words='english'). Demonstrate the root cause in code, fix it, and explain what you would do instead of aggressive text cleaning.
Key concepts: stop-word removal; negation handling; word bigrams; CountVectorizer; token pattern; ablation; feature collision
Cause: scikit-learn's built-in english stop-word list contains negators such as not, no, never, nor and cannot (check with `"not" in ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS`), so with stop_words='english' the texts 'good' and 'not good' become the same feature vector, as do 'bad' and 'not bad'. The model cannot represent negation, and the opposite sentiments collide. The default tokenizer also drops single-character tokens and punctuation, so emoticons and '!' disappear.
```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

def fit_predict(vec, train_texts, train_y, test_texts):
    X = vec.fit_transform(train_texts)
    clf = LogisticRegression(C=10, max_iter=1000).fit(X, train_y)
    return clf.predict(vec.transform(test_texts))

def broken_vec():
    return CountVectorizer(stop_words="english")                  # drops "not", "no", "never", "very"...

def fixed_vec():
    return CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2))                    # keeps negators; bigram "not good" is a feature
```

```python
      "great and not boring"]

for w in ["not", "no", "never", "nor", "cannot"]:
```

Backpropagation
A single neuron computes a = sigmoid(X @ w + b) and is trained with L = (1/(2N)) * sum_i (a_i - y_i)^2. Derive dL/dw and dL/db, implement them in numpy, and write a numerical gradient check that would catch a forgotten sigmoid-derivative term. What step size and relative error do you expect for a correct implementation?
Key concepts: chain rule; sigmoid derivative a(1-a); central difference gradient check; relative error; MSE loss; vanishing gradient from saturation
With z = Xw + b and a = sigmoid(z), the chain rule gives dL/dz_i = (a_i - y_i) * a_i * (1 - a_i) / N, because sigmoid'(z) = a(1 - a). Then dL/dw = X^T dL/dz and dL/db = sum_i dL/dz_i. The check compares these against central differences (L(theta + eps) - L(theta - eps)) / (2 eps) for each parameter, using float64 and eps around 1e-6, and reports a relative error ||g_a - g_n|| / (||g_a|| + ||g_n||). A correct implementation typically lands around 1e-7 or smaller (about 3e-10 for a random 20x4 example with eps=1e-6); omitting the a(1 - a) factor gave about 0.8 on that example (X.T @ ((a - y) / N) versus the numeric gradient), so the check catches it clearly.

```python
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))

def forward(w, b, X, y):
    a = sigmoid(X @ w + b)
    loss = 0.5 * np.mean((a - y) ** 2)
    return a, loss

def grads(w, b, X, y):
    a, _ = forward(w, b, X, y)
    n = X.shape[0]
    dz = (a - y) * a * (1 - a) / n      # dL/dz_i, includes sigmoid'(z) = a(1-a)
    return X.T @ dz, dz.sum()           # dL/dw, dL/db

def numeric_grads(w, b, X, y, eps=1e-6):
    gw = np.zeros_like(w)
    for i in range(w.size):
        wp, wm = w.copy(), w.copy()
        wp[i] += eps
        wm[i] -= eps
        gw[i] = (forward(wp, b, X, y)[1] - forward(wm, b, X, y)[1]) / (2 * eps)
    gb = (forward(w, b + eps, X, y)[1] - forward(w, b - eps, X, y)[1]) / (2 * eps)
    return gw, gb

def rel_error(a, b):
    return np.linalg.norm(a - b) / max(np.linalg.norm(a) + np.linalg.norm(b), 1e-12)
```

Practical points: use float64 (float32 noise swamps the finite difference), check at a random non-saturated point, and perturb one parameter at a time. Note also that with MSE the a(1 - a) factor makes gradients vanish when the neuron saturates on a wrong answer, which is one reason cross-entropy is preferred for sigmoid outputs.

Initialisation and optimisation
Write out Adam's update rule and explain what m and v each track and why bias correction is needed. Implement one Adam step in numpy and test it against a hand-computed first step. Then say when SGD with momentum might still be a better choice.
Key concepts: Adam update rule; first moment (m); second moment (v); bias correction; per-parameter adaptive step; SGD with momentum; AdamW decoupled weight decay
Adam keeps two exponential moving averages per parameter: m = beta1*m + (1-beta1)*g (a smoothed gradient direction) and v = beta2*v + (1-beta2)*g^2 (a smoothed gradient scale). Both start at zero, so early on they are biased toward zero. Bias correction divides by (1 - beta^t): m_hat = m/(1-beta1^t), v_hat = v/(1-beta2^t). The update is theta -= lr * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps). On step 1, m = 0.1g and v = 0.001g^2; after correction m_hat = g and v_hat = g^2, so the step is lr*g/(|g|+eps), essentially lr*sign(g) as long as |g| is much larger than eps. Without correction the first step would be about 3.16 times lr (0.1/sqrt(0.001)), which is why it matters, especially with beta2 = 0.999.

```python
import numpy as np

def adam_step(theta, grad, m, v, t, lr=1e-3, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8):
    """One Adam update; t is the 1-based step count. Returns new (theta, m, v)."""
    m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * grad
    v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * grad ** 2
    m_hat = m / (1 - beta1 ** t)
    v_hat = v / (1 - beta2 ** t)
    theta = theta - lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + eps)
    return theta, m, v
```

Check:
```python
theta = np.array([1.0, -1.0, 0.5]); g = np.array([0.5, -2.0, 0.0])
theta1, m1, v1 = adam_step(theta, g, np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3), t=1)
assert np.allclose(m1, 0.1 * g) and np.allclose(v1, 0.001 * g ** 2)   # hand-computed m, v
assert np.allclose(theta - theta1, [1e-3, -1e-3, 0.0], atol=1e-9)    # each nonzero coordinate moves by ~lr
```

SGD with momentum is worth trying when Adam fits training data fine but generalises worse, which some practitioners observe in certain vision tasks; this is empirical and not guaranteed, and it needs more learning-rate tuning. Also, adding L2 to the gradient under Adam is not the same as weight decay, because the term is rescaled by 1/sqrt(v); AdamW decouples decay from the adaptive step, which is usually the fairer comparison.

Normalisation
You move a model from a CNN with batch norm to a transformer and someone asks why the transformer uses layer norm. Over which axes does each compute its statistics, how does each behave at training versus inference, and what goes wrong with batch norm for small batches or variable-length sequences?
Key concepts: batch normalisation; layer normalisation; normalisation axes; running mean and variance; train/inference discrepancy; small-batch noise; group normalisation
For an activation tensor, batch norm computes mean and variance per feature/channel across the batch (and spatial positions for a conv layer, i.e. over N, H, W for each channel). Layer norm computes them per sample across the feature dimension (for a transformer, over d_model of each token independently). Both then apply a learned scale and shift.

Training vs inference: batch norm normalises with the current mini-batch statistics during training while updating exponential moving averages of mean and variance; at inference it uses those running estimates so a prediction does not depend on the other examples in the batch. Layer norm uses the same computation in both modes, with no batch dependence and no running statistics.

Problems for batch norm: with very small batches the statistics are noisy and the train-time (batch) and test-time (running) normalisation differ; with variable-length padded sequences the statistics are contaminated by padding positions; in recurrent or step-by-step models, per-time-step batch statistics are awkward to maintain and do not carry over to sequence lengths unseen in training; in distributed training the statistics are per device unless synchronised. Layer norm avoids all of these, which is why it is the standard choice in transformers and recurrent models. For CNNs with small batches, group norm is a common alternative.

Training diagnostics and debugging
You train an image classifier on 15,000 labelled images and see three different runs. Run A: training loss keeps falling towards zero while validation loss bottoms out around epoch 8 and then rises; validation accuracy stalls near 71%. Run B: training and validation loss both flatten at similar, high values after 5 epochs. Run A is overfitting. Priority: (1) checkpoint/early-stop at the best validation epoch; (2) more or stronger data augmentation, or more data; (3) regularise: weight decay, dropout, label smoothing, or a smaller or more heavily pretrained model; (4) confirm the validation split has no distribution shift from train. Run C is a noisy evaluation, not necessarily a model problem. With 300 images and accuracy near 70%, the binomial standard error is sqrt(0.7*0.3/300), about 2.6 points, and each image is worth 0.33 points, so a gap of a few points between epochs is within noise; on a fixed set the swings come from SGD noise flipping a few predictions (learning rate still high, no averaging). Priority: (1) enlarge the validation set or use cross-validation; (2) average over seeds or use a weight moving average; (3) decay the learning rate; (4) do not pick epochs or hyperparameters from differences within the noise.

Loss functions
For a classifier with softmax followed by cross-entropy, show that the gradient of the loss with respect to the logits is p - y. Verify it numerically in numpy against finite differences, and explain why frameworks offer a fused cross-entropy-from-logits function instead of softmax followed by log.
Key concepts: softmax Jacobian; cross-entropy gradient p - y; finite-difference gradient check; log-sum-exp stability; fused loss op; batch mean scaling 1/N
Let p = softmax(z) and L = -sum_k y_k log p_k. The softmax Jacobian is dp_k/dz_j = p_k (delta_kj - p_j). Then dL/dz_j = -sum_k y_k (1/p_k) p_k (delta_kj - p_j) = -(y_j - p_j sum_k y_k) = p_j - y_j, using sum_k y_k = 1 (one-hot or any label distribution). For a batch mean over N examples the gradient is (p - y)/N. It is simple: the error is predicted probability minus target, and each row sums to zero.

```python
import numpy as np

def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

def ce_loss(z, y_onehot):
    zs = z - z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    log_p = zs - np.log(np.exp(zs).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return -(y_onehot * log_p).sum(axis=1).mean()

def ce_grad(z, y_onehot):
    """dLoss/dlogits for the batch-mean loss: (p - y) / N."""
    return (softmax(z) - y_onehot) / z.shape[0]

def numeric_grad(z, y_onehot, eps=1e-6):
    g = np.zeros_like(z)
    for idx in np.ndindex(*z.shape):
        zp, zm = z.copy(), z.copy()
        zp[idx] += eps
        zm[idx] -= eps
        g[idx] = (ce_loss(zp, y_onehot) - ce_loss(zm, y_onehot)) / (2 * eps)
    return g
```

Check it with: z = rng.normal(size=(5, 4)) * 3; y = np.eye(4)[rng.integers(0, 4, 5)]; assert np.allclose(ce_grad(z, y), numeric_grad(z, y), atol=1e-8) and np.allclose(ce_grad(z, y).sum(axis=1), 0). Central differences with eps=1e-6 agree to about 1.6e-10 in the run, and the row sums are zero.

Why fuse: (1) numerical stability - computing log(softmax(z)) separately can give -inf (probability underflows to 0), whereas the fused form uses log-softmax via log-sum-exp and stays finite, as logits [0, -800] with the true class at index 1 show: log(softmax(z)) gives -inf (0 * -inf even gives nan with a one-hot product), while the fused form returns a loss of exactly 800; (2) the backward pass is the cheap p - y instead of multiplying through the full softmax Jacobian and 1/p, which also avoids dividing by tiny probabilities; (3) the forward loss never needs the explicit probabilities, only log-softmax (the backward pass recomputes or reuses p).

Regularisation and hyperparameters
Implement inverted dropout in numpy with separate training and evaluation behaviour, including the backward pass. Why do we scale by 1/(1-p) during training rather than at test time? Write a test with a fixed seed that checks the expectation of the activations is preserved.
Key concepts: inverted dropout; drop vs keep probability; 1/(1-p) scaling; expectation preservation; train vs eval mode; dropout mask in backward pass
In inverted dropout, p is the probability of dropping a unit. During training each unit is kept with probability 1-p and the kept values are multiplied by 1/(1-p), so E[out] = (1-p) * x/(1-p) = x. At evaluation the layer is the identity. Scaling at train time means the test-time network needs no change and no extra multiplication; the alternative (scale by 1-p at test) works but puts the correction in every deployed model. The backward pass multiplies the upstream gradient by the same mask (including the 1/(1-p) factor) and a fresh mask must be drawn on every forward pass.

```python
import numpy as np

def dropout_forward(x, p, training, rng):
    """Inverted dropout. p = probability of dropping a unit. Returns (out, mask)."""
    if not 0.0 <= p < 1.0:
        raise ValueError("p must be in [0, 1)")
    if not training or p == 0.0:
        return x, None
        raise ValueError("p must be in [0, 1)")
    mask = ((rng.random(x.shape) >= p) / (1.0 - p)).astype(x.dtype, copy=False)   # 0 or 1/(1-p)
    return x * mask, mask

def dropout_backward(dout, mask):
    return dout if mask is None else dout * mask
```

The test uses one million ones with seed 42 and p = 0.3: the mean after dropout is 1.0002 (standard error about 0.0007, tolerance 0.005), the dropped fraction is 0.2999, and the unscaled variant has mean 0.6998, showing what goes wrong without scaling. Pitfalls: some libraries parameterise by drop probability and others by keep probability, so check the convention; and forgetting to switch to eval mode makes predictions stochastic and noisy (the expectation is preserved, but individual outputs are perturbed).

Architectures
Very deep plain convolutional networks were observed to get worse training error than shallower ones. How do residual (skip) connections address this, what is the gradient argument, and what do you do when the input and output of a residual block have different shapes?
Key concepts: residual connection; identity mapping; degradation problem; gradient path; projection shortcut (1x1 conv); y = x + F(x)
That observation is the degradation problem: deeper plain networks can show higher training error than shallower ones, so it is an optimisation difficulty rather than overfitting. A residual block computes y = x + F(x). If an identity mapping is optimal, the layers only need to drive F towards zero, which is easier than making a stack of nonlinear layers approximate the identity.

Gradient argument: dy/dx = I + dF/dx, so the backward signal has a direct additive identity path from later layers to earlier ones instead of only a product of many layer Jacobians. This helps gradients reach early layers and eases optimisation. The identity path is exact in pre-activation blocks; the original ResNet applies a ReLU after the addition. He et al. also argue the degradation is unlikely to be caused by vanishing gradients (the plain nets use batch norm), so read the identity path as easing optimisation, not only as a vanishing-gradient fix. It does not remove every training difficulty (normalisation, initialisation and learning rate still matter).

When shapes differ, the element-wise addition needs matching dimensions: use a projection shortcut, typically a 1x1 convolution (with the same stride) on the skip path to match channels and spatial size, or in some designs pad extra channels with zeros and subsample. Concatenation (as in DenseNet) is a different design that grows the channel count instead of adding.

Transfer learning
You have about 2,000 labelled images from a specialised domain (for example industrial surface defects or microscopy) and a CNN pretrained on a large natural-image dataset. Describe how you would decide between feature extraction and fine-tuning, which layers to unfreeze, what learning rates to start with, what augmentation to use, and how you would validate the result.
Key concepts: feature extraction versus fine-tuning; gradual unfreezing; discriminative learning rates; domain gap; label-preserving augmentation; group-aware validation split; frozen batch norm statistics
Start with a cheap baseline: freeze the backbone, extract features (or train only a new classification head). With 2,000 images this is fast, low-variance and gives a number any fine-tuning must beat. Then fine-tune if it beats the baseline on validation: frozen features are often enough when the domain is close to the pretraining data, while a large domain gap (defects, microscopy) usually favours fine-tuning, with only 2,000 images limiting how much you can unfreeze. unfreeze gradually from the top (last block first, then more blocks) while comparing validation results; the further the domain is from the pretraining data, the more layers usually need to adapt, while early layers (edges, textures) transfer most readily. Use the pretraining input normalisation; start at the pretraining resolution but try higher resolution if the defects or structures are small, since downscaling can erase them.

Learning rates (starting points to tune, not rules): head around 1e-3 and backbone 10 to 100 times smaller (about 1e-4 to 1e-5 with AdamW), or SGD with momentum 0.9 around 1e-2 for the head and 1e-3 for the backbone, with warmup and a decay schedule. Keep weight decay modest. With small batches consider keeping batch-norm layers in eval mode (frozen statistics) because noisy batch statistics can hurt.

Augmentation must preserve the label: flips/rotations only if the class is invariant to them, colour jitter only if colour is not the signal; crops, mild scale and noise are usual. Validation: with 2,000 images use stratified k-fold or a fixed hold-out, split by the unit that can leak (patient, part, session, scene) rather than by image, keep a test set untouched until the end, and report per-class precision/recall (or F1/PR-AUC if classes are imbalanced, with class weighting or oversampling) against the frozen-feature baseline and a majority-class baseline. If domain gap is large, consider domain-specific or self-supervised pretrained weights.

Convolutional networks
Write a helper that computes the output spatial size of a convolution given input size, kernel size, padding, stride and dilation, and another that counts the parameters of a conv layer (with optional groups and bias). Test them on worked examples, including a 7x7 stride-2 stem on a 224x224 input and a depthwise-separable pair.
Key concepts: convolution output size formula; padding and stride; dilation and effective kernel; conv parameter count; depthwise separable convolution; floor in output size
Effective kernel extent is d*(k-1)+1, and the output size is floor((n + 2p - d*(k-1) - 1)/s) + 1. Parameters: c_out * (c_in/groups) * k * k, plus c_out if there is a bias. The floor means trailing positions that do not fit a full window are ignored.

```python
import numpy as np

def conv_out_size(n, k, padding=0, stride=1, dilation=1):
    eff_k = dilation * (k - 1) + 1                 # effective kernel extent
    if n + 2 * padding < eff_k:
        raise ValueError("kernel larger than padded input")
    return (n + 2 * padding - eff_k) // stride + 1

def conv_params(c_in, c_out, k, groups=1, bias=True):
    if c_in % groups or c_out % groups:
        raise ValueError("groups must divide c_in and c_out")
    return c_out * (c_in // groups) * k * k + (c_out if bias else 0)
```

Worked results (the output sizes were cross-checked by brute-force counting of window positions; the parameter counts are hand arithmetic; the stem assumes the usual ResNet setting of 3 input channels, 64 output channels and padding 3): 224 with k=7, p=3, s=2 gives 112; then a 3x3, stride-2, pad-1 pool gives 56; a 3x3 kernel with dilation 2 and pad 2 keeps size 32; the same without padding gives 28; n=10, k=3, s=2 gives 4. Parameters: a 7x7 conv from 3 to 64 channels has 9,472; a 3x3 conv from 64 to 128 has 73,856; a depthwise 3x3 on 64 channels (groups=64) has 640 and a following 1x1 pointwise conv from 64 to 128 has 8,320, so the separable pair has 8,960 versus 73,856 for the standard conv. Parameter count does not depend on input size, unlike FLOPs.

Embeddings
An embedding layer is described as 'a lookup table'. Show in numpy that looking up rows of an embedding matrix equals multiplying one-hot vectors by that matrix, implement the gradient for both, and explain why the lookup form is used and how gradients reach only the rows that were used.
Key concepts: embedding lookup; one-hot matrix multiplication equivalence; sparse gradient; scatter-add for repeated indices; vocabulary size cost; gradient flow to used rows
With E of shape (V, d) and token ids idx, E[idx] equals onehot(idx) @ E. In backward, with upstream gradient dout of shape (len(idx), d), dE = onehot^T @ dout: row v of dE is the sum of dout rows for positions where idx == v. Rows of tokens not in the batch get exactly zero gradient, and a token that appears several times gets the sum of its gradients, so use np.add.at (or an equivalent scatter-add) rather than assignment.

```python
import numpy as np

def embed_lookup(E, idx):
    return E[idx]                                   # row gather: O(len(idx) * d)

def embed_onehot(E, idx):
    onehot = np.zeros((len(idx), E.shape[0]))
    onehot[np.arange(len(idx)), idx] = 1.0
    return onehot @ E                               # O(len(idx) * V * d)

def embed_grad_lookup(V, idx, dout):
    dE = np.zeros((V, dout.shape[1]))
    np.add.at(dE, idx, dout)                        # accumulates repeated indices
    return dE

def embed_grad_onehot(V, idx, dout):
    onehot = np.zeros((len(idx), V))
    onehot[np.arange(len(idx)), idx] = 1.0
    return onehot.T @ dout
```

Check (idx is 1-D here; for (batch, seq) ids flatten idx and dout first):
```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
E = rng.normal(size=(10, 4)); idx = np.array([2, 7, 2, 5]); dout = rng.normal(size=(4, 4))
assert np.allclose(embed_lookup(E, idx), embed_onehot(E, idx))
g = embed_grad_lookup(10, idx, dout)
assert np.allclose(g, embed_grad_onehot(10, idx, dout))
assert np.allclose(g[2], dout[0] + dout[2])      # repeated index accumulates
assert np.all(g[[0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9]] == 0)     # unused rows get exactly zero
```

Why lookup is used: the one-hot matmul costs O(len(idx) * V * d) time and needs a (len(idx), V) matrix, which is infeasible for vocabularies of tens of thousands or more, while gathering rows costs O(len(idx) * d). The mathematics is identical. Practical consequence: the gradient is sparse, so optimisers with per-parameter state (Adam) or weight decay can behave differently on rarely seen rows, and some frameworks offer sparse-gradient options for embeddings (check the docs of the framework you use).

Model compression and deployment
A trained model is too slow and too large for its target hardware (say a mid-range phone or a small CPU-only server). Walk through how you would shrink and speed it up using quantisation, pruning, distillation, architecture changes and batching, what the trade-offs are, and how you would validate that accuracy loss is acceptable.
Key concepts: post-training quantisation; quantisation-aware training; structured versus unstructured pruning; knowledge distillation; profiling on target hardware; dynamic batching; accuracy regression validation
First define the target: latency percentile, memory budget, throughput, and an agreed accuracy budget; then profile on the real hardware to see whether the bottleneck is compute, memory bandwidth, preprocessing or the runtime. Go roughly from cheap to costly; steps 3 to 5 all need training, so pick by expected gain on your hardware.

1. Engineering: export to an optimised inference runtime, fuse operators, use half precision where supported, and batch or dynamically batch requests when throughput matters (batching raises throughput but can raise per-request latency).
2. Post-training quantisation, e.g. int8: weights take a quarter of the memory of float32, and speedups depend on hardware int8 support. Use representative calibration data; if accuracy drops, use quantisation-aware training or keep sensitive layers in higher precision.
3. Pruning: unstructured sparsity shrinks the stored model but gives little speed on dense hardware without sparse kernels; structured pruning (channels, heads, layers) gives real speedups but usually needs fine-tuning.
4. Distillation: train a smaller student on the teacher's soft outputs (plus labels); costs a training run but changes the architecture freely.
5. Architecture changes: efficient blocks such as depthwise separable convolutions, a smaller backbone or lower input resolution. These need retraining, and the cost is accuracy (lower resolution loses small objects); depthwise convolutions cut FLOPs but can be memory-bound, so check real latency.

Validation: a frozen held-out set matching production, compare the compressed model against the original on the overall metric and on important slices and classes, check calibration, measure latency on the target device with warm-up and report p50/p95/p99, then run shadow or canary traffic before rollout. Expect trade-offs to be task- and hardware-specific; measure rather than assume.

Write one query that returns the employees in the top 3 salary levels of each department (ties share a level, so a department may return more than 3 people). Output columns: dept, name, salary, rn, rnk, drnk, where rn, rnk and drnk are ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK over salary DESC within the department (break the ROW_NUMBER tie by name). Order by dept, salary DESC, name. Then explain, using your output, how the three functions differ and which one you would pick for "top 3 people" versus "top 3 salary levels".
Key concepts: ROW_NUMBER; RANK; DENSE_RANK; PARTITION BY; window function in subquery; ties; deterministic tiebreaker
Compute all three ranking functions in a subquery partitioned by dept and filter on the outer query, because window functions are only allowed in the select list and ORDER BY, not in WHERE. Filtering drnk <= 3 gives the top 3 salary levels.

```sql
SELECT dept, name, salary, rn, rnk, drnk
FROM (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, name) AS rn,
         RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)       AS rnk,
```

Reading the output: in Eng, Ben and Cy both earn 140. ROW_NUMBER still gives them 2 and 3 (the order between them is arbitrary unless you add a tiebreaker, here name). In Sales, Fay, Gus and Hal all have rank 1 and dense rank 1, but ROW_NUMBER numbers them 1, 2, 3, and Ivy has rnk 4 but drnk 2. Choosing: ROW_NUMBER <= 3 for exactly 3 people per department (needs a deterministic tiebreaker, otherwise the cut-off among tied people is arbitrary); RANK <= 3 for "everyone who finishes in the top 3 positions" (Sales would return 3 people at rank 1, Ivy excluded, Eng returns Ana, Ben, Cy); DENSE_RANK <= 3 for the top 3 distinct salary values.

Table contacts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, name TEXT, created_at TEXT NOT NULL) was loaded from several imports and now contains duplicates. Sample rows (id, email, created_at):
1 'sam@example.com' 2024-01-03 09:00:00
2 'Sam@Example.com' 2024-01-01 12:30:00
3 'lee@example.com' 2024-01-05 10:00:00
4 'sam@example.com ' (trailing space) 2024-02-01 08:00:00
5 'lee@example.com' 2024-01-05 10:00:00
6 NULL 2024-01-02 00:00:00
7 NULL 2024-01-04 00:00:00
8 'kai@example.com' 2024-03-01 00:00:00
(a) Write a query listing the duplicated emails and how many copies each has, treating emails as duplicates when they match after trim and lower-casing. (b) Write the DELETE that keeps only the earliest row (by created_at, then lowest id) per email and leaves rows with NULL email alone. Show which ids survive.
Key concepts: ROW_NUMBER; PARTITION BY; de-duplication; DELETE with subquery; NULL grouping; email normalisation; deterministic tiebreaker
(a) Group on the normalised email and keep groups with more than one row, excluding NULLs:

```sql
SELECT lower(trim(email)) AS norm_email, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM contacts WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY lower(trim(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY norm_email;
```
On the sample this returns lee@example.com with 2 and sam@example.com with 3.

(b) Number the rows inside each normalised-email group with ROW_NUMBER, earliest first with id as tiebreaker, and delete everything numbered above 1:

```sql
DELETE FROM contacts
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id
  FROM (
    SELECT id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY lower(trim(email))
                              ORDER BY created_at, id) AS rn
    FROM contacts
    WHERE email IS NOT NULL
  )
  WHERE rn > 1
);
SELECT id, email, created_at FROM contacts ORDER BY id;
```

Surviving ids are 2 (the 2024-01-01 Sam row, the earliest even though its id is not the lowest), 3 (Lee: tie on created_at with id 5, the lower id wins), 6 and 7 (NULL emails, untouched) and 8. Ids 1, 4 and 5 are deleted.

Details that matter: the WHERE email IS NOT NULL inside the subquery is essential, because PARTITION BY puts all NULLs into one partition and rows 6 and 7 would otherwise count as duplicates of each other. The ORDER BY must include a unique tiebreaker so the survivor is deterministic. Before running a delete like this in production, run the subquery as a SELECT first to review the doomed rows, and do the delete inside a transaction. Afterwards add a unique index on the normalised email so duplicates cannot come back.

Table daily_sales(day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue INTEGER) stores ISO dates. Rows (day, revenue): 2024-03-01 100, 2024-03-02 200, 2024-03-03 150, 2024-03-06 300, 2024-03-07 250, 2024-03-08 50. Note that 03-04 and 03-05 have no row.
Write one query returning day, revenue, cumulative_revenue (running total), avg_last_3_rows (average of the current and previous 2 rows) and avg_last_3_days (average of the rows whose day lies within the current day and the 2 days before it), both averages rounded to 2 decimals, ordered by day. Explain why the last two columns differ, and what the default window frame does when you write only ORDER BY.
Key concepts: running total; window frame; ROWS vs RANGE; default frame; moving average; peer rows; missing dates
```sql
SELECT day, revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS cumulative_revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day
             ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg_last_3_rows,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY julianday(day)
             RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg_last_3_days
FROM daily_sales
ORDER BY day;
```

Cumulative revenue is a window SUM with ORDER BY and no explicit frame. The default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes the current row and all its peers (rows with the same ORDER BY value). Here days are unique so it equals a plain running total (100, 300, 450, 750, 1000, 1050). If two rows shared the same day, both would show the same running total including each other, whereas ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING would advance row by row. For deterministic row-level running totals, state ROWS explicitly and order by a unique key.

avg_last_3_rows uses ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which counts physical rows. On 03-06 that averages 03-02, 03-03 and 03-06 = 216.67, silently reaching back across the missing days. The calendar version orders by julianday(day), a number, and uses RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, so the window is days within 2 days of the current one: on 03-06 only itself (300.0), on 03-07 03-06 and 03-07 (275.0). SQLite requires exactly one ORDER BY term and a constant non-negative offset for RANGE with an offset, and the offset arithmetic only works on numbers: ordering by the text date does not raise an error, the frame just collapses to the current row's peers, so the date is converted with julianday. The first rows have fewer than 3 inputs and average whatever exists. If you need a true 'N full days' metric, generate a calendar and fill missing days with 0 first, because AVG over an incomplete window is not the same as a 3-day average.

Table logins(user_id INTEGER, login_date TEXT) records one row per login with an ISO date; a user can log in several times a day. Sample rows (user_id: dates):
1: 2024-05-01, 05-02, 05-02, 05-03, 05-05, 05-06
2: 2024-05-01, 05-03, 05-04, 05-06
3: 2024-04-29, 04-30, 05-01, 05-02, 05-10, 05-11, 05-12, 05-13
For each user return their longest streak of consecutive calendar days with at least one login: user_id, streak_len, streak_start, streak_end. If a user has several streaks of the maximum length, return the earliest. Order by user_id. Explain why the date-minus-row-number trick identifies streaks.
Key concepts: gaps and islands; ROW_NUMBER; date arithmetic; consecutive days; deduplicate before ranking; GROUP BY island label; tie-breaking
```sql
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
),
numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn
  FROM days
),
islands AS (
  SELECT user_id,
         date(login_date, '-' || rn || ' days') AS grp,
         MIN(login_date) AS streak_start,
         MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
         COUNT(*)        AS streak_len
  FROM numbered
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                               ORDER BY streak_len DESC, streak_start) AS pick
  FROM islands
)
SELECT user_id, streak_len, streak_start, streak_end
FROM ranked
WHERE pick = 1
ORDER BY user_id;
```

Steps: (1) DISTINCT user_id, login_date so repeated same-day logins do not inflate the row numbers. (2) ROW_NUMBER per user ordered by date. (3) Subtract rn days from the date. Within a run of consecutive days the date rises by exactly 1 per row and rn also rises by 1, so date minus rn is constant; whenever a day is skipped the date jumps by more than 1 while rn increases by 1, so the difference changes. That difference (grp) is just a label for an island, and GROUP BY user_id, grp gives each streak with MIN, MAX and COUNT. (4) Rank the streaks per user by length descending then start ascending and keep the first.

Expected result: user 1 has a 3-day streak 05-01 to 05-03 (the duplicate login on 05-02 is collapsed); user 2 has longest streak 2 days (05-03 to 05-04); user 3 has two streaks of 4 days (04-29 to 05-02 and 05-10 to 05-13, which also crosses a month boundary) and the tiebreak returns the earlier one.

Pitfalls: skipping the DISTINCT breaks the arithmetic, because two rows on one day add 2 to rn but 0 to the date. It also requires one row per user-day, and the trick only works for consecutive integers/days; for other gap definitions use LAG and a running sum of 'new island' flags. The date() modifier syntax used to subtract days is SQLite's; other engines have their own date arithmetic.

NULL handling
A catalogue report is meant to list products that are not discontinued, but it returns zero rows. Tables: products(id, name) = (1,'Aviator'), (2,'Wayfarer'), (3,'Round'), (4,'Cat-eye'), (5,'Shield'); discontinued(product_id INTEGER NULL, reason TEXT) = (2,'low sales'), (4,'supplier closed'), (NULL,'legacy import, no id').
SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM discontinued) ORDER BY id;
Explain exactly why this returns nothing (three-valued logic), then give a correct query that returns Aviator, Round and Shield, and say which fix you would choose.
Key concepts: NOT IN; NULL; three-valued logic; UNKNOWN; NOT EXISTS; anti-join; IS NOT NULL / NOT NULL constraint
NOT IN with a list that contains a NULL can never be TRUE. x NOT IN (2, 4, NULL) is x <> 2 AND x <> 4 AND x <> NULL. For id 1 the first two parts are TRUE but x <> NULL is UNKNOWN, and TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE, so UNKNOWN rows are dropped. For ids 2 and 4 a comparison is FALSE, so they are dropped as well. Result: zero rows, with no error, which is why this bug is easy to ship. It starts the day one NULL appears in the subquery column.

Fix with NOT EXISTS, which tests whether any matching row exists and does not get poisoned by NULLs because d.product_id = p.id with a NULL is simply not a match:

```sql
SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products AS p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM discontinued AS d WHERE d.product_id = p.id
)
ORDER BY p.id;
```

This returns Aviator (1), Round (3) and Shield (5).

Alternative: add WHERE product_id IS NOT NULL inside the NOT IN subquery. That also returns the three rows, but it only works if you remember it every time, and it breaks again if someone changes the subquery. I would choose NOT EXISTS (or a LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL anti-join) as the default, and also add NOT NULL on discontinued.product_id plus a foreign key, since a NULL id here is a data-quality defect.
