Your team wants to pick between BM25 and a dense retriever for a 20,000-chunk internal knowledge base. The plan: sample 500 chunks uniformly at random, prompt an LLM to 'write a question that this chunk answers', mark that chunk as the single gold chunk, and compare recall@5.

Critique this golden-set plan. Name the specific biases it introduces and which retriever it is likely to favour, and describe a better construction, including how you would validate it and keep it from going stale.
Key concepts: synthetic question generation; lexical leakage; single gold chunk; query distribution shift; near-duplicate chunks; held-out split
Problems with the plan:

1. Lexical leakage. A question written while looking at a chunk tends to reuse its distinctive terms and phrasing. That is an easy case for BM25 and also for dense models, but it systematically flatters term-matching systems relative to real users, who paraphrase, use abbreviations, or describe a problem without knowing the document's vocabulary. The comparison may therefore be biased towards BM25 (the direction is likely, not guaranteed; measure it).
2. Distribution mismatch. Real queries are shorter, vaguer, sometimes multi-part, sometimes unanswerable, and concentrated on popular topics. Uniform chunk sampling gives the opposite: equal weight to rarely used pages, boilerplate (headers, legal footers, tables of contents) and chunks that cannot yield a self-contained question.
3. Context-dependent questions. 'What does the table above show?' is not retrievable. Generated questions need a standalone-answerable filter.
4. A single gold chunk. Duplicated content, overlapping chunks and other pages stating the same fact are scored as misses, which adds noise and penalises retrievers that find a valid alternative.
5. No hard cases: multi-hop questions needing two chunks, questions whose answer changed over time, and questions with no answer in the corpus.
6. Size and overfitting: 500 items give wide intervals on differences between systems, and reusing the set for tuning inflates the final numbers.

A better construction: start from real query logs (anonymised) or support tickets where available; add synthetic questions for coverage but instruct the generator to paraphrase and avoid copying rare terms, then filter by standalone-answerability and by a second check that a human or strong model agrees the chunk answers it. Collect candidates by pooling the top results from several diverse retrievers (BM25, dense, hybrid) and have annotators mark every pooled candidate as relevant or not, allowing multiple gold chunks. Stratify by question type and topic, include unanswerable items, and split into a development set and a frozen test set. Version the set, store corpus snapshot IDs with it, and review it when documents change.

RAG evaluation (recall@k, MRR, nDCG, faithfulness, golden sets, LLM judges)
You replace the embedding model in a RAG pipeline that passes the top 5 retrieved chunks to the generator. On a 200-question golden set, recall@10 rises from 0.78 to 0.84. Human-graded answer correctness barely moves: 61% to 62.5%. The team wonders if retrieval metrics 'don't matter'.

Give at least four distinct reasons this can happen, say how you would tell them apart with the data you already have, and what extra experiment establishes the ceiling on what better retrieval can deliver.
Key concepts: recall@k at the k actually used; oracle context ablation; transition table; generator bottleneck; parametric knowledge; paired noise
Recall@10 counts gold chunks in 10 positions, but the generator sees 5. Candidate explanations:

1. The gain sits at ranks 6-10. Recall@5 may not have moved at all. Always report recall at the k actually passed to the generator (and the rank distribution of the gold chunk).
2. The generator is the bottleneck. Many remaining failures happen with the right chunk in context: misreading, ignoring it, over-compressing, or hallucinating. Better retrieval cannot fix those.
3. The new hits are on questions the model already answered correctly from parametric knowledge, or on easy single-hop questions, while the hard ones (multi-hop, tables, negation) are unchanged.
4. Position and distraction effects: with long contexts, models often use evidence in the middle less reliably than at the edges, and extra irrelevant chunks can distract; a better embedder may reorder chunks without making the context cleaner.
5. Label problems: 'gold chunk retrieved' can overstate sufficiency (the chunk is relevant but incomplete, so the answer needs a second chunk) or the answer grader may be noisy.
6. Noise. A single 61% accuracy on n = 200 has a standard error of about 3.4 points, but for a before/after change on the same questions the relevant SE is about sqrt(number of flipped questions) / 200, for example 1.7 points if 11 questions flip (say 7 improved, 4 got worse). A net change of 3 questions (1.5 points) is within one standard error, so it says almost nothing alone.

Telling them apart: build a per-query transition table (retrieval hit before/after at the used k vs answer correct before/after) and look only at queries whose retrieval status changed. Check the rank of the gold chunk for the newly hit queries. Break results down by question type. Hand-read a sample of failures that have the gold chunk in context.

Ceiling experiment: run the generator with the gold chunk(s) injected as the context (oracle context). If correctness only rises to, say, the mid-70s, retrieval can at most close a limited gap and the generator or labels need attention; if oracle accuracy is far higher than current accuracy, retrieval and context assembly still have headroom. Also run a no-context baseline to measure parametric knowledge.

RAG evaluation (recall@k, MRR, nDCG, faithfulness, golden sets, LLM judges)
Your retrieval golden set was built by annotators who judged only the top 10 results of the existing BM25 system for each query. You now evaluate a new dense retriever against it: its recall@10 and nDCG@10 come out lower than BM25's, yet when you read its results for 20 queries by hand, they look as good or better. Why can the metrics say this, and how would you fix the evaluation?
Key concepts: pooling; unjudged documents; incomplete relevance labels; judged fraction at k; condensed lists; candidate pool diversity
Recall, precision and nDCG all treat a document as relevant only if it appears in the judged-relevant set; unjudged documents count as non-relevant. When the labelled set came from the top 10 of BM25 only, relevant documents that BM25 cannot find were never shown to annotators, so they have no label. A dense retriever that surfaces such documents is penalised for exactly the behaviour you want, while BM25 is flattered because its own top results are the ones that got judged. This is pooling bias, and the metrics are biased towards systems similar to the one that built the pool.

Small example: the labelled relevant set for a query is {d1, d2, d3}. The dense system returns [d1, x, y, d2, z]. If x and y are truly relevant but never judged, measured recall@5 is 2/3 and precision@5 is 2/5, while the real precision@5 is 4/5 (if z is not relevant).

Diagnose it by computing the judged fraction at k (the share of each system's top-k that has any label). If BM25 is near 100% and the dense system is much lower, the comparison is unreliable. Also sample the unjudged dense results and have a human (or a carefully validated LLM judge) label them to estimate how many are relevant.

Fixes: (1) pool the top results from several different systems (BM25, dense, hybrid, the new candidate) before annotating, and re-pool when you add a new system; (2) judge the unjudged documents in the new system's top k, which is usually a small extra batch; (3) as a sensitivity check, report metrics on 'condensed lists' that drop unjudged documents; (4) keep the judged fraction as a standard column in every eval report; (5) when labels are partial, treat measured precision@k as a lower bound (unjudged hits count as misses); measured recall is biased too, but its denominator is also incomplete, so it is not a strict bound. More queries do not help because the missing labels bias every query in the same direction.

RAG evaluation (recall@k, MRR, nDCG, faithfulness, golden sets, LLM judges)
Some of your RAG questions need several pieces of evidence (for example a policy rule plus its exception), and for each piece there may be several acceptable chunks because the corpus contains near-duplicates. Averaging plain recall@k over queries hides whether the generator actually receives everything it needs.

Implement evidence_coverage(ranked, groups, k), where groups is a list of sets of chunk ids and a group counts as covered if any of its chunks is in the top k, returning (fraction of groups covered, whether all groups are covered), and aggregate(runs, k) returning (mean coverage, full-coverage rate). Here runs is a list of (ranked, groups) pairs. Use these four queries: (1) ranked [c1, c9, c2, c7], groups [{c1}, {c2, c20}]; (2) [c5, c3, c8, c4], [{c3}, {c6}]; (3) [c10, c11], [{c12}]; (4) [c1, c2, c3, c4], [{c4}, {c3}, {c40}]. Explain why mean coverage and full-coverage rate move differently when k goes from 3 to 4.
Key concepts: evidence groups; full coverage rate; mean coverage; context sufficiency; multi-hop retrieval; duplicate chunks
Plain recall@k averages over gold chunks. For a question that needs two chunks, retrieving one of them gives recall 0.5 but usually gives a generator that cannot answer correctly, because the second piece (the exception, the second hop) is missing. What matters for answerability is whether all required pieces are present, so report both: mean coverage (partial credit, a smooth signal for tuning) and the full-coverage rate (the share of questions whose evidence is complete, closer to the answer-correctness ceiling).

Modelling evidence as groups of acceptable chunks handles duplicates and overlapping chunk boundaries: a group is covered if any member is retrieved, so retrieving the equivalent duplicate is not penalised, and several retrieved duplicates of the same group count once (a chunk listed in two groups would cover both, so keep groups disjoint). Define the groups when building the golden set (by pooling and judging, not just by the chunk the question came from).

In the four-query example, at k = 3 the per-query coverages are 1.0, 0.5, 0.0 and 1/3, so mean coverage is 0.458, and only the first query is fully covered (rate 0.25). Going to k = 4 raises the fourth query to 2/3 and mean coverage to 0.542, but the full-coverage rate stays at 0.25, because the second query still misses its second group and the fourth has a group (c40) that is nowhere in the ranking. A larger k can look like progress on the mean while giving the generator no more complete evidence sets. Note too that a larger k means more context tokens and more distractors for generation.

Caveats: coverage says nothing about rank order (pair it with MRR or nDCG), about whether the chunk is sufficient on its own, or about whether the generator uses it. Edge cases: no groups is an invalid question (unanswerable questions need their own handling), and k = 0 gives zero coverage.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
A 20M-chunk collection sits in an HNSW index. Queries always carry a metadata filter. For a filter such as department='legal' AND year=2019, only about 0.5% of vectors match (roughly 100,000 chunks). With ef_search=100 and top_k=10, the service often returns only 0 to 2 results, though the same query unfiltered returns 10 sensible hits and an exact scan with the filter returns 10 good ones.

Explain why this happens with post-filtering, what in-graph (filtered) traversal and pre-filtering change, and how you would choose a strategy by selectivity.
Key concepts: post-filtering; pre-filtering; filter selectivity; ef_search; graph connectivity under filters; query planner / fallback to exact scan
Post-filtering: the index returns the ef_search nearest candidates ignoring the filter, then the engine discards non-matching ones. If the filter is roughly independent of the query, the expected number of survivors is ef_search x selectivity = 100 x 0.005 = 0.5, far below top_k = 10. To get 10 survivors on average you would need ef around 2,000 (10 / 0.005), which costs latency and still fails when the filter correlates with the query (a query about a topic that lies mostly outside 'legal 2019' will rarely have matching items among its nearest neighbours). Raising top_k does not help for the same reason.

Pre-filtering with exact scan: evaluate the filter first (inverted index or bitmap), giving about 100,000 ids, then compute exact distances for just those. For 768-d float32 vectors that is about 100,000 x 768 x 4 bytes = 307 MB of vector data to read, acceptable for a rare query pattern and perfect recall within the filter, but too heavy at high QPS or when the filter passes millions of vectors.

Traversal-time (in-graph) filtering: search the graph but only admit matching nodes to the result set, in some engines still walking through non-matching nodes and in others restricting the walk to matching ones. It works well for moderate selectivity, but when matching nodes are very sparse, the search wanders through mostly non-matching regions, the effective graph of matching nodes can become disconnected, and recall or latency degrades; implementations differ in how they handle this (for example by switching to a brute-force path when the filter is selective enough).

Partitioning: if a few filter fields are used on nearly every query (tenant, year, language), build separate indexes or partitions per value so that the ANN index only holds eligible vectors.

Choosing: estimate selectivity per query from filter statistics; use post-filter with generous ef when most data matches (for example more than half); use traversal-time filtering in the middle range; use pre-filter plus exact scan when the matching set is small enough to scan within the latency budget. Always measure recall against an exact filtered search on a sample of real filter/query combinations, split by selectivity band, since average recall hides the selective cases.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
You must serve 50 million chunks, 768-d float32 embeddings, from an in-memory HNSW index with M=16, with 3 replicas for availability and throughput. Each node has about 100 GB usable for the index. Estimate memory for the base design, work out how many nodes it needs, and compare it with int8 scalar quantisation and product quantisation with 96-byte codes. Which would you choose and what would you verify before deciding?
Key concepts: vector memory arithmetic; HNSW link overhead; scalar quantisation; product quantisation; sharding vs replication; re-ranking with full vectors
Assumptions (state them in the interview; real engines differ): decimal GB; layer 0 stores up to 2M = 32 neighbour ids of 4 bytes per node; upper layers add roughly n/(M-1) node-layer entries with up to M links each; per-node headers, ids, allocator overhead and metadata are ignored and typically add more.

Base design: vectors = 50e6 x 768 x 4 B = 153.6 GB. Layer-0 links = 50e6 x 32 x 4 B = 6.4 GB. Upper layers add about 0.2 GB. Total about 160.2 GB per full copy. Three replicas = about 480.6 GB cluster-wide.

Nodes: one copy does not fit within 100 GB, so shard it: ceil(160.2 / 100) = 2 shards of about 80 GB each, times 3 replicas = 6 nodes. Replicas multiply cost but not capacity.

int8 scalar quantisation: 1 byte per dimension gives 38.4 GB for vectors plus 6.6 GB for the graph = 45.0 GB per copy, which fits on one node, so 3 nodes with 3 replicas. The recall loss is often small but data- and model-dependent, so measure it.

Product quantisation with 96 one-byte codes per vector (8 dimensions per sub-vector): 4.8 GB + 6.6 GB = 11.4 GB per copy. Each copy fits on one node, so it still needs 3 nodes (the replica count is the floor), the same as int8; the gain is only that nodes could be much smaller. It is lossy: distances are approximate, so many setups re-rank the top candidates with full-precision vectors stored on SSD or in object storage (153.6 GB on disk), adding latency and I/O. The graph links, not the vectors, dominate once codes are this small.

Decision: with these assumptions, int8 gets from 6 nodes to 3 and is a reasonable first step; PQ pays off when memory is the binding constraint. Before deciding, compare recall@k and end-to-end answer quality against the float32 index on a real query set, measure latency under load at the intended QPS and ef_search, and check the build and rebuild time and cost, since sharded indexes also need a fan-out and merge of per-shard top-k results.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
A RAG service re-ingests documents weekly; each document is split into chunks and upserted into an HNSW-based vector store, and deleted documents are removed with a 'delete by chunk id' call. Six months in, you see: memory and disk keep growing though the corpus is stable, p95 latency is creeping up, recall on a fixed monitoring set has dropped a little, and legal reports that a withdrawn document still appears in answers.

Explain the likely mechanisms and design the update and delete path properly.
Key concepts: tombstone deletes; index compaction / rebuild; stable chunk ids; orphaned chunks; alias swap; query-time validity filter
Likely mechanisms:

1. Soft deletes. Many ANN implementations mark deleted vectors (tombstones) and filter them from results but leave them in the graph and storage until a compaction or rebuild. Memory and disk do not shrink; searches can still traverse deleted nodes, which may consume part of the ef budget (implementation-dependent; Qdrant documents graph disconnection with many soft-deleted points); and repeatedly inserting into a graph around deleted nodes can reduce graph quality. This fits growing memory, slower queries and mildly lower recall. Behaviour varies by engine, so check the one you use.
2. Orphaned chunks. If chunk ids are random per ingest, or are position-based (doc42_chunk_11) while a document shrinks from 12 to 9 chunks, then re-upserting by id overwrites some chunks and leaves chunks 10 to 12 of the old version alive. Edited text also shifts chunk boundaries, so the old and new versions coexist and the corpus quietly grows with stale, contradictory text.
3. The withdrawn document: the delete was keyed on chunk ids the pipeline no longer had (or ran before the index refresh made it visible), so some chunks survive.

Design: (a) store doc_id, doc_version and chunk ordinal as metadata, with chunk ids derived from doc_id and version; (b) update = write the new version, then delete everything for that doc_id with an older version (a delete-by-filter on doc_id, not a list of ids you remember); (c) add a query-time filter on an 'active' flag or valid_to timestamp so removals take effect for retrieval immediately even before physical deletion, which is what a compliance deletion needs; (d) monitor the deleted/live ratio and run compaction or a rebuild based on it, validating recall against an exact search on a held-out query set; (e) for large rebuilds build a new index in the background and switch an alias or pointer atomically, with the ability to roll back; (f) reconcile periodically: compare doc ids in the source of truth against the index and fix drift; (g) remember that other copies (caches, reranker caches, backups, answer logs) may also contain the withdrawn text.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
Users of a news-assistant RAG product expect a newly published article to be answerable within about 30 seconds. Today the vector index is rebuilt every night, ingestion runs at roughly 200 new chunks per second at peak, and queries must stay under 200 ms at p95.

Design how new documents become searchable quickly without rebuilding the whole index, say where the 30 seconds actually go, and discuss the consistency and cost trade-offs.
Key concepts: fresh segment; brute-force scan of a small segment; segment merge / compaction; refresh interval; embedding pipeline latency; read-your-writes
Architecture: a main index (ANN, large, rebuilt or compacted in the background) and a delta/fresh segment that accepts writes. Ingestion path: document arrives, is queued, chunked, embedded (often a batched model call), written to a durable log, then added to the fresh segment. A query searches main and fresh in parallel and merges the two top-k lists by similarity (valid because both use the same embedding model and metric; for hybrid keyword scores, normalise or fuse by rank since term statistics differ across segments).

Fresh segment sizing: at 200 chunks per second, an hour accumulates 720,000 chunks. Brute-forcing 768-d float32 vectors for that many chunks means reading about 720,000 x 768 x 4 B = 2.2 GB per query, which is too heavy at high QPS if you let the segment grow for an hour. So flush frequently: after, say, a few minutes (tens of thousands of chunks, tens of MB to a few hundred MB per scan, depending on the interval), convert the segment to a small ANN index or keep it exact, and start a new fresh segment. Many segments increase query fan-out and tail latency, so a background compaction merges small segments into larger ones, in the style of log-structured merge designs.

Where the 30 seconds go: measure end to end. Message-queue delay, fetching and cleaning documents, chunking, the embedding call (rate limits and batching delays), the index refresh interval (a newly written vector is often invisible until the next refresh or commit), and replication to read replicas. Optimising index internals will not help if embedding batches wait 20 seconds to fill.

Trade-offs: a shorter refresh interval gives fresher results but creates more tiny segments and write amplification; read-your-writes consistency for the publishing user may need a routing hint or a direct lookup; deletes and updates must be applied to both main and fresh segments (see tombstone handling); recall of ANN on the main index is not the same as exact scan on the fresh one, but that mismatch is usually acceptable; and failures need a durable log so the fresh segment can be rebuilt after a crash. Nightly rebuilds then become compaction jobs rather than the freshness mechanism.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
A SaaS RAG product serves 3,000 tenants. Sizes are heavily skewed: most have a few hundred chunks, a handful have millions. Candidate designs: (a) one shared index with a tenant_id filter, (b) a separate index per tenant, (c) a hybrid. Customers require that one tenant can never retrieve another's data, and that deleting a tenant removes all its vectors.

Compare the designs on isolation, search quality and latency, cost, noisy neighbours and erasure, and say which you would build.
Key concepts: shared index with filter; index per tenant; hybrid tiering; isolation enforced server-side; noisy neighbour; tenant deletion
(a) Shared index with a tenant_id filter. Cheapest for many small tenants and simple to operate, but: isolation depends on every query path adding the filter, so one missing clause is a cross-tenant leak; a tenant with 300 chunks among 100M has selectivity around 3e-6, so post-filtered ANN returns nothing or poor results (see filtered-ANN behaviour) unless the engine pre-filters or scans exactly; one heavy tenant's queries or ingestion can consume shared capacity (noisy neighbour); deleting a tenant means many deletes with tombstones, compaction and no hard proof of removal.

(b) One index (or collection) per tenant. Strong logical isolation, per-tenant tuning, simple erasure (drop the index) and the ability to place a large tenant on its own hardware. But fixed overhead per index (memory, file handles, background threads, cluster metadata) multiplies by thousands, and tiny tenants waste it. Engines differ in how many indexes they handle well, so test your own.

(c) Hybrid, which I would choose. Tier 1: very small tenants (a few hundred to a few thousand chunks) live in shared partitions keyed by tenant. At that size an exact scan within the tenant's partition is cheap (a few hundred 768-d vectors is trivial) and avoids ANN recall problems entirely. Tier 2: large tenants get dedicated indexes or shards, so they are isolated, tuned and scaled independently; a tenant graduates when its size or traffic passes a threshold. A routing layer maps tenant to location.

Isolation controls beyond the filter: derive the tenant from the authenticated token in a gateway, not from user input; make the data layer enforce scoping (per-tenant namespaces, row-level policies, or credentials limited to a tenant's collection) so a forgotten filter cannot cross tenants; test with canary documents per tenant and automated cross-tenant queries; include tenant id in cache keys for retrieval and generation caches; consider per-tenant encryption keys where regulations demand. Erasure: dedicated index drops cleanly; shared partitions need delete-by-tenant plus compaction and a verification query; remember backups, logs and caches.

Monitor per-tenant latency and size, set rate limits per tenant, and automate promotion between tiers.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
A hybrid search service runs BM25 and dense retrieval across 8 shards. Each shard computes BM25 with its own local statistics, returns its top 20, and the coordinator merges the lists by raw score and then fuses with the dense list. After the corpus was resharded unevenly, queries with rare terms started returning odd rankings, and the hybrid scores seem on a different scale than the dense ones.

Why does this happen, and how should the merging and fusion work?
Key concepts: shard-local IDF; global statistics; scatter-gather top-k; reciprocal rank fusion; score scale mismatch; candidate depth
Why raw merging fails: BM25 weights terms by IDF, computed from document frequency and collection size. Using the common Lucene-style form idf = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)), a term that appears in 5 of 250,000 documents on one shard has idf of about 10.72, while on another shard where it appears in 40 of 250,000 it has about 8.73. For the same term frequency and document length, the first shard produces larger scores. Merging by raw score then favours shards where the term happens to be locally rare, a bias that grows with uneven resharding (for example one shard holding a topical cluster). When the corpus was split randomly, local statistics approximate the global ones for common terms and the problem is usually small (very rare terms stay noisy even then); after skewed resharding it is not.

Fixes: (1) compute or distribute global term statistics (a first pass collects document frequencies from all shards, or a periodically refreshed global dictionary), at the cost of an extra round trip or stale stats; many distributed search engines support such a mode. (2) Route documents so each shard is a statistically fair sample of the corpus. (3) Avoid relying on raw cross-shard BM25 scores: per-query score normalisation or merging by per-shard rank are only fallbacks, because both remain unsafe when shards differ in size or content, so prefer global statistics or even routing.

Hybrid fusion: BM25 scores are unbounded and corpus-dependent; cosine similarities lie in [-1, 1] and often cluster in a narrow band. Adding them directly gives one signal dominance. Reciprocal rank fusion scores a document as the sum of 1 / (c + rank) over lists (c = 60 is a widely used default), which needs no calibration: a document ranked 1st in BM25 and 3rd in dense gets 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.03227, just above one ranked 2nd in both (2/62 = 0.03226), so the two are nearly tied: RRF rewards a top rank only slightly more than consistent agreement. The alternative is min-max or z-score normalisation per list, which is sensitive to outliers and list length, plus a tuned weight.

Candidate depth: each shard must return at least the number of candidates you want globally (to guarantee an exact merged top-k each shard must return k), and for fusion take more than the final k from each retriever (for example 50 to 100 for a final 10) because a document ranked 30th in one list may be 2nd in the other. ANN recall also applies per shard. Evaluate on judged queries with rare terms, since that is where lexical retrieval adds value.

RAG failure diagnosis
A RAG assistant answers 'What is the notice period for terminating the Enterprise plan?' with '30 days', but the policy says 60 days. Logging shows the correct policy chunk was retrieved at rank 2 and is in the prompt. Lay out a step-by-step triage to find out why the answer is wrong, with the experiment that separates each cause.
Key concepts: triage ladder; context ablation; conflicting evidence; parametric override; gold-chunk-only test; chunk position; quote-then-answer; faithfulness conditional on retrieval
Retrieval recall is not the problem if the correct chunk is truly in the prompt (retrieval precision may still be), so the question is why the generator did not use it correctly. Candidate causes and the discriminating checks:

1. A conflicting chunk is also in the prompt (for example an older policy or a different plan saying 30 days). Check: read the whole prompt, not just rank 2. If another chunk says 30 days, this is a retrieval/versioning problem after all (stale or wrong-plan chunk), and the fix is filtering by version or plan.
2. The chunk is present but the relevant sentence is truncated, mangled by extraction or separated from its table header (so '60' is not attached to 'Enterprise'). Check: print the exact chunk text as the model saw it.
3. Parametric override: the model answers from memory or from a common default ('30 days' is a typical notice period) instead of the context. Check: run the same prompt with the chunk removed; if the answer is still '30 days', that value comes from the model's prior or from another chunk, so the gold chunk is not what drives the answer; also run with only the correct chunk. If it then answers 60, distractors are the problem; if it still answers 30 with only the gold chunk, the model is overriding or misreading the context (see 6).
4. Position or distraction effects with many chunks: move the chunk to the first position and reduce k. A model-dependent effect, so test.
5. Prompt instructions that allow or encourage outside knowledge, or conflict (for example 'be concise' leading to dropping conditions). Check: re-run with a strict 'answer only from the context, say not found otherwise' instruction and compare.
6. Reasoning or reading error on a complex clause ('60 days, or 30 days for plans under 10 seats'): the model took the wrong branch. Check: ask for the supporting quote; if the quote is correct but the conclusion is wrong, it is a reasoning failure.

Run these as controlled ablations on the failing example and then on a set of similar failures, since one example can mislead. The measure that separates generation from retrieval is faithfulness/correctness conditional on the gold chunk being supplied: if accuracy is high with the gold chunk alone and low with the production context, the context assembly is at fault.

RAG failure diagnosis
Answers are fluent and confident, but spot checks show many sentences are not in any retrieved chunk. Some are true, some are wrong. How do you determine whether the model is drawing on its own training knowledge, over-generalising from the chunks, or being fed irrelevant context, and what does each finding imply for the fix?
Key concepts: atomic claims; faithfulness; closed-book test; parametric knowledge; over-generalisation; abstention; context recall; verifier step
'Unsupported' is a property of claim versus context; the causes differ in where the claim came from, so the first step is to measure support at claim level, then run tests that vary the context.

Step 1: split answers into atomic claims and label each as supported, contradicted or not found in the provided context (human labels on a sample, or a calibrated entailment judge). This gives the unsupported-claim rate, and shows whether unsupported claims are mostly true (suggesting parametric knowledge or sensible inference) or mostly wrong (confabulation or over-generalisation).

Step 2: closed-book test. Ask the same questions with no retrieved context. If the unsupported claims in the RAG answer reappear in the closed-book answer, they come from the model's parametric knowledge. Fix: stronger instructions to answer only from context, a requirement to cite per claim, an abstain option, and possibly a verifier that removes unsupported claims.

Step 3: relevance test. Measure whether the retrieved chunks actually contain the answer (context recall against a labelled answer span, or a manual check of 30 cases). If answer-bearing text is absent, the model fills gaps because the question cannot be answered from its context; the fix is retrieval, plus abstention when evidence is weak.

Step 4: over-generalisation test. When the answer-bearing text is present but the output states more than it says (a rule extended to all regions, a number rounded or merged), check the claim against the cited quote. Fix: quote-first prompting, lower generation temperature (helps variability, not the cause), and a verifier step.

Interpretation caution: a true but unsupported claim is still a policy risk when the system promises answers 'from the documents', and the correct fraction does not make the system faithful. The metrics to report are faithfulness (claims supported by context) separately from correctness (claims true), because the two diverge in exactly this scenario.

RAG failure diagnosis
Offline, your RAG system scores recall@5 of 0.92 and faithfulness 0.95 on the golden set, yet thumbs-down feedback is high, and users say answers are 'not what I asked' or 'outdated'. List the plausible reasons offline metrics and user feedback disagree and the analysis you would run to find which applies.
Key concepts: distribution shift; golden set coverage; stale evaluation; user feedback bias; faithfulness versus usefulness; failure classification; production query sampling; multi-turn queries
The two signals measure different things, so the mismatch is informative.

Possible causes:
1. Query distribution shift. Golden queries are often written by the team, clean and well-formed; real users write short, vague, typo-laden, multi-part or follow-up queries ('what about for contractors?') that need conversation context. Retrieval and answers on those can be much worse.
2. Stale evaluation. The golden set labelled last quarter's corpus; new or changed documents are not represented, and 'outdated' complaints reflect freshness failures that offline sets cannot see.
3. Metric blind spots. Recall@5 shows the evidence was retrieved, not that the answer was complete or well-formed; faithfulness measures support, not usefulness: a faithful but evasive or overly narrow answer scores well. Answer relevance and completeness may not be tracked.
4. Coverage gaps. Users ask things the corpus cannot answer; the offline set may only include answerable questions, so abstention behaviour is untested.
5. Feedback bias. Unhappy users are more likely to click, and thumbs-down can reflect latency, tone, UI or a missing feature, not answer quality.
6. Judge or label issues: if faithfulness is scored by an LLM judge, it may be lenient and miscalibrated against humans.

Analysis: (a) sample 100 thumbs-down interactions and classify them (wrong retrieval, stale source, wrong intent, missing content, tone/format, unrelated to answer); (b) compare real query logs to the golden set by length, type, language and topic, and add a stratified slice of real queries (with consent and privacy handling) to the eval; (c) slice feedback rate by feature (conversation turn, doc type, age of source); (d) check whether the golden-set metrics predict feedback at the query level (do low-recall queries get more thumbs-down?). The change that comes out of it is usually a refreshed, production-sampled eval set, not a tweak to the model.

RAG failure diagnosis
After a weekend re-index in which you also switched to a newer embedding model and changed chunk size from 512 to 256, answer quality drops and some previously working queries now fail. Without being able to blame one change by intuition, how do you isolate the cause, and what would you have done before the migration to make this easy?
Key concepts: regression set; factor isolation; index versioning; embedding model change; chunk size effect on top-k; blue-green index; canary queries; metadata loss
Three changes were made at once: embedding model, chunk size, and (implicitly) a full re-ingest that may have altered parsing, filters or metadata. Isolate by changing one factor at a time against a fixed labelled query set, and do not rely on intuition about which factor is likely.

Isolation procedure:
1. Reproduce with a regression set: take queries that worked before (from logs or the golden set) and measure recall@k and answer quality on the old and new index. Identify the queries that regressed; patterns (long queries, identifiers, tables) hint at the cause.
2. Build a factor grid if the old index is still available: old model with 512 chunks (baseline), new model with 512, old model with 256, new model with 256. Compare each against baseline, scoring hits by whether a retrieved chunk contains the labelled answer span (chunk IDs differ across chunk sizes), and keep in mind that the same k covers half as much text at 256 tokens. Interactions matter too, and the new model may need a different query/document prefix or normalisation, and the embedding dimension or similarity metric may differ.
3. Check for plain bugs unrelated to the factors: query and document embedded by different model versions (a mixed index or an unchanged query encoder), wrong distance metric for the new model, missing normalisation, lost metadata fields so filters match nothing, a truncated input exceeding the new model's token limit, different parsing, or an incomplete index (count of chunks versus expectation).
4. Chunk size effect on the prompt: 256-token chunks double the chunk count per document, so the same top-k now covers half the text; if k and the context budget were not retuned, the model sees less evidence per query.
5. Verify end-to-end separately from retrieval, since a retrieval gain can still reduce answer quality.

Prevention: version the index (blue/green with an alias), keep the old index until the new one passes the regression set, change one thing per release, keep a frozen canary query set with expected sources, and log the model and chunker versions in the chunk metadata. Rolling back then takes one alias flip back to the old collection (alias changes are atomic), provided the old collection was kept.

RAG failure diagnosis
Users of an internal assistant complain that questions containing acronyms and IDs ('What does SLA-7 cover?', 'Status of ticket INC-48213?', 'Is DPA required?') get wrong or irrelevant answers, while natural-language questions work well. The system uses dense retrieval only. Explain why, how you would confirm the diagnosis with measurements, and the fixes in order of cost.
Key concepts: exact-match retrieval; subword tokenisation; BM25; hybrid retrieval; reciprocal rank fusion; acronym expansion; query routing; identifier lookup
Why: a dense embedding encodes semantic similarity of text pieces learned from training data. Rare strings such as 'INC-48213' or a company-specific acronym are tokenised into subword fragments with little meaning, so their embeddings are plausibly weakly informative and may sit close to many other IDs (dense retrievers are documented to underperform sparse methods on entity-centric questions); 'SLA-7' may be close to 'SLA-8' or generic SLA text. Exact-match signals (BM25 or keyword search) handle these naturally because the token is rare and highly discriminative. Acronyms add ambiguity (DPA could mean data processing agreement or something else) which dense models may resolve using general-world knowledge, not your domain.

Confirm: (1) split the query log into identifier/acronym queries and others (regex for IDs, a dictionary for acronyms), compare recall@k on the labelled subset of each; (2) run BM25 or hybrid on the same subset and check whether recall jumps; (3) inspect the top results for failures: if near-miss IDs (SLA-8) appear, that is the embedding conflation signature; (4) for acronyms, check whether the chunk uses the long form only (so the acronym never appears in the text) or the reverse.

Fixes in order of cost:
1. Add lexical retrieval and fuse with dense (RRF or weighted fusion); cheap and usually effective for exact tokens. Make sure the analyser does not split or drop the ID format.
2. Query-side handling: detect IDs and route them to exact lookup in a structured store or metadata filter (ticket status belongs in a ticket API, not a document index).
3. Acronym expansion: glossary mapping applied to both queries and chunks at indexing time, or to the query by rewriting.
4. Domain adaptation: fine-tune the embedder with domain pairs; the highest cost and least certain, and it still handles arbitrary IDs poorly.

Also note that live-status questions like ticket state need live data, so the answer should come from a tool call rather than a stale index.

Prompting and structured output (few-shot, CoT caveats, schemas, determinism)
An invoice-extraction service forces the model to emit JSON that matches a schema (total: number, currency: one of three enum values, due_date: string). Parse errors fell to zero, yet finance still finds about 4% of records with a wrong total (usually the pre-tax subtotal was picked) and some due dates that are invented when the invoice shows none. Why does schema enforcement not fix this, and which extra layers would you add?
Key concepts: constrained decoding; schema validity vs semantic correctness; nullable fields; cross-field invariants; grounding check; field-level accuracy; human review routing
A schema or constrained decoder only guarantees syntax and types: the value is valid JSON of the right shape, not a true statement about the document.

Schema-constrained decoding (the strict structured-output modes some providers offer) restricts which token sequences can be produced, so the result parses and has the declared types and enum values. Plain JSON mode promises only syntactically valid JSON, and ordinary function calling without a strict mode may not even guarantee the schema, so check which guarantee your provider documents. They say nothing about whether a number was read from the right place. The model still chooses the value by the same probabilistic process as free text, and a constraint can even push it to emit something plausible for a required field it could not find: if due_date is a required string, the model must still output some string, and an invented date is a likely one (an empty string or 'N/A' would also pass the schema, but nothing steers the model there).

So treat the output as untrusted data and add layers.
1. Make absence representable: allow null or an explicit 'not_found' marker, and say in the prompt when to use it. Required-and-non-nullable fields invite fabrication.
2. Cross-field invariants checked in code: sum(line_items) + tax should equal total within a rounding tolerance; due_date should not precede issue_date; currency should match the symbol in the source. Violations trigger a retry with the error message or human review.
3. Grounding checks: for extraction tasks the value (normalised) should occur in the source text; a total that appears nowhere in the document is suspect. This catches invention but not 'picked the wrong number that does appear'.
4. Disambiguating schema design: separate fields (subtotal, tax, total_due) force the model to place each number, which often reduces confusion versus a single ambiguous 'amount'. Field descriptions help, though how much is model-dependent.
5. Evaluate per field on a labelled sample (exact match for total, not just 'valid JSON rate'), and track it as a regression metric.
6. Route by risk: records failing any check, or where two independent extractions disagree, go to review.

Pitfall: reporting 'valid JSON rate = 100%' as quality. Syntactic validity and semantic accuracy are different metrics.

Prompting and structured output (few-shot, CoT caveats, schemas, determinism)
Model replies are sometimes wrapped in prose or Markdown fences, sometimes contain a trailing comma, sometimes quote an example object before the real answer, and sometimes violate the requested schema. Implement, with the standard library only and no network, (1) extract_json_values(text) returning every top-level JSON object/array found in free text (braces inside strings must not confuse it, a truncated value must not be silently completed), (2) validate(value, schema) for a small JSON-Schema subset returning a list of readable violations, and (3) parse_with_retries(call_model, prompt, schema, max_attempts=3) that feeds the violations back to the model on retry, returns (value, attempts) only for schema-valid data and otherwise raises ParseFailure. Explain your design choices and what the retry loop cannot guarantee.
Key concepts: string-aware bracket matching; trailing-comma repair; schema validation; error feedback retry; bounded retries; truncation handling; bool vs integer
Design points.
- Extraction: scan for '{' or '[', find the bracket-balanced end with a string-aware pass (track quotes and backslash escapes so a '}' inside a string value does not end the object), then json.loads the slice. A conservative repair strips trailing commas outside strings. Truncated output has no balanced end, so it is skipped rather than 'completed': guessing the missing tail can turn a cut-off reply into a plausible but wrong record. Caveat: scanning resumes after the skipped opener, so a complete inner object of a truncated outer value (for example '{"a": {"b": 1}') is still returned as a candidate; the schema's required keys usually reject it, and a reply that ended mid-value should be treated as suspect.
- All candidates, not the first: a model often quotes an example object before its answer. Returning every parsed value lets the caller pick the first one that passes the schema instead of the first one that parses.
- Validation is a separate, explicit step. The subset covers type (with bool excluded from integer, since bool is an int subclass in Python), enum, required, additionalProperties false, numeric bounds, string length and array items. Errors carry a path such as $.priority so they can be fed back to the model.
- Retry loop: on failure, append the concrete violations to the original prompt (not to the previous, already polluted prompt) and ask for corrected JSON. Attempts are capped, max_attempts is validated, and invalid data is never returned.

Limits. A retry can fix format and constraint violations; it cannot make the values true, so semantic checks (cross-field rules, grounding) still belong after validation. Retries cost latency and tokens, and sampling means attempt 2 is not guaranteed to differ. A hand-rolled subset validator is acceptable for a closed schema; for broad schemas use a full JSON-Schema library, which is outside this stdlib-only exercise. Log the failure reasons per attempt: a rising retry rate is an early signal of a prompt or model regression.

Prompting and structured output (few-shot, CoT caveats, schemas, determinism)
A 5-class ticket-routing prompt uses 10 fixed few-shot examples and scores 81% on a 300-item dev set. A colleague merely reorders the same 10 examples and gets 76%. Another colleague replaces them with 10 examples retrieved per query by similarity and gets 85%. How do you interpret these numbers, and how would you test for ordering and example-selection effects before shipping?
Key concepts: example ordering sensitivity; recency bias; label balance in demonstrations; similarity-based example retrieval; permutation testing; paired comparison; near-duplicate leakage
Reading the numbers. On 300 items at about 80% accuracy the binomial standard error is sqrt(0.8*0.2/300), roughly 2.3 points, and treating the two scores as independent the standard error of a 5-point difference is about 3.3 points (1.5 standard errors). The two runs share the same items, so a paired comparison is the right tool and is more sensitive, but 300 items alone cannot settle a 5-point gap. If decoding is sampled, also repeat each ordering a few times: run-to-run variation on the same items is a separate noise source from item sampling. The literature on in-context learning reports that accuracy can depend on prompt format, which examples are chosen and their order, with effects that persist across model sizes in those studies; the size of the effect for your model is an empirical question. Commonly proposed mechanisms are bias toward labels that are frequent in the examples, toward the label of the last example (recency), and toward tokens common in pre-training data. Treat these as hypotheses to check, not guarantees.

How to test.
1. Fix everything except order. Run K random permutations of the same 10 examples (for instance K=20) on a dev set not used to choose the examples, and report mean, standard deviation and worst case. If the spread is large, a single 'good' order is a lucky draw, and shipping it means a prompt that is brittle to small edits.
2. Check label balance: count each class among the 10 examples and the label of the final example; test a version with balanced classes and shuffled order.
3. Compare selection strategies fairly: fixed set vs similarity-retrieved vs random-retrieved, on a separate test split, with paired differences and a confidence interval. Retrieved examples can win because they leak near-duplicates of the test item; check that the example pool and test set do not overlap.
4. Remember retrieved selection makes the prompt vary per request, which hurts prompt caching, reproducibility and debugging; include that cost in the decision.
5. Decide using the unseen test split, and keep the winning prompt as a versioned artifact with the permutation spread recorded.

Prompting and structured output (few-shot, CoT caveats, schemas, determinism)
Your team plans to (a) show the model's step-by-step reasoning to loan officers as 'the explanation' for a triage recommendation, and (b) switch on chain-of-thought for a simple three-class sentiment tagger 'to be safe'. What are the caveats for each, and how would you decide with data whether chain-of-thought is worth it for (b)?
Key concepts: chain-of-thought faithfulness; post-hoc rationalisation; output-token latency cost; paired A/B on labelled data; explanation vs evidence citation; parse failures from free-text reasoning
(a) Explanation. A chain of thought is generated text conditioned on the input, like any other output. Research on chain-of-thought faithfulness reports cases where the stated reasoning does not mention a factor that demonstrably changed the answer (for example a bias introduced through the prompt) and where models produce a fluent justification for a wrong answer. That does not mean the reasoning is always misleading, and it often does help accuracy on multi-step problems; it means it cannot be relied on as evidence of the actual decision process. For a regulated decision like lending this matters: showing it as 'the reason' can give officers false confidence and can misstate grounds. Better options: base the recommendation on features you can inspect, show cited evidence (fields and documents the answer relied on), keep reasoning text as a convenience labelled as model-generated, and keep a human accountable. Check any legal requirements with the relevant experts rather than assuming the text satisfies them.

(b) Cost-benefit. Reasoning tokens are generated sequentially, so output tokens, cost and latency rise roughly with their number, and parsing gets harder because the label has to be separated from the prose. For a coarse classification the answer may not need intermediate steps, and extra text can sometimes introduce errors. Whether it helps is task- and model-dependent, so measure it rather than assume it.

Decision rule: adopt chain-of-thought only if the accuracy gain, with its confidence interval, justifies the added latency and cost for the product's budget, and if the extra parsing failures do not cancel the gain.

Prompting and structured output (few-shot, CoT caveats, schemas, determinism)
A CI job sends 50 fixed prompts at temperature 0 and asserts that each reply equals a stored string. It passes locally but fails on about 3 of 50 prompts at random in CI, and the failing replies diverge at some token and then differ in wording. A teammate insists 'temperature 0 is deterministic, so this is a bug in our code'. Diagnose it and redesign the tests.
Key concepts: greedy decoding; floating-point non-associativity; batch-dependent numerics; record and replay tests; property-based assertions; flake rate measurement; model version pinning
Temperature 0 means 'pick the highest-probability token' (greedy), but the probabilities themselves can differ slightly between runs, and greedy decoding is a discontinuous function: if two top candidates are within floating-point noise, a tiny change flips the choice and every later token conditions on it, so the text diverges.

Where the noise can come from (which apply depends on the serving stack):
- Floating-point addition is not associative. In plain Python, (0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3 gives 0.6000000000000001 while 0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3) gives 0.6. Parallel reductions on accelerators sum in orders that can depend on kernel choice, batch size or how work is split, so the same input can give slightly different logits.
- Batching: your request is processed alongside other, varying requests, which can change kernel shapes and reduction order.
- Different hardware, library versions or replicas behind a load balancer.
- The provider may update the model or serving stack behind a fixed name; some APIs only offer 'best effort' seed behaviour or none.
- Tokenisation or prompt template differences (whitespace, timestamps, ordering of retrieved items) are deterministic but easy to overlook: diff the exact prompts first.

So the test is wrong, not necessarily the code: it asserts something the system never promised. Redesign.
1. Unit tests of your own code should not call the live model. Record real responses once and replay them (a cassette or stub), so parsing, routing and prompt assembly are tested deterministically.
2. Tests that do call the model assert properties, not strings: valid schema, required fields, label equals expected class, contains a citation, within a length bound.
3. Quantify flakiness: run each prompt N times and track pass rate per prompt; quarantine prompts with unstable outcomes and look at them as prompt-design problems (borderline cases).
4. Pin model identifiers where possible, and rerun the suite on a schedule to detect silent upstream changes.

Prompting and structured output (few-shot, CoT caveats, schemas, determinism)
Three people edit the production system prompt through an admin page. After one 'small wording tweak', downstream JSON parse failures rose from 0.5% to 3% and nobody noticed for two days; nobody could even say which prompt text served which request. Design prompt versioning, change control and a regression gate for this system.
Key concepts: prompt versioning; content hash; regression gate; canary rollout; rollback; online guardrail metrics; prompt changelog
Treat prompts as code: store them in version control with a content hash or version id, render them from typed templates, log the id with every request, and require every change to pass an automated regression suite (parse rate, field accuracy, safety checks) before a staged rollout with a quick rollback.

Failure analysis: there was no version identity (cannot attribute), no pre-deployment test (the change shipped untested), no online monitoring on a cheap proxy metric (parse failure rate), and no rollback path.

Design.
1. Source of truth: prompt templates live in the repository, reviewed like code. The admin page may exist but should create a pull request or a draft that goes through the same gate, not edit production in place.
2. Identity: each deployed prompt configuration has a version id (for example the hash of template text plus its static configuration plus the model identifier and sampling settings); optionally also log a hash of the fully rendered prompt per request when you need to reconstruct exactly what was sent. Log this id on every request, with the model identifier. A change to any of those counts as a new version, because model or setting changes can break prompts that did not change.
3. Templates with explicit variables: validate that all placeholders are filled and that untrusted text goes only in data slots; this prevents silent breakage like an empty variable.
4. Regression gate in CI: a fixed set of cases (typical, edge and previously failed examples) run on the candidate and the current version, checking cheap deterministic properties first (valid schema, parse rate), then task accuracy or judge scores, with paired comparison and thresholds that fail the build. Add every production incident as a new case.
5. Staged rollout: shadow or small-percentage canary comparing online metrics (parse failures, retries, latency, token counts, thumbs-down) between versions; automatic rollback when a guardrail metric crosses its threshold.
6. Observability and ownership: dashboards per prompt version, alerts on parse-failure rate and retry rate, a changelog with the reason for each edit, and a named owner.

Trade-off: heavier process slows small edits; keep the suite fast (minutes) and tier it so cheap checks run on every change and the expensive judge-based run on release candidates.

Tool use and agents (function calling, loops, failure modes, action guardrails)
A support agent has four tools: get_order(order_id), lookup_order(query), get_customer_orders(email) and cancel(order_id). In logs, about 30% of the time the model calls lookup_order with a bare order number, and about 10% of the time it calls get_order with a customer's name, which errors. How would you redesign the tool definitions so the model picks the right tool and arguments, and how would you verify the fix?
Key concepts: tool descriptions; overlapping tools; argument schema constraints; server-side validation; actionable error messages; tool-selection accuracy; tool subset per task
The model chooses tools from names, descriptions and parameter schemas, so overlapping tools with vague descriptions cause confusion.

Diagnosis. Function calling gives the model a list of tool names, descriptions and argument schemas, and it picks by matching the request to that text. lookup_order and get_order overlap, 'query' is free text so a bare order number looks acceptable, and nothing tells the model that get_order wants a specific id format. The errors are a design problem more than a model problem.

Redesign.
1. Reduce overlap: fewer, clearly separated tools. Perhaps one find_orders tool with explicit mutually exclusive parameters (order_id or customer_email or free-text search), or keep separate tools with disjoint inputs.
2. Descriptions that say when to use it AND when not to: 'Use when the user supplies an order number such as ORD-123456. Do not use to search by customer name; use get_customer_orders with an email.' Put the distinguishing facts early; descriptions are the model's only documentation.
3. Constrain arguments in the schema: a pattern for order ids, enums for status values, units and formats stated (currency, ISO dates), required vs optional marked. Validate server-side anyway: unless the provider's strict tool-schema mode is on, the schema is guidance rather than a guarantee, and even in strict mode it enforces shape, not that the order exists or belongs to this customer.
4. Informative errors: return 'order_id must match ORD-######; for a name use get_customer_orders(email)' rather than a bare 400, so the next step can self-correct (and count self-corrections as a metric).
5. Keep side-effecting tools (cancel) separate and clearly marked, with their confirmation requirement in the description and enforced in code.
6. Tool count and description length cost context tokens and can degrade selection when the list gets long; prune or route to a subset of tools per task.

Verification: build 100 to 200 labelled requests including ambiguous ones (name only, number plus typo, two identifiers), record which tool and arguments an ideal call would use, and measure tool-choice accuracy, argument validity and error rate before and after, using the same sampling settings and several runs per request.

Tool use and agents (function calling, loops, failure modes, action guardrails)
A research agent sometimes runs 40+ steps, repeating essentially the same web_search with slightly reworded queries. Each tool result adds about 1,500 tokens and the full history is resent at every step. Explain what is going wrong in cost and quality terms, and which guards you would add to the loop.
Key concepts: agent loop termination; step and token budgets; repeated-call detection; quadratic context cost; tool-result truncation; retryable vs non-retryable errors; no-progress detection
Two problems compound.

1. Loop without progress. The model has no built-in notion of 'I already tried this'. If results do not satisfy it, rewording the query is a locally reasonable next action. Nothing in the loop enforces termination, so the stopping condition is only the model's own judgement.

2. Context growth makes cost superlinear in steps. If the whole transcript is resent each step (no truncation, and ignoring any provider-side prompt caching, which can reduce price or latency but not the size of the context the model must attend to), step k processes about base + k x 1,500 tokens, so total input over n steps grows roughly with n squared. Long, repetitive contexts can also make the model less likely to use the useful parts, an effect that depends on the model.

Guards, in the orchestration code rather than in the prompt:
- Hard step limit and wall-clock/token/cost budgets per task, with a defined end state when they are hit (return best partial result and say so).
- Repeat detection: hash normalised (tool, arguments) and block or warn on exact repeats; add near-duplicate detection for reworded queries (for example high overlap of tokens or embedding similarity with earlier queries).
- No-progress check: if the last K results added no new URLs or facts, force a different strategy or stop.
- Return structured, actionable tool errors and distinguish retryable errors (timeout) from non-retryable ones (invalid argument, not found) so the agent does not retry blindly.
- Context management: truncate or summarise old tool outputs, keep only the extracted facts, cap tool-result size.
- Escalation: after the budget, hand off to a human or return what is known rather than looping.

Monitor distributions (steps per task, repeated calls, budget hits), because a few runaway runs can dominate cost.

Tool use and agents (function calling, loops, failure modes, action guardrails)
A refund agent calls issue_refund(order_id, amount). Last week a tool call timed out at the payment service although the refund had actually gone through; the agent retried, and the customer was refunded twice. In a separate case a prompt-confused agent refunded an order that had been delivered fine. Redesign the action path so duplicate and unauthorised refunds are prevented, and say where a human should be in the loop.
Key concepts: idempotency key; ambiguous timeout; status check before retry; server-side authorisation; propose and commit; approval thresholds; audit log
Two different failure classes.

1. Duplicates after ambiguous failure. A timeout means 'unknown outcome', not 'failed'. Blind retry of a non-idempotent call can repeat the side effect. Fix: make the operation idempotent. The orchestrator (not the model) generates an idempotency key per intended action, for example derived from the conversation id, order id and refund intent, and passes it with the call. The payment service stores the key with the result and returns the stored result on repeats. On timeout, the agent must query the status ('is there a refund for this key/order?') before any retry.

2. Wrong or unauthorised action. The model's decision is probabilistic and can be steered by user text or tool output, so authorisation must not live in the prompt. Enforce in code:
- Server-side eligibility rules: order delivered or not, refund window, remaining refundable amount (order total minus prior refunds), one refund per line item. The tool rejects violations regardless of what the model asked.
- Narrow the tool: no free-form amount beyond the remaining balance; the credential used by the agent may only issue refunds up to a per-transaction and per-day cap.
- Two-step propose/commit: the agent proposes an action; the system shows the exact order, amount and reason, and commits only after confirmation. Confirmation can be the end user for low-risk cases, and a human reviewer above a threshold or when risk signals fire (high amount, new account, repeated refunds, injected-looking content in the conversation).
- Audit log of every proposal, approval and result, with the key.

Human placement: the more irreversible and costly the action, the earlier the human; review the exact structured action, not the model's prose summary, and tune thresholds from measured error costs. Reversible low-value actions can be automatic with after-the-fact sampling.

Residual risk: confirmation fatigue (people click through), and rules that are too tight create escalations. Measure both.

Tool use and agents (function calling, loops, failure modes, action guardrails)
An email-and-web agent can read web pages, read the user's inbox and send email. Explain, in terms of the agent's control flow, why a web page that the agent merely 'reads' can end up causing the agent to send mail to an outside address, and what design rule would limit the damage without removing the web tool.
Key concepts: indirect prompt injection; tool-result append; data vs instruction confusion; lethal combination of exposure, sensitive data and outward channel; tainted session; quarantined sub-agent; recipient allowlist
Control-flow view. The loop is: model reads context, emits a tool call, the runtime executes it, the result is appended, repeat. Untrusted content (a web page, an email body, a file) enters at the 'append result' step and is then processed by the same model, with the same authority to choose the next call, as the user's request. The research on indirect prompt injection describes this as LLM-integrated applications blurring the line between data and instructions, with injected text in retrieved data able to influence how and whether other tools or APIs are called. The model is trained to follow instructions in text, and instruction-like text inside a page is still text in its context; there is no dependable in-band marker that the model will always honour as 'this is only data'.

Why the damage is possible: it needs three ingredients together. (1) Exposure to untrusted content (the web tool). (2) Access to sensitive data (the inbox). (3) An outward channel (send email, or a call whose arguments reach an attacker). With all three in one session, a successful steering of the model can move data out. Removing the web tool removes the feature, so cut a different leg.

Design rules.
- Treat the session as tainted after untrusted content enters; after that point, tools that read private data or communicate externally are disabled or need explicit user confirmation showing the exact recipient and content.
- Split roles: a quarantined sub-agent reads untrusted pages and returns only a constrained, validated summary (fixed schema, no free-form instructions), while the privileged agent that can send mail never sees the raw page.
- Fix recipients from an allowlist or the user's own address book; arguments are validated by code.
- Least privilege per task: a 'summarise this page' task gets no send tool at all.
Honest limit: filtering prompts for suspicious phrases is unreliable, since attackers can phrase injections in endless ways; structural limits on what a compromised model can do are more dependable, though they cost usability.

Tool use and agents (function calling, loops, failure modes, action guardrails)
A product manager wants an 'autonomous AI agent' to process expense claims: read the receipt, check it against the policy, then approve, reject or flag. The steps and their order are the same for every claim. Argue for or against building it as a free-running agent, and describe the alternative, including a rough reliability argument.
Key concepts: workflow vs agent; control of sequence; per-step testability; compounding error; bounded cost and latency; agentic step inside workflow; audit trail
Agent versus workflow is a choice about who controls the sequence. A workflow is code that calls the model at fixed points; an agent lets the model decide which tool to call next, how often, and when to stop. Autonomy buys flexibility for open-ended tasks and costs predictability.

For expense claims the sequence is known: extract fields, validate (date, currency, amount, category), look up the policy, compare, decide, route. Reasons to use a workflow:
- Testability: each step has a defined input and output and can be unit-tested and evaluated separately (extraction accuracy, policy-match accuracy), and failures can be located.
- Bounded cost and latency: the number of model calls is fixed, no runaway loops.
- Determinism where possible: the policy comparison (amount over a cap, missing receipt) can be plain code rather than model judgement.
- Smaller attack surface and simpler permissions: the model never chooses to call a payment tool.
- Auditability: the path is the same each time.

Rough reliability argument: if a free-running agent must get 6 decisions right in sequence and each is right with probability 0.95 independently, and any error spoils the result, the end-to-end success is 0.95^6, about 0.74. A workflow does not repair per-step accuracy, but it can add targeted checks (schema validation, rules, a second extraction on low confidence) at the weak steps, and the risky ones can be done in code, whereas in an agent the error rate of the planning itself adds to the product. The independence assumption is rough and optimistic or pessimistic depending on the setting, so treat the number as an illustration.

When the agent is the right tool: investigations where which tool comes next depends on what was found (debugging an incident, open-ended research), many possible tools and paths, tolerance for variable cost, and strong guardrails. A good pattern is workflow by default, with an agentic step inside it for the genuinely open part (for example 'ambiguous receipt, investigate'), under a step budget.

Tool use and agents (function calling, loops, failure modes, action guardrails)
You evaluate a ticket-resolution agent that can read a customer database, update ticket status and issue credits. In a 200-task suite it ends with the correct final reply 80% of the time. Why is that number insufficient, how would you evaluate trajectories as well as outcomes, and how do you handle run-to-run variation?
Key concepts: state-diff evaluation; trajectory metrics; policy-violation gate; run-to-run variance; all-runs-pass rate; tool error recovery; sandboxed deterministic tools
A correct final message does not show that the right things happened. The agent may have changed the wrong record, issued an unauthorised credit, taken 11 calls where 3 suffice, or got lucky; and a wrong message may follow a correct state change. For agents with side effects, evaluate three layers.

1. Outcome in the environment. Check the end state, not the prose: ticket status, credit ledger, no unintended changes. Build a sandbox with a known initial state and a function that compares the final state with the expected one (a state diff). This is more reliable than judging the reply text.
2. Trajectory quality. Log each step and score: tool-call validity (schema errors, wrong tool), policy violations (any forbidden action, even if the result was fine; usually a hard fail), number of steps and tokens versus a reference, repeated or unnecessary calls, recovery from tool errors. Use deterministic checks where possible; an LLM judge for subjective parts is an AI label and should itself be validated on human-labelled examples. Do not require an exact reference trajectory when several valid paths exist; check required milestones and forbidden actions instead.
3. Final answer quality: correctness, grounding in tool results, tone.

Variation. The same task can succeed or fail across runs because sampling and tool timing vary. Run each task several times (for example 5) and report both the average success and a stricter 'all runs succeed' rate. If per-run success is p and runs were independent, all 5 pass with probability p^5, so a task suite that looks fine on a single run can hide an unreliable agent. Report confidence intervals over tasks (not runs of the same task) since tasks are the sampling unit.

Also keep the suite honest: mock tools deterministically, cover error and adversarial cases (tool failure, ambiguous request, injected text in a ticket), and split safety metrics from helpfulness.

Tool use and agents (function calling, loops, failure modes, action guardrails)
A data-analyst assistant is given three tools: run_sql, read_file and send_report_email. The team plans to use one service account with broad access for all users because 'the prompt tells the model to stay within the user's data'. How would you scope permissions properly?
Key concepts: least privilege; confused deputy; user-scoped credentials; read-only database role; argument validation in code; recipient allowlist; audit logging
Do not make the prompt the access-control layer. The model's behaviour is probabilistic and can be influenced by user text and by anything it reads, so every permission must be enforced by the tools and the systems behind them, as if the model were an untrusted client that might emit any call.

Concrete design:
- Act as the user, not as a superuser. Pass the end user's identity or a scoped token derived from it to the tool, so the database applies that user's row-level and table permissions. A single broad service account turns any steering of the model into access to everyone's data (a confused-deputy problem).
- Least privilege per tool. run_sql uses a read-only role limited to the needed schemas; deny DDL and writes at the database level; add statement timeouts, row limits and cost limits. read_file is confined to an allowed directory with path normalisation to block traversal. send_report_email may only send to the user's own address or an approved domain list, with attachments produced by the system.
- Per-task tool set. A request to 'explain this query result' needs no email tool; grant tools for the task at hand rather than everything always.
- Validate arguments in code, independently of the schema shown to the model: parse SQL or use parameterised, pre-approved query templates for sensitive tables; check recipient addresses; reject unexpected arguments.
- Rate limits and quotas per user and per session, to bound the damage of a runaway or hijacked loop.
- Confirmation for outward or irreversible effects (email with data), showing the exact recipient and content.
- Audit log tying every call to the user, session and prompt version, with alerting on unusual volume.
- Secrets never in the prompt or tool output.

Trade-offs: finer scoping means more engineering and sometimes refused legitimate queries; start with the highest-impact controls (user-scoped read-only data access and a recipient allowlist) and expand. No scoping removes all risk, but it bounds what a mistaken or manipulated model can do.

LLM evaluation (benchmarks, contamination, LLM-as-judge bias, regression suites)
A new model scores 4 points higher than your current one on a public reasoning benchmark, and leadership wants to swap it into your contract-clause extraction pipeline. Why might that gain not carry over, and what would you do before agreeing?
Key concepts: benchmark transfer; contamination risk; evaluation protocol sensitivity; paired confidence interval; representative held-out set; slice analysis; decision gate defined in advance
Public scores measure the benchmark's task mix, prompt format, answer extraction and scoring, not your task.

Reasons a benchmark gain may not transfer.
1. Different distribution and skill: a reasoning benchmark of short puzzles exercises different abilities from locating and normalising clauses in 40-page contracts (long-context use, formatting fidelity, domain vocabulary, refusal behaviour).
2. Contamination or overfitting to the benchmark: if test items or close variants appear in training or in tuning data, scores overstate general ability. You usually cannot verify this from outside; treat it as a risk, not as a conclusion.
3. Evaluation protocol differences: the reported number depends on the prompt template, number of shots, answer-extraction rules, sampling settings and sometimes multiple attempts. Your pipeline's prompt differs, and models can differ in prompt sensitivity.
4. Noise and saturation: a 4-point gap on a few hundred items may be within sampling error, and benchmarks near the ceiling separate models poorly.
5. Metric mismatch: the benchmark measures accuracy; you care about field-level precision and recall, calibrated abstention, latency, cost and failure severity (a missed termination clause matters more than a missed footnote).
6. Behavioural changes unrelated to capability: different output formatting, verbosity or instruction following can break your parser even if the model is 'better'.

What to do.
- Build or reuse a labelled, representative eval set of real documents (stratified by contract type and length, kept out of any prompt tuning), with an agreed labelling guide.
- Run both models with the same pipeline, and also with per-model prompt tuning if you plan to tune, to avoid favouring the incumbent.
- Report per-field precision/recall with paired bootstrap or paired-test intervals, plus parse failure rate, latency and cost per document.
- Check slices (long documents, scanned text, rare clause types) and safety/regression cases.
- Use public benchmarks only as a shortlist signal. Decide with a gate defined in advance, for example 'no field drops by more than X and the overall gain exceeds the interval'.

LLM evaluation (benchmarks, contamination, LLM-as-judge bias, regression suites)
You have a 200-case regression suite for a support-answer prompt. The old prompt passes 168 cases; the new prompt passes 174. Looking case by case, the new prompt fixes 15 cases and breaks 9.
