Key concepts: citation presence vs support; claim-level citations; highlighted evidence span; abstention in the UI; calibrated wording; over-trust measurement
The badge asserts verification, but the audit shows 70 of 500 badged answers (14%) are only partly supported (45, 9%) or unsupported (25, 5%). A binary badge based on citation presence measures the wrong thing: the model can cite a real document that does not contain the claim, or support one clause while an adjacent clause is invented. It also invites over-trust: users who see an authoritative marker may check less (automation bias is plausible here, and worth measuring rather than assuming).

Changes. (1) Do not show a badge unless support is checked: run a claim-to-passage support check before display and show the badge only when it passes; remember this check has its own error rate. (2) Cite per claim, not per answer, and show the supporting passage with the relevant span highlighted next to the claim, so verification takes one click. (3) Tell the user what the answer is based on ('From the 2024 returns policy, section 4.2') including the document version or date, and say explicitly when evidence is missing, partial or conflicting ('I couldn't find this in the policy; here is the closest text'). (4) Use plain-language confidence only if it is tied to measured accuracy (for example 'checked against the source' versus 'not checked'); avoid invented percentages. (5) For high-stakes actions add friction, such as asking the user to confirm against the source or offering a human handoff. (6) Provide a one-click 'this is wrong' report that feeds the evaluation set.

Test it with a randomised experiment with enough users per arm to detect the difference you care about: show users answers of which a known fraction are wrong, compare designs (old badge, new evidence display) on the rate at which users catch wrong answers and on the rate at which they wrongly reject right ones, plus task completion and escalation rate. Keep auditing a random sample of badged answers each week, with confidence intervals, and set a launch gate on the unsupported-citation rate.

GenAI product scenarios (support bot, document QA)
A retailer's support team handles about 12,000 conversations a month. The ten most common intents (order status, returns, delivery changes and so on) make up roughly 45% of volume. Leadership wants an LLM support bot live in 8 weeks and quotes 'containment rate' as the success target. Design the launch: scope, escalation, rollout, metrics beyond containment, how to handle wrong answers and legal risk, and a measurable go/no-go gate.
Key concepts: containment vs resolution; scope limiting; human handoff; shadow mode; re-contact within 7 days; Wilson lower bound; rollback
Scope. Roughly 45% of volume sits in ten intents, which is where to start. Pick intents with stable policies and low harm if wrong (order status, standard return window). Keep money-moving, legal, safety and complaint-escalation topics out of the first release, and route anything off-scope or low-confidence to a human with the conversation summary attached so customers do not repeat themselves. Make the human route visible at any point; hiding it inflates containment and damages trust.

Metrics. Containment (no human involved) rewards deflection, including useless deflection. Add: resolution (contained and no re-contact on the same issue within 7 days), customer satisfaction on contained and escalated chats separately (watching survey response bias), correct-and-policy-compliant rate from sampled human review, escalation rate and handoff quality, and average handling time of escalated chats. Track wrong-answer severity separately: a wrong tracking number is not a wrong refund promise.

Rollout. Weeks 1-3: build against recorded conversations with grounded answers from policy and order systems, and define review rubrics. Weeks 4-5: shadow mode, where the bot drafts answers that are scored but not sent. Weeks 6-7: limited live traffic, for example 5% then 20%, randomised, with a human fallback and daily review. Week 8: decide.

Wrong answers and legal risk. Ground replies in approved policy text and live order data, not model memory; show what was used; avoid making commitments (refunds, compensation) outside policy; keep logs and versions of policy/prompt so you can reconstruct what a customer was told; let customers reach a person; have legal review of disclosures and of what the bot may promise. A kill switch and a fast correction process matter as much as accuracy. Regulations on automated customer interaction differ by jurisdiction, so involve counsel.

GenAI product scenarios (support bot, document QA)
A legal-tech team is building a contract question-answering product. Lawyers upload their own contracts, ask things like 'what is the notice period for termination?' and expect answers with exact clause references. Say what you would and would not promise users, how you would present answers and citations, how access control must work, and what evaluation results you would require before launch.
Key concepts: clause-level citation; abstention on missing information; per-document access control; quote verification; scope of promise; evaluation set from real contracts; human review for high stakes
What to promise. Position the product as an assistant that finds and summarises relevant text with traceable references, not as legal advice. Promise things the system can show: here is the clause, here is the quoted text, here is a plain-language reading. Do not promise that it catches every relevant clause, or that its interpretation is correct. State that lawyers remain responsible for conclusions, and make that visible in the interface.

Answers and citations. Each claim should link to a specific passage (document, page, clause number) and show the quoted text beside the answer. Verify citations programmatically: confirm that the quoted span actually exists in the cited document, and flag answers that contain statements with no supporting quote. Handle contract-specific difficulty: definitions that change a term's meaning, amendments and side letters that override earlier clauses, cross-references (see Section 12), and tables or scanned pages where text extraction fails. When information is absent or contradictory, the product should say so (and show the competing clauses) instead of choosing one.

Access control. Contracts are confidential. Enforce permissions in the retrieval layer using the user's identity and the document ACL, so text from documents the user cannot see never enters the prompt. Isolate customers, log access, and treat uploaded contracts as untrusted content that may contain instruction-like text.

Evaluation before launch. Build a test set from real contracts (with consent and redaction) across types, lengths, scanned and native files, and questions that include unanswerable and multi-clause cases. Measure answer correctness graded by lawyers, citation validity (does the quoted text support the claim), recall of relevant clauses, abstention behaviour, and latency. Report results by contract type and by question type, with confidence intervals, and decide thresholds with the lawyers who will use it.

GenAI product scenarios (support bot, document QA)
An A/B test of a support bot ran on 10,000 conversations, 5,000 per arm. The bot arm resolves 39% of conversations without a human versus 31% for the control (which has a simple FAQ widget). However, among conversations marked 'resolved without a human', 21% of the bot arm contacted support again within 7 days about the same issue versus 12% in the control. Customer satisfaction scores are 0.1 points lower in the bot arm on a 5-point scale, from a survey answered by about 8% of users. Should you ship? Argue with the numbers.
Key concepts: containment; true resolution; re-contact within 7 days; guardrail metrics; survey non-response; two-proportion test; segment analysis
Headline versus net. Containment rose by 8 points (31% to 39%), but a contained conversation that comes back is not resolved. Computing net resolution: control 31% x (1 - 0.12) = 27.3%; bot 39% x (1 - 0.21) = 30.8%. So the real gain is about 3.5 points, less than half the headline, and each re-contact costs the customer effort.

Is the re-contact difference noise? Contained counts are about 1,550 (control) and 1,950 (bot). Re-contact rates of 12% (about 186 people) and 21% (about 410) differ by 9 points; a two-proportion z-test gives z of about 7, so chance is not a plausible explanation, and the 95% intervals (roughly 10.5% to 13.7% versus 19.3% to 22.9%) do not overlap. The headline containment gain (z of about 8) is also clearly real. Both are statistically clear, but the re-contact comparison is among different subsets of users (those each arm contained), so treat it as a warning sign and rely on the randomised conversation-level net resolution for the causal estimate.

Satisfaction. A 0.1 point difference on a 5-point scale with only 8% responding is weak evidence either way, because responders differ systematically from non-responders (very happy and very unhappy users answer more). Do not use it as the deciding metric; supplement with behavioural signals such as re-contact, abandonment and escalation request rates.

Decision. Do not ship to all traffic yet: net resolution is up about 3.5 points (conversation-level z of about 3.9) but re-contact among contained conversations is far worse (21% versus 12%). Break results down by intent. If a few intents drive the re-contact (for example answers that sound final but leave a step undone), restrict the bot to intents where re-contact is no worse than control, improve the rest, and re-test. Check whether the bot's wrong 'resolved' judgments come from users leaving rather than being helped. Define the success metric as net resolution with a guardrail on re-contact and satisfaction proxies, and agree it before the next test.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
A teammate hands you a notebook that reported 0.87 F1 on the validation set and says 'just rerun it to get the same number'. Which pieces of information must have been recorded for the run so that someone else can re-create that result, and which of them are most often forgotten?
Key concepts: run record; code commit hash; dataset snapshot identity; split rule; random seed; environment lockfile; fitted preprocessing artifacts
A reproducible run record has to pin down every input that influences the number, not just the model code. At minimum:

1. Code identity: the commit hash, plus a note (or saved diff) if the working tree had uncommitted changes. A notebook with out-of-order cells is a classic way to lose this.
2. Data identity: which dataset snapshot or content hash was read, and exactly how the train/validation split was made (rule, key and seed). 'The latest table' is not an identity.
3. Configuration: hyperparameters, feature list, preprocessing options, and any defaults that were silently applied.
4. Randomness: the seed(s) used for initialisation, shuffling, sampling and augmentation.
5. Environment: interpreter and library versions (ideally a lockfile or image digest), and hardware/driver details when they can change numerics.
6. Outputs: the metrics, the evaluation set used, and the fitted artifacts (model weights, but also scalers, vocabularies and encoders fitted on the training data).

The most commonly forgotten items are the data version and the split rule (data changed underneath a fixed query), uncommitted code changes, fitted preprocessing artifacts, and the library versions. Tracking tools exist to capture these automatically: for example, MLflow Tracking describes itself as an API and UI for logging parameters, code versions, metrics and output files. Even with all of this recorded, bit-exact reruns may still differ slightly because of hardware nondeterminism, so a good record also states the expected run-to-run spread.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
Why does 'it works on my machine' cause more trouble in machine-learning projects than in ordinary application code?
Key concepts: silent failure; unpinned dependencies; container image; data version; hardware nondeterminism; run-to-run variance
Because an ML result depends on more than the code, and many of the extra dependencies fail silently. In ordinary software a missing library or wrong version usually crashes or fails a test. In ML the program still runs and simply returns a slightly different number or a slightly different model.

Typical sources of 'my machine vs yours' differences:
- Data: your laptop has a sample or an older extract; the pipeline reads a table that has since been refreshed.
- Library versions: an unpinned dependency can resolve to a newer release with changed defaults, a different tokeniser, a different numerical kernel or changed random-number behaviour.
- Hardware and drivers: CPU versus GPU, different GPU generations, or different driver/runtime libraries can change floating-point results and which algorithm is chosen.
- Randomness: unseeded shuffling, initialisation or dropout gives different runs even on one machine.
- Hidden state: fitted preprocessors, cached features, and notebook cell execution order.

So 'it works' can mean 'accuracy was 0.91 here and 0.88 there' with nothing obviously broken, and nobody notices until a metric is compared. The remedies are to make the environment explicit (lockfile and container image, pinned by digest rather than a moving tag), version the data by identity rather than by path, record seeds and configuration with each run, and compare runs with a known noise level in mind so a real regression can be told apart from run-to-run variation.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
Three weeks ago a run on branch main reported 0.842 AUC on a fixed validation set. Today, the same script on main gives 0.829, and nobody changed the code on purpose. Give an ordered checklist for finding out why, and say how you would decide whether 0.829 is a real regression at all.
Key concepts: run-to-run variance; bisecting one factor at a time; data snapshot hash; lockfile; moving image tag; moved validation set; run manifest
Work from the cheapest and most likely explanations to the most expensive, and change one factor at a time.

0. Check the comparison itself. Is it the same evaluation set (same rows, same ordering of any sampling), the same metric code and the same threshold/averaging convention? A moved validation set explains many 'regressions'.
1. Measure the noise first. Re-run the old configuration with several seeds. If run-to-run spread is, say, a standard deviation of 0.005 AUC, a 0.013 gap is about 2.6 seed SDs if the old number is treated as exact, but only about 1.8 SDs (0.013 / (0.005 x 1.41)) when both numbers are single runs: suggestive but not conclusive; if the spread is 0.012, the gap may be noise. Only then chase causes.
2. Code: confirm the commit actually used three weeks ago (the branch may have moved; uncommitted changes are not in the history). Diff that commit against today's HEAD, including config files and default values.
3. Data: was the input a mutable path or a query that returns 'latest'? Compare row counts, null rates, label rates and a content hash with the recorded snapshot. Check whether the split is random per run or derived from a stable key.
4. Environment: compare the resolved package versions (lockfile or a freeze listing) and the base image digest. Loose requirements and moving tags such as 'latest' are frequent culprits, because library defaults and numerical kernels change.
5. Hardware and nondeterminism: different GPU type, driver, thread count, non-deterministic kernels and data-loader ordering.
6. Only after the above, suspect the model: a real data shift or a real bug.

Decision rule: call it a regression only if the gap exceeds the measured seed spread on the same data and environment, or if re-running the exact recorded configuration (old commit, old data snapshot, old environment) reproduces 0.842 while today's setup does not.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
You fix every random seed in a training script, yet two runs on the same GPU box differ in the third decimal of validation loss, and a colleague's run on a different machine differs more. Why is setting the seed necessary but not sufficient, and what else would you control or accept?
Key concepts: floating-point non-associativity; parallel reduction order; cuDNN algorithm selection; DataLoader worker seeding; SeedSequence.spawn; deterministic algorithms mode; seed variance
A seed only initialises pseudo-random generators. It does not make the rest of the computation identical.

1. Floating-point order. Floating-point addition is not associative, so summing the same numbers in a different order can give a different result. Parallel reductions, tiled matrix multiplies and, in some GPU kernels, accumulation whose order depends on scheduling can change the order from run to run. Differences are tiny per operation but can compound over many training steps.
2. Algorithm selection. Libraries may auto-tune and pick different convolution or matmul algorithms. PyTorch's reproducibility notes say that cuDNN benchmark mode may select different algorithms on subsequent runs even on the same machine, and that switching it off gives deterministic selection at a possible cost in performance.
3. Platform and version. The same notes state that completely reproducible results are not guaranteed across releases, individual commits or platforms, and that CPU and GPU results may differ even with identical seeds.
4. Data loading. Multi-process loaders need each worker to have a well-defined stream. PyTorch documents using a worker init function and a seeded generator for this. With NumPy, the documented approach is to derive child streams with SeedSequence.spawn rather than computing seeds such as root_seed + worker_id, because overlapping worker seeds across invocations can cause bias.
5. Everything else: hash-randomised iteration order of sets of strings (PYTHONHASHSEED), multithreaded preprocessing, and data that changed.

What to do: fix and record all seeds (framework, NumPy, Python, loader workers); enable deterministic algorithm modes where available and accept the slowdown and the errors they may raise for operations without a deterministic implementation; pin the whole stack (libraries, drivers, image digest) and the hardware class; keep batch order fixed. Where bit-exactness is not achievable, treat the noise as a property of the training procedure: run several seeds and report mean and spread, and compare candidates against that spread instead of expecting identical numbers.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
Your team logs every training run to an experiment tracker and also keeps a model registry. A new hire asks why one of them is not enough. What belongs in each, and how would you answer 'which code, data and run produced the model that is serving traffic right now?'
Key concepts: experiment tracker; model registry; immutable model version; alias or stage pointer; lineage; data snapshot hash; serving-time version logging
Different jobs, different lifecycles.

Experiment tracker: high volume, mostly disposable. For each run it stores parameters, metrics over time, tags, evaluation plots and output artifacts, plus the identity of the inputs (code commit, data snapshot id, config, seeds, environment). MLflow Tracking, for instance, describes logging parameters, code versions, metrics and output files, with a run holding metadata and artifacts. Use it to compare, filter and debug experiments; runs that never get promoted are still valuable evidence of what was tried.

Model registry: low volume, governed. It stores promoted model versions as entries that should be treated as immutable, with a name, a version number, a movable pointer (alias or stage) such as 'candidate' or 'production', the input/output signature, the validation results that justified promotion, who approved it, and a reference to the training run. The pointer move is the deployment-relevant event, and it can be audited and reversed. A plain file bucket typically has none of this by default: no enforced immutability (unless object lock or versioning is configured and used consistently), no pointer semantics, no approval trail, no link to evidence.

Answering the serving question is a chain of links, and every link must be recorded: (1) the serving process logs the model version it loaded (and the artifact checksum) with each prediction or at least at start-up; (2) the registry entry for that version points to the training run; (3) the run holds the commit hash, the data snapshot hash, the config, the seeds, and the environment (lockfile hash, image digest). If any link is only a convention ('the file name has the date'), lineage breaks the first time someone copies a file by hand.

Pitfalls: registering a model without the preprocessing/fitted artifacts it needs; promoting by overwriting a file in place so that the version number no longer identifies bytes; and logging the run id in the tracker but not carrying it into the registry or into the serving logs.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
Your training set is 400 GB of images plus a labels file. About 2% of the files are added or relabelled each week, and models from the last year must stay reproducible. Compare keeping a dated full copy of the dataset every week with content-hash versioning using small pointer files, say what each training run records, and name what can still go wrong.
Key concepts: content-addressable storage; manifest hash; pointer file in Git; immutable snapshot; deduplication; garbage collection and retention; split rule
Full dated copies are simple but scale linearly with the number of versions and give no cheap way to answer 'what changed'. Content-addressed versioning stores each distinct file once, keyed by a hash of its bytes, and a small manifest or pointer file maps names to hashes. The pointer file is what lives in version control, so a Git commit pins an exact dataset state.

DVC is one concrete example: its documentation describes a small .dvc metadata file, kept in Git, that records an MD5 hash and acts as a placeholder for the data; the data lives in a hash-addressed cache, and checking out a Git commit followed by a data checkout restores the matching version. The same idea can be built with any object store plus manifests.

What a training run records: the commit (which includes the pointer files), or equivalently the dataset manifest hash, plus the split rule. The aim is that the manifest hash alone identifies the exact bytes.

Properties that matter:
- Immutability: a version must never be modified in place. If someone fixes a label by overwriting a file in a shared bucket, every old manifest silently points to different content. Content addressing detects this because the hash of the new bytes differs; path-based copying does not.
- Deduplication: only changed files take new space, and diffs between versions are cheap to compute.
- Directory entries: a directory is represented by a manifest (in DVC a .dir entry) that lists its files and their hashes, so adding one file changes the directory entry but leaves the other files' objects shared.

What can go wrong: garbage collection deleting objects that old manifests still reference (keep retention rules tied to registered models); the pointer files being updated but the underlying objects never pushed to remote storage, so a colleague cannot fetch them; very many small files making hashing and checkout slow (pack them or use a manifest format designed for it); labels stored outside the versioned set; and legal deletion requests that require removing objects while old runs still reference them (record that the data is unavailable rather than silently failing).

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
Two training configurations, A and B, are each run with 5 seeds on the same data split. Validation accuracy for A is 0.912, 0.905, 0.918, 0.909, 0.915 and for B is 0.917, 0.908, 0.921, 0.913, 0.919 (seed i uses the same initial weights and data order in both). A teammate wants to ship B because 'it won in every seed'. How would you compare the two fairly, and how strong is the evidence?
Key concepts: seed variance; paired comparison; standard error of a difference; best-of-n selection bias; sign test limits; minimum worthwhile effect
Principles for comparing runs: use the same data split and evaluation set for both; run several seeds because a single run mixes real differences with seed noise; report mean and spread (standard deviation), not the best run; and never pick the best of many runs for one configuration and compare it with a single run of the other, which builds in selection bias.

Here, A has mean 0.9118 and sample standard deviation about 0.0051; B has mean 0.9156 and about 0.0052. The mean difference is 0.0038, which is smaller than the seed-to-seed spread of either configuration. Treating the runs as independent samples, the standard error of the difference is about 0.0032, so the difference is about 1.2 standard errors: not convincing.

But the setup is paired: seed i shares initial weights and data order across configurations, so a lucky seed tends to be lucky for both. Pairing removes that shared noise. The per-seed differences are 0.005, 0.003, 0.003, 0.004, 0.004: mean 0.0038, with a standard error of about 0.00037, i.e. about 10 standard errors. That is much stronger evidence that B is better on this split.

Caveats keep this honest. (1) Pairing is only valid if the seed really controls shared sources of noise; otherwise the independent analysis applies. (2) Five pairs is a small sample; a sign test on 5 out of 5 wins has a two-sided p-value of 2 x (1/2)^5 = 0.0625, which cannot reach 0.05 at all. (3) Both configurations were evaluated on one validation split, so split noise is not captured; also, the gain of 0.0038 may be below what matters for the product. (4) If B was chosen after many trials, the effect is optimistic.

A sensible recommendation: B is probably slightly better; confirm with more seeds and a different split or fold, check the practical size of the gain, then decide.

CI/CD for ML (data and model tests, gating, rollback) - includes data and model validation
Where in an ML pipeline would you put data validation, and which kinds of failures would you block the pipeline on versus only warn about? Use training data and live serving requests separately in your answer.
Key concepts: data schema; contract checks vs statistical checks; fail closed in training; serving-time validation; null-rate threshold; reference statistics; feature logging
Think of validation as tests on data, placed where bad data does the most damage and is cheapest to stop.

Training side:
1. At ingestion/feature build: structural and semantic checks derived from a schema: required columns, types, allowed categories, value ranges, null-rate limits, uniqueness of keys, row counts versus the previous run. These are contract checks, so a violation should block the pipeline; training on a feed that silently renamed a column or changed units wastes compute and can ship a worse model.
2. Before training: statistical comparison with a reference (previous accepted data): distribution summaries, label rate, category frequencies. Large shifts are not always errors (seasonality, a campaign), so these usually warn or require sign-off, with thresholds tuned to keep false alarms low.

Serving side:
3. On each request or batch: schema, type and range checks on the features. One malformed request should not crash the service: reject it with a clear error, or substitute a documented fallback, and count it. A rising rate of violations is the alerting signal (it often means an upstream change). Log the served features so that they can be compared with the training data; Google's Rules of ML recommends saving the features used at serving time to a log.
4. The ML Test Score rubric lists these concerns explicitly: feature expectations captured in a schema, and data invariants holding in both training and serving inputs.

Fail versus warn is a cost judgement: block where an error is unambiguous and the downstream cost high; warn where the check is statistical and has a false-positive rate. Pitfalls: a schema never updated, so alerts get ignored; thresholds copied from one dataset; and checks that run only on a sample missing a rare corruption.

CI/CD for ML (data and model tests, gating, rollback) - includes data and model validation
Write validate_batch(rows, schema) in plain Python (standard library only) that checks a batch of feature rows before training or scoring and returns structured violations. rows is a list of dicts; schema maps a column name to a dict with optional keys type ('int', 'float' or 'str'), min, max, allowed, max_null_rate (default 0.0) and severity ('error' or 'warn', default 'error'). A missing key, None or NaN counts as null. Report: an empty batch, a column absent from every row, a null rate above its limit, a wrong type (bools are not ints; ints are acceptable as floats), values outside [min, max], and values not in allowed. Return a list of dicts with column, check, severity and detail, in a deterministic order, plus a has_errors(violations) helper. Then explain how you would wire it into a pipeline.
Key concepts: schema validation; null rate; bool-is-int pitfall; structured violations; severity levels; missing column detection; fail vs warn
Design decisions behind the function:

- Structure first, content second. A column missing from every row is reported as a single missing_column error and the other checks on that column are skipped, because null-rate and range failures would just repeat the same root cause (a renamed or dropped upstream field). Likewise, a type error stops the range/allowed checks for that column, since comparing strings to numeric bounds is meaningless.
- Nulls are separated from bad values. Null rate is computed over all rows (a missing key, None or NaN), and range/allowed checks run on non-null values only, so a column with 5% nulls and 0 out-of-range values is reported only as a null-rate problem.
- Severity is per column for statistical-looking checks (null rate, range, allowed), but structural problems (empty batch, missing column, wrong type) are always errors.
- Bool is a subclass of int in Python, so isinstance(True, int) is True; the code excludes it explicitly. Otherwise a flag column accidentally passed as a feature would pass an int check.
- Output is structured (column, check, severity, detail) and sorted by column so that tests, logs and alert grouping are stable.
- Limitations: it is a batch check; it does not compare distributions with a reference (that is a separate, statistical step), does not check cross-column constraints, and a rate threshold of 0 on range violations is deliberately strict. Infinite floats are caught only if min/max is given.

The pipeline wiring is below; the function itself is in the practical answer.

CI/CD for ML (data and model tests, gating, rollback) - includes data and model validation
A retrained churn model scores 0.871 AUC against 0.866 for the production model on the same fresh holdout. The pipeline is about to promote it automatically. Besides the overall AUC, what would you require before promotion, and in what order would you run the checks? Give one concrete example of a check that overall AUC can hide.
Key concepts: promotion gate; slice metrics; calibration; non-regression tolerance; operating-point metric; latency budget; behavioural tests
Overall AUC on one holdout is necessary, not sufficient. A gain of 0.005 may be inside noise, and an aggregate can hide regressions where it matters. The checks I would require, cheapest first, so that failures stop the pipeline early:

1. Sanity and integrity: the model loads, produces outputs of the right shape and range for a fixed smoke input set, with no NaN; its training/serving signature matches the endpoint (Google's Rules of ML advises sanity checks right before exporting a model).
2. Budgets: size and latency on the target hardware against the budget (for example p95 under a stated limit), since a better but slower model can break the service.
3. Comparison with the incumbent on the same data: a candidate-minus-baseline difference with an uncertainty estimate, and a minimum worthwhile improvement. 0.005 might not clear that bar or the confidence bound.
4. Slices: metrics on important segments (new customers, regions, device types, high-value accounts) with a non-regression tolerance, and a minimum sample size so noisy small slices do not trigger or hide failures. The ML Test Score rubric lists model quality on important data slices and checking that a simpler model is not better.
5. Calibration: if scores drive thresholds, budgets or expected-value calculations, compare reliability (for example expected calibration error or a reliability table). Two models with similar AUC can have very different probabilities.
6. Behavioural tests: invariance and directional tests (changing a field that should be irrelevant does not change the score materially; increasing support tickets should not decrease predicted risk).
7. Operational decision metric: at the operating threshold used in production (for example the top 10% of scores contacted), compare precision/recall or expected value, since AUC averages over thresholds nobody uses.
8. Staging then canary before full traffic.

Example hidden by AUC: the candidate improves on long-tenure customers (80% of the data) but loses 0.03 AUC on customers in their first 60 days (6% of the data), exactly the group the retention campaign targets. The overall number rises while the business-critical slice degrades.

CI/CD for ML (data and model tests, gating, rollback) - includes data and model validation
Implement promotion_gate(candidate, baseline, min_improvement=0.002, slice_tolerance=0.01, min_slice_n=200, z=1.96) for a higher-is-better metric. Each side is {'overall': (value, std_err), 'slices': {name: (value, std_err, n)}}. Promote only if the overall gain is at least min_improvement and its lower confidence bound (using independent standard errors) is above zero; reject if any baseline slice with at least min_slice_n examples regresses by more than slice_tolerance, or if any baseline slice of any size is missing from the candidate; if only small slices regress, return needs_review. Return {'decision': ..., 'reasons': [...]}. Then discuss what this rule does not protect against.
Key concepts: promotion gate; minimum improvement; confidence lower bound; slice non-regression; minimum slice size; fail closed; multiple comparisons
Design choices and why:

- Two separate overall conditions. 'Gain at least min_improvement' is a business threshold (is it worth the operational risk of a change?). 'Lower confidence bound above zero' is a statistical condition (is the gain distinguishable from noise?). Either can fail alone: 0.0015 with tiny error bars fails the first; 0.005 with a standard error of 0.02 fails the second.
- Independent standard errors: the standard error of the difference is sqrt(se_c^2 + se_b^2). If both models are scored on the same examples, their errors are positively correlated, so the true standard error of the difference is smaller; ignoring that makes this gate conservative. A paired bootstrap on per-example scores is better when the data is available.
- Slice rule: the tolerance allows small, expected movements on a slice (otherwise a gate with many slices would reject nearly everything by chance); the minimum slice size stops a 40-example slice from deciding the outcome in either direction. Small regressing slices produce needs_review instead of silent promotion, so a human sees them.
- A slice missing from the candidate's evaluation, and any NaN or infinite metric, is a hard failure: fail closed, because a missing metric often means a broken evaluation job and a NaN makes every comparison False, which would otherwise read as a pass.
- Three outcomes rather than two keep ambiguity visible.

What it does not protect against: many slices tested at once raise the chance of a spurious slice failure (and a real one hiding inside the tolerance); a gain on the offline set that does not transfer online (the ML Test Score lists 'offline and online metrics correlate' as its own test); slice regressions judged on point estimates (a 200-example slice at accuracy 0.85 has a standard error near 0.025, over twice the 0.01 tolerance, so the slice rule is noisy at the default minimum size); label leakage in the holdout; distribution shift between holdout and tomorrow's traffic; latency, size, and calibration limits (which need their own checks); and the baseline being a stale number rather than a re-evaluation of the current production model on the same data.

CI/CD for ML (data and model tests, gating, rollback) - includes data and model validation
A pull-request check trains a small model on a 200-row fixture and asserts validation accuracy >= 0.75. It fails in roughly one build in seven even when no relevant code changed, and engineers have started re-running it until it is green. Diagnose the problem and redesign the check, saying what a PR-level test can and cannot establish about a model.
Key concepts: flaky test; seed variance; smoke test floor; overfit-a-tiny-batch test; small fixtures; PR check vs post-merge evaluation; quarantining flaky tests
The test asserts a statistical outcome of a stochastic process against a threshold that sits inside the process's own noise, so it is flaky by construction. Re-running until green trains the team to ignore the check, which is arguably worse than having none.

What a PR check can establish: the pipeline code runs end to end on a small fixture; shapes, dtypes and value ranges are right; the loss decreases on a few steps or the model can overfit a tiny batch (a strong signal the training loop and loss are wired correctly); the data-validation and feature code behave on edge cases (unseen categories, nulls); predictions are deterministic given fixed inputs and weights; saved and reloaded models give the same outputs; and invariants hold (probabilities in [0, 1], outputs sum to 1).

What it cannot establish: that the model's quality on real data is acceptable. A 200-row fixture says almost nothing about that, and quality needs the full evaluation on a proper holdout in a scheduled or post-merge pipeline with a promotion gate.

Redesign: (1) keep seeds fixed in tests, and measure the spread rather than guessing: train with many seeds and set the assertion well below the observed minimum, or assert a very loose sanity floor (for example better than the majority-class baseline by a margin). (2) Replace the metric assertion with property tests (overfit 16 examples to near-zero loss; loss at step 20 is below loss at step 0). (3) Keep fixtures tiny so the check runs in seconds; run the expensive training in a separate nightly or on-demand job. (4) Quarantine and fix flaky tests promptly. The ML Test Score rubric lists training reproducibility and pipeline integration tests among its infrastructure tests, and Google's Rules of ML recommends testing the infrastructure independently from the machine learning.

CI/CD for ML (data and model tests, gating, rollback) - includes data and model validation
A newly promoted model passes every offline gate and goes to full traffic at 14:00. At 14:40 the endpoint's error rate is normal but the business metric 'orders per 1,000 sessions' looks 6% lower than the same hour last week. Define the rollback criteria you would have agreed in advance, and what has to be true for the rollback to be quick and safe.
Key concepts: rollback criteria; hard vs soft signals; canary before full traffic; concurrent control; previous artifact retention; expand-contract schema change; model version in logs
Rollback criteria should be written, with thresholds, before the promotion, because deciding during an incident is when people rationalise.

Hard signals, automatic: error and timeout rate above a limit for N minutes; p95 or p99 latency breaching the SLO; prediction health checks such as a share of NaN, constant or out-of-range outputs; a sudden shift in the output score distribution against the previous model on the same traffic. These are cheap to evaluate and rarely ambiguous.

Soft signals, human decision with a pre-agreed protocol: business or proxy metrics (conversion, click-through, orders per session). They are noisy, seasonal and sometimes delayed. A 6% drop in one hour may be within normal hour-to-hour variation, a time-of-day pattern, or a concurrent change (promotion, outage). Compare against a concurrent control (the old model on a slice of traffic, a canary) rather than against last week, and require a minimum sample before acting. The ML Test Score rubric lists canarying models before serving and being able to roll back to a previous serving version as distinct tests; in that setup the 14:00 launch would have been a canary first, which answers this question directly.

What must hold for a fast, safe rollback:
- The previous model version stays in the registry, immutable, with its container image or runtime and dependencies still available (do not garbage-collect it during the cooling-off period).
- Its input features are still produced. If the new release also changed the feature pipeline or schema, rolling back the model alone can break serving; use backward-compatible (expand then contract) schema changes so that both versions can run.
- Rollback is a pointer or traffic change, not a rebuild, and has been rehearsed in staging.
- State is considered: caches keyed by model output, downstream consumers that stored scores from the new model, and any feature or embedding store the new model wrote.
- The incident record keeps the data needed to diagnose: model version in each prediction log.

Decision at 14:40 in this scenario: shift part of traffic back to the old model for a controlled comparison, rather than guessing from a single hour.

CI/CD for ML (data and model tests, gating, rollback) - includes data and model validation
A nightly retraining DAG runs ingest -> validate -> build_features -> train -> evaluate -> register. After a transient failure in train, the orchestrator retried the whole run from build_features. The next morning the feature table has duplicated rows for 3 days, two models are registered under the same version tag, and a colleague's backfill of last week's partitions produced different features than the originals. List the design faults and how you would fix each, including how a step's cache key should be formed.
Key concepts: idempotent step; atomic commit of outputs; overwrite by partition; cache key from input hashes; logical date parameter; retry vs fail-fast; backfill; resume from failed step
Each symptom points to a step that is not idempotent, or to an ambiguous identity of inputs.

1. Duplicated rows after a retry: build_features appended to the table. A retried step must produce the same final state as a single successful run. Fix: write by partition key with overwrite or upsert (replace partition for date D), or write to a temporary location and atomically swap or commit on success, so a partial first attempt is discarded.
2. Two models with the same version tag: register created a new entry with a caller-chosen name. Fix: derive identity from content or run (training run id plus input hashes), make registration idempotent (registering the same run twice returns the same version), and never let a step overwrite an existing version.
3. Backfill produced different features: the step read something that is not a pure function of the partition: 'now', 'latest' reference tables, current code, or an unpinned join. Fix: pass the logical date as an explicit parameter; read versioned or as-of snapshots of reference data; pin code and environment versions; record them in the step's outputs.
4. Retry granularity: restarting the whole run repeats successful steps. Fix: persist each step's output as an artifact addressed by its inputs, and let a retry resume from the failed step; cap retries and use backoff for transient errors, but fail fast on deterministic ones (a schema violation will fail identically every time).
5. Failed attempts left partial artifacts behind (a half-written feature partition, a stored but unregistered model) that later attempts could pick up. Fix: write to a temporary location, commit or rename only on success, and let downstream steps read only committed outputs.

Cache key: a step's output can be reused only if everything that influences it is unchanged. So the key is a hash of (step name, code version or hash of the step's code and its dependencies, parameters, and the content hashes of every input artifact), using a canonical serialisation (sorted keys). Do not include volatile values such as wall-clock time. Unhashable hidden inputs (an external table read by name, an unpinned model download) break caching correctness, so they must be turned into explicit versioned inputs.

CI/CD for ML (data and model tests, gating, rollback) - includes data and model validation
Your team has: a feature-engineering code repository, a weekly-refreshed training table, a model that ages quickly, and a data-quality alert system. Which events would you let trigger which pipeline (PR checks, full retraining, evaluation only, redeploy), and what would each pipeline run versus skip?
Key concepts: pipeline triggers; path-filtered triggers; smoke test on fixture; retrain on new data after validation; model staleness; promotion gate; alert-driven investigation
Think of triggers as events, each mapped to the cheapest pipeline that can detect the risk it brings.

1. Pull request touching feature or model code: run in minutes. Static checks, unit tests of feature functions on edge cases, a pipeline smoke test on a tiny fixture (ingest through train through evaluate with a handful of rows), schema and config validation. It cannot judge model quality; do not train on full data here.
2. Merge to main: heavier integration run on a fixed, versioned sample with a baseline comparison, producing a candidate and its report. This answers 'did the change alter metrics, latency or outputs'. Often only paths that matter (feature code, training code, config) should trigger it.
3. New training data lands (weekly table): validation first (schema, null rates, row counts against the last accepted run). If it passes, retrain on the new snapshot, evaluate against the current production model on the same holdout, and apply the promotion gate. If it fails, stop and alert; do not retrain on data you do not trust.
4. Schedule: Google's Rules of ML suggests knowing the system's freshness requirements, that is, measuring how quickly performance degrades as the model ages. A model that loses measurable value in a few days justifies a more frequent schedule; one that holds for months does not. Schedule is a floor, not the only trigger.
5. Monitoring alerts (data quality, performance regression): usually trigger investigation or a protective action (switch to a fallback, pause automatic promotion), not an automatic retrain, because retraining does not fix a broken feed or a labelling issue. An automated retrain on drift can be appropriate when the process is mature and gated.
6. Config or dependency change: treat like code (a pinned-dependency update triggers the integration run); a registry alias change triggers redeploy, not retraining.

Rule of thumb: each trigger gets a pipeline whose runtime is proportional to how often it fires, and every path that ends in production passes the same promotion gate.

Model registry and packaging (containers, ONNX, signatures, dependency pinning)
A teammate argues: 'We already save every trained model into a versioned folder in object storage, so a model registry is redundant.' What does a registry add beyond that folder, and in what situation would the folder genuinely be enough?
Key concepts: model registry; model version; alias; lineage; signature; metadata and tags; approval and audit trail
A registry turns 'a file somewhere' into a managed, addressable model with history. The folder gives you bytes with a naming convention; a registry typically adds:

1. Version identity. Each registration under a model name gets a new, immutable version number (MLflow's registry documents the incrementing version number; treating a version as immutable is the intended usage rather than something that page spells out), so 'model X v12' means one specific artifact.
2. Lineage. Each version links back to what produced it: the training run, code commit, data snapshot and config, so you can answer 'how was the model in production built?'
3. Metadata. Tags, descriptions, evaluation results and the input/output signature travel with the version, so a consumer can validate requests without opening the artifact.
4. Named pointers. Consumers ask for 'production' (an alias or stage) instead of a path. Promotion and rollback become re-pointing that name, and a registry with auditing enabled can record who moved it and when. MLflow documents aliases as mutable named references to a version.
5. Governance. Access control, approvals and an audit trail around who may promote.

The folder is genuinely enough when there is one model, one author and one consumer, nothing is promoted through environments, and nobody will ever ask for provenance. Even then, the convention you invent (latest, final, v2) tends to be a hand-built registry with fewer guarantees.

Pitfall: a registry does not create reproducibility on its own. If the training job does not log the data version, seeds and environment, the lineage field is empty or misleading.

Model registry and packaging (containers, ONNX, signatures, dependency pinning)
Your team stores scikit-learn pipelines as joblib files in a shared bucket that several teams, and one external partner, can write to. The serving image loads whichever file is newest at startup. After a base-image refresh the service starts logging version warnings and a handful of predictions change; separately, the security team flags the loading step. Explain both problems and what you would change in the loading path.
Key concepts: pickle deserialization; arbitrary code execution on load; library version coupling; joblib; artifact integrity (hash/signature); environment pinning; fail-fast version check
Two different problems share one loading step.

Compatibility. A pickle records instance state plus references to classes by import path; it does not embed the class code (the Python docs say only instance data is pickled). Loading therefore needs a compatible version of the library that defined the classes. scikit-learn's persistence guide says loading a model trained with a different scikit-learn version is not supported, may emit an inconsistent-version warning, and can give different results or crash. A base-image refresh that bumped a library is the classic trigger: the file loads, so nothing fails loudly, but internals have changed. Small output changes are consistent with changed internals, but only a replay against the old environment would prove the cause.

Security. Unpickling calls whatever callables the byte stream names, so crafted data can execute arbitrary code during loading (Python's pickle documentation carries an explicit warning). scikit-learn states that joblib is pickle-based and shares the risk. Because several teams and an outside partner can write to the bucket, anyone with write access can run code inside the serving process with its credentials. 'Newest file wins' makes it worse: an overwritten or planted file is promoted automatically.

Changes: (1) serve only artifacts that a registry has promoted, referenced by explicit version, never 'latest'; (2) restrict who can write promoted artifacts; (3) verify integrity against a digest or signature recorded where the artifact writers cannot edit it (the Python docs suggest signing pickled data with HMAC); (4) record training-time library versions with the model and refuse to load on mismatch, instead of warning; (5) build the serving image from the same lockfile as training; (6) where feasible, move to a format that does not execute code on load, accepting its limits (an exchange format may not cover every estimator or custom step).

Model registry and packaging (containers, ONNX, signatures, dependency pinning)
A fraud model (a scikit-learn pipeline: one-hot encoding, scaling, then gradient-boosted trees) is exported to ONNX so it can be served without a Python environment. In a shadow comparison, 0.8% of rows get a different predicted class from the original pipeline, and the ops lead asks whether ONNX 'guarantees identical behaviour'. What does an exchange format like this actually fix, what can still make outputs differ, and how would you test the export before it ships?
Key concepts: ONNX computation graph; operator set (opset); custom operators; preprocessing outside the graph; float32 vs float64 precision; decision threshold flips; parity testing
What it fixes. ONNX specifies a portable, serialized computation graph plus named operator sets (the IR specification). The serving side needs a runtime that implements those operators, not the training Python environment, and loading a model does not unpickle Python objects. scikit-learn's guide lists these as advantages and also notes that arbitrary computation can be expressed in ONNX, so untrusted models should still run in a sandbox.

What it does not guarantee:
1. Semantics come from the converter. Not every estimator is supported, and custom transformers need custom conversion work; the original Python object is lost.
2. Operator sets. A model must name the operator sets it needs, and a runtime must support them all or reject the model. A runtime that is too old fails loudly; custom operators from non-default domains require the runtime to have them.
3. Anything outside the graph. Pandas feature engineering, text cleaning or tokenization done before the pipeline is not exported unless you convert it too. Re-implementing it in the service creates exactly the skew you wanted to avoid.
4. Numerics. Exported graphs often compute in float32 where training used float64. Tree models compare a feature to a threshold, so a value very close to a split can go to the other branch; summed leaf scores then shift slightly, and a row sitting near the decision threshold flips class. Float32 rounding alone usually flips far fewer rows than 0.8% (it needs that share of rows to sit within rounding error of a split or of the decision threshold; the skl2onnx documentation says float and double comparisons give the same result in most cases, though the same page shows a regression example where casting to float produced large errors, so this is an expectation, not a guarantee), so treat a 0.8% difference as a sign of a real discrepancy, such as unseen-category or missing-value handling, scaler dtype, or preprocessing outside the graph, until the margin analysis shows otherwise.

Test: run both models on a large representative sample, compare probabilities (not just labels), and check whether every flipped row has a score within the numeric tolerance of the decision threshold.

Model registry and packaging (containers, ONNX, signatures, dependency pinning)
A registered model has an input signature of {age: double, plan_id: string, days_active: long}. Three clients misbehave: one sends age as the string '34'; one sends days_active as 3.7; a third sends perfectly typed rows but days_active measured in hours instead of days. Which of these can a signature-based schema check catch, which can it not, and what would you add around it?
Key concepts: model signature; input schema validation; type coercion; range and unit validation; contract test; signature inference from an example
A signature is a declared contract on input and output names, types and (for tensors) shapes that travels with the model version. MLflow's documentation describes it this way and notes it can be generated automatically when you log an input example, which is convenient but means the signature only reflects that one example: a column whose example values are integers (for instance Python ints or an int64 column) is inferred as an integer type even if the model should accept doubles. Review inferred signatures.

What it can catch:
- The string '34' for a double column: a type mismatch. A strict check rejects it with a clear client error; a lenient one coerces it. Decide which behaviour you want and test it, because coercion rules differ between serving layers.
- days_active = 3.7 for a long column: this is a lossy conversion (3.7 to 3). A good check rejects it rather than truncating, because truncation hides a client bug.
- Missing columns and wrong shapes. Extra columns are a policy choice: MLflow's schema enforcement ignores them with a warning, so reject them explicitly if you want strictness.

What it cannot catch: the third client. 'Hours instead of days' is type-correct but semantically wrong, and every type check passes while predictions degrade silently. Neither can it catch out-of-range values (age = -4 or 900), new categories in plan_id, an unusual null rate, or a shifted distribution.

Complement it with:
1. Constraint checks derived from training data: ranges, allowed categories, maximum null rate, applied at the endpoint (reject or flag) and in the pipeline.
2. Unit conventions in the field names or schema documentation (days_active_days), and contract tests that replay each client's sample payloads against the endpoint in CI.
3. Logging of rejected and clamped requests per client, so a unit mix-up shows up as a changed distribution for one client.
4. Versioning of the signature with the model so a schema change is a deliberate, reviewed event.

Model registry and packaging (containers, ONNX, signatures, dependency pinning)
Auditors ask you to bring back, with behaviour equivalent to the original, the model that served customers 14 months ago, and to show how it was built. Design what each registry version must record and how the model is packaged, then describe how promotion and rollback should work using aliases, including what is and is not atomic.
Key concepts: immutable model version; alias promotion; lineage (code, data, config); lockfile and base-image digest; packaged preprocessing; deployment record; replay test
Record per version (immutable once registered):
- Artifact in the chosen format with a content digest, plus the preprocessing it depends on, packaged inside it or versioned and referenced explicitly.
- Lineage: training run, code commit, data snapshot identifier or hash, configuration, seeds, and the feature definitions' version. MLflow's registry documents linking a version to the run that produced it, which is the pattern to copy.
- Signature, evaluation results against the baseline, who approved the promotion.
- Environment: dependency lockfile with hashes, base image referenced by digest (tags are mutable), hardware class.

Equivalent behaviour needs more than the weights: if the feature pipeline or an encoder lives outside the artifact, the old version of that code must also be recoverable. Exact bit-for-bit equality can be unrealistic across hardware, so define 'equivalent' as agreement within a stated tolerance on a replay set.

Aliases. Versions should never change (treat them as immutable by convention); aliases (for example 'production') are mutable named pointers, which MLflow documents. Promotion moves the alias from v39 to v41. A single alias update is one registry write (atomic in typical database-backed registries; MLflow's documentation does not state this), but running replicas do not notice unless they re-resolve it. A safe pattern is to resolve the alias to an explicit version when you create the deployment, and record that version, not the alias, in the deployment record. Rollback is then the same operation in reverse (alias back to v39, redeploy v39), which only works if v39's artifact and image are still retained. Retention policy is therefore part of the design: cleanup jobs that delete 'old' images silently destroy your ability to roll back or to answer an audit.

Serving patterns (batch, online, streaming, REST/gRPC, autoscaling, batching) - includes monitoring fundamentals for serving
Choose batch, online (request/response) or streaming inference for each case and justify it on latency, freshness, cost and failure handling: (a) re-ranking 3 million product pages once a week for a newsletter; (b) a card-payment risk score that must return in about 100 ms at checkout and should reflect the cardholder's last 10 minutes of activity; (c) 50,000 sensor readings per second where an alert must fire within a few seconds of a pattern. Where would a hybrid beat a pure choice?
Key concepts: batch inference; online inference; streaming inference; feature freshness; latency budget; idempotent writes; fallback decision
(a) Batch. Nobody waits on an individual prediction, the entity set is known in advance, and staleness of a week is acceptable. Run it as a scheduled job that is partitioned and retried per partition, with idempotent writes (overwrite by partition or upsert by key) so a rerun cannot duplicate. Cost is paid only while the job runs, and if a run fails the previous week's output simply stays in place.

(b) Online, with a hybrid feature path. The score is on the checkout critical path, so it needs a synchronous endpoint with a latency budget (for example 100 ms end to end, meaning only a few tens of ms for the model). Slow-moving features are precomputed in batch and read from a key-value store; the 'last 10 minutes' aggregates are maintained by a streaming job into the same store. Capacity must cover peak traffic, so cost is higher than batch. Failure handling is a business decision made in advance: on timeout, return a rules-based or default decision (for example allow with step-up verification) and flag it, rather than blocking checkout.

(c) Streaming. Events arrive continuously and the answer is needed within seconds, so a stateful stream processor keeps windows per sensor and applies a small model per event or window. Design for event time versus arrival time, late and out-of-order events, checkpointing, and at-least-once delivery, which means alerts must be deduplicated or idempotent. Prefer backpressure or a durable buffer to silent drops (sensors often cannot be slowed, so if load must be shed, do it deliberately and count it). Cost is a continuously running, stateful cluster sized for the peak of 50,000 events/s, so keep the per-event model light.

Hybrid beats pure modes when the expensive part is stable: precompute embeddings or heavy scores in batch, then run a light model online on top of fresh signals. Also, if the set of entities is finite, an 'online' product can often be a lookup of batch-precomputed predictions, which removes inference from the request path entirely.

Serving patterns (batch, online, streaming, REST/gRPC, autoscaling, batching) - includes monitoring fundamentals for serving
An image-embedding model sits behind an endpoint called by other backend services at about 300 requests/s with a 150 ms client budget. Each request currently carries a decoded 224x224x3 float32 tensor (150,528 values) as JSON over REST. A browser dashboard also calls a separate, low-volume prediction route. Would you move the main route to gRPC with protobuf, and what would you check before and after the move?
Key concepts: REST/JSON vs gRPC/protobuf; payload size and serialization cost; HTTP/2 multiplexing and load balancing; deadlines; schema contract (.proto); browser clients; sending compressed image bytes
Start with the arithmetic, because it may make the protocol question secondary. 150,528 float32 values are 602,112 bytes raw. Serialised as JSON text with float64 digits (random float32 values converted by numpy tolist and dumped with Python's json module; shortest float32 text would be about 1.75 MB) the same tensor was about 3.05 MB, roughly five times larger; rounding to four decimals brought it to about 1.19 MB. At 300 requests/s the JSON route moves on the order of 0.9 GB/s, which is about 7 Gbit/s before overhead, so the network and the JSON encode/decode cost may already eat the 150 ms budget. Raw binary is 0.18 GB/s. Sending the encoded image (typically a small fraction of the raw tensor size) and preprocessing on the server is usually the bigger win, and keeps preprocessing in one place.

gRPC advantages for the internal route: a binary protobuf encoding, a .proto contract with generated clients that catches schema drift at build time, HTTP/2 multiplexing and streaming. Its docs recommend always setting an explicit, realistic deadline and note that gRPC sets none by default, so a client could wait indefinitely; deadlines can be propagated to downstream calls. Decide them from your measured latency plus margin.

Costs and checks: (1) load balancing, since many requests share one long-lived HTTP/2 connection, a connection-level balancer can leave some replicas idle; verify per-request balancing; (2) browsers generally cannot speak native gRPC directly, so the dashboard keeps REST or goes through a gRPC-Web proxy (the gRPC-Web guide's example uses Envoy); (3) debugging is harder than curl, so keep a REST health and admin path; (4) benchmark both under your real payload, not assumptions.

After the move, compare p50/p95/p99 and CPU per request for old and new routes, and keep both routes for a deprecation period.

Serving patterns (batch, online, streaming, REST/gRPC, autoscaling, batching) - includes monitoring fundamentals for serving
Implement a deterministic simulator for dynamic request batching on a single worker, plus a percentile helper.

simulate_microbatch(arrivals, max_batch, max_wait, overhead, per_item) -> (latencies, batch_sizes)

arrivals is a sorted list of arrival times in ms (ValueError if unsorted; ValueError if max_batch < 1 or max_wait < 0). Requests are served FIFO. A batch is dispatched at the first moment the worker is free AND (max_batch requests are waiting OR the oldest waiting request has waited max_wait ms). It contains the waiting requests up to max_batch (a request arriving exactly at the dispatch instant counts as waiting). Service time is overhead + per_item * batch_size, and the worker is busy for that time. Latency of a request is its finish time minus its arrival time. Also write percentile(values, p) using the nearest-rank definition. Then use it to explain, with an arrival every 1 ms (1000 requests/s) and every 20 ms, why max_batch and max_wait must be chosen from the load, using overhead=10 ms and per_item=0.5 ms.
Key concepts: dynamic batching; max batch size and max wait; fixed overhead vs per-item cost; queueing delay; throughput capacity; p95 latency; head-of-line wait
Why batching exists. Many accelerators and runtimes pay a mostly fixed cost per call (launching kernels, moving data, framework overhead) and a smaller marginal cost per item, so a batch of n costs overhead + per_item * n. Throughput per worker is then n / (overhead + per_item * n), which rises with n and approaches 1/per_item. Batching trades latency for throughput: the first request in a batch waits for others to arrive (bounded by max_wait), and a larger batch also takes longer to compute.

The dispatch rule has two cases. If the worker is idle, the batch goes at min(time the max_batch-th request arrives, oldest arrival + max_wait). If the worker is busy, requests accumulate and the batch goes as soon as the worker frees if the full or timeout condition already held by then. Both cases are captured by max(free_time, min(full_time, oldest_arrival + max_wait)). Under heavy load the worker is always busy, so the wait window barely matters and batches fill toward max_batch; under light load the window is pure added delay.

Edge cases to test: a single request with a timer-based dispatch; max_wait = 0 (a batch contains only requests already waiting, so batching still occurs under backlog or simultaneous arrivals; only max_batch=1 disables it); a request that arrives just inside versus just outside the window; unsorted input.

Interpretation of the experiment: with one request per ms and no batching, service takes 10.5 ms per request but only 1 ms passes between arrivals, so the queue grows without bound; with max_batch 32 the worker handles 32 requests per 26 ms, which exceeds the arrival rate, and latency stays bounded. At one request per 20 ms the opposite holds: batching only adds waiting.

Serving patterns (batch, online, streaming, REST/gRPC, autoscaling, batching) - includes monitoring fundamentals for serving
A model endpoint scales out when average CPU passes 70%. Each replica serves about 4 requests at a time at roughly 120 ms each and takes about 90 s to become useful (image pull, model load, warm-up). Normally 3 replicas handle 50 requests/s. At 09:00 traffic ramps to 200 requests/s within two minutes. p99 goes to timeouts for several minutes even though CPU graphs look unremarkable (the work happens on an accelerator). Diagnose the failure and redesign the scaling policy.
Key concepts: autoscaling signal; Little's law (concurrency = rate x latency); saturation; cold start and warm-up; readiness gating; scale-up lag; bounded queue and load shedding
Diagnosis. Capacity per replica is about 4 in flight / 0.12 s = 33 requests/s. Three replicas give about 100 requests/s, which is fine for 50 requests/s (50% busy) but not for 200. The excess is about 100 requests/s. Even if scaling reacted instantly at 09:00, new replicas are only useful after about 90 s, plus the metric scrape and decision delay, so on the order of 9,000 requests (100 requests/s of excess times 90 s, an upper figure that assumes demand is already at 200 requests/s; the two-minute ramp lowers it, scrape and decision delay raise it) arrive faster than they can be served. With an unbounded queue they wait until clients time out, and retries add load. CPU never signalled because the work runs on an accelerator, so the chosen signal does not measure saturation (one of the four golden signals in Google's SRE book: how full the service is).

Redesign.
1. Scale on a signal that tracks saturation: in-flight requests (concurrency) per replica, or queue depth or queue wait, optionally together with accelerator utilisation. Little's law gives the target: required in-flight = rate x latency = 200 x 0.12 = 24, so at least 6 replicas at 100% utilisation.
2. Keep headroom: target about 60% of per-replica concurrency (2.4 in flight), so 24 / 2.4 = 10 replicas at the new peak, and about 3 at 50 requests/s (6 in flight / 2.4 = 2.5, rounded up).
3. Respect the lag: pre-scale on a schedule or forecast for known 09:00 ramps; keep a minimum replica count; scale up aggressively and down slowly with a stabilisation window.
4. Make readiness mean 'model loaded and warmed up' (run a few dummy requests so the first real request does not pay for lazy initialisation), so the balancer never sends traffic to a cold replica.
5. Bound the queue and shed load early (fast 429/503 or a cheaper fallback) so overload degrades part of the traffic instead of all of it.

Serving patterns (batch, online, streaming, REST/gRPC, autoscaling, batching) - includes monitoring fundamentals for serving
During a deploy, a prediction service's p99 rises from 200 ms to 1.5 s. Its callers use a 1 s timeout and retry up to 3 times immediately. Within minutes the service, which normally runs at about 80% of capacity, is completely down. Explain the mechanism and describe the client and server changes (timeouts, retries, idempotency, fallbacks) that would have contained it.
Key concepts: retry storm; timeouts and deadlines; retry budget; exponential backoff with jitter; idempotency; load shedding; fallback prediction; circuit breaker
Mechanism. The slow deploy pushes some requests past the 1 s client timeout. Each timeout triggers an immediate retry, so offered load grows. If a fraction f of attempts fail, a client with up to 3 retries sends about 1 + f + f^2 + f^3 attempts per original request; at f = 0.5 that is 1.875x. A service at 80% of capacity has only 25% headroom, so 1.875x load takes it to about 150% of capacity, which makes more requests time out, which raises f: positive feedback. A second effect makes it worse: when a client times out, the server often keeps processing the abandoned request, so capacity is spent on answers nobody is waiting for.

Client changes.
- Set explicit deadlines, derived from the end-to-end budget, and pass the remaining deadline downstream (gRPC documents propagating deadlines, and notes it sets none by default).
- Retry only on retryable errors, with a retry budget (for example retries limited to about 10% of recent request volume), exponential backoff with jitter, and a low attempt cap.
- Add a circuit breaker so a failing dependency is skipped for a short period.
- Define a fallback: a cached score, a simpler model or rule, or a safe default, marked as fallback in the response.

Server changes.
- Reject or skip work whose deadline has already passed; cancel in-flight inference when the client disconnects where the stack allows.
- Bound queues and shed load quickly (fast 503/429) instead of queueing past the point where answers are useful.
- Make deploys gradual with readiness gates so a slow version never takes full traffic.

Idempotency. Pure scoring is safe to retry, but if the endpoint also writes a decision, charges, or sends a notification, a retry can repeat the side effect. Use a client-generated request id as an idempotency key so repeats return the stored result. Monitor retry rate, fallback rate and the latency of failed requests separately from successful ones.

Serving patterns (batch, online, streaming, REST/gRPC, autoscaling, batching) - includes monitoring fundamentals for serving
You are about to put a recommendation-scoring endpoint (about 500 requests/s) into production. Define what you log for every prediction, which dashboard panels and alerts you build from the four golden signals (and which latency statistic you alert on), and what you deliberately do not page on. Mention the cost and privacy side of logging at this volume.
Key concepts: per-prediction log record; model version tag; four golden signals; percentile latency; symptom-based alerting; fallback rate; log sampling and privacy
Log per prediction (structured, one record per request): request id or trace id; timestamp; model version and the version of preprocessing/feature definitions; a pseudonymised entity id; the model's output (score, chosen items) and any threshold applied; fallback flag and reason; status code; latency broken into queue wait, preprocessing and inference; and either a hash of the input features or, for a small sample, the features themselves. Request id plus model version lets you join later outcomes (clicks, labels) back to the exact prediction.

Golden signals (Google SRE book): latency, traffic, errors, saturation.
- Latency: p50, p95 and p99 per model version, not the mean (averages hide the tail), and track failed requests separately from successful ones, since fast failures can make averages look good.
- Traffic: requests per second, split by route, client and model version.
- Errors: explicit (5xx, timeouts) and implicit ones such as malformed outputs, NaN scores, or responses served by the fallback.
- Saturation: concurrency or queue depth against the measured limit, accelerator and memory utilisation.

Alert on symptoms users feel: error ratio and latency SLO burn. The latency statistic you alert on is the fraction of requests slower than the objective (for example 300 ms) burning the budget quickly, not the mean; p95/p99 panels support diagnosis. Do not page on drift statistics, offline accuracy, or a single noisy metric; send them to dashboards and tickets because they need labels, windows or judgment.

Volume: 500 requests/s is 43.2 million requests a day; at about 1 KB per record that is roughly 43 GB/day. Keep a compact record for every request and the full feature payload for a sample (say 1%), set retention periods, restrict access, and avoid raw identifiers or free text where a keyed hash is enough (a plain hash of a low-entropy identifier can be reversed, and pseudonymised data is still personal data).

Serving patterns (batch, online, streaming, REST/gRPC, autoscaling, batching) - includes monitoring fundamentals for serving
Your scoring API has a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, where a request is 'good' only if it returns a valid score within 300 ms. In the last hour 1.5% of requests were bad; in the last 5 minutes 0.4% were bad. How fast is the error budget burning, how much of the monthly budget did that hour use (assume uniform traffic), would a multiwindow policy that pages at a 14.4x burn rate over 1 hour and 5 minutes fire, and how should responses served by a fallback model be counted?
Key concepts: error budget; burn rate; multiwindow alert; SLI definition (valid and within 300 ms); fallback accounting; long and short window
The error budget is the allowed bad fraction: 100% - 99.9% = 0.1%. Burn rate is observed bad ratio divided by that: over the last hour 1.5% / 0.1% = 15x; over the last 5 minutes 0.4% / 0.1% = 4x. Google's SRE workbook defines burn rate as how fast the service consumes error budget relative to the SLO.

Budget used by the hour: the hour is 1/720 of a 30-day window (720 hours), so at 15x it consumed 15 / 720 = 2.08% of the monthly budget (assuming uniform traffic). At a sustained 15x the whole budget would be gone in 30 / 15 = 2 days. As a sanity check, the monthly budget corresponds to 0.1% of 43,200 minutes = 43.2 minutes of total outage, and a 15x burn for an hour spends 15 x 60 x 0.001 = 0.9 minutes' worth of that.

Would it page? The rule needs both windows above 14.4x. The 1-hour window is at 15x (above), the 5-minute window is at 4x (below), so it would not fire. That is the point of the short window: the long window alone would keep alerting for up to an hour after a problem ended, while the short window shows the problem is already receding. The SRE workbook's suggested starting parameters for a 99.9% SLO page at 14.4x over 1 hour with a 5-minute short window, corresponding to 2% of the budget. You would still want a lower-severity alert such as a 6x burn over 6 hours, and a ticket-level alert for slow burns.

Fallbacks. Define 'good' by what the user receives. A valid, in-time response from the fallback is good for the availability SLO, but a fallback model is usually lower quality, so track the fallback rate as its own SLI with its own objective (and alert), otherwise a long fallback period looks perfectly healthy.

Deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, rollback)
How does a canary release of a new model differ from a blue-green deployment, and what does each one cost you?
