Key concepts: canary release; blue-green deployment; traffic shifting; control group; instant rollback; duplicate capacity; blast radius
Canary. Google's SRE workbook defines canarying as a partial, time-limited deployment of a change and its evaluation, with the rest of the service acting as control. For a model: route, say, 5% of requests to the new version, compare error rate, latency and behavioural metrics against the concurrent baseline, and increase the share in stages. Benefits: small blast radius, real-traffic evidence, gradual capacity growth. Costs: you need weighted routing and a way to compare the two groups; the canary must be large and long enough to be representative (the workbook says so), and a small slice can be too small to detect rare or slow-to-appear problems.

Blue-green. You keep the current ('blue') environment and bring up the new model fully in a separate ('green') one, warm it up and test it, then switch the router. Benefits: the cutover is a single routing change, and if something is wrong, switching back is just as fast because blue is still running. Costs: duplicate capacity for the overlap (significant for GPU-backed services), and everyone is exposed at the moment of the flip, so a defect that only appears under real traffic hits 100% of users until you notice.

They combine well: build green as a separate environment, shift traffic to it in canary steps, and keep blue until the new model has proven itself. Neither helps if both versions share state that has changed incompatibly, such as a feature table or schema; that needs compatible, staged data changes.

Deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, rollback)
A team replacing a ranking model proposes: 'We will shadow the new model for two weeks. If its offline metrics on the logged shadow outputs and its latency look good, we go straight to 100%.' What can shadow deployment tell you, what can it not, and how would you sequence shadow, canary and A/B testing instead?
Key concepts: shadow deployment; canary release; A/B test; feedback effects; selection bias in logged data; guardrail metrics; staged rollout
Shadow deployment sends copies of live requests to the new model while only the old model's output is used. What it can tell you: whether the new model runs reliably on real inputs (errors, malformed outputs), how latency and resource use behave under real traffic, how its output distribution compares with the old model's, and how often the two agree. If you log the shadow outputs you can also compute offline metrics once outcomes arrive, with care.

What it cannot tell you:
1. User response. Shadow outputs are never shown, so clicks, purchases or complaints about them never happen. Anything that depends on how users react to the new ranking is invisible.
2. Feedback effects. A different ranking changes what users see, which changes what data you collect and how the system evolves. Shadow runs in a world still shaped by the old model.
3. Unbiased labels. In ranking, outcomes usually exist only for items the old model displayed. Scoring the shadow model on those is biased toward the old model's choices, and it cannot reward items the old model never showed.
4. Side-effect paths. If the model call has side effects (writes, cache fills), shadowing must be isolated; also shadow adds compute cost and may perturb latency if it shares resources.

So 'looks good in shadow, go to 100%' is unsafe. A sound sequence is: shadow for crash, latency and distribution sanity; a small canary (a few percent) with guardrail metrics and automatic rollback to prove safety on real user-facing traffic; then a properly sized randomized A/B test on the business metric to measure impact, including feedback effects; then a staged ramp. The canary is usually too small and short to estimate business impact, and the A/B test is the step that does.

Deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, rollback)
Your service handles 2 million requests per day. A new model is canaried at 1% of traffic for one day. The guardrail is the complaint rate, baseline 0.20%, and you do not want it to rise by more than 30% relative (to 0.26%). At the end of the day the canary shows 50 complaints in 20,000 requests (0.25%). One colleague says 'not statistically significant, so it is safe'; another says 'close enough to the limit, ship'. Evaluate both, and say how you would design the check. Complaints are only reliably known after a week.
Key concepts: canary statistical power; non-inferiority margin; confidence bound; event counts; delayed labels; proxy metrics; traffic share vs duration
Neither colleague is right. Expected complaints at baseline in 20,000 requests are 0.20% x 20,000 = 40, so 50 observed is within ordinary noise of 40 (Poisson standard deviation about 6.3). The canary rate is 0.25% against a control of about 0.20%; with the large control group, the standard error of the difference is about 0.035 percentage points. The difference of 0.05 points gives z of about 1.4 to 1.6 (two-sided p about 0.11 to 0.16, depending on whether the observed or the baseline rate sets the variance), so it is not significant. That is not evidence of safety: a one-sided 95% upper bound on the canary rate is roughly 0.31%, about 54% above baseline, well past the 30% margin. The data are consistent with both 'no change' and 'unacceptable'.

Power. Using a normal approximation for two proportions with a large control, detecting a rise from 0.20% to 0.26% with 80% power needs roughly 57,000 canary requests (about 48,000 with the usual formula that uses baseline variance under the null; two-sided 5% test, 80% power). One day at 1% (20,000) gives only about 38 to 48% power depending on the formula; it takes about 3 days at 1%, or under a day at 5% (100,000 requests/day). So size the canary by required events (here, about 114 complaints expected at baseline across 57,000 requests), not by a fixed share or day count. The guardrail should be framed as non-inferiority: promote only if the upper confidence bound of the increase stays under the 30% margin.

Practical design. (1) Use fast, high-volume metrics for the automatic gate: errors, timeouts, latency percentiles, fallback rate, score distribution, decision or flag rate, support-contact rate. They are well powered even at 1% because they are common. (2) Treat the week-delayed complaint rate as a delayed guardrail: hold at a modest share long enough to accumulate the needed events, then ramp only once enough matured outcomes are in. (3) Outcomes cluster by user, so effective sample size is smaller than the request count; assign by user. Also, one day can miss weekly seasonality, so the canary window should span a representative period.

Deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, rollback)
Design the automatic promote/rollback policy for a canary that ramps a new fraud-scoring model through 5%, 25% and 100% of traffic (150 requests/s overall). Chargeback labels arrive up to 45 days late. Specify the comparison baseline, the guardrail metrics, minimum samples before each decision, example thresholds, and what stays manual. Explain why 'roll back if the canary's error rate is ever higher than control's' is a poor rule.
Key concepts: concurrent control comparison; guardrail metrics; minimum sample size; rollback threshold; consecutive-window rule; delayed labels; proxy metrics; human sign-off
Baseline. Compare the canary with a concurrent control receiving the old model, as Google's SRE workbook frames canarying (the rest of the service is the control). This removes time-of-day and traffic-mix effects that a comparison with yesterday would mix in. Keep assignment sticky by user or account so the two groups are comparable and customers do not flip between models.

Tiered metrics.
1. Operational guardrails (auto-rollback): 5xx and timeout rate, p99 latency, saturation, fallback rate, invalid or NaN scores. These are frequent, so a few thousand requests give a usable signal.
2. Behavioural proxies (banded checks): approval/decline/flag rate, manual-review queue rate, score quantiles versus control. A shift beyond a band blocks promotion and goes to a human, because it may be an intended change in strictness or a defect.
3. Outcomes (chargebacks, 45-day delay): cannot gate a stage lasting hours. Limit exposure while they mature, and verify later with a matured-label comparison or an A/B analysis.

Minimum samples. At 150 requests/s, a 5% canary sees 7.5 requests/s, so 27,000 per hour and 4,500 per 10 minutes. With a 0.5% baseline error rate, the standard error of an observed 4,500-request rate is about 0.1 percentage points (sqrt(0.005 x 0.995 / 4500)), so thresholds must sit well outside that noise.

Why the naive rule fails. With small samples the canary's rate will exceed control's by chance about half the time, causing spurious rollbacks; it ignores effect size; and checking repeatedly multiplies false alarms. The SRE workbook warns that a handful of queries gives no useful signal. Require a minimum count, a margin, and persistence (consecutive windows).

Deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, rollback)
Model v7 was released together with a feature pipeline change: the feature merchant_category moved from 12 integer codes to 40 string categories and the old column was dropped from the online store. Two hours in, v7 regresses, so you roll back to v6, and v6's predictions collapse to near the default value. Explain why rollback failed, and how to structure the release so that rolling back a model is safe even when its inputs change.
Key concepts: expand-contract (parallel change); rollback compatibility; feature versioning; feature store / schema coupling; backward-compatible schema change; deployment contract test; retention window before removal
Why it failed. A model is deployed together with the feature definitions it was trained on: a model plus a schema and encoding contract. Rolling back v7 to v6 restores the model weights, but the feature pipeline kept running the new definition, and the old column is gone. v6 now receives missing or unrecognised values for merchant_category and falls into its default branch (null handling, unseen-category handling). The predictions look 'valid' to the endpoint, so nothing errors, but quality collapses. The release combined two changes that were not independently reversible.

Expand-contract (parallel change). Make the data change in backward-compatible steps:
1. Expand: add merchant_category_v2 (the new 40-string encoding) next to the old column and keep populating both, online and offline, including a backfill for training history. Existing models are unaffected.
2. Migrate: train and release v7 reading only the new feature. v6 still reads the old one, so both models run correctly against the live data.
3. Observe: canary v7; rolling back is just switching the model.
4. Contract: only after v7 is stable, v6 is retired and the rollback window (for example, a few weeks of retained v6 artifacts) has passed, stop writing and then delete the old column.

Supporting controls. Version feature definitions rather than editing them in place and record the feature-set version in the model's registry entry. Add a pre-deploy compatibility check: every feature that a model version declares (name, type, version) must exist in the serving store; run it both on release and on rollback. Package fitted encoders with the model. Replay logged requests from before the change through the older model against the new pipeline in CI. Cost: dual-write storage and compute for the window, which is the price of a safe rollback.

Deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, rollback)
A marketplace tests a new ranking model with a 50/50 split. One engineer wants to randomise each request; another wants to hash the user ID. The 'recommended for you' carousel shows a +6% click lift in week 1 that decays to +1.5% by week 3. Compare the two ways of splitting traffic for consistency and interference, explain the decay, and say what you would put in place.
Key concepts: split unit (request vs user); sticky assignment by hashing; experiment-specific salt; interference between arms; novelty effect; switchback test; sample ratio check
Per-request randomisation gives many independent assignments and the highest statistical power for request-level outcomes (for example, 'was this impression clicked'), but each user sees both models. The experience is inconsistent, and outcomes that accumulate over a user (retention, repeat purchase, trust) are blended across arms, so they cannot be attributed to either model. It suits stateless, memoryless situations such as a latency or error comparison.

Hashing the user ID (with an experiment-specific salt, so assignments are not correlated with other concurrent tests) gives sticky assignment: a user always sees the same model, user-level metrics are interpretable, and the same user cannot learn from one arm and act in the other. Cost: fewer independent units, and analysis must treat users, not requests, as the unit. Verify the split is balanced with a sample-ratio check; a deviation from 50/50 beyond chance indicates an assignment or logging bug.

Neither method fixes interference. In a marketplace, arms compete for shared inventory, shared caches or a model that retrains on logged feedback from both arms, so one arm's gains can come at the other's expense and the measured difference is not what a full rollout would give. Where interference is likely, consider randomising by cluster (market, region, seller group) or alternating whole-system time blocks (switchback), and watch for effects on shared resources.

The decay from +6% to +1.5% is consistent with a novelty effect: users click on something that looks different, then adapt. Other explanations exist (a differing mix of new and returning users, seasonality, or a feedback loop), so I would: run long enough for the effect to stabilise; report the metric by week and by new versus returning users; use holdout users who keep the old model for the longer term; decide on the stabilised effect; and avoid shipping on early lift.

Containers, orchestration and ML pipelines in practice (Docker, Kubernetes basics, GPU scheduling, pipeline steps)
A teammate's Dockerfile for a model-serving API is: a slim Python base image, WORKDIR /app, COPY . ., RUN pip install -r requirements.txt, then CMD to start the server. Editing one line of application code makes CI take about 8 minutes, because every large dependency wheel is downloaded and installed again. Why does that happen, and how would you restructure the file? What else would you tighten in this image before it goes to production?
Key concepts: layer caching; cache invalidation; COPY ordering; lock file; base image digest; dockerignore; non-root user; multi-stage build
Docker builds an image as a stack of layers and caches each instruction's result. Per Docker's build-cache documentation, when a layer changes every layer after it must be rebuilt. In the original file, COPY . . comes before the install step, and that copy includes the application source. Any edited line changes the content of the copied files, so the COPY layer is invalidated, and the pip install layer below it is invalidated too, even though requirements.txt did not change. That is why each code edit re-downloads and re-installs every dependency.

The fix is to order instructions from least to most frequently changing. Copy only the dependency manifest, install, and only then copy the source. Now a code-only change invalidates only the last COPY layer and everything after it, and the expensive install layer is reused from cache. Docker's optimisation guidance describes exactly this split: expensive, stable steps early, frequently changing source late.

Other tightening worth mentioning: (1) Pin dependencies in a lock file with exact versions, otherwise the cached install layer can hide that a fresh build would resolve different packages. (2) Pin the base image, ideally by digest, because a tag can move; Docker documents digest pinning as a supply-chain measure. (3) Add a .dockerignore so datasets, .git, notebooks and local virtualenvs are not sent in the build context or copied into the image, which also keeps COPY layers from being invalidated by irrelevant files. (4) Run as a non-root user with USER if the service needs no privileges. (5) Decide deliberately where model weights live: baking them in makes the image self-contained but large, and a new layer for weights should sit before the code layer so code changes do not re-push them; downloading at start-up keeps the image small but makes start-up depend on external storage. (6) Consider a multi-stage build if compilers or build tools are only needed to install dependencies.

Containers, orchestration and ML pipelines in practice (Docker, Kubernetes basics, GPU scheduling, pipeline steps)
A scoring service runs fine with docker run on a 32 GB workstation, but in Kubernetes with a memory limit of 4 GiB (request 2 GiB) the pod restarts every few hours, and kubectl describe shows the last state as terminated with reason OOMKilled. The container starts 2 server worker processes, each of which loads a model that takes 1.4 GiB in memory; a batch endpoint also uses a data loader with 4 worker processes that exchange tensors through shared memory (/dev/shm). Why did it not fail locally, how would you find the real memory need, and what would you change?
Key concepts: OOMKilled; memory limit; memory request; CPU throttling; shared memory; emptyDir medium Memory; worker processes; peak memory measurement
Locally there was no limit, so nothing stopped the container from using whatever the processes wanted; the 32 GB machine simply never hit pressure. In Kubernetes the memory limit is enforced by the kernel: Kubernetes documents that memory limits are enforced through out-of-memory kills, and that an OOMKilled reason means the container tried to use more memory than its limit. The container is killed and restarted, which matches the periodic restarts. (CPU behaves differently: a CPU limit throttles, it does not kill.)

Add up what the container really holds. Two workers times 1.4 GiB of model is 2.8 GiB before anything else. Add per-process framework and interpreter overhead (suppose a measured 0.4 GiB each for the two server workers, 0.8 GiB; the 4 data-loader workers run only during batch calls, so assume their own interpreter overhead is folded into the 0.6 GiB request-peak figure below, and confirm by measuring every process), and the container is at about 3.6 GiB while idle. A request spike, for instance a large batch plus intermediate tensors (suppose 0.6 GiB), takes the peak to about 4.2 GiB, above the 4 GiB limit. Memory-backed shared memory makes it worse: Kubernetes documents that files written to an emptyDir with medium Memory count against the memory limit of the container that wrote them, so tensors the data loader places in shared memory are part of the same budget. Do not assume forked workers share the model for free; whether pages stay shared depends on how and when the model is loaded and on copy-on-write behaviour, so measure rather than assume.

Finding the real need: run the container locally with representative traffic including the largest batch you allow, observe peak resident memory of all processes (not just one), and repeat under a limit equal to the intended one to see where it dies. Also watch memory over hours, because a slow upward trend points to a leak, not to a too-small limit.

Changes, in order of leverage: reduce duplication (one process with threads, or load the model once per pod and scale out with replicas), cap batch size and concurrency, size the limit from measured peak plus margin, and set the request from measured typical busy-state usage so the scheduler packs nodes honestly (the example below uses 3Gi, near the estimated peak, which is conservative). Raising the limit alone treats the symptom if the cause is a leak.

Containers, orchestration and ML pipelines in practice (Docker, Kubernetes basics, GPU scheduling, pipeline steps)
A model service takes 60 to 150 seconds to become usable: it downloads about 1 GB of weights and then warms up. Its Deployment has a liveness probe on /health with initialDelaySeconds 20, periodSeconds 10 and failureThreshold 3, and no readiness or startup probe. Pods enter CrashLoopBackOff and never serve. Explain what is happening and design the probe configuration, including what each endpoint should check and one way your design could still go wrong.
Key concepts: liveness probe; readiness probe; startup probe; CrashLoopBackOff; failureThreshold; model warm-up; dependency checks in probes; Service endpoints
What happens: Kubernetes documents that a failed liveness check makes the kubelet kill the container and restart it. With these settings the first check starts about 20 s after start-up, and three consecutive failures at 10 s intervals take it to roughly 40 to 50 s. The model needs up to 150 s, so the container is killed before it is ever ready, restarts, repeats, and eventually backs off. Nothing is wrong with the application; the probe is judging a slow start as a deadlock.

Design: use three probes with different jobs. (1) A startup probe on the same endpoint as liveness. Kubernetes documents that liveness and readiness probes are not run until the startup probe succeeds, and that startup probes are meant for slow-starting containers; if it never succeeds the kubelet kills the container. Its budget is about failureThreshold x periodSeconds, so with a 10 s period and a threshold of 30 you allow roughly 300 s, comfortably above the 150 s worst case, without weakening the liveness settings. (2) A readiness probe that returns success only when weights are loaded and a trivial inference has run; Kubernetes documents that pods not ready receive no traffic through Services, and that readiness probes run for the container's whole lifecycle, so it also protects against a pod that becomes unable to serve later. (3) A liveness probe that is cheap and local: is the event loop responding. Keep it short-fused (the original 10 s x 3 is fine once startup is handled) because its job is to detect a hung process.

What can still go wrong: if liveness checks a downstream dependency (feature store, database), an outage of that dependency restarts every pod at once and turns a partial failure into a total one. Likewise, a readiness probe that includes an expensive inference or depends on a shared backend can flap under load, removing pods and pushing more traffic onto the rest; keep the probe cheap and give it a sensible timeout. Also, a startup budget that is too tight causes restarts after a slow storage day, so set it from the observed worst case plus margin.

Containers, orchestration and ML pipelines in practice (Docker, Kubernetes basics, GPU scheduling, pipeline steps)
Your GPU inference Deployment has 4 replicas, each requesting 1 GPU, on a node pool that currently has exactly 4 GPUs in total, all occupied by those replicas. A model release is rolled out with maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0, and the rollout never completes. A new pod sits in Pending while the 4 old pods keep serving. Why, what are your options, and what does each cost? Assume a pod needs about 90 s to load the model.
Key concepts: maxSurge; maxUnavailable; Pending pod; GPU capacity; rolling update; minReadySeconds; revision history; rollback
With maxSurge 1 the Deployment is allowed to create one pod above the desired 4, and maxUnavailable 0 forbids taking any old pod down until a new one is available. The surge pod needs a free GPU, but all 4 are held by old pods, so the scheduler cannot place it; Kubernetes documents that a pod stays Pending as long as its resource request cannot be satisfied. Since the old pods may not be removed until a new pod is available, the rollout deadlocks. Serving is unaffected, which is the safe failure mode, but the release never lands.

Options:
1. Switch to maxSurge 0 and maxUnavailable 1. The documented rule is that these cannot both be 0; this setting replaces in place: one old pod is terminated, freeing its GPU, then a new pod is scheduled onto it. Cost: capacity drops to 3 of 4 replicas for the whole update (a pod that is still loading its model counts as unavailable, provided readiness is gated on model load), and the update takes at least 4 x 90 s = 6 minutes because each replacement loads before the next old pod is removed. If 3 replicas cannot carry peak traffic, schedule the rollout off-peak.
2. Keep surge but make room: temporarily add a fifth GPU (autoscaling the pool or reserving spare capacity). Cost: paying for an idle GPU most of the time, or waiting for node provisioning. It preserves full capacity and fast rollback, since old pods keep serving until new ones are available.
3. Use a different release shape, such as a separate second Deployment at small scale on a spare GPU for a canary before replacing the main one. Cost: requires spare GPUs again and extra routing configuration.

Also relevant: minReadySeconds delays counting a new pod as available, which slows the rollout further but gives a window that catches pods which crash shortly after becoming ready. Rollback is available because Deployments keep old ReplicaSets as revision history by default, but under option 1 a failed new version has already consumed capacity, so decide on readiness-based abort criteria before starting.

Containers, orchestration and ML pipelines in practice (Docker, Kubernetes basics, GPU scheduling, pipeline steps)
A shared Kubernetes cluster has several 8-GPU nodes. A researcher requests nvidia.com/gpu: 0.5 for a small embedding service and the API server rejects it. Another job requests 'requests: 1, limits: 2'. Meanwhile an 8-GPU training job stays Pending even though the cluster shows 10 free GPUs in total, because small CPU-heavy pods and 1-GPU services have spread across the nodes. Explain the GPU resource rules, why the big job is stuck, and how you would organise scheduling.
Key concepts: extended resource; GPU limits; whole-number devices; no overcommit; fragmentation; taints and tolerations; node selector; dedicated node pool
Rules. In Kubernetes a GPU is exposed as an extended resource. The documentation says GPUs are specified in limits; a limit given alone is used as the request; if you specify both they must be equal, and requests without limits are not allowed. The resource-management docs add that extended resources are restricted to whole numbers and cannot be overcommitted. So nvidia.com/gpu: 0.5 is rejected, and 'requests 1, limits 2' is invalid because they differ. A container asks for whole devices, so an ordinary resource request cannot express sharing one GPU. Sharing one physical GPU between several pods (time-slicing, partitioning) is possible only through vendor or operator mechanisms layered on top, which differ by setup and are not part of the plain resource request; whether they fit depends on your cluster and workload isolation needs, so verify with your platform team.

Why the training job is stuck. An 8-GPU pod must be placed on one node that has 8 GPUs free at once. The scheduler places a pod on a single node, so 10 free GPUs spread as, say, 2 or 3 per node are useless to it. This is fragmentation: each small 1-GPU service lands wherever it fits, and once every node has at least one GPU taken, no node can ever offer 8. CPU-only pods landing on GPU nodes also consume CPU and memory the GPU job needs on that node.

Organising scheduling. Separate pools by workload shape. Taint GPU nodes so that only pods with a matching toleration are scheduled there (the taints documentation describes dedicating nodes this way), and give GPU workloads a node selector or affinity for the right GPU type. Put small services on a node pool sized for them, or on specific nodes, so they do not fragment the large-job nodes. Gang scheduling and job queueing (a batch scheduler or job-queue controller) address fairness and all-or-nothing placement for multi-pod training jobs and have mostly been provided by add-ons beyond the core scheduler (recent Kubernetes versions are adding feature-gated gang scheduling to the core scheduler, so check your cluster version); pod priority and preemption are core features and can also let an important job displace lower-priority pods.

Containers, orchestration and ML pipelines in practice (Docker, Kubernetes basics, GPU scheduling, pipeline steps)
A nightly ML pipeline runs five steps as containerised jobs: extract, build_features, train, evaluate, register_model. Two incidents occurred this week. First, train was OOM-killed at 90% and retried automatically; register_model then ran twice for that day and created two registry versions with identical weights. Second, a retried build_features step overwrote its output directory while train was starting, and train read a half-written dataset without error. Explain what properties each step needs, how you would pass artifacts between steps, and where caching and retries fit.
Key concepts: at-least-once execution; idempotent step; idempotency key; atomic publish; completion manifest; artifact checksum; cache key; retry policy
Root cause: orchestrators and job controllers give at-least-once execution. Kubernetes documents that for Jobs the same program may sometimes be started twice, so a step must tolerate duplicate runs. So each step has to be safe to run more than once and safe to be observed mid-run.

Properties each step needs. (1) Idempotent: running it again with the same inputs yields the same outcome and no duplicate side effects. register_model is the offender in the first incident; make it a get-or-create keyed by an idempotency key such as the training run id or the model artifact hash, so a second attempt finds the existing version and returns it. (2) Atomic publication of outputs: build_features should write to a temporary location unique to the attempt and publish only at the end (an atomic rename where the filesystem guarantees it, or, on object stores without atomic directory rename, a completion marker such as a manifest listing files and checksums). Downstream steps read only complete, marked outputs. That removes the half-written read in the second incident, and it works because train is told which committed output to read, rather than listing a directory that something else may still be writing. (3) Deterministic output location: key outputs by a content address or by pipeline-run id plus step name, so retries overwrite their own attempt, never another run's data.

Passing artifacts. Steps exchange references, not large payloads: a URI plus checksum (and schema version) stored by the orchestrator, with the artifact in object or shared storage. The downstream step verifies the checksum before use, which catches truncation.

Caching. A step's cache key is a hash of its code version (image digest or commit), its configuration, and the digests of its input artifacts. If the key matches a completed, committed run, skip execution and reuse the output. This makes retries and backfills cheap, but only if steps are deterministic enough that reuse is acceptable; non-deterministic training should record its seed and be cached by key anyway, treating the stored result as the canonical one. Include anything that changes the output in the key, including the data snapshot id, otherwise stale results are reused.

Retries. Retry only transient failures (node loss, network blips). An OOM kill usually repeats for the same resources and input (though node memory pressure can make it intermittent), so identical retries often waste time: fail fast, or (if your orchestrator supports per-attempt resources) retry once with a larger memory request, and alert. Cap attempts and make failure visible rather than silently looping.

Feature stores and training-serving skew
What is training-serving skew, and how is it different from data drift? Use a small concrete example, and say how you would tell which one you are looking at.
Key concepts: training-serving skew; data drift; feature computation paths; unit mismatch; default value handling; distribution comparison; replay of raw events
Training-serving skew is a difference between the data a model sees during training and the data it sees when serving, caused by how the data is produced, not by the world changing. A typical case is a feature computed by different code in each path: a price stored in cents in the training table but sent in dollars by the live service, or a missing value filled with -1 offline and 0 online. The same real-world event yields different feature values in the two places, so the model's learned relationships no longer apply.

Data drift is a change over time in the distribution of inputs (or labels) in the real world, for example customer behaviour shifting after a price change. The pipelines may be perfectly consistent; the population simply moved away from the training window.

The tools for them overlap, which is why people confuse them. TensorFlow Data Validation, for instance, documents distribution skew as a difference between training and serving data, and drift as a comparison between consecutive spans of data.

How to tell which: (1) Skew typically shows up immediately after deployment (or after a change to one of the paths): serving feature statistics differ from the training statistics from day one, and an offline replay of logged production requests through the training code produces different feature values than the live service did. (2) Drift typically appears over time (though it can also be abrupt): day-one serving statistics match training, then diverge as time passes, and a replay of today's raw data through the training pipeline gives the same features the service computed. A direct test is to take a sample of raw events, run them through both the offline and the online feature path, and compare outputs row by row: any difference is skew. Comparing the training distribution with the served distribution tells you something is off but not which cause.

The fixes differ too: skew is a bug to be fixed by sharing code or definitions; drift calls for monitoring, retraining or redesign.

Feature stores and training-serving skew
You are building training data for a churn model. Feature rows are (entity, feature_ts, value) and labelled events are (entity, event_ts). A colleague joins each event to the newest feature row per entity and gets a surprisingly high validation score. Explain what is wrong, then implement point_in_time_join(events, feature_rows, ttl) returning, for each event, the latest value with feature_ts <= event_ts and event_ts - feature_ts <= ttl, else None. Say how you treat ties on feature_ts.
Key concepts: point-in-time join; temporal leakage; as-of join; feature TTL; binary search; tie-breaking; event timestamp
The colleague's join uses information from the future. A label event at time t should be paired with the feature values that were known at t, but the 'newest row per entity' includes updates made after t, for example a ticket count that already reflects the complaint that preceded the churn. The model then learns from signals that cannot exist at prediction time, so validation looks better than production will. This is temporal leakage, and it also creates skew, because the live system by construction can only see the past.

A point-in-time (as-of) join fixes this by selecting, per event, the most recent feature row with feature_ts <= event_ts. Feast documents this behaviour as joining features onto an entity dataframe in a point-in-time correct way, reproducing the state at each entity timestamp, and also scanning backward from that timestamp up to a TTL. The TTL bounds staleness: a feature last updated a year ago should usually not be treated as current, so beyond the TTL the value is missing (None), mirroring what a serving system that treats old values as expired would return.

Implementation notes. Group rows by entity and sort by timestamp, then use binary search (bisect_right on the timestamps) to find the last row not after the event; that is O(log n) per event after an O(n log n) sort. The comparison must be less-or-equal on the timestamp: a row stamped exactly at the event time was available then. In the tests, with TTL 300, an event at 250 sees the value written at 200, an event at 800 sees nothing because the newest row (t=400) is 400 s old, and the naive join returns the t=400 value for every u1 event, including the one at t=99 where nothing was yet known. Ties: when two rows share a timestamp, I let the one appearing later in the input win, which is a convention you must make deterministic and document; in practice a separate ingestion or created-at timestamp is a better tie-breaker. One more subtlety: feature_ts here is the time the value was true; if data arrives late, you also need the time it became known (see backfill questions).

Feature stores and training-serving skew
A three-person team has one churn model. Features come from a data warehouse, the model scores 200,000 customers once a night, and results are written back to a table. The CTO wants to introduce a feature store with online and offline stores. What problems does a feature store solve, why do such systems usually have two stores, and would you adopt one here? Say what would change your answer.
Key concepts: feature store; offline store; online store; materialization; point-in-time correctness; shared feature definitions; batch scoring
What it solves. A feature store addresses three recurring problems: (1) one definition of each feature, reused across training and serving and across models, so teams do not re-implement it in different languages; (2) point-in-time correct training sets, so training rows get the feature values known at the label time and not later values; (3) serving features at low latency by key. Feast's documentation describes joining features onto an entity dataframe in a point-in-time correct way, and ingesting values into an online store so features can be served in real time with low latency.

Why two stores. The access patterns conflict. Training needs historical values across millions of entities and timestamps, read as large scans, which suits warehouse or lake storage (the offline store). An online prediction needs the latest value for one or a few entities within a few milliseconds, which suits a key-value store (the online store). A single store rarely does both well at reasonable cost. A process, often called materialization, loads recent values from the offline side into the online side; this process and its freshness are where much of the operational work lies.

This team. Nightly batch scoring means no online store is needed: the scoring job can read the same warehouse tables the training job reads. The point-in-time logic can be a tested SQL or Python function, as in a small as-of join, and the feature code can be one shared module or SQL view used by both training and scoring. A feature store would add infrastructure to run, a new abstraction and a migration for a team with little capacity.

What would change the answer: real-time scoring (the online store becomes necessary); several models or teams reusing the same features and duplicating logic; recurring skew or leakage incidents despite shared code; features with complex time windows where hand-written as-of joins keep going wrong; or audit needs for feature lineage. Even then I would start with the smallest step, such as a shared definitions repo with parity tests, and only adopt a store when the pain is demonstrated.

Feature stores and training-serving skew
Training features come from warehouse SQL; the live service recomputes the same features in application code written by another team. Audits keep finding differences: rounding, a 30-day window that is 'last 30 calendar days' in one place and '720 hours' in the other, and unknown categories mapped to different defaults. Propose how to give training and serving a single transformation definition, compare at least three approaches with their trade-offs, and explain how you would prove parity before and after the change.
Key concepts: single source of truth; on-demand transformation; parity test; shared library; window semantics; default handling; feature logging; replay of raw events
The root problem is two independent implementations of one specification. Any duplicated logic drifts, and each choice (window boundaries, rounding, default) is a place where they can differ silently. The goal is that exactly one artifact defines the transformation, and that anything else is generated from it or tested against it.

Approaches:
1. Single computation, two destinations. Compute features once in a pipeline (batch or streaming), write them to the offline store with timestamps and push the latest values to the online store, so serving reads, never recomputes. Pros: no second implementation. Cons: only works for features that can be computed ahead of the request; request-time inputs (the current cart) cannot be precomputed, and freshness is bounded by pipeline latency.
2. One transformation function executed in both paths. Feast documents on-demand (an alpha feature in its docs) transformations as Python logic executed in both the historical retrieval and online retrieval paths; a shared library imported by both the training job and the service achieves the same. Pros: one definition for request-time features. Cons: both environments must run the same language and runtime; library versions must be pinned and equal; per-request latency cost.
3. Declarative spec compiled to both targets (a feature DSL generates SQL and service code). Pros: language-independent. Cons: a new language to maintain; generator bugs affect everyone; limited expressiveness.
4. Keep two implementations but enforce parity with tests. Pros: no re-architecture. Cons: parity is only as good as test coverage, and it is a recurring cost. This is the fallback when 1 to 3 are impractical.
5. Log-and-wait: log the features the service actually computed at prediction time and train on the logs. Pros: eliminates skew by construction for the logged features. Cons: needs a history of logs before you can train, hard to add new features retrospectively, and it can bake in the live service's bugs.

Specify the semantics regardless of choice: window definition (calendar vs hours, timezone), rounding rule, null and unknown-category defaults, and the time at which a value is considered known.

Proving parity: replay a sample of raw entities through both implementations and compare values, categorising mismatches. Do this before the change to baseline the problem, and in CI after the change so that any later edit that breaks equivalence fails the build.

Feature stores and training-serving skew
A fraud model uses orders_last_24h per customer. About 3% of order records reach the warehouse 1 to 3 days after the order time, and cancelled orders are later deleted. Training features for the past year were backfilled last month with a single SQL query over the current orders table, using order_ts for the 24-hour window. Offline AUC is excellent but production is clearly worse, and logged online feature values for orders_last_24h are systematically lower than the backfilled values for the same transactions. Explain the mechanism and how to repair the training data and the process.
Key concepts: knowledge time; event time; late-arriving data; backfill; bitemporal data; temporal leakage; feature logging; feature TTL
The backfill answers a different question from the one the online path answers. The backfill ran today over the complete, corrected orders table, so for a transaction last March it counts every order in the 24 hours before the transaction, including orders that only arrived in the warehouse days later and excluding orders that were later cancelled and deleted. The online feature, computed at the time of the transaction, could only count orders that had arrived by then and still existed. Hence the logged online values are lower because of the late orders (deleted orders push the other way, since online counts them and the backfill does not; the observed systematic gap implies late arrivals dominate) and the backfilled values are, in this respect, cleaner than anything the live system ever sees. The model learns relationships on idealised features and meets noisier ones in production: training-serving skew caused by data availability, a form of temporal leakage, since information that was not yet known at the prediction time is used. Event-time-only correctness is not enough; the join must also respect when each record became known.

Repair. (1) Track two times per record: event time (order_ts, when it happened) and knowledge time (ingestion or loaded_at, when the system could see it), and keep history of deletions or status changes instead of overwriting. With both, the backfill can ask 'what did the table look like at time t': include a row only if loaded_at <= t and it was not yet deleted at t. (2) If history is unavailable, you cannot reproduce past knowledge exactly; use logged online feature values for the period where they exist, and for the rest consider simulating the delay (drop each order from the window with the observed delay distribution) as an approximation, flagged as such. (3) Going forward, log the features served with each prediction and use them for training and for skew checks. (4) Compare distributions of backfilled versus logged values for the same transactions before trusting any backfill, and re-evaluate the model on the logged features, which is the number that predicts production.

A related freshness point: whatever pipeline fills the online store has its own lag, and its TTL (in stores that enforce one) decides when a stale value is treated as missing; reproduce that lag in training as well, or the same kind of skew returns.

Feature stores and training-serving skew
You log 1,000 served values of a categorical feature 'country' and have the training sample. After release, the offline-to-online metric gap is large. Implement categorical_skew(train, served, ...) that reports null rates, the L-infinity distance between category frequencies, and the share of served values whose category never appears in training, plus a list of threshold violations. Then say what each statistic would tell you, what mistake in the pipeline it would reveal, and what its limits are.
Key concepts: L-infinity distance; null rate; unseen categories; category frequency; served feature logging; skew threshold; sampling noise
Each statistic points at a different failure. The null-rate gap tells you about missing-value handling: the training data may have imputed, filtered or never contained nulls, while the live path sends them (or the reverse). The unseen-category rate detects vocabulary mismatches: spelling or case differences ('gb' vs 'GB'), new categories after the training cut-off, or a different normalisation function; those values hit the encoder's unknown-category branch, often silently mapped to a default. The L-infinity distance, the largest absolute difference in any single category's relative frequency, gives a worst-case view of distribution shift between the two samples. TensorFlow Data Validation documents expressing drift for categorical features in terms of L-infinity distance, and it supports detecting distribution skew between training and serving data; a similar statistic is a reasonable, interpretable check.

Design choices in the function: compute category frequencies over non-missing values only, so that a null-rate difference is reported separately and does not distort the frequency comparison; report which category produced the maximum gap, because 'country=gb' immediately suggests a casing bug; treat thresholds as parameters. In the test, serving sends 240 of 960 non-null values in lower case ('gb'), which the training data never contains: unseen rate 25%, L-infinity 0.25 on 'gb', and the 'GB' frequency falls from 0.60 to 0.375. 4% nulls in serving versus none in training triggers the null violation.

Limits. Sample sizes matter: with small samples, the maximum gap fluctuates by chance, so thresholds need calibrating on two training-like samples (the test checks that a 100-row sample constructed with near-training proportions, 58/31/11 against 60/30/10, does not fire at the default 0.10 threshold). The statistic is insensitive to long tails, since a thousand rare categories can each shift by little but together matter, which the unseen rate catches only for new values. It compares marginal distributions only, so a joint shift (feature relationships) goes unnoticed, and a matching distribution does not prove per-row equality: two implementations can disagree row by row yet produce the same aggregate. Row-level replay remains the definitive check.

Production monitoring and drift operations (input/prediction drift, PSI/KS, delayed labels, alert design)
Implement psi(reference, current, n_bins=10, eps=1e-4) with numpy only. Bin edges must come from quantiles of the reference sample, current values outside the reference range must still be counted, and empty bins must not produce log(0) or a division by zero. Then explain why a PSI computed from 200 reference rows, 200 current rows and 40 bins is a poor drift signal even when nothing has changed.
Key concepts: PSI; quantile bins; reference sample; empty-bin floor (eps); out-of-range values; sampling noise floor; number of bins
Design choices. Quantile edges taken from the reference give roughly equal reference mass per bin, which copes with skewed features; the edges are frozen so every later window is compared on the same bins. np.unique collapses duplicate edges, so a feature with a large spike (say many zeros) simply ends up with fewer bins. If only one or two distinct edges survive (a constant, or a binary feature so imbalanced that the interpolated quantiles stay at 0 and 1; a 50/50 binary feature keeps an interior edge at 0.5) there are no interior edges, so the code falls back to one bin per distinct value plus open bins on both sides; otherwise any change would score 0. Searching only the interior edges sends values below the reference minimum to the first bin and values above its maximum to the last, so out-of-range data is counted rather than dropped. Proportions are floored at eps because (q - p) * log(q / p) is undefined when either proportion is 0.

The floor makes the output an artefact once a bin is empty. With a 20,000-row N(0,1) reference and 1,000 current values all equal to 5.0, the PSI was about 12.4 with eps=1e-6 and about 3.9 with eps=1e-2. Read such a value as 'enormous', not as a magnitude to compare across runs.

Why 200 rows and 40 bins is a bad signal: PSI is a sum over bins of sampling noise even without drift. A rough chi-square-style argument gives an expected null value near (B - 1) * (1/n + 1/m): for B=10 and n=m=200 that is 0.09, and a 300-repetition simulation with two samples from the same normal distribution gave a mean of 0.089 (sd 0.046). With 40 bins (about 5 expected rows per bin) the approximation breaks down and the simulated mean was 0.50 (sd 0.15). Commonly quoted rule-of-thumb cutoffs such as 0.1 and 0.25 are not statistical thresholds, and with 40 bins both would be exceeded in nearly every run with no change at all (a 2,000-run check gave 98% above 0.25). Remedies: fewer bins, more rows, a longer window, or calibrating the alert threshold against the noise floor measured on same-distribution splits.

Production monitoring and drift operations (input/prediction drift, PSI/KS, delayed labels, alert design)
On Monday 06:10 the drift job pages you: txn_amount has PSI 8.3 against the training reference, and the model's score distribution has collapsed to near-constant high scores. The same report shows discount_pct at PSI 0.05, below the team's 0.1 'investigate' line, yet a colleague points out its null rate went from 0.2% to 9% on Friday after an upstream ETL release; downstream code imputes nulls with 0. Product's first instinct is to retrain. How do you triage, what do the two numbers tell you, and what changes in monitoring?
Key concepts: unit change; null-rate monitoring; PSI insensitivity; quantile ratio check; data-quality incident; schema/data contract; imputation before monitoring
Do not retrain yet; treat both as data-quality incidents until proven otherwise.

txn_amount: a PSI of 8.3 means essentially all current values fall in bins that held little reference mass. A change of units by a large factor such as 100 does exactly that for a narrowly spread amount distribution; with a wider spread the PSI is lower (about 4 for a lognormal with sigma 2) but still far above any threshold. In a simulation (50,000 lognormal amounts each side), multiplying every value by 100, as dollars-to-cents would, gave PSI about 8.2 with 10 quantile bins and eps=1e-4 (the ceiling for that setup is about 8.3) while two plain samples gave about 0.0003 (lognormal with sigma 1). Real behavioural drift rarely multiplies every quantile by the same constant. Check: compare quantiles (p10, p50, p99) of current vs reference; a near-constant ratio such as 100 points to a unit or schema change. Then confirm in raw logs, the upstream release notes and the data contract, and look for a step at a deploy timestamp across all slices. The collapsed scores are most likely a consequence: the model is probably being fed out-of-support inputs (confirm by re-scoring a sample with the amounts rescaled). Fix at the source (or add an explicit conversion in the feature pipeline), backfill or mark the affected window, and exclude it from training data. Retraining on a mix of units would bake the bug into the model.

discount_pct: a null-to-zero spike moves about 9% of the mass into the lowest bin. In a simulation with a continuous discount_pct and no reference zeros, PSI was only about 0.055 with 10 bins (about 0.09 to 0.10 with 20); with 20% of the reference already at zero it was about 0.015 to 0.03 (depending on how the ties at zero are binned). At 10 bins all are under the 0.1 line (20 bins sit right at it), although the feature is broken. Binned distribution distances are weak at detecting a modest mass moving inside a single bin. Add explicit data-quality monitors measured before imputation: null rate, zero rate, min/max and unit-sanity bounds, schema and type checks, each with absolute bands from history. The ML Test Score paper lists matching data against a schema and alerting when it diverges as a monitoring test.

Routing: data-quality alerts go to the data owner and block automated retraining; distribution drift goes to the model owner.

Production monitoring and drift operations (input/prediction drift, PSI/KS, delayed labels, alert design)
A churn model has 120 input features. A daily job runs a two-sample test per feature at p < 0.01 and posts every hit to a Slack channel. Typically one to three features alert each day, nobody reads the channel any more, and last month a real null-rate regression went unnoticed. Redesign the alerting so that someone acts on what fires.
Key concepts: alert fatigue; multiple testing; effect size vs p-value; historical thresholds; persistence window; severity tiers; symptom-based alerting
Start from why it is noisy. With 120 features tested at p < 0.01, even if nothing changes you expect 120 x 0.01 = 1.2 false hits per day, and if the tests were independent the chance of at least one hit is 1 - 0.99^120, about 70%. Correlated features change that arithmetic but not the conclusion. In addition, with large daily volumes a p-value flags differences far too small to matter, so alerts are dominated by statistical significance rather than importance.

Principles for the redesign:
1. Alert on model-level symptoms and hard data-quality invariants first. The model's output distribution (score histogram, positive rate), data-quality invariants (schema, null rate, range) and, when available, quality proxies are what someone should be paged for. Per-feature distribution changes are diagnostic detail.
2. Use an effect size, not a p-value, and set thresholds from the metric's own history (for example a high percentile of the last 60-90 daily values, compared on the same weekday where there is weekly seasonality). The ML Test Score paper notes that alert thresholds need careful tuning to balance false positives against false negatives.
3. Require persistence: fire only if the condition holds for k of the last n windows, except for hard failures such as schema violations.
4. Tier the severity by feature importance and failure type, and route each tier to an owner.
5. Review the alerts: track which were actionable and retire or retune rules that never lead to action. Sculley et al. make a related point about action limits on a system's real-world actions: they should be broad enough not to trigger spuriously, and when one trips an alert should lead to investigation.

This design also fixes the missed incident: a null-rate regression becomes a data-quality rule with its own absolute band instead of one of 120 anonymous drift hits.

Production monitoring and drift operations (input/prediction drift, PSI/KS, delayed labels, alert design)
A daily job runs a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on each numeric feature, yesterday's 1,000,000 logged rows against a 1,000,000-row reference, and alerts at p < 0.05. It alerts on almost every feature every day. Another team uses PSI with 10 quantile bins and alerts above 0.1. Compare what the two signals measure, explain the alert storm, and say what neither tells you.
Key concepts: KS statistic; p-value vs effect size; sample size sensitivity; PSI binning; ties and discrete features; noise floor; prediction impact
The storm is most likely a sample-size effect rather than a bug (rule out a systematic logging difference between reference and yesterday). A KS p-value answers 'is there any difference between the two distributions?', and with a million rows per side almost any real difference, however small, is significant. In a simulation with two N(0,1) samples of 1,000,000 rows where one was shifted by 0.01 standard deviations, the KS statistic was about 0.004 (0.0035 to 0.0055 over eight seeds) and the p-value between about 1e-5 and 1e-13, far below 0.05 every time, while PSI with 10 bins was about 0.0001. At the other extreme, 1,000 rows per side with a 0.3 sd shift gave, in one draw, KS statistic 0.14 (p about 8e-9) and PSI about 0.10 (PSI varied roughly 0.07 to 0.16 across draws). So p-values track evidence, not size.

What each measures. SciPy documents the KS statistic as the maximum absolute difference between the two empirical CDFs, with a null hypothesis of identical distributions, and assumes continuous inputs. The statistic itself is a bounded effect size and is the thing to threshold (ideally against its historical variation). PSI is not a test: it bins the data, and sums (q - p) * log(q / p) over bins, so it depends on the bin count and any empty-bin floor, is sensitive to where mass moves between bins, and has a noise floor of roughly (B - 1) * (1/n + 1/m).

Caveats. KS on features with many ties (spikes at 0, integer counts, sentinel values) violates the continuity assumption, so use PSI or a chi-square-type comparison on bins or categories instead. KS is often more sensitive to changes in the bulk of the distribution than to far tails, so pair it with min/max or tail-quantile checks when tails matter.

Neither tells you whether the model cares: that needs feature importance, prediction drift, and eventually labels. Neither sees changes in joint structure (correlations) when marginals stay the same, and neither reports why the shift happened, such as a data-quality bug.

Production monitoring and drift operations (input/prediction drift, PSI/KS, delayed labels, alert design)
After a marketing campaign, the drift dashboard shows PSI above 0.25 on 14 of a fraud model's 120 features, while the score distribution and the review-queue rate look unchanged. Product wants to retrain tonight. With labels arriving weeks later, how do you decide whether this drift is harmful, and what would change your answer?
Key concepts: harmless vs harmful drift; feature importance weighting; counterfactual feature replacement; training support; slice analysis; concept drift without labels; proxy labels
Treat the dashboard as a lead, not a verdict. Feature drift is harmless when the model's behaviour on the new inputs is still what it learned; it is harmful when the inputs leave the region where the model is reliable or when the input-to-label relationship has changed. Without labels you can test the first part cheaply.

Triage steps:
1. Weight by importance. Rank the 14 drifted features by the model's importance (permutation importance on labelled validation data, or attribution mass such as mean absolute SHAP on a recent sample). Drift in low-importance or redundant features matters little.
2. Counterfactual replacement. Re-score a recent sample after replacing each drifted feature (or the group) with values resampled from the reference. Independent resampling breaks correlations with the other features, so treat the result as a sensitivity check, not an exact estimate. If the scores barely move, the drift is not driving predictions; if they move a lot, find out in which direction.
3. Support check. What fraction of current rows lie outside the training range or in sparsely populated regions? Inputs inside the training support are interpolation; far outside they are extrapolation, where tree-based models predict a constant beyond the observed range and neural nets can behave unpredictably.
4. Slice the output. Check score distributions and queue rates for campaign-acquired cohorts vs the rest, since an unchanged aggregate can hide a changed slice.
5. Get cheap labels. Have analysts review a small random sample of campaign traffic, or use early proxies such as confirmed customer disputes.

What changes the answer: scores shifting, rows outside support, or analyst labels disagreeing with the model are signs of possible harm. Unchanged scores do not rule out concept drift, because the model can still output the same scores for inputs whose fraud rate changed; only labels settle that.

Retraining tonight on a few days of campaign-skewed data risks fitting a transient and makes it harder to attribute any change. Prefer monitoring, targeted checks and a scheduled retrain once labels mature.

Production monitoring and drift operations (input/prediction drift, PSI/KS, delayed labels, alert design)
Your monitor computes one PSI per feature over all traffic and has stayed green for weeks. Customer support then reports that a newly launched market, about 10% of traffic, gets poor recommendations. The offending feature, basket_value, was roughly N(50, 10) in training for everyone and is now about N(80, 10) in that market only. Why did the aggregate monitor stay quiet, how would you change the monitoring, and what does it cost?
Key concepts: metric dilution; slice-level monitoring; mix shift; PSI noise floor; minimum slice size; multiplicity; unseen category share
Dilution. In a simulation of 100,000 rows with 10% from the new market, basket_value shifted from N(50, 10) to N(80, 10) in that market only. The overall mean moved just from about 50 to 53, and aggregate PSI (10 quantile bins) was about 0.06, below a typical 0.1 line, while PSI on the new-market slice alone was above 5 (the exact figure depends on the empty-bin floor) and about 0.0002 on the rest. A shift that is huge for 10% of users is small in the pooled distribution, and PSI grows with both the size of the shift and the share of traffic affected.

Fix: compute the drift and quality metrics per slice as well as overall. Choose slices by what the business and risk owners care about: market/country, new vs returning users, acquisition channel, device, and any segment with a distinct policy. The ML Test Score paper makes a parallel point for prediction bias: models should have zero bias in aggregate and on slices.

Costs and limits:
- Multiplicity: F features x S slices x metrics multiplies the false-alarm opportunities, so use effect-size thresholds, persistence and a ranking by slice size times severity rather than paging on each pair.
- Sample size: a small slice has a high noise floor of roughly (B - 1) * (1/n + 1/m) for PSI, so enforce a minimum row count and use longer windows for small slices, or sample them at a higher rate.
- Interpretation: when the aggregate drifts but each slice is stable, the cause is a mix shift (traffic composition changed). That can be harmless if the model performs well in each slice; compare aggregate and per-slice results to tell the two cases apart.
- New slices that did not exist at training time cannot appear in a reference, so also alert on previously unseen category values and sharp changes in slice share.

Production monitoring and drift operations (input/prediction drift, PSI/KS, delayed labels, alert design)
A scoring service handles 2 million predictions a day. A full feature payload is about 4 KB, so logging everything is 8 GB a day, and the security team also wants less raw data retained. You must support daily PSI checks per feature, hourly checks for a slice that is 0.5% of traffic, and a join with labels arriving weeks later. Design what you log and how you sample, and show that the sample is big enough.
Key concepts: deterministic hash sampling; streaming aggregates; sampling weights; PSI noise floor; oversampling small slices; label join key; privacy minimisation
Separate three needs, because they have different cost profiles.

1. Always-on aggregates, computed in the stream with no raw rows retained: request counts, null and zero rates, min/max, quantile sketches or histograms on the frozen reference bin edges, score histograms, category counts, per slice and per model version. Counters and histograms are exact over all traffic (quantile sketches are approximate) and tiny, and they serve the data-quality and drift dashboards.

2. A sampled set of raw feature rows for investigation, drift tests that need raw values, and the label join. Sample deterministically from a hash of the request ID, for example keep the row if a stable hash of the ID (for example SHA-256 or xxHash, not Python's salted built-in hash()) mod 10,000 is below 100 for a 1% rate. The decision is reproducible, uncorrelated with feature values as long as request IDs are not derived from user or feature data, and needs no coordination, and the same ID can later be joined to labels. Always store the sampling rate or weight on each row so estimates can be re-weighted.

3. Higher or full capture where rarity matters: errors, low-confidence scores and small but important slices.

Sizing. At 1%, 2,000,000 x 0.01 = 20,000 rows a day, about 80 MB at 4 KB instead of 8 GB. The PSI noise floor is roughly (B - 1) * (1/n + 1/m); with B=10, a 100,000-row reference and 20,000 daily rows, that is 9 x (0.00001 + 0.00005), about 0.0005, negligible. But the 0.5% slice gets only 2,000,000 x 0.005 x 0.01 = 100 rows a day, about 4 per hour, which is useless; even 50 rows gives roughly 9 x (0.00001 + 0.02), about 0.18 (the approximation is rough at so few rows; a simulation gave roughly 0.2 to 0.25), above a typical 0.1 line with no drift at all. So the slice should be covered at 100%, either by its streamed per-slice histograms (item 1) or by raw capture when rows are needed for investigation, which is 10,000 rows a day, about 417 an hour on average (fewer overnight, where the floor is higher), and the hourly floor becomes about 9 x (0.00001 + 1/417), about 0.02 (assuming a 100,000-row reference for the slice; if the slice reference holds only its own 0.5% share, about 500 rows, the floor is 9 x (1/500 + 1/417), about 0.04).

Privacy: log the model's input features rather than raw free text or identifiers where possible, pseudonymise IDs, and set retention limits; what is permitted depends on jurisdiction and legal advice.

Production monitoring and drift operations (input/prediction drift, PSI/KS, delayed labels, alert design)
daily_orders_per_user has a strong weekly cycle (weekends about 25% higher). You are choosing the reference for a daily drift check: (A) the training set, (B) yesterday, (C) the pooled previous 7 days, or (D) the same weekday over the previous 4 weeks. Separately, the true feature mean has been creeping up by 0.05 standard deviations per day. Compare the four options on false alarms and on detecting the slow creep, and recommend a setup.
Key concepts: reference window; weekly seasonality; slow drift; lagging baseline; same-weekday comparison; training reference; retrain staleness
Each reference answers a different question, so use two.

(A) Training set: answers 'how far is today from what the model learned?', which is the question that matters for model validity. Weekly seasonality still causes recurring weekend alarms when a single day is compared with the all-days training mixture, unless you compare like with like (same weekday or weekday-adjusted), but it does catch the creep: after 60 days the mean has moved 60 x 0.05 = 3 sd. Downsides: once the shift is real it stays red permanently and says nothing about when it started.

(B) Yesterday: compares Monday to Sunday, so the weekly cycle produces false alarms every week. It is also nearly blind to the creep: a day-over-day change of 0.05 sd is smaller than the weekly swing (unless the standard deviation exceeds about five times the mean) and, unless daily volume is large (about 7,200 rows per day are needed to see it at 3 standard errors), within sampling noise.

(C) Pooled previous 7 days: the reference averages out the weekly cycle, but today is a single day, so it is still compared with a weekly mixture. With weekends 25% higher, the weekly average is about 7% above a weekday level, so a weekend day sits about 17% above the pool and a weekday about 7% below it; seasonal false alarms remain unless today is also a 7-day window or the comparison is weekday-adjusted. Its lag is also large: the average age of the pooled days is (1 + ... + 7) / 7 = 4 days, so under steady creep today sits about 4 x 0.05 = 0.2 sd above the reference. That is a constant small offset, easy to miss when seasonal swings and alert tolerances are of similar size, and it does not accumulate.

(D) Same weekday, previous 4 weeks: removes the weekday effect if the weekly pattern is stable; the average age is (7 + 14 + 21 + 28) / 4 = 17.5 days, so the creep offset is about 17.5 x 0.05 = 0.875 sd, much more visible, though each weekday sample is only 4 pooled days, so its noise floor is higher than C's 7-day pool (4 days of rows instead of 7) and holidays contaminate it.

Recommendation: keep a seasonal-aware rolling reference (D, or C with weekday adjustment) to catch recent changes with few false alarms, plus a fixed training reference tracked as a slowly moving 'distance from training' trend with a staleness limit that triggers a retrain review. Reset the fixed reference only when you retrain. Compare both against historical variability, not a constant threshold.

Retraining and automation (triggers, continuous training, champion/challenger, rollback of a retrain)
What does 'continuous training' mean in an ML system, and how does it differ from CI/CD for ordinary application code?
Key concepts: continuous training; retraining triggers; data validation; model validation; CI/CD for ML; artifact lineage and metadata
In application software, behaviour changes only when someone changes the code, so CI/CD (build, test, deploy) is enough to keep production current. In an ML system the model is a product of code plus data, so the same code can yield a different, and eventually staler, model as the world and the data change. Continuous training automates that second loop: a pipeline that can be triggered repeatedly, retrains the model, checks it and, if it passes, hands it to deployment. Google's MLOps architecture guidance describes CT as a property unique to ML systems concerned with automatically retraining and serving models, and lists triggers such as a schedule, availability of new training data, performance degradation and significant changes in data distributions.

Differences from code CI/CD:
- What is tested: besides code and components, CI/CD for ML also covers data (schema, distribution checks) and models (quality against a baseline).
- Two extra gates: data validation before training decides whether it is worth, or safe, to retrain; model validation after training decides whether the new model may replace the current one.
- Artifacts: the pipeline must record the data version, features, parameters and metrics, since the result is not reproducible from code alone.
- Triggers: not only commits but also time, data arrival and monitoring signals.

Common pitfalls: 'continuous' does not mean retraining all the time. Retraining has cost and risk, so the trigger policy and the validation gates matter more than the frequency. Automating retraining without data validation and model validation simply automates the production of bad models. CT also does not replace CI/CD: pipeline code still needs ordinary testing and deployment.

Retraining and automation (triggers, continuous training, champion/challenger, rollback of a retrain)
A lender's credit model approves applicants scoring above a threshold (about 40% of 50,000 monthly applications). Each month the team retrains on repayment outcomes of the approved loans and keeps the score threshold. After six months offline metrics on the newest approved loans look better than ever, yet approval volume is flat, losses are not improving, and risk managers suspect good applicants are being turned away. What is going on, and how would you redesign the retraining data?
Key concepts: selection bias; feedback loop; exploration; inverse propensity weighting; reject inference; propensity logging; policy-independent evaluation
This is a selection-bias feedback loop. Outcomes (repayment or default) are observed only for approved applicants, so the training set is truncated to people the previous model already liked. The model never sees what happens to rejected applicants, cannot learn that some of them would have repaid, and is evaluated on a population it pre-filtered. Each retrain makes the model better at ranking within the approved region and leaves its behaviour outside that region untested. Sculley et al. describe the general case: a model may directly influence the selection of its own future training data.

Why the offline numbers mislead: they are computed on loans the model chose, where its scores are concentrated and the outcome range is narrow, so improvements say little about the rejected 60%, and the extra confidence never gets challenged.

Redesign:
- Exploration: approve a small random sample of applicants who would have been rejected, ideally concentrated near the threshold, record the approval probability (propensity) and the outcome. This gives unbiased labels for a part of the rejected region at a known business cost.
- Weighting: use inverse-propensity weights in training and evaluation so that the explored cases represent the rejected population they were drawn from.
- Evaluation: judge challengers on the exploration slice and on any data from policy-independent sources, not on the approved set alone.
- Logging: store the model version, score, threshold and decision with every application so you can tell how the data was selected.
- Alternatives such as reject inference (imputing outcomes for rejected applicants) rely on modelling assumptions and are best treated as supplementary, not as a replacement for real outcomes.

Exploration has a direct cost and may need risk and compliance approval; what is allowed depends on jurisdiction and legal advice.

Retraining and automation (triggers, continuous training, champion/challenger, rollback of a retrain)
Your pipeline retrains automatically whenever PSI on any of five key features exceeds 0.25, evaluates on the latest 7 days and promotes the result if AUC beats the champion. Last week an upstream bug wrote income = 0 for six hours. The monitor fired, the pipeline retrained on a window that included those rows, and the new model passed the gate because the 7-day holdout contained the same corrupted rows. Which guardrails would have stopped this, and where in the pipeline does each sit?
Key concepts: data validation before training; quarantine bad partitions; trusted holdout; action limits; cooldown; human approval; data-quality vs drift trigger
The root problem is a pipeline that treats every drift alarm as a reason to learn and uses the same possibly corrupted data to train and to judge. Guardrails, in pipeline order:

1. Trigger: separate data-quality alerts (null/zero rate, range, schema) from distribution drift. A data-quality failure should block automated retraining and go to the data owner, not start it. Add persistence (the condition holds for several windows) and a cooldown or maximum retrains per period, so a flapping alarm cannot cause a chain of retrains.

2. Data validation before training: Google's MLOps guidance states that data validation is required before training to decide whether to retrain. Run it on the whole training window: schema, null and zero rates, ranges, row counts and label rates compared with their usual bands. Quarantine bad partitions (here the six hours) instead of training on them, and fail the run if the failures are too large.

3. Trusted evaluation data: the holdout must pass the same validation and should not be allowed to share the defect that the training data had. Prefer a time-based holdout of validated data, plus a fixed, curated reference set that rarely changes, so a corrupted recent window cannot grade itself.

4. Model validation after training: besides AUC against the champion, compare the new model's predictions against the champion's on the trusted set and on the champion's slices, and bound the change. Sculley et al. suggest action limits on a system's real-world actions as sanity checks that are broad enough not to trigger spuriously; a similar bound on champion/challenger change (a sudden large shift in score distribution or in the importance of income) should stop promotion.

5. Approval and rollout: require human approval when the model affects money or when the behaviour change exceeds a limit, and release through a staged rollout with a rollback path.

6. Record data versions and excluded partitions so the incident can be audited.

Guardrails 1 and 2 alone would very likely have stopped this incident; the later layers are defence in depth, covering a missed quality check, a corrupted holdout, or a model that passes AUC but behaves abnormally.

Retraining and automation (triggers, continuous training, champion/challenger, rollback of a retrain)
A full retrain of your ranking model on the last 180 days takes about 14 hours on a shared cluster, and the business wants daily updates. A teammate proposes warm-starting from yesterday's model and training only on the last day's data, which takes about 40 minutes. Compare this with a full retrain on a sliding window, say what can go wrong with the warm start, and how you would decide with data.
Key concepts: warm start; sliding-window retrain; catastrophic forgetting; error persistence; lineage; hybrid schedule; rolling-origin backtest
