You are sizing an A/B test on checkout conversion. The control converts at about 10%, and the smallest lift worth detecting is an absolute 1 percentage point (10% -> 11%). The test is two-sided with alpha = 0.05 and 80% power, users are split 50/50, and a user is the unit of randomisation.

Write sample_size_two_proportions(p_base, mde_abs, alpha=0.05, power=0.8) -> int using only the standard library (statistics.NormalDist), returning the required number of users PER GROUP. Example: sample_size_two_proportions(0.10, 0.02) should return 3841. Then explain how n moves when the MDE, the baseline rate, the power and alpha change, and which pitfalls make real tests need more traffic than this number.

You run an A/A test (both arms identical, true conversion 10%, 500 users per arm per day for 14 days) and a colleague checks a two-proportion z-test every morning, stopping the experiment and declaring a winner the first time p < 0.05.

Write simulate_peeking(n_sims=4000, days=14, users_per_day=500, p=0.10, seed=0) -> (peeking_rate, fixed_rate) with numpy default_rng, where peeking_rate is the share of simulated experiments that are ever significant at any daily look and fixed_rate is the share significant on one test at day 14 only. Say what values you expect, why the peeking rate is not simply 14 x 5%, and what remedies exist.

An experiment was configured for a 50/50 split. After a week the analysis table shows 50,000 users in control and 51,200 in treatment. A PM says "that's only 2.4% off, close enough".

Implement srm_check(counts, expected_ratios, alpha=0.001) -> (chi2, df, p_value, mismatch_flag), a chi-square goodness-of-fit test for sample ratio mismatch, with no scipy (use math.erfc for df = 1). Example: srm_check([50000, 51200], [1, 1]) should give chi2 about 14.23 with a very small p-value and a True flag. Then say how you would interpret this, which causes you would investigate first, and what you do with the experiment's results.

In an experiment on a signup flow, variant A shows 17.5% overall conversion and variant B shows 8.7%, so B looks much worse. Broken down by device, however, B converts better than A on both desktop and mobile.

Write simpson_report(df) -> dict for a DataFrame with columns variant, segment, users, conversions. It should return the pooled rate per variant, the per-segment rates (segment x variant), the pooled winner, the variant that wins in every segment (or None), a boolean reversal flag, and mix-standardised rates (each variant re-weighted to the overall segment mix). Use this data: A desktop 1000 users / 200 conversions, A mobile 200 / 10, B desktop 200 / 44, B mobile 1000 / 60. Explain what causes the reversal and which comparison you would trust.

Revenue per order for an online shop is heavily right-skewed. A sample of 10 order values is [18, 22, 25, 27, 30, 31, 34, 38, 41, 950].

Implement mad_outliers(values, threshold=3.5) using the MAD-based modified z-score M_i = 0.6745 * (x_i - median) / MAD (with a documented fallback when MAD is 0), alongside zscore_outliers (|z| > 3) and iqr_outliers (1.5 x IQR fences), all returning boolean numpy arrays. Show which of the three flags the 950 order on this sample, explain why, and say how the methods behave on a large log-normal sample and what you do with flagged points.

You have 10 page-load times in seconds: [12, 15, 11, 40, 13, 14, 90, 16, 12, 18] and want a 95% interval for the median.

Write bootstrap_median_ci(x, n_boot=5000, alpha=0.05, seed=0) -> (lo, hi) returning a percentile bootstrap interval using numpy default_rng (vectorised: resample indices with replacement, take medians, take the alpha/2 and 1 - alpha/2 quantiles). Explain exactly what the interval does and does not mean, when the percentile bootstrap is unreliable (small samples, dependence, other statistics), and what you can assert in a deterministic test.

A dashboard test reports 20 independent metrics, each tested at alpha = 0.05, and the team is excited that two are significant. First say how many false positives you expect if no metric truly changed and the chance of at least one.

Then implement bonferroni(pvals, alpha=0.05) and benjamini_hochberg(pvals, q=0.05), each returning a list of booleans in the ORIGINAL order of the p-values. Test input: [0.200, 0.021, 0.001, 0.600, 0.022, 0.008, 0.900, 0.029, 0.400, 0.0045] (10 tests). Explain what each controls and when to prefer which.

You have two tables: signups(user_id, signup_date) and events(user_id, event_date), one row per user action (many per user, possibly several per day). Define weekly retention precisely and implement weekly_retention(signups, events, as_of, max_week=None) with pandas.

Definitions to use: weeks start on Monday; a user's cohort is the week of their signup; retention at week k = fraction of the cohort with at least one event in week (cohort week + k), so week 0 is the signup week itself; users with no events still count in the cohort size; events before signup and events by users without a signup row are ignored; cells whose week had not fully elapsed before the exclusive end date as_of are NaN. Return a DataFrame indexed by cohort week with a cohort_size column and columns 0..max_week. Example: with 6 signups across two cohorts and as_of='2024-01-22' the first cohort's row is [1.0, 0.667, 0.333] and the second is [1.0, 0.0, NaN].

Overall checkout conversion fell from 3.00% to 2.71% between two weeks (100,000 sessions in each). Sessions and orders by device:
- Week 0: desktop 45,000 sessions / 1,800 orders; mobile 50,000 / 900; tablet 5,000 / 300.
- Week 1: desktop 38,000 / 1,482; mobile 57,000 / 969; tablet 5,000 / 255.

Write decompose_conversion_change(df) -> DataFrame for columns segment, sessions_0, orders_0, sessions_1, orders_1 that splits the total change into a mix effect and a within-segment rate effect per segment so that they sum exactly to the change. Report the numbers, say whether the drop is statistically distinguishable from noise, and list the next diagnostic steps.

A customer-satisfaction survey (score 1-5) was emailed to all customers. You received 500 responses: 50 from customers with under 1 year of tenure (mean 3.0), 150 with 1-3 years (mean 3.8) and 300 with over 3 years (mean 4.5). The CRM shows the customer base is 50% under-1-year, 30% 1-3 years and 20% over 3 years.

Name the bias, say how you would check for it, and implement poststratify(df, stratum_col, value_col, population_share) -> dict returning the raw mean, the post-stratified mean, the weights and Kish's effective sample size. Report the worked numbers and the limits of reweighting.

You have 48 months of sales data (4 years) with a clear upward trend and a repeating yearly pattern. Implement decompose_classical(y, period, model='additive') -> DataFrame with columns observed, trend, seasonal, resid using only numpy and pandas: trend from a centred moving average (a 2 x period moving average when period is even), seasonal indices as the per-position average of the detrended series re-centred to sum to 0 (additive) or to average 1 (multiplicative), and the remainder as residual. Trend and residual are NaN at the first and last period//2 points.

Test on a synthetic series 100 + 2t + a known monthly pattern; then explain when a multiplicative model is better and what this classical method cannot do.

A dashboard shows that product pages with more images have a higher conversion rate: pages with 8+ images convert at about 6% and pages with 1-3 images at about 2%. A product manager proposes adding images to every page to triple conversion.

Explain why this is not evidence of a causal effect, name specific confounders, design an experiment that would test the causal claim (what you randomise, the unit, the metric and the analysis), and give observational fallbacks with their assumptions. To illustrate confounding, write simulate_confounding(n=40000, seed=0) -> (naive_slope, adjusted_slope, randomised_slope) in which product tier drives both image count and conversion while images have zero true effect.

Two teammates both say their model 'has leakage'. One means a feature in the training table that is only populated after a customer cancels; the other means the scaler was fitted on the whole dataset before the split. Define target leakage and train-test contamination, give a concrete example of each, and explain how each inflates offline metrics.

A churn model trained on 400,000 customer-month rows reaches 0.99 AUC on a random 80/20 validation split; the previous model scored about 0.78. Before celebrating, list the most likely leakage sources in this setup and, for each, give a concrete check you would run.

A gradient-boosted classifier for loan default has 0.88 ROC-AUC, but when it outputs 0.30 for a group of applicants, roughly 12% of them actually default. What does it mean for a model to be calibrated, how would you measure it with a reliability diagram and expected calibration error, why does the high AUC not tell you the probabilities are right, and when does calibration matter?

You must calibrate a fraud classifier's probabilities. Option A has only 2,000 labelled validation rows (about 60 positives); option B has 200,000 (about 6,000 positives). Compare Platt scaling and isotonic regression for each case, explain why the calibrator must not be fitted on the training data, and say what calibration does to ROC-AUC.

Your team's dashboards mention 'covariate drift', 'label drift' and 'concept drift' as if they were the same thing. Define each, give one example each for a credit-risk model, and say which of the three you can detect without waiting for ground-truth labels.

A card-fraud model flags transactions for manual review. Analysts feel precision has been falling for a month, but chargeback labels take 30-60 days to arrive, so the weekly precision report is always stale. Design a monitoring plan that can warn you earlier, covering input checks, score checks, proxy metrics, delayed-label evaluation, alert thresholds and retraining triggers, and say what trade-offs each choice brings.

In a fraud problem only 1% of 100,000 transactions are fraudulent. Model X has ROC-AUC 0.96 and the team is happy; the investigators, who can review 500 alerts a day, are not. Explain why PR-AUC and precision@k are more informative than ROC-AUC here, and how you would choose the operating threshold if a missed fraud costs about 100 and a false alert costs about 5.

You have two years of event data (about 3 million rows) from 80,000 customers, each with many events over time, and you want to predict whether a customer will upgrade in the next 30 days. A colleague proposes shuffled 5-fold cross-validation. Compare random k-fold, GroupKFold by customer, and a time-based split: what leaks in each, which fits this problem, and how should you report the final performance estimate?

A new churn model beats the old one in offline evaluation (higher AUC on a held-out month), but in an online A/B test its retention uplift is clearly worse than the old model's. Give the causes of training-serving skew you would suspect, and describe how you would isolate which one is responsible.

A 3-class support-ticket classifier is tested on 1,000 tickets: 900 are 'billing', 80 'outage' and 20 'legal'. The confusion matrix (rows true, columns predicted; order billing, outage, legal) is [[860, 30, 10], [20, 50, 10], [5, 5, 10]]. Compute per-class F1, macro-F1, weighted-F1 and micro-F1, explain why they differ so much, and say which you would report for (a) a leadership dashboard about overall correctness and (b) making sure the rare 'legal' tickets are handled well.

Two tables hold sign-up emails: web_signups(email) with rows 'a@x.com', 'b@x.com', 'b@x.com', NULL, and newsletter(email) with rows 'b@x.com', 'c@x.com', NULL. A teammate combines them with UNION and is surprised the result has 4 rows, not 7. Explain the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, say what each costs, and state the rules a compound SELECT imposes on its column lists and on ORDER BY. Then write one query that returns the row count of the UNION result and of the UNION ALL result as two rows (columns op, n_rows), ordered by n_rows.

purchases(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, product TEXT NOT NULL) has one row per item bought. Rows (customer_id, product): 1 Aviator; 1 Aviator; 2 Aviator; 2 Wayfarer; 3 Wayfarer; 4 Aviator; 4 Round; 5 Aviator; 5 Wayfarer; 5 Aviator. Return the customers who bought 'Aviator' but never bought 'Wayfarer' (expected 1 and 4), one row per customer, column customer_id, ordered by customer_id. Write it with EXCEPT, then compare it with the NOT EXISTS version: what does each return for customer 1, and when would you prefer which?

Two nightly snapshots of the same contact list should match. crm_contacts(id, email, phone) has rows (1,'a@x.com','111'), (2,'b@x.com',NULL), (3,'c@x.com','333'), (4,'d@x.com',NULL); billing_contacts(id, email, phone) has rows (1,'a@x.com','111'), (2,'b@x.com',NULL), (3,'c@x.com','999'), (5,'e@x.com',NULL). List every row that is present in only one snapshot, with columns side ('crm_only' or 'billing_only'), id, email, phone, ordered by id then side. Row 2 is identical in both (phone is NULL in both) and must not be reported. Explain why a join on phone = phone gets row 2 wrong and why EXCEPT does not.

logins(user_id INTEGER NOT NULL, login_date TEXT NOT NULL) holds ISO dates, several rows per user possible. Rows (user_id: dates): 1: 2024-09-03, 09-17, 10-02, 10-05, 10-09; 2: 09-12, 09-12; 3: 10-01, 10-31; 4: 09-30, 10-01; 5: 09-05, 09-06, 10-20 (all 2024). Return the users who logged in during September 2024 and also during October 2024, one row per user, column user_id, ordered by user_id (expected 1, 4, 5). Use INTERSECT, then compare with the equivalent self-join and IN versions: what does the plain join return for this data and why?

employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT, salary INTEGER) has rows (name, dept, salary): Ana Eng 150, Ben Eng 140, Cy Eng 140, Dee Eng 130, Eli Eng 120; Fay Sales 100, Gus Sales 90, Hal Sales 90, Ivy Sales 60; Jo HR 80, Kim HR 70; Lou Ops 50, Max Ops 70, Ned Ops NULL (not yet set), Oda Ops 60. Assume no built-in MEDIAN aggregate (the 3.37.2 library has none; recent SQLite releases only ship median()/percentile() in the CLI or as an optional extension). Write one query returning dept and median_salary (the middle value, or the mean of the two middle values when the count is even), ignoring NULL salaries, ordered by dept. Explain how you handle odd and even counts and what goes wrong if the NULL row is not excluded.

sales(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category TEXT, product TEXT, amount INTEGER) has one row per order line. Rows (category, product, amount): Sunglasses: Aviator 200, Aviator 100, Wayfarer 250, Round 150, Round 100, Shield 100; Frames: Slim 400, Bold 250, Bold 150, Retro 100; Lenses: A 90, B 80, C 50, C 30, D 80; Accessories: Case 50, Cloth 20. The homepage has exactly two featured slots per category, filled by the top two products by total revenue. Return category, product, revenue, rn, rnk and cutoff_tie for the products that fill the slots, where rn is ROW_NUMBER (ties broken by product name), rnk is RANK, and cutoff_tie is 1 when the product's revenue is shared with a product that missed the cut. Order by category, rn. Explain what each ranking function would do with the ties, and the business consequence.

events(user_id INTEGER NOT NULL, event_ts TEXT NOT NULL, event_name TEXT) stores 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' timestamps in one time zone. Rows (user_id, event_ts): user 1: 2024-06-01 09:00:00, 09:10:00, 09:40:00, 10:11:00, 10:12:00; user 2: 2024-06-01 23:50:00, 2024-06-02 00:10:00, 2024-06-02 00:10:00 (two events at the same second), 2024-06-02 12:00:00; user 3: 2024-06-01 08:00:00. A new session starts at a user's first event, and whenever the gap to that user's previous event is strictly more than 30 minutes (a gap of exactly 30:00 stays in the session). Return user_id, session_id (1, 2, ... per user), session_start, session_end and n_events, ordered by user_id, session_id, using LAG and a running SUM. Explain why the running SUM works and which edge cases matter.

events(user_id INTEGER NOT NULL, event_name TEXT NOT NULL, event_ts TEXT NOT NULL) logs a shop funnel with event_name in 'view', 'add_to_cart', 'purchase'. Rows (user_id: event@ts, all 2024-05): 1: view 05-01 10:00, view 10:05, add_to_cart 10:06, purchase 10:20; 2: view 05-01 11:00, add_to_cart 11:02; 3: view 05-02 09:00; 4: view 05-02 12:00, view 12:30, view 05-03 08:00; 5: view 05-03 14:00, add_to_cart 14:01, add_to_cart 14:02, purchase 14:10; 6: purchase 05-04 09:00 only; 7: add_to_cart 05-04 10:00, then view 10:05; 8: view 05-04 15:00, add_to_cart 15:03, purchase 15:30. Count USERS (not events) at each step, where a user reaches add_to_cart only if their first cart event is at or after their first view, and reaches purchase only if their first purchase is at or after their first cart event. Return one row: viewed, carted, purchased, view_to_cart_pct, cart_to_purchase_pct, overall_pct (1 decimal). Explain the design choices.

revenue(region TEXT NOT NULL, year INTEGER NOT NULL, amount INTEGER NOT NULL) has rows (region, year, amount): North 2021 400, North 2022 500, North 2023 450; South 2021 300, South 2022 0, South 2023 250; East 2021 300, East 2023 300 (East has no 2022 row). Return region, year, revenue, share_pct (the region's percentage of that year's total revenue, 1 decimal), prev_revenue (the same region's revenue in year-1) and yoy_pct (year-over-year % change, 1 decimal), ordered by year, region. prev_revenue and yoy_pct must be NULL for a region's first year, when the previous calendar year has no row, and yoy_pct must also be NULL when the previous year's revenue is 0. Explain the traps.

user_plans(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user_id INTEGER NOT NULL, plan TEXT NOT NULL, updated_at TEXT) is an append-style history. Rows (id, user_id, plan, updated_at): (1,1,free,'2024-01-10 09:00:00'), (2,1,pro,'2024-03-02 12:00:00'), (3,1,team,'2024-02-01 08:30:00'), (4,2,free,'2024-02-14 10:00:00'), (5,2,pro,'2024-02-20 17:45:00'), (6,2,team,'2024-02-20 17:45:00'), (7,3,free,'2024-01-05 00:00:00'), (8,4,free,NULL), (9,4,pro,'2024-03-01 00:00:00'). Return exactly one current row per user (id, user_id, plan, updated_at), the one with the latest updated_at, ordered by user_id. For the tie of user 2's rows 5 and 6, the higher id wins. Show the ROW_NUMBER version, then compare it with the correlated-subquery and the GROUP BY ... MAX() versions: what does each do with ties and the NULL?

A nightly job must count the lines containing ' ERROR ' in a 40 GB application log on a machine with 8 GB of RAM. The file is mostly UTF-8 but a few lines contain stray invalid bytes, and some lines end in \r\n. A colleague wrote `data = open('app.log').read().splitlines()`. What is wrong with that, and how would you write it? Show a function plus a test.

Your team's scripts build paths like `base + '/' + name + '.csv'` and `os.path.join(...)`, and a Windows colleague's run fails on paths copied from Linux. Argue for or against moving to pathlib, naming concrete things Path objects give you and the cases where you would still need care.

A service rewrites its config file with `open(path, 'w').write(json.dumps(cfg))`. After a kill -9 during a deploy, the file was empty and the service would not start. Explain why this happens and write a safer function. Include a test that shows the old file survives a failed write.

A teammate parses a CSV export with `for line in f: a, b, c = line.strip().split(',')` and it crashes on some rows; another row is split into two records. The file contains values like `"Smith, J"` and a multi-line comment field. Explain what is going wrong, show the correct reading code, and say why csv documentation tells you to open files with newline=''. Include a test.

Two modules, `orders.py` and `customers.py`, each start with an import of the other: orders has `from customers import get_customer` and customers has `from orders import latest_order`. Running `import orders` fails with `ImportError: cannot import name 'latest_order' from partially initialized module 'orders' (most likely due to a circular import)`. Walk through exactly why, and give three fixes in order of preference.

You have a project folder `shop/` with `shop/__init__.py`, `shop/cli.py` and `shop/db.py`, and cli.py contains `from . import db`. `python shop/cli.py` fails with `ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package`, but `python -m shop.cli` works. Explain why, what `__init__.py` is for, and what `if __name__ == '__main__':` actually tests.

You inherit a small internal Flask service and a reusable parsing library, both of which 'work on my laptop' because everything was pip-installed into the system Python. Describe how you would set both up properly: virtual environments, what goes in pyproject.toml, and how you would pin dependencies differently for the service and for the library.

You are writing a small library, `acmeconf`, that reads configuration files. Design its exception hierarchy. A caller should be able to catch 'anything this library raised' with one clause, but also handle a bad value differently from a missing file. Inside the library you call int() on a port string; show how to re-raise as your own type while keeping the original error visible, and explain `__cause__` versus `__context__` and when `from None` is appropriate.

A script that splits a list of records into batches of 100 for an API upload reports success, but the vendor says the last few records are missing. There is no traceback. Describe, step by step, how you would find and prove the bug, and then show a minimal reproduction with a fix and a test. Cover how you would use the traceback when there is one, logging versus print, breakpoint(), assertions and shrinking the input.

You are handed a 2.4M-row customer table (one export, no documentation) and asked to 'see what is in there' before anyone builds a churn analysis. What do you check, in what order, and what do you write down?
Average order value on your shop is 84 but most customers seem to spend far less, and the median is 41. A manager asks which number to put on the dashboard. What do you tell them?

A customer survey has 30 percent of income answers missing. Explain how you would decide whether the missingness is MCAR, MAR or MNAR using business examples, what happens if you just drop those rows versus impute, and what you can actually test.

Product wants to test a redesigned checkout button on a site with about 40,000 eligible visitors per day and a 4.0 percent checkout conversion. Design the experiment: primary and guardrail metrics, randomisation unit, sample size and duration, novelty effects, and the stopping rule.

A teammate says 'the 95 percent confidence interval for the mean delivery time is 31 to 35 minutes, so there is a 95 percent chance the true mean is between 31 and 35.' Is that right? What does the interval mean and what makes it wider or narrower?

An A/B test reports that the variant lifts conversion by +2.0 percent relative, with a 95 percent CI of [-0.5, +4.5] percent relative, and baseline conversion is 5 percent. The PM asks whether to ship. What do you conclude and recommend, and what extra information would change your decision?

You are testing a new ride-matching algorithm in a two-sided marketplace (riders and drivers share the same supply). A colleague proposes randomising riders 50/50 and comparing outcomes. Why might that give a biased estimate, and what alternatives would you consider?

An analyst computes average customer tenure and satisfaction using only customers who are active today, and reports 'average tenure is 4.1 years and satisfaction is 8.2 out of 10'. What is wrong, which way is the bias, how would you detect it, and how would you fix or reframe the analysis?

Monthly active users on the dashboard drop 12 percent the week after an app release that also changed how 'active' is logged. Leadership is alarmed. How do you work out whether it is a real decline or a measurement artefact, reconcile the numbers, and explain it to stakeholders?

Conversion rose from 2.0 percent to 2.5 percent after a redesign. One slide says 'up 0.5 percent', another says 'up 25 percent'. Which is right, how would you write it, and why does the base rate matter? Include the same absolute change on a 20 percent baseline.

You must pick an ANN index for 50 million 768-d float32 chunk embeddings. Constraints: about 1 million new chunks per day plus a few thousand deletions, a target of roughly 0.95 recall@10 against exact search, p95 latency under 50 ms, and 64 GB of RAM per node. Compare HNSW, IVF-Flat and IVF-PQ (with and without re-ranking from full vectors) on recall, latency, memory, build cost and update behaviour, and say which you would shortlist and why.

Your team says the new vector index 'has 98% recall' but nobody can say how that was measured. Describe how to measure ANN recall@k properly, then implement it: write exact_topk(queries, base, k) (brute-force L2 ground truth), ann_recall_at_k(exact_ids, approx_ids) (mean overlap fraction, ignoring -1 padding) and a small inverted-file index ToyIVF(base, nlist, seed) with search(queries, k, nprobe). Show how recall changes with nprobe and what happens when nprobe equals nlist.

A team switched their vector index from L2 to inner-product 'because cosine is better for text'. They changed only the index metric flag. Afterwards: similarity scores returned to the app range from about 0.4 to 3.1, a hard-coded 'relevant if score > 0.75' rule now passes almost everything, and some long, generic chunks appear at the top for unrelated queries. Diagnose the problem and give the fix, including what to do about the existing index.

You maintain a 20-million-chunk vector index built with embedding model A (1024-d). A newer model B, also 1024-d, scores better on your eval set. To save time, a colleague proposes embedding only new documents and all queries with model B and adding them to the same index, backfilling old documents 'later'. Is this safe? What happens, and how would you roll out the upgrade?

A colleague says: 'In 1,024 dimensions all distances are basically equal, so nearest-neighbour search on our embeddings is meaningless and we should stop using vector search.' Evaluate the claim. What does distance concentration actually say, when does it apply, and why does ANN search still work on real text embeddings?

You are choosing among a 384-d, 768-d and 1,024-d embedding model for 20 million chunks, and the vector index must fit in a 64 GB node (with some headroom for the OS, metadata and query processing). Do the memory arithmetic for float32, float16 and int8 storage, add the graph overhead for HNSW with M = 16, and explain which options fit and what you would do beyond arithmetic to decide.

An IVF index (nlist = 4,096) was trained eight months ago on a 200k sample, when the corpus was mostly consumer-electronics documents. The corpus has since grown to 30 million vectors, largely from a new product line. At launch nprobe = 16 gave about 0.95 recall@10 on exact-search checks; today the same setting gives about 0.80 on a fresh query set, and p95 latency has roughly doubled. Some inverted lists now hold more than 100 times the mean list size. Explain what happened and how you would fix and monitor it.

Your RAG team splits every document into 512-token chunks with no overlap and gets noticeably worse answers on questions whose answer straddles a paragraph boundary. A colleague says 'just raise the overlap to 128'. Estimate what that does to index size for a 10,000-token document, and describe how you would decide on chunk size and overlap using retrieval measurements rather than intuition.

After ingesting 3,000 two-column PDF reports, your retrieval returns chunks that read like 'The revenue grew by Table 3 shows 12% in the Page 14 of 62 Confidential region'. Queries on the report body are poor, though simple title lookups work. Diagnose the likely extraction problems, how you would confirm each, and what you would change in the ingestion pipeline.

Your knowledge base is Markdown documentation containing headings, long tables (pricing tiers, parameter references) and fenced code blocks. A fixed-size splitter cuts a 40-row table in half and a code sample in the middle of a function. What goes wrong at retrieval and generation time, and how would you split each of the three content types?

A nightly job re-ingests your wiki. Over three weeks, users report answers quoting removed policies, the same paragraph appearing three times in the cited sources, and the vector index growing about 4% a night even though the wiki barely grows. Explain the likely ingestion design bug and how you would redesign the update path so re-ingestion is idempotent, handles edits and deletions, and can be rolled back.

Explain parent-child (small-to-big) retrieval. Using child chunks of 128 tokens and parent sections of 1,024 tokens, say what is embedded, what is returned to the LLM, and one situation where it helps and one where it can hurt.
Besides the text itself, what metadata would you store with every chunk in a RAG index, and what is each field used for?

An IT-helpdesk assistant retrieves from 40,000 knowledge-base articles. Three real-style queries fail in different ways: (a) 'what does error E-4417 mean?'; (b) 'laptop will not wake up after closing the lid' (the relevant article is titled 'Resume from suspend fails on battery'); (c) 'how do I request SKU AG-2291-B for a new hire?'. For each, say whether a dense retriever or BM25 is more likely to succeed, and why. What does this imply for the retrieval design?

In a hybrid search system, a teammate computes final_score = bm25_score + cosine_score for each candidate and sorts. In testing, BM25 values look like 14.2, 9.8 and 3.1, while cosine scores are 0.71, 0.69 and 0.64 for the same documents. Why is this wrong, and what are the options for combining the two retrievers properly, with their trade-offs?

Implement reciprocal rank fusion: rrf(rankings, k=60, top_n=None) takes several ranked lists of document ids (best first) and returns [(doc, score)] best first, with score = sum over lists of 1 / (k + rank), rank starting at 1. Repeats inside one list count once (first occurrence), exact ties go to the document that appears earlier (earlier list, then earlier position), and empty inputs return an empty list. Explain what k does.

Implement Okapi BM25 over tokenised documents with a class BM25(docs, k1=1.2, b=0.75) offering idf(term), score(query_tokens, doc_index) and rank(query_tokens, top_n). Use the non-negative idf ln(1 + (N - df + 0.5)/(df + 0.5)) and count repeated query terms once. Then explain, with your code, what tf saturation and length normalisation do and what happens when b = 0 or b = 1.

A RAG retriever's top-5 contains four near-identical paragraphs from different copies of the same policy, which wastes context. Implement Maximal Marginal Relevance mmr(query, docs, k, lam=0.5) over cosine similarity (greedy; score = lam x sim(q, d) - (1 - lam) x max similarity to already selected; ties to the lower index; zero vectors score 0). Explain how lam behaves and where MMR is not the right tool.

Users of a document-QA chatbot type very short or chatty queries ('and the notice period?', 'termination'), and recall@5 is low. A teammate proposes three changes: (1) LLM query rewriting using chat history, (2) HyDE (embed an LLM-written hypothetical answer instead of the query), and (3) multi-query expansion with fusion. Explain what each does, when each helps or hurts, and what you would test before adding them.

A multi-tenant RAG service has 80 million chunks in an ANN index, with metadata for tenant, language and date. A query is restricted to one tenant that owns 1% of the chunks. The current code retrieves the top-10 vectors then drops those whose tenant does not match, and users often see 0-2 results. Explain why, compare post-filtering, pre-filtering and filter-aware ANN, and recommend a strategy as a function of filter selectivity.

On 300 labelled queries, a hypothetical evaluation reports MRR@10 of 0.41 for BM25, 0.49 for dense and 0.52 for hybrid (RRF). The product team wants to ship hybrid and to tune the RRF k and a dense/sparse weight on the same 300 queries. The relevance judgements were originally collected by annotators reviewing the top results of the current dense system. What is wrong with this evaluation, and how would you evaluate and tune the hybrid system properly?

Why can't you replace your first-stage vector search with a cross-encoder that scores every document against the query, even though cross-encoders are usually more accurate? Use a 1,000,000-chunk corpus and a hypothetical 4 ms per query-document pair to make the point, and say where a cross-encoder does fit.

Your pipeline retrieves the top-N with hybrid search, reranks with a cross-encoder, and gives the top 5 to the LLM. On a labelled set, hypothetically, recall@50 of the first stage is 0.86 and recall@200 is 0.93; reranker cost is about 4 ms per pair when batched, and the product's retrieval budget is 400 ms. How do you choose N, and what other measurements would change your decision?

You assemble 10 retrieved chunks into a prompt. The best evidence is usually chunk 1, but you notice answers degrade when the key chunk lands in the middle of a long context. What is this effect, how reliable is the evidence for it, and what would you do about ordering and context size?

Users report that the assistant's context often shows the same paragraph three times, or the same policy in three slightly different versions, and answers feel repetitive or inconsistent. The top-8 chunks come from an index with 15% overlap chunking and several document versions. Describe how you would deduplicate and compress retrieved context before the prompt is built, and what each technique risks.

Compliance requires that every claim in the assistant's answer can be traced to a source passage the user can open. How would you implement citation and attribution in a RAG answer pipeline, and how do you check that a citation actually supports the claim it is attached to?

Your model has a hypothetical 8,192-token context window. The prompt has a 600-token system message, a 100-token user question and up to 1,200 tokens of conversation history, and you must reserve 1,000 tokens for the answer. Chunks average 450 tokens plus about 30 tokens of per-chunk formatting (ID and title). How many chunks fit, what happens when some chunks are much longer than average, and how would you design the token budget so it degrades gracefully?

You compare two retrievers on 40 labelled queries using hit@5 (1 if a gold chunk is in the top 5, else 0). Retriever A scores 0.50 and B scores 0.60: B hits where A misses on 6 queries, A hits where B misses on 2, and they agree on the other 32. A teammate wants to ship B because 'it is 10 points better'.

Write paired_bootstrap_ci(a, b, n_boot=10000, alpha=0.05, seed=0) that takes per-query scores for the two systems and returns (mean difference b - a, lower, upper) using a percentile bootstrap over queries. Then say what the interval tells you, why resampling pairs beats treating the two scores as independent samples, and what you would do next.

You use an LLM judge to label RAG answers as 'ok' (faithful to the retrieved context) or 'bad'. On 100 answers a human reviewer also labelled, the two agree on 91. The human marked 90 answers ok and 10 bad; the judge marked 95 ok and 5 bad. A colleague says 'it agrees 91% of the time, so we can trust it as our faithfulness gate'.

Reconstruct the confusion matrix, compute Cohen's kappa, and explain why the headline agreement is misleading here. Then implement cohen_kappa(human, judge) and say what else you would report before relying on the judge.

A RAG bot is asked: 'How many days of notice are needed to cancel the contract?' The retriever returns only a superseded policy page saying 30 days (the current policy says 60). Three candidate answers:

A: 'You need 30 days of notice.'
B: 'You need 60 days of notice.' (no retrieved text mentions 60)
C: 'Cancellations must be made in writing and follow the contract terms.'

For each answer say whether it is faithful, relevant and correct, state which inputs each of those three judgements needs, and explain what this implies for choosing the headline metric of a RAG evaluation.

You use an LLM as a pairwise judge to compare a new prompt (B) against the current prompt (A) on 200 questions. The judge prefers B on 62% of pairs. Before reporting it, you re-run the same 200 pairs with the answer order swapped, and the judge's verdict changes (it picks the other system) on 31% of the pairs. The new prompt's answers are on average about 40% longer than the old prompt's.

What is going on, which other judge biases should you test for, and how do you turn this judge into a usable measurement?

Your team wants to pick between BM25 and a dense retriever for a 20,000-chunk internal knowledge base. The plan: sample 500 chunks uniformly at random, prompt an LLM to 'write a question that this chunk answers', mark that chunk as the single gold chunk, and compare recall@5.

Critique this golden-set plan. Name the specific biases it introduces and which retriever it is likely to favour, and describe a better construction, including how you would validate it and keep it from going stale.

You replace the embedding model in a RAG pipeline that passes the top 5 retrieved chunks to the generator. On a 200-question golden set, recall@10 rises from 0.78 to 0.84. Human-graded answer correctness barely moves: 61% to 62.5%. The team wonders if retrieval metrics 'don't matter'.

Give at least four distinct reasons this can happen, say how you would tell them apart with the data you already have, and what extra experiment establishes the ceiling on what better retrieval can deliver.

Your retrieval golden set was built by annotators who judged only the top 10 results of the existing BM25 system for each query. You now evaluate a new dense retriever against it: its recall@10 and nDCG@10 come out lower than BM25's, yet when you read its results for 20 queries by hand, they look as good or better. Why can the metrics say this, and how would you fix the evaluation?

Some of your RAG questions need several pieces of evidence (for example a policy rule plus its exception), and for each piece there may be several acceptable chunks because the corpus contains near-duplicates. Averaging plain recall@k over queries hides whether the generator actually receives everything it needs.

Implement evidence_coverage(ranked, groups, k), where groups is a list of sets of chunk ids and a group counts as covered if any of its chunks is in the top k, returning (fraction of groups covered, whether all groups are covered), and aggregate(runs, k) returning (mean coverage, full-coverage rate). Here runs is a list of (ranked, groups) pairs. Use these four queries: (1) ranked [c1, c9, c2, c7], groups [{c1}, {c2, c20}]; (2) [c5, c3, c8, c4], [{c3}, {c6}]; (3) [c10, c11], [{c12}]; (4) [c1, c2, c3, c4], [{c4}, {c3}, {c40}]. Explain why mean coverage and full-coverage rate move differently when k goes from 3 to 4.

A 20M-chunk collection sits in an HNSW index. Queries always carry a metadata filter. For a filter such as department='legal' AND year=2019, only about 0.5% of vectors match (roughly 100,000 chunks). With ef_search=100 and top_k=10, the service often returns only 0 to 2 results, though the same query unfiltered returns 10 sensible hits and an exact scan with the filter returns 10 good ones.

Explain why this happens with post-filtering, what in-graph (filtered) traversal and pre-filtering change, and how you would choose a strategy by selectivity.

You must serve 50 million chunks, 768-d float32 embeddings, from an in-memory HNSW index with M=16, with 3 replicas for availability and throughput. Each node has about 100 GB usable for the index. Estimate memory for the base design, work out how many nodes it needs, and compare it with int8 scalar quantisation and product quantisation with 96-byte codes. Which would you choose and what would you verify before deciding?

A RAG service re-ingests documents weekly; each document is split into chunks and upserted into an HNSW-based vector store, and deleted documents are removed with a 'delete by chunk id' call. Six months in, you see: memory and disk keep growing though the corpus is stable, p95 latency is creeping up, recall on a fixed monitoring set has dropped a little, and legal reports that a withdrawn document still appears in answers.

Explain the likely mechanisms and design the update and delete path properly.

Users of a news-assistant RAG product expect a newly published article to be answerable within about 30 seconds. Today the vector index is rebuilt every night, ingestion runs at roughly 200 new chunks per second at peak, and queries must stay under 200 ms at p95.

Design how new documents become searchable quickly without rebuilding the whole index, say where the 30 seconds actually go, and discuss the consistency and cost trade-offs.

A SaaS RAG product serves 3,000 tenants. Sizes are heavily skewed: most have a few hundred chunks, a handful have millions. Candidate designs: (a) one shared index with a tenant_id filter, (b) a separate index per tenant, (c) a hybrid. Customers require that one tenant can never retrieve another's data, and that deleting a tenant removes all its vectors.

Compare the designs on isolation, search quality and latency, cost, noisy neighbours and erasure, and say which you would build.

A hybrid search service runs BM25 and dense retrieval across 8 shards. Each shard computes BM25 with its own local statistics, returns its top 20, and the coordinator merges the lists by raw score and then fuses with the dense list. After the corpus was resharded unevenly, queries with rare terms started returning odd rankings, and the hybrid scores seem on a different scale than the dense ones.

Why does this happen, and how should the merging and fusion work?

A RAG assistant answers 'What is the notice period for terminating the Enterprise plan?' with '30 days', but the policy says 60 days. Logging shows the correct policy chunk was retrieved at rank 2 and is in the prompt. Lay out a step-by-step triage to find out why the answer is wrong, with the experiment that separates each cause.

Answers are fluent and confident, but spot checks show many sentences are not in any retrieved chunk. Some are true, some are wrong. How do you determine whether the model is drawing on its own training knowledge, over-generalising from the chunks, or being fed irrelevant context, and what does each finding imply for the fix?

Offline, your RAG system scores recall@5 of 0.92 and faithfulness 0.95 on the golden set, yet thumbs-down feedback is high, and users say answers are 'not what I asked' or 'outdated'. List the plausible reasons offline metrics and user feedback disagree and the analysis you would run to find which applies.

After a weekend re-index in which you also switched to a newer embedding model and changed chunk size from 512 to 256, answer quality drops and some previously working queries now fail. Without being able to blame one change by intuition, how do you isolate the cause, and what would you have done before the migration to make this easy?

Users of an internal assistant complain that questions containing acronyms and IDs ('What does SLA-7 cover?', 'Status of ticket INC-48213?', 'Is DPA required?') get wrong or irrelevant answers, while natural-language questions work well. The system uses dense retrieval only. Explain why, how you would confirm the diagnosis with measurements, and the fixes in order of cost.

An invoice-extraction service forces the model to emit JSON that matches a schema (total: number, currency: one of three enum values, due_date: string). Parse errors fell to zero, yet finance still finds about 4% of records with a wrong total (usually the pre-tax subtotal was picked) and some due dates that are invented when the invoice shows none. Why does schema enforcement not fix this, and which extra layers would you add?

Model replies are sometimes wrapped in prose or Markdown fences, sometimes contain a trailing comma, sometimes quote an example object before the real answer, and sometimes violate the requested schema. Implement, with the standard library only and no network, (1) extract_json_values(text) returning every top-level JSON object/array found in free text (braces inside strings must not confuse it, a truncated value must not be silently completed), (2) validate(value, schema) for a small JSON-Schema subset returning a list of readable violations, and (3) parse_with_retries(call_model, prompt, schema, max_attempts=3) that feeds the violations back to the model on retry, returns (value, attempts) only for schema-valid data and otherwise raises ParseFailure. Explain your design choices and what the retry loop cannot guarantee.

A 5-class ticket-routing prompt uses 10 fixed few-shot examples and scores 81% on a 300-item dev set. A colleague merely reorders the same 10 examples and gets 76%. Another colleague replaces them with 10 examples retrieved per query by similarity and gets 85%. How do you interpret these numbers, and how would you test for ordering and example-selection effects before shipping?

Your team plans to (a) show the model's step-by-step reasoning to loan officers as 'the explanation' for a triage recommendation, and (b) switch on chain-of-thought for a simple three-class sentiment tagger 'to be safe'. What are the caveats for each, and how would you decide with data whether chain-of-thought is worth it for (b)?

A CI job sends 50 fixed prompts at temperature 0 and asserts that each reply equals a stored string. It passes locally but fails on about 3 of 50 prompts at random in CI, and the failing replies diverge at some token and then differ in wording. A teammate insists 'temperature 0 is deterministic, so this is a bug in our code'. Diagnose it and redesign the tests.

Three people edit the production system prompt through an admin page. After one 'small wording tweak', downstream JSON parse failures rose from 0.5% to 3% and nobody noticed for two days; nobody could even say which prompt text served which request. Design prompt versioning, change control and a regression gate for this system.

A support agent has four tools: get_order(order_id), lookup_order(query), get_customer_orders(email) and cancel(order_id). In logs, about 30% of the time the model calls lookup_order with a bare order number, and about 10% of the time it calls get_order with a customer's name, which errors. How would you redesign the tool definitions so the model picks the right tool and arguments, and how would you verify the fix?

A research agent sometimes runs 40+ steps, repeating essentially the same web_search with slightly reworded queries. Each tool result adds about 1,500 tokens and the full history is resent at every step. Explain what is going wrong in cost and quality terms, and which guards you would add to the loop.

A refund agent calls issue_refund(order_id, amount). Last week a tool call timed out at the payment service although the refund had actually gone through; the agent retried, and the customer was refunded twice. In a separate case a prompt-confused agent refunded an order that had been delivered fine. Redesign the action path so duplicate and unauthorised refunds are prevented, and say where a human should be in the loop.

An email-and-web agent can read web pages, read the user's inbox and send email. Explain, in terms of the agent's control flow, why a web page that the agent merely 'reads' can end up causing the agent to send mail to an outside address, and what design rule would limit the damage without removing the web tool.

A product manager wants an 'autonomous AI agent' to process expense claims: read the receipt, check it against the policy, then approve, reject or flag. The steps and their order are the same for every claim. Argue for or against building it as a free-running agent, and describe the alternative, including a rough reliability argument.

You evaluate a ticket-resolution agent that can read a customer database, update ticket status and issue credits. In a 200-task suite it ends with the correct final reply 80% of the time. Why is that number insufficient, how would you evaluate trajectories as well as outcomes, and how do you handle run-to-run variation?

A data-analyst assistant is given three tools: run_sql, read_file and send_report_email. The team plans to use one service account with broad access for all users because 'the prompt tells the model to stay within the user's data'. How would you scope permissions properly?

A new model scores 4 points higher than your current one on a public reasoning benchmark, and leadership wants to swap it into your contract-clause extraction pipeline. Why might that gain not carry over, and what would you do before agreeing?

You have a 200-case regression suite for a support-answer prompt. The old prompt passes 168 cases; the new prompt passes 174. Looking case by case, the new prompt fixes 15 cases and breaks 9. Is the new prompt better? Explain how to analyse this properly, how sampling variance and flaky cases change the picture, and how many cases you would want for a regression gate.

You must compare four candidate answer styles for a help-centre assistant using an LLM judge. Should the judge score each answer on an absolute 1-5 scale or compare pairs? How would you treat ties and judge inconsistency, and what are the cost implications?

You want to use an LLM judge to label support answers as 'acceptable' or 'not acceptable'. On 150 answers that a human reviewer also labelled, the counts are: both acceptable 120, judge acceptable but human not 10, judge not acceptable but human acceptable 5, both not acceptable 15. The vendor says '90% agreement, so it's good enough'. Evaluate that claim, state how you would calibrate the judge, and say how to treat the two kinds of labels honestly.

Over six weeks a team iterated its assistant prompt against a fixed 300-item dev set scored by an LLM judge. The judge score rose from 3.1 to 4.2 out of 5, but thumbs-up rate in production is flat and the average answer length is up 40%. What happened, and how do you change the evaluation process so improvements are real?

A stricter system prompt raises the refusal rate on your 200 clearly harmful test requests from 188 to 196 (94% to 98%). The team celebrates. Your 200 benign-but-sensitive requests (for example medical or security questions with legitimate purposes) show refusals going from 8 to 22. Evaluate the change and describe how you would build and report safety and helpfulness measures together.

A prompt change passes 27 of 30 smoke-test cases and an engineer reports '90% pass rate'. Implement in Python (standard library only) a function wilson_interval(successes, n, z=1.96) with input validation, compare it with the naive normal-approximation interval on this data, and explain what the interval does and does not tell you at n=30, and how many cases you would need for a +/-3 point interval at about 90%.

A 40-agent helpdesk wants every internal ticket summary in one fixed five-section layout (Issue, Impact, Steps tried, Current status, Next action). A developer proposes fine-tuning a model on 300 past summaries. Today, a plain zero-shot prompt produces the layout correctly in about 60% of cases, and the content is usually accurate. A manager asks if fine-tuning is the right first move. What do you recommend, and what result would change your mind?

A product team lists three needs for a single assistant: (A) answer HR questions from policy documents that are edited every week, (B) always reply in a warm, concise brand voice with a fixed sign-off, and (C) pull 12 fields from scanned expense reports into a strict schema with at least 98% field accuracy. Someone says 'just fine-tune one model for all three'. How would you map each need to prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning, and which of your choices is the weakest?

After LoRA supervised fine-tuning, your support-intent classifier scores 80% on a 400-item held-out set. Your best hand-tuned prompt on the untuned model scored 74% on the same 400 items. The team wants to declare that fine-tuning beat prompting. What would you check before accepting this, and how would you decide whether a 6-point gap is real?

A team ran full-parameter supervised fine-tuning for 3 epochs on 6,000 internal ticket-classification examples. The classifier meets its target. During release testing, though, the model ignores formatting rules in the system prompt, answers unrelated general questions more tersely, and declines clearly out-of-scope requests less often than before. What probably happened, what checks should have caught it, and how would you change the training pipeline?

Your team can LoRA fine-tune a mid-sized decoder on two GPUs, but only one is available this quarter, and someone suggests QLoRA. Describe what QLoRA changes relative to plain LoRA, what you give up, and what you would verify before shipping an adapter trained that way.

A team has 200 high-quality human-written support replies and plans to prompt a larger model to generate 20,000 more, then run supervised fine-tuning on all 20,200 to improve a smaller deployed model. What are the main risks, which controls would you add, and how would you decide whether the synthetic expansion actually helped?

An email-triage assistant summarises a user's inbox and can draft replies. A security reviewer shows that a message from an external sender can steer the assistant's behaviour even though the user never typed anything unusual. The team's first fix is a filter that blocks emails containing phrases such as 'ignore previous instructions'. Explain the distinction between direct and indirect prompt injection here, and why that filter is a weak defence.

You are asked to ship an assistant that can read a user's email and calendar, search the web, and (when asked) send email and create events. Design a layered defence against prompt injection from external content. For each layer say what it stops and what it cannot stop, and be explicit about the residual risk.

A chat assistant renders model output as markdown, including images. A security test shows that after the assistant summarised a shared document, the user's browser made an outbound request to an unfamiliar domain, and the request contained fragments of the user's earlier conversation. No tool call was involved. Walk through how this can happen, why it is hard to notice, and what you would change. Describe the mechanism and fixes, not attack text.

A support-copilot stores full prompts, retrieved chunks and model responses in application logs for 90 days. Retrieved chunks come from past tickets that contain names, emails, order numbers and sometimes health information. All tenants share one vector index with a tenant_id filter. Design the privacy controls for this system across prompts, logs, retrieval and deletion requests, and say where each control is weakest.

You must red-team a customer-facing assistant that has read access to internal knowledge and one write tool, before launch. Describe a red-team plan, how you would define and measure attack success rate (ASR), and what you would conclude if 200 attack attempts all fail. Include how to treat adaptive attackers and what the plan cannot prove.

In a security review a colleague says 'jailbreaks and prompt injection are the same thing, so one safety classifier covers both'. Give a precise distinction between the two, say who the attacker and the victim are in each case, and explain why the mitigations only partly overlap.

A team hosting a decoder-only model wants a small capacity-planning helper. Write two functions.

kv_cache_bytes(n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1, bytes_per_elem=2) returns the bytes needed to cache keys and values for `batch` sequences of `seq_len` tokens.

max_concurrent_sequences(total_bytes, weight_bytes, reserve_bytes, n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, bytes_per_elem=2) returns how many full-length sequences fit after subtracting the weights and a fixed reserve (activations, runtime overhead) from the device memory. It returns 0 if not even one fits, and raises ValueError if weights plus reserve already exceed total memory.

Validate inputs: every size must be an int (bool and float rejected with TypeError) and positive (ValueError); reserve_bytes may be 0. Then, for a hypothetical 32-layer model with head_dim 128, 4,096-token sequences, an fp16 cache, an 80 GiB device, 14e9 bytes of weights and a 6 GiB reserve, report how many sequences fit with 32 KV heads versus 8 KV heads, and what that tells you about the design of the attention layer.

On a hypothetical accelerator with 300 TFLOP/s of usable fp16 compute and 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth, you serve a 7B-parameter fp16 model (14 GB of weights) with 32 layers, 32 KV heads and head_dim 128. A colleague says: "Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound, so just keep growing the decode batch until the GPU is saturated." Using a back-of-envelope roofline, show why batch-1 decode is bandwidth-bound, how far batching really helps with 2,000-token contexts, and what the numbers say about prefill.

Write a small simulator that compares static and continuous batching. All requests arrive at time 0 and are served in FIFO order; request i needs lengths[i] decode steps; one decode step costs one time unit regardless of batch size, and prefill is ignored.

static_batching(lengths, max_batch): requests are taken in groups of max_batch; a group runs until its longest member finishes, and every member is returned when the group ends.
continuous_batching(lengths, max_batch): at every step boundary free slots are filled from the queue in FIFO order, and a request leaves after exactly its own number of steps.

Both return {"total_steps": int, "completion": [finish time of each request, in input order]} and raise ValueError for a non-positive max_batch or a non-positive or non-int length. Run them on lengths = [2, 10, 3, 9] with max_batch = 2, and say what this model leaves out that matters for a real serving system.

A chat feature sends about 3,000-token prompts and gets about 400-token answers. Measured per request: 0.2 s queueing, 0.3 s prefill, 0.1 s network, then 25 ms for each generated token after the first. Ops proposes raising concurrency from 16 to 32 streams per GPU; a load test says per-token time becomes 40 ms (assume queueing and prefill are unchanged). Compute time to first token and total latency before and after, and the per-GPU token throughput. Then decide whether to ship the change for (a) the streamed chat UI and (b) a nightly job that needs the full JSON answer, and say which latency metric you would put the SLO on in each case.

You quantise a 13B-parameter model's weights from fp16 to 4-bit (group size 128, one fp16 scale per group) so it fits a smaller GPU. The team reports the aggregate benchmark score dropped by a margin they call negligible, yet support reports wrong digits in long extracted tables and occasional broken JSON. (a) How much weight memory does this save, and what does it not save? (b) How do weight-only and weight-plus-activation quantisation differ in speed benefit and quality risk? (c) What checks would you run before approving the change?

Your support assistant has a response cache keyed on embedding similarity: if a new query has cosine similarity of at least 0.92 to a cached query, the cached answer is returned and the model is skipped. It serves 30% of 1,000,000 daily queries; a human reviews a random sample of 500 cache hits and finds 10 wrong answers. (a) Estimate daily wrong answers with a rough 95% interval. (b) Name the failure modes that tuning the threshold cannot remove (tenants, personal data, staleness, near-miss questions). (c) Redesign the cache key and invalidation, and say when you would not cache at all.

A serving stack reserves a contiguous KV-cache region for the maximum 4,096-token length for every request at admission. The model has 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, an fp16 cache, and 60 GiB is available for cache. In your traffic a typical request ends at about 700 tokens (prompt plus output). (a) How many concurrent requests fit, and what fraction of the reserved memory is actually used? (b) A paged scheme allocates 16-token blocks on demand: roughly how many requests fit and how much is wasted per request? (c) Why will the real throughput gain be smaller than the capacity ratio, and what else does block-level allocation enable?

A model asked for references on a niche topic returns three plausible-looking papers with authors, titles, venues and years; two of them do not exist. A colleague asks: "It clearly knows how to say 'I don't know' in other chats, so why did training leave it guessing here?" Describe how the pretraining objective and the way answers are typically scored encourage confident guessing, why facts seen once or never are especially at risk, and which part of the problem retrieval can and cannot fix.

A policy Q&A assistant outputs an answer and a confidence score. On 1,000 held-out questions the confidence bands look like this (hypothetical): at least 0.9: 400 questions, 380 correct; 0.7 to 0.9: 300 questions, 210 correct; 0.5 to 0.7: 200 questions, 90 correct; below 0.5: 100 questions, 20 correct. When the bot abstains the user is routed to a human, at a cost of 1 unit; a wrong answer costs 10 units. Where should the abstention threshold sit, what changes if a wrong answer costs only 3, and what must you verify before trusting these numbers?

Your company has a 300,000-token body of product manuals, updated weekly, and about 50,000 questions a day from customers with different entitlements. A manager says a hypothetical 400,000-token context model makes RAG unnecessary: "just paste all the manuals into every prompt." Assume prefill runs at 10,000 tokens/s per GPU, a typical RAG prompt is 6,000 tokens, and the KV cache costs 128 KiB per token. Compare the two designs on latency, compute, memory, freshness and access control, and say when long context is the right choice.

To catch hallucinations cheaply, a team proposes two signals: (1) flag any answer whose average token log-probability falls below a threshold; (2) sample the model 5 times at a non-zero temperature and flag the answer when fewer than 4 of the samples agree. Where would each signal be informative, where would it fail, and how would you decide whether to deploy either?

You build a hallucination detector for a RAG assistant: split each answer into sentences, run an NLI-style entailment model of (retrieved passages, sentence), and flag sentences that are not entailed. On 10,000 production sentences, 3% are truly unsupported by the retrieved context (hypothetical). The detector has 80% recall and a 5% false-positive rate. (a) What share of flags are real problems, and what does that imply for how you use the detector? (b) Beyond the threshold, what systematic error modes does this approach have? (c) How would you validate and improve it?

A product team wants to show a green "Verified by sources" badge whenever an assistant answer includes at least one citation. A hypothetical audit of 500 badged answers found that in 430 the cited passage supports the claim, in 45 it supports only part of the claim, and in 25 it does not support it at all. What is wrong with the badge, how would you change the UI and wording to reduce over-trust, and how would you test that the change works?

A retailer's support team handles about 12,000 conversations a month. The ten most common intents (order status, returns, delivery changes and so on) make up roughly 45% of volume. Leadership wants an LLM support bot live in 8 weeks and quotes 'containment rate' as the success target. Design the launch: scope, escalation, rollout, metrics beyond containment, how to handle wrong answers and legal risk, and a measurable go/no-go gate.

A legal-tech team is building a contract question-answering product. Lawyers upload their own contracts, ask things like 'what is the notice period for termination?' and expect answers with exact clause references. Say what you would and would not promise users, how you would present answers and citations, how access control must work, and what evaluation results you would require before launch.

An A/B test of a support bot ran on 10,000 conversations, 5,000 per arm. The bot arm resolves 39% of conversations without a human versus 31% for the control (which has a simple FAQ widget). However, among conversations marked 'resolved without a human', 21% of the bot arm contacted support again within 7 days about the same issue versus 12% in the control. Customer satisfaction scores are 0.1 points lower in the bot arm on a 5-point scale, from a survey answered by about 8% of users. Should you ship? Argue with the numbers.

A teammate hands you a notebook that reported 0.87 F1 on the validation set and says 'just rerun it to get the same number'. Which pieces of information must have been recorded for the run so that someone else can re-create that result, and which of them are most often forgotten?
Why does 'it works on my machine' cause more trouble in machine-learning projects than in ordinary application code?

Three weeks ago a run on branch main reported 0.842 AUC on a fixed validation set. Today, the same script on main gives 0.829, and nobody changed the code on purpose. Give an ordered checklist for finding out why, and say how you would decide whether 0.829 is a real regression at all.

You fix every random seed in a training script, yet two runs on the same GPU box differ in the third decimal of validation loss, and a colleague's run on a different machine differs more. Why is setting the seed necessary but not sufficient, and what else would you control or accept?

Your team logs every training run to an experiment tracker and also keeps a model registry. A new hire asks why one of them is not enough. What belongs in each, and how would you answer 'which code, data and run produced the model that is serving traffic right now?'

Your training set is 400 GB of images plus a labels file. About 2% of the files are added or relabelled each week, and models from the last year must stay reproducible. Compare keeping a dated full copy of the dataset every week with content-hash versioning using small pointer files, say what each training run records, and name what can still go wrong.

Two training configurations, A and B, are each run with 5 seeds on the same data split. Validation accuracy for A is 0.912, 0.905, 0.918, 0.909, 0.915 and for B is 0.917, 0.908, 0.921, 0.913, 0.919 (seed i uses the same initial weights and data order in both). A teammate wants to ship B because 'it won in every seed'. How would you compare the two fairly, and how strong is the evidence?

Where in an ML pipeline would you put data validation, and which kinds of failures would you block the pipeline on versus only warn about? Use training data and live serving requests separately in your answer.

Write validate_batch(rows, schema) in plain Python (standard library only) that checks a batch of feature rows before training or scoring and returns structured violations. rows is a list of dicts; schema maps a column name to a dict with optional keys type ('int', 'float' or 'str'), min, max, allowed, max_null_rate (default 0.0) and severity ('error' or 'warn', default 'error'). A missing key, None or NaN counts as null. Report: an empty batch, a column absent from every row, a null rate above its limit, a wrong type (bools are not ints; ints are acceptable as floats), values outside [min, max], and values not in allowed. Return a list of dicts with column, check, severity and detail, in a deterministic order, plus a has_errors(violations) helper. Then explain how you would wire it into a pipeline.

A retrained churn model scores 0.871 AUC against 0.866 for the production model on the same fresh holdout. The pipeline is about to promote it automatically. Besides the overall AUC, what would you require before promotion, and in what order would you run the checks? Give one concrete example of a check that overall AUC can hide.

Implement promotion_gate(candidate, baseline, min_improvement=0.002, slice_tolerance=0.01, min_slice_n=200, z=1.96) for a higher-is-better metric. Each side is {'overall': (value, std_err), 'slices': {name: (value, std_err, n)}}. Promote only if the overall gain is at least min_improvement and its lower confidence bound (using independent standard errors) is above zero; reject if any baseline slice with at least min_slice_n examples regresses by more than slice_tolerance, or if any baseline slice of any size is missing from the candidate; if only small slices regress, return needs_review. Return {'decision': ..., 'reasons': [...]}. Then discuss what this rule does not protect against.

A pull-request check trains a small model on a 200-row fixture and asserts validation accuracy >= 0.75. It fails in roughly one build in seven even when no relevant code changed, and engineers have started re-running it until it is green. Diagnose the problem and redesign the check, saying what a PR-level test can and cannot establish about a model.

A newly promoted model passes every offline gate and goes to full traffic at 14:00. At 14:40 the endpoint's error rate is normal but the business metric 'orders per 1,000 sessions' looks 6% lower than the same hour last week. Define the rollback criteria you would have agreed in advance, and what has to be true for the rollback to be quick and safe.

A nightly retraining DAG runs ingest -> validate -> build_features -> train -> evaluate -> register. After a transient failure in train, the orchestrator retried the whole run from build_features. The next morning the feature table has duplicated rows for 3 days, two models are registered under the same version tag, and a colleague's backfill of last week's partitions produced different features than the originals. List the design faults and how you would fix each, including how a step's cache key should be formed.

Your team has: a feature-engineering code repository, a weekly-refreshed training table, a model that ages quickly, and a data-quality alert system. Which events would you let trigger which pipeline (PR checks, full retraining, evaluation only, redeploy), and what would each pipeline run versus skip?

A teammate argues: 'We already save every trained model into a versioned folder in object storage, so a model registry is redundant.' What does a registry add beyond that folder, and in what situation would the folder genuinely be enough?

Your team stores scikit-learn pipelines as joblib files in a shared bucket that several teams, and one external partner, can write to. The serving image loads whichever file is newest at startup. After a base-image refresh the service starts logging version warnings and a handful of predictions change; separately, the security team flags the loading step. Explain both problems and what you would change in the loading path.

A fraud model (a scikit-learn pipeline: one-hot encoding, scaling, then gradient-boosted trees) is exported to ONNX so it can be served without a Python environment. In a shadow comparison, 0.8% of rows get a different predicted class from the original pipeline, and the ops lead asks whether ONNX 'guarantees identical behaviour'. What does an exchange format like this actually fix, what can still make outputs differ, and how would you test the export before it ships?

A registered model has an input signature of {age: double, plan_id: string, days_active: long}. Three clients misbehave: one sends age as the string '34'; one sends days_active as 3.7; a third sends perfectly typed rows but days_active measured in hours instead of days. Which of these can a signature-based schema check catch, which can it not, and what would you add around it?

Auditors ask you to bring back, with behaviour equivalent to the original, the model that served customers 14 months ago, and to show how it was built. Design what each registry version must record and how the model is packaged, then describe how promotion and rollback should work using aliases, including what is and is not atomic.

Choose batch, online (request/response) or streaming inference for each case and justify it on latency, freshness, cost and failure handling: (a) re-ranking 3 million product pages once a week for a newsletter; (b) a card-payment risk score that must return in about 100 ms at checkout and should reflect the cardholder's last 10 minutes of activity; (c) 50,000 sensor readings per second where an alert must fire within a few seconds of a pattern. Where would a hybrid beat a pure choice?

An image-embedding model sits behind an endpoint called by other backend services at about 300 requests/s with a 150 ms client budget. Each request currently carries a decoded 224x224x3 float32 tensor (150,528 values) as JSON over REST. A browser dashboard also calls a separate, low-volume prediction route. Would you move the main route to gRPC with protobuf, and what would you check before and after the move?

Implement a deterministic simulator for dynamic request batching on a single worker, plus a percentile helper.

simulate_microbatch(arrivals, max_batch, max_wait, overhead, per_item) -> (latencies, batch_sizes)

arrivals is a sorted list of arrival times in ms (ValueError if unsorted; ValueError if max_batch < 1 or max_wait < 0). Requests are served FIFO. A batch is dispatched at the first moment the worker is free AND (max_batch requests are waiting OR the oldest waiting request has waited max_wait ms). It contains the waiting requests up to max_batch (a request arriving exactly at the dispatch instant counts as waiting). Service time is overhead + per_item * batch_size, and the worker is busy for that time. Latency of a request is its finish time minus its arrival time. Also write percentile(values, p) using the nearest-rank definition. Then use it to explain, with an arrival every 1 ms (1000 requests/s) and every 20 ms, why max_batch and max_wait must be chosen from the load, using overhead=10 ms and per_item=0.5 ms.

A model endpoint scales out when average CPU passes 70%. Each replica serves about 4 requests at a time at roughly 120 ms each and takes about 90 s to become useful (image pull, model load, warm-up). Normally 3 replicas handle 50 requests/s. At 09:00 traffic ramps to 200 requests/s within two minutes. p99 goes to timeouts for several minutes even though CPU graphs look unremarkable (the work happens on an accelerator). Diagnose the failure and redesign the scaling policy.

During a deploy, a prediction service's p99 rises from 200 ms to 1.5 s. Its callers use a 1 s timeout and retry up to 3 times immediately. Within minutes the service, which normally runs at about 80% of capacity, is completely down. Explain the mechanism and describe the client and server changes (timeouts, retries, idempotency, fallbacks) that would have contained it.

You are about to put a recommendation-scoring endpoint (about 500 requests/s) into production. Define what you log for every prediction, which dashboard panels and alerts you build from the four golden signals (and which latency statistic you alert on), and what you deliberately do not page on. Mention the cost and privacy side of logging at this volume.

Your scoring API has a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, where a request is 'good' only if it returns a valid score within 300 ms. In the last hour 1.5% of requests were bad; in the last 5 minutes 0.4% were bad. How fast is the error budget burning, how much of the monthly budget did that hour use (assume uniform traffic), would a multiwindow policy that pages at a 14.4x burn rate over 1 hour and 5 minutes fire, and how should responses served by a fallback model be counted?
How does a canary release of a new model differ from a blue-green deployment, and what does each one cost you?

A team replacing a ranking model proposes: 'We will shadow the new model for two weeks. If its offline metrics on the logged shadow outputs and its latency look good, we go straight to 100%.' What can shadow deployment tell you, what can it not, and how would you sequence shadow, canary and A/B testing instead?

Your service handles 2 million requests per day. A new model is canaried at 1% of traffic for one day. The guardrail is the complaint rate, baseline 0.20%, and you do not want it to rise by more than 30% relative (to 0.26%). At the end of the day the canary shows 50 complaints in 20,000 requests (0.25%). One colleague says 'not statistically significant, so it is safe'; another says 'close enough to the limit, ship'. Evaluate both, and say how you would design the check. Complaints are only reliably known after a week.

Design the automatic promote/rollback policy for a canary that ramps a new fraud-scoring model through 5%, 25% and 100% of traffic (150 requests/s overall). Chargeback labels arrive up to 45 days late. Specify the comparison baseline, the guardrail metrics, minimum samples before each decision, example thresholds, and what stays manual. Explain why 'roll back if the canary's error rate is ever higher than control's' is a poor rule.

Model v7 was released together with a feature pipeline change: the feature merchant_category moved from 12 integer codes to 40 string categories and the old column was dropped from the online store. Two hours in, v7 regresses, so you roll back to v6, and v6's predictions collapse to near the default value. Explain why rollback failed, and how to structure the release so that rolling back a model is safe even when its inputs change.

A marketplace tests a new ranking model with a 50/50 split. One engineer wants to randomise each request; another wants to hash the user ID. The 'recommended for you' carousel shows a +6% click lift in week 1 that decays to +1.5% by week 3. Compare the two ways of splitting traffic for consistency and interference, explain the decay, and say what you would put in place.

A teammate's Dockerfile for a model-serving API is: a slim Python base image, WORKDIR /app, COPY . ., RUN pip install -r requirements.txt, then CMD to start the server. Editing one line of application code makes CI take about 8 minutes, because every large dependency wheel is downloaded and installed again. Why does that happen, and how would you restructure the file? What else would you tighten in this image before it goes to production?

A scoring service runs fine with docker run on a 32 GB workstation, but in Kubernetes with a memory limit of 4 GiB (request 2 GiB) the pod restarts every few hours, and kubectl describe shows the last state as terminated with reason OOMKilled. The container starts 2 server worker processes, each of which loads a model that takes 1.4 GiB in memory; a batch endpoint also uses a data loader with 4 worker processes that exchange tensors through shared memory (/dev/shm). Why did it not fail locally, how would you find the real memory need, and what would you change?

A model service takes 60 to 150 seconds to become usable: it downloads about 1 GB of weights and then warms up.
