Its Deployment has a liveness probe on /health with initialDelaySeconds 20, periodSeconds 10 and failureThreshold 3, and no readiness or startup probe. Pods enter CrashLoopBackOff and never serve. Explain what is happening and design the probe configuration, including what each endpoint should check and one way your design could still go wrong.

Your GPU inference Deployment has 4 replicas, each requesting 1 GPU, on a node pool that currently has exactly 4 GPUs in total, all occupied by those replicas. A model release is rolled out with maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0, and the rollout never completes. A new pod sits in Pending while the 4 old pods keep serving. Why, what are your options, and what does each cost? Assume a pod needs about 90 s to load the model.

A shared Kubernetes cluster has several 8-GPU nodes. A researcher requests nvidia.com/gpu: 0.5 for a small embedding service and the API server rejects it. Another job requests 'requests: 1, limits: 2'. Meanwhile an 8-GPU training job stays Pending even though the cluster shows 10 free GPUs in total, because small CPU-heavy pods and 1-GPU services have spread across the nodes. Explain the GPU resource rules, why the big job is stuck, and how you would organise scheduling.

A nightly ML pipeline runs five steps as containerised jobs: extract, build_features, train, evaluate, register_model. Two incidents occurred this week. First, train was OOM-killed at 90% and retried automatically; register_model then ran twice for that day and created two registry versions with identical weights. Second, a retried build_features step overwrote its output directory while train was starting, and train read a half-written dataset without error. Explain what properties each step needs, how you would pass artifacts between steps, and where caching and retries fit.
What is training-serving skew, and how is it different from data drift? Use a small concrete example, and say how you would tell which one you are looking at.

You are building training data for a churn model. Feature rows are (entity, feature_ts, value) and labelled events are (entity, event_ts). A colleague joins each event to the newest feature row per entity and gets a surprisingly high validation score. Explain what is wrong, then implement point_in_time_join(events, feature_rows, ttl) returning, for each event, the latest value with feature_ts <= event_ts and event_ts - feature_ts <= ttl, else None. Say how you treat ties on feature_ts.

A three-person team has one churn model. Features come from a data warehouse, the model scores 200,000 customers once a night, and results are written back to a table. The CTO wants to introduce a feature store with online and offline stores. What problems does a feature store solve, why do such systems usually have two stores, and would you adopt one here? Say what would change your answer.

Training features come from warehouse SQL; the live service recomputes the same features in application code written by another team. Audits keep finding differences: rounding, a 30-day window that is 'last 30 calendar days' in one place and '720 hours' in the other, and unknown categories mapped to different defaults. Propose how to give training and serving a single transformation definition, compare at least three approaches with their trade-offs, and explain how you would prove parity before and after the change.

A fraud model uses orders_last_24h per customer. About 3% of order records reach the warehouse 1 to 3 days after the order time, and cancelled orders are later deleted. Training features for the past year were backfilled last month with a single SQL query over the current orders table, using order_ts for the 24-hour window. Offline AUC is excellent but production is clearly worse, and logged online feature values for orders_last_24h are systematically lower than the backfilled values for the same transactions. Explain the mechanism and how to repair the training data and the process.

You log 1,000 served values of a categorical feature 'country' and have the training sample. After release, the offline-to-online metric gap is large. Implement categorical_skew(train, served, ...) that reports null rates, the L-infinity distance between category frequencies, and the share of served values whose category never appears in training, plus a list of threshold violations. Then say what each statistic would tell you, what mistake in the pipeline it would reveal, and what its limits are.

Implement psi(reference, current, n_bins=10, eps=1e-4) with numpy only. Bin edges must come from quantiles of the reference sample, current values outside the reference range must still be counted, and empty bins must not produce log(0) or a division by zero. Then explain why a PSI computed from 200 reference rows, 200 current rows and 40 bins is a poor drift signal even when nothing has changed.

On Monday 06:10 the drift job pages you: txn_amount has PSI 8.3 against the training reference, and the model's score distribution has collapsed to near-constant high scores. The same report shows discount_pct at PSI 0.05, below the team's 0.1 'investigate' line, yet a colleague points out its null rate went from 0.2% to 9% on Friday after an upstream ETL release; downstream code imputes nulls with 0. Product's first instinct is to retrain. How do you triage, what do the two numbers tell you, and what changes in monitoring?

A churn model has 120 input features. A daily job runs a two-sample test per feature at p < 0.01 and posts every hit to a Slack channel. Typically one to three features alert each day, nobody reads the channel any more, and last month a real null-rate regression went unnoticed. Redesign the alerting so that someone acts on what fires.

A daily job runs a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on each numeric feature, yesterday's 1,000,000 logged rows against a 1,000,000-row reference, and alerts at p < 0.05. It alerts on almost every feature every day. Another team uses PSI with 10 quantile bins and alerts above 0.1. Compare what the two signals measure, explain the alert storm, and say what neither tells you.

After a marketing campaign, the drift dashboard shows PSI above 0.25 on 14 of a fraud model's 120 features, while the score distribution and the review-queue rate look unchanged. Product wants to retrain tonight. With labels arriving weeks later, how do you decide whether this drift is harmful, and what would change your answer?

Your monitor computes one PSI per feature over all traffic and has stayed green for weeks. Customer support then reports that a newly launched market, about 10% of traffic, gets poor recommendations. The offending feature, basket_value, was roughly N(50, 10) in training for everyone and is now about N(80, 10) in that market only. Why did the aggregate monitor stay quiet, how would you change the monitoring, and what does it cost?

A scoring service handles 2 million predictions a day. A full feature payload is about 4 KB, so logging everything is 8 GB a day, and the security team also wants less raw data retained. You must support daily PSI checks per feature, hourly checks for a slice that is 0.5% of traffic, and a join with labels arriving weeks later. Design what you log and how you sample, and show that the sample is big enough.

daily_orders_per_user has a strong weekly cycle (weekends about 25% higher). You are choosing the reference for a daily drift check: (A) the training set, (B) yesterday, (C) the pooled previous 7 days, or (D) the same weekday over the previous 4 weeks. Separately, the true feature mean has been creeping up by 0.05 standard deviations per day. Compare the four options on false alarms and on detecting the slow creep, and recommend a setup.
What does 'continuous training' mean in an ML system, and how does it differ from CI/CD for ordinary application code?

A lender's credit model approves applicants scoring above a threshold (about 40% of 50,000 monthly applications). Each month the team retrains on repayment outcomes of the approved loans and keeps the score threshold. After six months offline metrics on the newest approved loans look better than ever, yet approval volume is flat, losses are not improving, and risk managers suspect good applicants are being turned away. What is going on, and how would you redesign the retraining data?

Your pipeline retrains automatically whenever PSI on any of five key features exceeds 0.25, evaluates on the latest 7 days and promotes the result if AUC beats the champion. Last week an upstream bug wrote income = 0 for six hours. The monitor fired, the pipeline retrained on a window that included those rows, and the new model passed the gate because the 7-day holdout contained the same corrupted rows. Which guardrails would have stopped this, and where in the pipeline does each sit?

A full retrain of your ranking model on the last 180 days takes about 14 hours on a shared cluster, and the business wants daily updates. A teammate proposes warm-starting from yesterday's model and training only on the last day's data, which takes about 40 minutes. Compare this with a full retrain on a sliding window, say what can go wrong with the warm start, and how you would decide with data.

A retrained model v12 was promoted on Tuesday and rolled back to v11 on Thursday after conversions fell. The team plans to 'just redeploy v11 and carry on'. What else has to be checked or changed so the rollback really restores the previous state, and so the same thing does not happen again on the next automated retrain?

A credit-default model's aggregate AUC rose from 0.781 to 0.789 after a retrain and the promotion gate passes. Before shipping, you want behavioural tests that an aggregate metric cannot show. Using numpy only, write invariance_failures(predict, X, col, perturb, tol) returning the rows whose score moves by more than tol when an irrelevant column is changed; directional_failures(predict, X, col, step, direction, tol) returning rows where a change that should raise risk lowers it; and behavioural_report(predict, X, checks, max_fail_rate) that turns the failure rates into a pass/fail. Then say how you would set the tolerances and why strict monotonicity may not hold for a tree ensemble.

Your training data is stored as training_rows(row_id, entity_id, prediction_ts, label_ts) plus a long table training_features(row_id, feature, feature_ts) in which feature_ts says when each feature value was computed. A nightly snapshot job and a join on calendar date are suspected of leaking future information. Write one SQLite query that lists, per feature, how many training rows use a value computed after the row's prediction time, the share of rows, the worst case in hours ahead, and how many of those values are even later than the label time, returning only offending features. Then interpret the result on a small example and say what the query cannot catch.

A nightly step validates the candidate training table against 'expected statistics' and has been green for nine months. This week a join bug dropped every row for region 'EU' and one feature became 100% null, yet the step stayed green and nobody noticed until a model metric fell. Reading the code you find: expected statistics are recomputed each run from the table being validated; per-region checks loop over regions present in the data; the null-rate check is `if null_rate > limit: fail` and null_rate is NaN for an empty group; and the job exits non-zero only on an exception. List how the validator can pass silently and how you would fix it and test the validator itself.

Your team generates a data schema by running automatic inference on last month's training data and then uses it unchanged to check production requests. Within a quarter it blocks harmless traffic and also misses real problems. Which parts of an inferred schema need human review, and what do you have to add that inference from a single snapshot cannot supply?

Your ML platform has 40 data scientists, one shared object-store bucket that every training job can write models to, a registry whose 'production' alias any user token can move, and serving images built from requirements files with unpinned packages and a mutable base-image tag. A red-team exercise shows a compromised notebook could get attacker code running inside production inference. Design the controls that close that path without blocking everyday experimentation: identities and permissions, artifact integrity, dependency and image hygiene, and the approval flow. For each control say what it protects against and what it does not.

A churn model's service logs, for every request, the full feature vector and the score into a warehouse table retained indefinitely for retraining and debugging. Features include date_of_birth and postcode, and the user_id is replaced by an unsalted SHA-256 hash 'to anonymise it'. Labels (churned or not) mature after 90 days. A privacy review asks what is wrong with this and what you will change. Answer as an engineer, not as a lawyer.

A customer asks for their personal data to be deleted. Their records were in the warehouse, the online and offline feature stores, prediction logs, analysts' exported CSVs, and the training sets of three production models, one of which is retrained nightly. Legal asks what you can honestly promise about the trained models. What do you delete, what can and cannot be said about models already trained, and how do you design the system so the promise is cheap to keep? Treat the legal threshold as a question for counsel.
What is a model card, and which fields would you require in one before a credit-scoring model is allowed to be promoted to production?

You expose a risk-scoring model through a public API that returns the full probability vector with six decimals and allows 10,000 calls per key per day. A security reviewer says an outsider could learn whether a specific person's record was in the training set. Explain the risk in plain terms, what training and model conditions make it worse, and how you would rank cheap mitigations by what they do and do not achieve.

After promoting recommendation model v12, the endpoint's p50 latency went from 38 ms to 41 ms but p99 went from 120 ms to 410 ms. The error rate is unchanged and the offline latency benchmark of v12 looked fine. In what order do you investigate, and what does each observation rule in or out?

A routine dependency update moved the numeric and ML libraries and the base image of a fraud-scoring service. After the Friday deploy, about 3% of responses are NaN and, for the rest, the score distribution is suspiciously narrow compared with the previous week. Nothing in the application code changed. What do you do in the first hour, how do you find the cause, and what would have prevented the incident?

A scoring pod with a 2 GiB memory limit is OOMKilled about every 11 hours. Its resident memory climbs roughly linearly from 0.9 GiB just after start, traffic is flat at about 10 requests per second, and no heap profiling is set up. How do you tell a true leak from a bounded cache or allocator fragmentation, find the source, and keep the service healthy until it is fixed?

Forty minutes after a model rollout, a guardrail shows 4% fewer approved applications at similar approval quality. The cause is either a flaw in the new model, a bug in one newly added feature's pipeline, or both. A one-line fix for the feature bug is ready and takes about 25 minutes to ship through CI; the previous model bundle still exists but the new feature has been written for the last 30 minutes. How do you decide between rolling back and rolling forward, what do you need to know, and what do you do in the first five minutes?

An online scoring service with a 99.95% availability target needs the online feature store on every request and the model registry at replica start-up. Last month a feature-store outage returned errors for 22 minutes, and a separate registry outage stopped autoscaled replicas from starting during a traffic peak. Design the degradation and recovery strategy for both dependencies, including what you log so retraining is not polluted by degraded predictions, and how you would test it.

Your pricing model's API has availability and latency SLOs and an error budget policy that halts releases when the budget is exhausted. Last quarter the service met 99.95% availability while a stale feature quietly degraded pricing quality for nine days. Labels (realised outcomes) arrive about three weeks late. How would you extend SLIs, SLOs and the budget policy to cover model quality, and what should the policy say when the quality budget is burning?

A recommendation model's click-through rate drifted down about 7% relative over 19 days before a product manager noticed in a weekly review. The cause: an upstream team renamed a column, and one feature silently fell back to its default for every user. Outline the postmortem: how to quantify impact, why detection was slow, the action items, and what the runbook for the next silent quality failure should say. What should the postmortem avoid?

Finance asks why the fraud-scoring endpoint is expensive. It serves 4.3 million requests a day (peak 100 requests/s, low overnight) on 4 always-on replicas; a replica costs 12 abstract cost units per hour and meets the latency target at up to 40 requests/s. Compute the cost per 1,000 predictions today, then for (a) autoscaling replicas to load with a floor of 2 and a 70% target utilisation, (b) additionally a quantised model assumed to give 1.6x throughput, and (c) additionally a 20% cache hit rate. What do you report, and what must you verify before claiming these savings?

A team runs three GPU workloads: (1) a 7-hour nightly fine-tune on a multi-GPU node; (2) an internal document classifier used by about 30 staff, roughly 200 requests a day in office hours, with a 3-minute cold start from image pull and weight load; (3) a customer-facing endpoint with a p99 target of 300 ms around the clock. The platform offers on-demand capacity, discounted capacity that can be reclaimed at short notice (preemptible or spot), and scale-to-zero for endpoints. Choose a capacity strategy for each workload and say what would change your mind.

Your ticket-triage service calls a hosted LLM through a model name that the provider re-points to its newest release. One Monday the share of tickets routed to 'billing' drops from 31% to 22% and the thumbs-down rate rises, although you deployed no code and no prompt change. Design the release process so that a provider-side model change is handled like any other dependency upgrade: what you pin and record, what you test before switching, how you roll out, and what you do when the provider announces a retirement date for the model you use.

Your assistant has an input filter and a separate output-moderation classifier, and the dashboard shows one number, 'blocked responses'. After Tuesday's release it goes from 1.2% to 3.9% of requests and p95 latency is also up 15%. No one has filed an incident. How do you decide whether this is real harmful traffic, a prompt or model change, or a mis-calibrated guardrail, and what must already be logged so that this is a 30-minute job rather than a 3-day one?

A multi-tenant support assistant handles 300,000 requests/day. Each call sends about 2,400 tokens of fixed content (system prompt, policy text, tool definitions) plus about 800 variable tokens and produces about 350 output tokens. Finance reports that the LLM bill grew 40% in a month while traffic grew 8%, and one tenant looks responsible. Using relative units (1k input tokens = 1 unit, 1k output tokens = 4 units, hypothetical), compute the baseline cost per request, estimate the saving from an 80% prefix-cache hit rate (cached input at 0.5 units/1k) and from routing half the traffic to a smaller model at 0.25x cost, and describe the attribution, budget and alerting controls plus the release checks that stop quality loss.

A recommender model passes a 5% canary and a 2-week A/B test (click-through +4%, no latency or error regressions) and goes to 100%. Six weeks later, repeat purchases per active user are down 2% against the pre-launch trend while click-through is still up. List the plausible mechanisms, say what evidence would separate them, and explain what release practice would have caught this earlier or made it cheaper to resolve.

A new fraud-scoring model ran in shadow for three weeks: the shadow logged scores for all mirrored requests, 99.9% of them agreed with the expected output computed offline, and the shadow call's p99 latency was 70 ms. After promotion, p99 for the live decision is 400 ms, customers get duplicate 'transaction held' notifications, and live scores for similar customers are noticeably lower than what the shadow had logged. Which properties of the shadow setup could have produced a clean pass that did not predict this, and what would you change in the next shadow?

An A/B test of a new ranking model (planned 50/50 by user hash) reports +3.1% conversion for treatment. A reviewer notices that assignment counts are 51,000 vs 49,000 users out of 100,000, and that the serving stack has (a) a result cache keyed by (query, locale) with a 10-minute TTL and (b) an online-learning component that updates one shared set of item-popularity weights from clicks in both arms. Explain what each of these can do to the experiment, how you would test for them, and how you would fix the setup.

A product-search ranker trained on click logs raises offline AUC from 0.78 to 0.81 on a held-out week of logged impressions, but the online A/B test shows conversion of 3.10% vs 3.09% (not significant, with enough traffic that a 1% relative change would have been detectable). Give the explanations specific to logged-data evaluation that you would investigate, in the order you would check them, and how you would change the offline evaluation so it predicts the online result better.

A real-time pricing model is served from an online store, while training features come from an offline pipeline. You are asked to build a consistency check that would have caught an incident where a deploy silently shifted one windowed count by one. Design the check: what you log at serving time, how and when you recompute offline, how you define tolerances for different feature types, how you use timestamps to root-cause a mismatch, and what you alert on. Show the comparison as SQL that you have executed.

Your team has a quarter to spend and must choose between (A) building a new model and (B) investing in monitoring and feature-consistency checks for the existing one. Hypothetical numbers: the model influences about 24 million per year of margin. A: offline estimate +1.5% relative uplift, past launches realised about half of the offline uplift, cost 5 engineer-months at 20,000 per engineer-month. B: history shows about 3 silent degradations a year, each costing about 2% of the model's margin until noticed, which takes about 6 weeks today; with monitoring about 3 days. B costs 3 engineer-months to build plus about 3 engineer-months of ongoing care per year. Work out the expected value of each, show the sensitivity to the assumptions you trust least, and give a recommendation.

Key concepts: R-squared; adjusted R-squared; overfitting; cross-validation; RMSE; MAE; AIC/BIC

Exploratory analysis and methodology
What is the curse of dimensionality?
Key concepts: curse of dimensionality; high dimensionality; clustering

Exploratory analysis and methodology
Is more data always better?
Key concepts: more data; data quality; high bias

Exploratory analysis and methodology
What are the advantages of plotting your data before performing analysis?
Key concepts: plotting data; outliers; skewness; multimodal variables; arithmetic mean

Exploratory analysis and methodology
How can you make sure that you don’t analyze something that ends up meaningless?
Key concepts: exploratory data analysis; hypothesis generation; exploitatory phase; summary statistics

Feature engineering and data preparation
How can you determine which features are the most important in your model?
Key concepts: feature importance; gradient boosting machine; random forest; information gain; forward variable selection

Data preparation and cleaning
How do you deal with some of your predictors being missing?
Key concepts: missing values; removing rows; predictors

Exploratory analysis and methodology
You have several variables that are positively correlated with your response, and you think combining all of the variables could give you a good prediction of your response. However, you see that in the multiple linear regression, one of the weights on the predictors is negative. What could be the issue?
Key concepts: multicollinearity; multiple linear regression; VIF; suppressor effect; lasso

Feature engineering and data preparation
Let’s say you’re given an unfeasible amount of predictors in a predictive modeling task. What are some ways to make the prediction more feasible?
Key concepts: dimensionality reduction; PCA; feature selection; lasso

Feature engineering and data preparation
Now you have a feasible amount of predictors, but you’re fairly sure that you don’t need all of them. How would you perform feature selection on the dataset?
Key concepts: feature selection; filter methods; wrapper methods; recursive feature elimination; embedded methods

Exploratory analysis and methodology
Your linear regression didn’t run and communicates that there are an infinite number of best estimates for the regression coefficients. What could be wrong?
Key concepts: perfect multicollinearity; singular X'X matrix; rank-deficient design matrix; p > n; dummy variable trap; ridge regression

Exploratory analysis and methodology
You run your regression on different subsets of your data, and find that in each subset, the beta value for a certain variable varies wildly. What could be the issue here?
Key concepts: heterogeneity; small-sample variance; multicollinearity; interaction terms; outliers and leverage; tree-based models

Decision trees and ensembles
What is the main idea behind ensemble learning? If I had many different models that predicted the same response variable, what might I want to do to incorporate all of the models? Would you expect this to perform better than an individual model or worse?
Key concepts: ensemble learning; weak learners; bagging; variance

Analytical case studies
Given that you have wifi data in your office, how would you determine which rooms and areas are underutilized and overutilized?
Key concepts: occupancy estimation; utilisation vs capacity; peak vs average; ground-truth calibration; segmentation; MAC randomisation; privacy

Analytical case studies
How could you use GPS data from a car to determine the quality of a driver?
Key concepts: GPS noise smoothing; harsh braking; speeding; map matching; exposure normalisation; validation against claims

Analytical case studies
Given accelerometer, altitude, and fuel usage data from a car, how would you determine the optimum acceleration pattern to drive over hills?
Key concepts: fuel consumption model; road grade from altitude; vehicle power equation; dynamic programming; constrained optimisation; sensor noise

Analytical case studies
Given position data of NBA players in a season’s games, how would you evaluate a basketball player’s defensive ability?
Key concepts: tracking data; expected points model; shot contest; opponent FG%; on/off adjusted plus-minus; regularisation; shrinkage toward the mean; team scheme confounding

Analytical case studies
How would quantify the influence of a Twitter user?
Key concepts: PageRank; follower graph; eigenvector centrality; damping factor; engagement-weighted edges; topic-sensitive influence

Analytical case studies
Given location data of golf balls in games, how would construct a model that can advise golfers where to aim?
Key concepts: shot dispersion model; expected strokes; strokes gained; Monte Carlo simulation; hazard penalties

Analytical case studies
You have 5000 people that rank 10 sushis in terms of saltiness. How would you aggregate this data to estimate the true saltiness rank in each sushi?
Key concepts: mean rank; median; ordinal data; interval data

Analytical case studies
Given data on congressional bills and which congressional representatives co-sponsored the bills, how would you determine which other representatives are most similar to yours in voting behavior? How would you evaluate who is the most liberal? Most republican? Most bipartisan?
Key concepts: co-sponsorship matrix; cosine similarity; nearest neighbours; dimensionality reduction; ideal point estimation; bipartisanship score

Analytical case studies
How would you come up with an algorithm to detect plagiarism in online content?
Key concepts: text normalisation; shingling; winnowing fingerprints; MinHash and LSH; Jaccard similarity; paraphrase detection with embeddings

Analytical case studies
You have data on all purchases of customers at a grocery store. Describe to me how you would program an algorithm that would cluster the customers into groups. How would you determine the appropriate number of clusters to include?
Key concepts: k-means; RFM features; feature scaling; elbow method; silhouette score; gap statistic; k-means++ initialisation

Analytical case studies
Let's say you're building the recommended music engine at Spotify to recommend people music based on past listening history. How would you approach this problem?
Key concepts: implicit feedback; matrix factorisation; content-based filtering; cold start; candidate generation and ranking; A/B testing

Neural network fundamentals
Do you think that deep network is better than a shallow one?
Key concepts: deep network; shallow network; deep representations; number of parameters

What is Backpropagation?
Key concepts: backpropagation; multilayer neural network; gradient; training algorithm

Deep learning overview
What are the deep learning frameworks or tools?
Key concepts: PyTorch; TensorFlow; JAX; Keras 3 multi-backend; define-by-run vs graph compilation; Hugging Face Transformers

Key concepts: data hunger; compute cost; overfitting on small data; interpretability; transfer learning; hyperparameter tuning

Key concepts: weight initialization; convergence; biases

Key concepts: zero initialization; weight initialization; backpropagation; gradients

Neural network fundamentals
What are the main types of layers in a neural network?
Key concepts: input layer; hidden layer; output layer

Activation functions
What is the use of the Activation function?
Key concepts: activation function; non-linearity; weighted sum and bias

What is a binary step function?
Key concepts: binary step function; activation function; threshold

What is the sigmoid function?
Key concepts: sigmoid function; logistic function; vanishing gradient; saturation; zero-centred output; binary classification output

Key concepts: model alias; pinned model snapshot; release unit; dependency change; golden set replay; canary rollout; retirement date; rollback by configuration

LLMOps specifics (prompt versioning, eval gates, token cost, guardrail monitoring)
Your assistant has an input filter and a separate output-moderation classifier, and the dashboard shows one number, 'blocked responses'. After Tuesday's release it goes from 1.2% to 3.9% of requests and p95 latency is also up 15%. No one has filed an incident. How do you decide whether this is real harmful traffic, a prompt or model change, or a mis-calibrated guardrail, and what must already be logged so that this is a 30-minute job rather than a 3-day one?
Key concepts: guardrail trigger rate; block-and-regenerate loop; false-positive review; offline replay; prompt version logging; fail-open guardrail; per-stage latency

A multi-tenant support assistant handles 300,000 requests/day. Each call sends about 2,400 tokens of fixed content (system prompt, policy text, tool definitions) plus about 800 variable tokens and produces about 350 output tokens. Finance reports that the LLM bill grew 40% in a month while traffic grew 8%, and one tenant looks responsible. Using relative units (1k input tokens = 1 unit, 1k output tokens = 4 units, hypothetical), compute the baseline cost per request, estimate the saving from an 80% prefix-cache hit rate (cached input at 0.5 units/1k) and from routing half the traffic to a smaller model at 0.25x cost, and describe the attribution, budget and alerting controls plus the release checks that stop quality loss.
Key concepts: tokens per request; prefix caching; per-tenant attribution; budget alert; model routing; cost per resolved ticket; cached-token reporting

MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
A recommender model passes a 5% canary and a 2-week A/B test (click-through +4%, no latency or error regressions) and goes to 100%. Six weeks later, repeat purchases per active user are down 2% against the pre-launch trend while click-through is still up. List the plausible mechanisms, say what evidence would separate them, and explain what release practice would have caught this earlier or made it cheaper to resolve.
Key concepts: proxy metric; long-term holdback; novelty effect; outcome horizon; difference-in-differences; seasonality confound; exposure narrowing

A new fraud-scoring model ran in shadow for three weeks: the shadow logged scores for all mirrored requests, 99.9% of them agreed with the expected output computed offline, and the shadow call's p99 latency was 70 ms. After promotion, p99 for the live decision is 400 ms, customers get duplicate 'transaction held' notifications, and live scores for similar customers are noticeably lower than what the shadow had logged. Which properties of the shadow setup could have produced a clean pass that did not predict this, and what would you change in the next shadow?
Key concepts: shadow deployment; critical-path latency; side effects; idempotency key; feature freshness; serving-time feature logging; recording stubs

An A/B test of a new ranking model (planned 50/50 by user hash) reports +3.1% conversion for treatment. A reviewer notices that assignment counts are 51,000 vs 49,000 users out of 100,000, and that the serving stack has (a) a result cache keyed by (query, locale) with a 10-minute TTL and (b) an online-learning component that updates one shared set of item-popularity weights from clicks in both arms. Explain what each of these can do to the experiment, how you would test for them, and how you would fix the setup.
Key concepts: sample ratio mismatch; chi-square test; cache key contamination; shared online learner; interference (SUTVA); A/A test; served versus assigned variant

MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
A product-search ranker trained on click logs raises offline AUC from 0.78 to 0.81 on a held-out week of logged impressions, but the online A/B test shows conversion of 3.10% vs 3.09% (not significant, with enough traffic that a 1% relative change would have been detectable). Give the explanations specific to logged-data evaluation that you would investigate, in the order you would check them, and how you would change the offline evaluation so it predicts the online result better.
Key concepts: position bias; selection bias; logged propensities; inverse-propensity weighting; direct feedback loop; nDCG at top ranks; objective mismatch

MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
A real-time pricing model is served from an online store, while training features come from an offline pipeline. You are asked to build a consistency check that would have caught an incident where a deploy silently shifted one windowed count by one. Design the check: what you log at serving time, how and when you recompute offline, how you define tolerances for different feature types, how you use timestamps to root-cause a mismatch, and what you alert on. Show the comparison as SQL that you have executed.
Key concepts: serving-time feature logging; point-in-time recomputation; per-feature tolerance; mismatch rate by hour; rule of three; late-arriving events; NULL mismatch

MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
Your team has a quarter to spend and must choose between (A) building a new model and (B) investing in monitoring and feature-consistency checks for the existing one. Hypothetical numbers: the model influences about 24 million per year of margin. A: offline estimate +1.5% relative uplift, past launches realised about half of the offline uplift, cost 5 engineer-months at 20,000 per engineer-month. B: history shows about 3 silent degradations a year, each costing about 2% of the model's margin until noticed, which takes about 6 weeks today; with monitoring about 3 days. B costs 3 engineer-months to build plus about 3 engineer-months of ongoing care per year. Work out the expected value of each, show the sensitivity to the assumptions you trust least, and give a recommendation.

qk_concise.text:
Statistics fundamentals
What is R2? What are some other metrics that could be better than R2 and why?
Key concepts: R-squared; adjusted R-squared; overfitting; cross-validation; RMSE; MAE; AIC/BIC
R^2 (coefficient of determination) is 1 - SS_res/SS_tot: the fraction of the variance of y that the model explains relative to a mean-only baseline. For OLS with an intercept, evaluated on the training data, it lies in [0, 1] and cannot decrease when you add a predictor, so it rewards complexity and says nothing about overfitting. On held-out data it can be negative (worse than predicting the mean). It also does not show whether the model is correctly specified or whether errors are large in absolute terms. Better alternatives depend on the goal. Adjusted R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p - 1) penalises extra predictors, so it can fall when a useless variable is added.

Exploratory analysis and methodology
What is the curse of dimensionality?
Key concepts: curse of dimensionality; high dimensionality; clustering
High dimensionality makes clustering hard, because having lots of dimensions means that everything is "far away" from each other. For example, to cover a fraction of the volume of the data we need to capture a very wide range for each variable as the number of variables increases All samples are close to the edge of the sample. And this is a bad news because prediction is much more difficult near the edges of the training sample. The sampling density decreases exponentially as p increases and hence the data becomes much more sparse without significantly more data. We should conduct PCA to reduce dimensionality.

Exploratory analysis and methodology
Is more data always better?
Key concepts: more data; data quality; high bias
Statistically, It depends on the quality of your data, for example, if your data is biased, just getting more data won’t help. It depends on your model. If your model suffers from high bias, getting more data won’t improve your test results beyond a point. You’d need to add more features, etc. - Practically, Also there’s a tradeoff between having more data and the additional storage, computational power, memory it requires. Hence, always think about the cost of having more data.

Exploratory analysis and methodology
What are the advantages of plotting your data before performing analysis?
Key concepts: plotting data; outliers; skewness; multimodal variables; arithmetic mean
Data sets have errors. You won't find them all but you might find some. That 212 year old man. That 9 foot tall woman. Variables can have skewness, outliers etc. Then the arithmetic mean might not be useful. Which means the standard deviation isn't useful. Variables can be multimodal! If a variable is multimodal then anything based on its mean or median is going to be suspect.

Exploratory analysis and methodology
How can you make sure that you don’t analyze something that ends up meaningless?
Key concepts: exploratory data analysis; hypothesis generation; exploitatory phase; summary statistics
Proper exploratory data analysis. In every data analysis task, there's the exploratory phase where you're just graphing things, testing things on small sets of the data, summarizing simple statistics, and getting rough ideas of what hypotheses you might want to pursue further. Then there's the exploitatory phase, where you look deeply into a set of hypotheses. The exploratory phase will generate lots of possible hypotheses, and the exploitatory phase will let you really understand a few of them. Balance the two and you'll prevent yourself from wasting time on many things that end up meaningless, although not all.

Feature engineering and data preparation
How can you determine which features are the most important in your model?
Key concepts: feature importance; gradient boosting machine; random forest; information gain; forward variable selection
Run the features though a Gradient Boosting Machine or Random Forest to generate plots of relative importance and information gain for each feature in the ensembles. Look at the variables added in forward variable selection

Data preparation and cleaning
How do you deal with some of your predictors being missing?
Key concepts: missing values; removing rows; predictors
Remove rows with missing values - This works well if 1) the values are missing randomly 2) if you don't lose too much of the dataset after doing so. Build another predictive model to predict the missing values - This could be a whole project in itself, so simple techniques are usually used here. Use a model that can incorporate missing data \- Like a random forest, or any tree-based method.

Exploratory analysis and methodology
You have several variables that are positively correlated with your response, and you think combining all of the variables could give you a good prediction of your response. However, you see that in the multiple linear regression, one of the weights on the predictors is negative. What could be the issue?
Key concepts: multicollinearity; multiple linear regression; VIF; suppressor effect; lasso
Most likely multicollinearity (or a suppressor effect): a coefficient measures a predictor's effect holding the others fixed, so its sign can differ from its marginal correlation with the response. Check the correlation matrix / VIF. Options: drop or combine correlated predictors, use ridge/lasso, or principal component regression; if the goal is prediction rather than interpretation the model can be left as is.

Feature engineering and data preparation
Let’s say you’re given an unfeasible amount of predictors in a predictive modeling task. What are some ways to make the prediction more feasible?
Key concepts: dimensionality reduction; PCA; feature selection; lasso
Reduce dimensionality: PCA or other projections, feature selection (filter methods, L1/lasso), dropping low-variance or highly correlated features, using domain knowledge, or using regularised models / more data.

Feature engineering and data preparation
Now you have a feasible amount of predictors, but you’re fairly sure that you don’t need all of them. How would you perform feature selection on the dataset?
Key concepts: feature selection; filter methods; wrapper methods; recursive feature elimination; embedded methods
Filter methods (univariate statistical tests per feature), wrapper methods (recursive feature elimination: train, drop the weakest ~10% of features, retrain, stop when accuracy drops sharply), and embedded methods (lasso / elastic net, which can zero out coefficients; tree-based importances). Ridge shrinks coefficients but does not remove features.

Exploratory analysis and methodology
Your linear regression didn’t run and communicates that there are an infinite number of best estimates for the regression coefficients. What could be wrong?
Key concepts: perfect multicollinearity; singular X'X matrix; rank-deficient design matrix; p > n; dummy variable trap; ridge regression
The design matrix is rank-deficient, so X'X is singular and the least-squares normal equations have infinitely many solutions. The usual causes are perfect multicollinearity (one predictor is an exact linear combination of others, for example a duplicated column, a unit-converted copy, or a set of one-hot dummies for every category alongside an intercept, the dummy variable trap) and having more parameters than observations (p > n, counting the intercept), which forces the columns to be linearly dependent. Note that p > n is a sufficient cause but not the only one; perfect correlation between just two predictors is enough. Fitted values are still unique, only the individual coefficients are not identifiable. Fixes: drop or merge redundant columns, drop one dummy level, collect more observations, reduce dimensionality (PCA), or add regularisation.

Exploratory analysis and methodology
You run your regression on different subsets of your data, and find that in each subset, the beta value for a certain variable varies wildly. What could be the issue here?
Key concepts: heterogeneity; small-sample variance; multicollinearity; interaction terms; outliers and leverage; tree-based models
Several things can make a coefficient swing between subsets, and heterogeneity is only one of them. Check these in order: (1) high estimation variance: small subsets give large standard errors, so wild betas may just be noise (compare confidence intervals across subsets, or bootstrap); (2) multicollinearity: if the variable is correlated with others, its coefficient is unstable even though predictions are not (check VIF); (3) outliers or high-leverage points dominating some subsets; (4) true heterogeneity: the relationship really differs across segments, or an interaction or non-linear effect is missing from the model.

Decision trees and ensembles
What is the main idea behind ensemble learning? If I had many different models that predicted the same response variable, what might I want to do to incorporate all of the models? Would you expect this to perform better than an individual model or worse?
Key concepts: ensemble learning; weak learners; bagging; variance
The assumption is that a group of weak learners can be combined to form a strong learner. Hence the combined model is expected to perform better than an individual model. Assumptions: average out biases reduce variance Bagging works because some underlying learning algorithms are unstable: slightly different inputs leads to very different outputs. If you can take advantage of this instability by running multiple instances, it can be shown that the reduced instability leads to lower error. Boosting works because of the focus on better defining the "decision edge". By reweighting examples near the margin (the positive and negative examples) you get a reduced error. Use the outputs of your models as inputs to a meta-model. For example, if you're doing binary classification, you can use all the probability outputs of your individual models as inputs to a final logistic regression (or any model, really) that can combine the probability estimates.

Analytical case studies
Given that you have wifi data in your office, how would you determine which rooms and areas are underutilized and overutilized?
Key concepts: occupancy estimation; utilisation vs capacity; peak vs average; ground-truth calibration; segmentation; MAC randomisation; privacy
Frame it as estimating occupancy per room over time, then comparing it with capacity and opening hours. 1. Data and mapping: WiFi association logs (device ID, access point, timestamp) joined to a floor plan that maps each AP to rooms or zones. Aggregate to fixed intervals (e.g. 15 minutes) as the count of distinct devices per zone. 2. Turn devices into people: exclude static devices (printers, desktops, APs) and very short visits, deduplicate by user login where available, and calibrate devices-per-person against a ground-truth sample (manual counts, door sensors, badge swipes or room bookings). Randomised MAC addresses inflate counts unless handled. 3. Metrics per room: average and peak (e.g.

Analytical case studies
How could you use GPS data from a car to determine the quality of a driver?
Key concepts: GPS noise smoothing; harsh braking; speeding; map matching; exposure normalisation; validation against claims
Start by defining what 'quality' means (usually safety, sometimes efficiency) and then derive features from the GPS trace. Clean it first: GPS is noisy, so smooth positions and map-match to the road network. Speed and acceleration are derived from successive fixes, so sampling rate matters. Features: speeding relative to the posted limit (needs road-segment data), harsh braking and harsh acceleration events (deceleration or acceleration above calibrated thresholds), cornering speed, speed variance, time of day and road type, and mileage. Normalise by exposure (events per 100 km, not raw counts), otherwise heavy drivers look worse. Combine features into a score. A hand-weighted score is easy to explain, but a better approach is supervised: train a model on features to predict outcomes such as accident or insurance-claim history, and validate on held-out drivers. Route efficiency is a separate dimension and not a safety signal.

Analytical case studies
Given accelerometer, altitude, and fuel usage data from a car, how would you determine the optimum acceleration pattern to drive over hills?
Key concepts: fuel consumption model; road grade from altitude; vehicle power equation; dynamic programming; constrained optimisation; sensor noise
Split it into a model and an optimiser. Model: estimate the road grade from altitude against distance (smooth it, as altitude is noisy) and estimate fuel rate as a function of speed, acceleration and grade. A physics-based form is a good prior: required power = rolling resistance + aerodynamic drag + grade force (m g sin θ) + inertial term (m a) times speed, and fuel flow rises with power and depends on engine efficiency. Fit the unknown parameters, or a flexible model such as gradient boosting, to the logged data. The accelerometer measures a mix of true acceleration and gravity along the slope, so derive acceleration from speed or correct for the tilt. Optimiser: choose a speed profile v(s) along the route that minimises total fuel subject to speed limits, acceleration limits and a bound on total trip time (without the time constraint the answer is trivially 'drive slowly').

Analytical case studies
Given position data of NBA players in a season’s games, how would you evaluate a basketball player’s defensive ability?
Key concepts: tracking data; expected points model; shot contest; opponent FG%; on/off adjusted plus-minus; regularisation; shrinkage toward the mean; team scheme confounding
Defence is hard to measure from box scores, so use tracking data (player and ball x-y coordinates over time) together with play-by-play and build metrics that compare outcomes with what was expected. 1. Shot-level: model the expected make probability of each shot from shot location, distance to the nearest defender, shooter identity, shot type and game context. For shots a player contests, compute expected points minus actual points (points saved). A related view is opponent FG% at the rim when the player is the nearest defender versus the expected FG%. 2. Possession-level: opponent points per possession while the player is on court, adjusted for teammates and opponents (e.g. regularised regression on stints, RAPM-style) because raw on/off numbers are confounded by who else is playing. 3.

Analytical case studies
How would quantify the influence of a Twitter user?
Key concepts: PageRank; follower graph; eigenvector centrality; damping factor; engagement-weighted edges; topic-sensitive influence
Build a directed graph in which an edge goes from a follower to the account they follow, then run PageRank: a user's score is high if they are followed by many users who themselves have high scores. Iteratively, rank(i) = (1-d)/N + d * sum over followers j of rank(j)/outdegree(j), with damping factor d (commonly 0.85) and special handling of dangling nodes; it converges to the stationary distribution of a random walk and is the principal-eigenvector style of centrality. Plain follower count is easy to inflate with bots and says nothing about attention, so improve it with engagement-weighted edges (retweets, replies, mentions rather than just follows), retweet-cascade size, and bot filtering. Topic-sensitive PageRank (restarting the walk in a topic-specific seed set) gives influence per topic.

Analytical case studies
Given location data of golf balls in games, how would construct a model that can advise golfers where to aim?
Key concepts: shot dispersion model; expected strokes; strokes gained; Monte Carlo simulation; hazard penalties
Frame it as choosing an aim point that minimises expected strokes to finish the hole. Two components: (1) A value function E[strokes | ball location and lie], estimated from historical shots (average strokes remaining from each distance/lie, the basis of strokes-gained metrics, or fitted by regression or dynamic programming). Hazards such as water and bunkers enter naturally as locations with a higher expected-strokes value (penalty strokes). (2) A dispersion model: for a golfer and club, the distribution of landing positions relative to the aim point, often a bivariate Gaussian with distance and lateral spread (fitted per golfer, possibly shrunk toward a population mean when data are sparse). For each candidate aim point a, compute E[strokes | a] = integral of P(land at x | a, golfer) * value(x) dx, by grid integration or Monte Carlo sampling, and recommend the argmin.

Analytical case studies
You have 5000 people that rank 10 sushis in terms of saltiness. How would you aggregate this data to estimate the true saltiness rank in each sushi?
Key concepts: mean rank; median; ordinal data; interval data
Some people would take the mean rank of each sushi. If I wanted something simple, I would use the median, since ranks are (strictly speaking) ordinal and not interval, so adding them is a bit risque (but people do it all the time and you probably won't be far wrong).

Analytical case studies
Given data on congressional bills and which congressional representatives co-sponsored the bills, how would you determine which other representatives are most similar to yours in voting behavior? How would you evaluate who is the most liberal? Most republican? Most bipartisan?
Key concepts: co-sponsorship matrix; cosine similarity; nearest neighbours; dimensionality reduction; ideal point estimation; bipartisanship score
Build a representatives x bills matrix (1 if the representative sponsored or co-sponsored, or voted yes; 0 otherwise; or use +1/-1/0 for yes/no/missing if you have roll-call votes). Missing is not the same as opposition, so treat absences carefully. Similarity to your representative: compute cosine or Jaccard similarity between the row vectors and rank the others; the nearest neighbours are the most similar. This is neighbourhood-based collaborative filtering. Ideology: reduce the matrix with SVD/PCA (or a proper ideal-point model such as DW-NOMINATE used in political science) and read the first dimension, which in US data generally separates the parties; the extreme ends are the most liberal and most conservative.

Analytical case studies
How would you come up with an algorithm to detect plagiarism in online content?
Key concepts: text normalisation; shingling; winnowing fingerprints; MinHash and LSH; Jaccard similarity; paraphrase detection with embeddings
Pipeline: normalise text (lowercase, strip punctuation and markup), split into overlapping word k-grams (shingles), and hash them. Compare documents by Jaccard similarity of their shingle sets, or by containment (what fraction of the suspect text appears in the source). Comparing all pairs does not scale, so use fingerprinting: winnowing (as in MOSS) keeps a representative subset of hashes with a guarantee of detecting matches above a length threshold, and MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing finds candidate near-duplicates without pairwise comparison. A plain bag of words discards order and flags unrelated texts that share vocabulary, so shingles preserve local order and are better for copied passages.

Analytical case studies
You have data on all purchases of customers at a grocery store. Describe to me how you would program an algorithm that would cluster the customers into groups. How would you determine the appropriate number of clusters to include?
Key concepts: k-means; RFM features; feature scaling; elbow method; silhouette score; gap statistic; k-means++ initialisation
Aggregate transactions into one feature vector per customer: for example recency, frequency and monetary value, plus spend share per product category. Scale features (k-means uses Euclidean distance, so large-valued features dominate), and consider log-transforming skewed spend. Run k-means (with k-means++ initialisation and several restarts, since it finds local optima) for a range of k. Choosing k: SSE (inertia) always decreases as k grows, so look for the elbow where the improvement flattens; that is subjective, so confirm with the silhouette score (higher is better), the gap statistic, or stability across resamples. Finally check that the clusters are interpretable and actionable for the business, which often decides between neighbouring k values.

Analytical case studies
Let's say you're building the recommended music engine at Spotify to recommend people music based on past listening history. How would you approach this problem?
Key concepts: implicit feedback; matrix factorisation; content-based filtering; cold start; candidate generation and ranking; A/B testing
Define the goal and metric first (for example listening time or retention, not just clicks). Data is mostly implicit feedback (plays, skips, saves, completions), which is noisy: a play is not a like, so weight signals by confidence. Architecture: a two-stage system. Candidate generation narrows millions of tracks to hundreds, using collaborative filtering (matrix factorisation or embeddings learned from user-item interactions, item-to-item similarity) plus content-based retrieval from audio features, metadata and text. Content features also handle cold start, where new tracks or users have no interaction history. A ranking model (for example gradient boosted trees or a neural network) then scores candidates with user, item and context features (time, device) to predict something like the probability of a non-skipped listen. A re-ranking step enforces diversity, freshness and business rules.

Neural network fundamentals
Do you think that deep network is better than a shallow one?
Key concepts: deep network; shallow network; deep representations; number of parameters
Both shallow and deep networks are good enough and capable of approximating any function. But for the same level of accuracy, deeper networks can be much more efficient in terms of computation and number of parameters. Deeper networks can create deep representations. At every layer, the network learns a new, more abstract representation of the input.

Neural network fundamentals
What is Backpropagation?
Key concepts: backpropagation; multilayer neural network; gradient; training algorithm
Backpropagation is a training algorithm which is used for multilayer neural networks. It transfers the error information from the end of the network to all the weights inside the network. It allows the efficient computation of the gradient. Backpropagation can be divided into the following steps: It can forward propagation of training data through the network to generate output. It uses target value and output value to compute error derivative concerning output activations. It can backpropagate to compute the derivative of the error concerning output activations in the previous layer and continue for all hidden layers. It uses the previously calculated derivatives for output and all hidden layers to calculate the error derivative concerning weights. It updates the weights.

Deep learning overview
What are the deep learning frameworks or tools?
Key concepts: PyTorch; TensorFlow; JAX; Keras 3 multi-backend; define-by-run vs graph compilation; Hugging Face Transformers
The main general-purpose deep learning frameworks today are PyTorch, TensorFlow (usually used through its Keras API) and JAX. Keras 3 is multi-backend: it can run on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch (OpenVINO is supported for inference only). Higher-level libraries such as Hugging Face Transformers, PyTorch Lightning and fastai are built on top of these frameworks rather than replacing them. Several older frameworks are no longer a good default for new work: Theano and Microsoft CNTK are no longer actively developed, Caffe2 was merged into the PyTorch codebase, and Chainer is in maintenance mode (bug fixes only). Frameworks differ in their programming model (eager/imperative define-by-run versus graph compilation, e.g. via XLA in JAX), deployment tooling and ecosystem. The landscape changes, so check current documentation before choosing.

Neural network fundamentals
What are the disadvantages of deep learning?
Key concepts: data hunger; compute cost; overfitting on small data; interpretability; transfer learning; hyperparameter tuning
Main disadvantages: (1) Data hungry: deep nets usually need large labelled datasets; on small data they tend to overfit, although transfer learning, data augmentation and regularisation can reduce the problem. (2) Computationally expensive: training large models can take hours to days or longer on GPUs/TPUs depending on model size, data and hardware, which also costs money and energy. (3) Hard to interpret: they are largely black boxes, which is a problem in regulated or high-stakes settings. (4) Many hyperparameters and design choices (architecture, learning rate, regularisation) with costly tuning and sensitivity to initialisation. (5) Can be brittle: sensitive to distribution shift and adversarial examples, and may learn spurious correlations. For small tabular datasets, simpler models such as gradient boosted trees or linear models are often as good or better and far cheaper.

Initialisation and optimisation
What is the meaning of term weight initialization in neural networks?
Key concepts: weight initialization; convergence; biases
In neural networking, weight initialization is one of the essential factors. A bad weight initialization prevents a network from learning. On the other side, a good weight initialization helps in giving a quicker convergence and a better overall error. Biases can be initialized to zero. The standard rule for setting the weights is to be close to zero without being too small.

Initialisation and optimisation
Why is zero initialization not a good weight initialization process?
Key concepts: zero initialization; weight initialization; backpropagation; gradients
If the set of weights in the network is put to a zero, then all the neurons at each layer will start producing the same output and the same gradients during backpropagation. As a result, the network cannot learn at all because there is no source of asymmetry between neurons. That is the reason why we need to add randomness to the weight initialization process.

Neural network fundamentals
What are the main types of layers in a neural network?
Key concepts: input layer; hidden layer; output layer
Input Layer The input layer contains input neurons which send information to the hidden layer. Hidden Layer The hidden layer is used to send data to the output layer. Output Layer The data is made available at the output layer.

Activation functions
What is the use of the Activation function?
Key concepts: activation function; non-linearity; weighted sum and bias
The activation function is used to introduce nonlinearity into the neural network so that it can learn more complex function. Without the Activation function, the neural network would be only able to learn function, which is a linear combination of its input data. Activation function translates the inputs into outputs. The activation function is responsible for deciding whether a neuron should be activated or not. It makes the decision by calculating the weighted sum and further adding bias with it. The basic purpose of the activation function is to introduce non-linearity into the output of a neuron.

Activation functions
What is a binary step function?
Key concepts: binary step function; activation function; threshold
The binary step function is an activation function, which is usually based on a threshold. If the input value is above or below a particular threshold limit, the neuron is activated, then it sends the same signal to the next layer. This function does not allow multi-value outputs.

Activation functions
What is the sigmoid function?
Key concepts: sigmoid function; logistic function; vanishing gradient; saturation; zero-centred output; binary classification output
The sigmoid (logistic) function is sigma(x) = 1 / (1 + e^-x). It squashes any real input into the open interval (0, 1), is monotonic and smooth, equals 0.5 at x = 0, and saturates towards 1 for large positive x and towards 0 for large negative x (it never reaches them exactly in theory; in floating point it rounds to them). Uses: the output unit for binary classification (the output is read as a probability and paired with binary cross-entropy), and the gates of LSTM/GRU cells. As a hidden-layer activation it has fallen out of favour for three reasons: its derivative sigma(x)(1 - sigma(x)) is at most 0.25 and near zero in the saturated regions, so gradients vanish in deep networks; its outputs are not zero-centred, which makes updates to the next layer's weights share the same sign; and exp is relatively costly.

Activation functions
What is Tanh function?
Key concepts: tanh; hyperbolic tangent; activation function; sigmoid function
The hyperbolic tangent function, also known as tanh for short, is a similar shaped nonlinear activation function. It provides output values between -1.0 and 1.0. Later in the 1990s and through the 2000s, this function was preferred over the sigmoid activation function as models. It was easier to train and often had better predictive performance.

Activation functions
What is ReLU function?
Key concepts: ReLU; dying ReLU; vanishing gradient; sparse activations
ReLU is f(x) = max(0, x): positive inputs pass through unchanged and negative inputs become 0. It is cheap to compute, does not saturate for x > 0 (which eases vanishing gradients) and produces sparse activations; its drawback is the 'dying ReLU' problem, where a unit stuck in the negative region outputs 0 and gets no gradient.

Activation functions
What is the use of leaky ReLU function?
Key concepts: leaky ReLU; dying ReLU; non-zero gradient
Leaky ReLU outputs x for x > 0 and alpha*x for x <= 0, where alpha is a small constant (e.g. 0.01). Negative inputs therefore still produce a small non-zero gradient, which reduces the 'dying ReLU' problem.

Activation functions
What is the softmax function?
Key concepts: softmax function; probability distribution; multi-class classification
The softmax function is used to calculate the probability distribution of the event over 'n' different events. One of the main advantages of using softmax is the output probabilities range. The range will be between 0 to 1, and the sum of all the probabilities will be equal to one. When the softmax function is used for multi-classification model, it returns the probabilities of each class, and the target class will have a high probability.

Activation functions
Can Relu function be used in output layer?
Key concepts: ReLU; output layer; softmax; sigmoid; hidden layers
Usually not for classification outputs (use sigmoid for binary and softmax for multi-class). ReLU, or a similar non-negative activation, can be used on the output of a regression model whose target is non-negative. ReLU is mainly used in hidden layers.

Activation functions
In which layer softmax activation function used?
Key concepts: softmax; output layer; multi-class classification; cross-entropy; sigmoid for multi-label; logits; attention
Softmax is typically used in the output layer of a network for multi-class classification with mutually exclusive classes. It maps a vector of logits z to probabilities softmax(z)_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j), which are positive and sum to 1, and is paired with cross-entropy loss. For multi-label problems (classes not exclusive) use independent sigmoids instead, and for binary classification a single sigmoid. Softmax is not restricted to the output layer: attention mechanisms apply it to scores inside hidden layers, and mixture-of-experts gating uses it to weight experts. In practice frameworks often take raw logits in the loss (e.g. PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss) for numerical stability, so the softmax is folded into the loss rather than being a separate layer.

Autoencoders and generative models
What do you understand by Autoencoder?
Key concepts: autoencoder; representation learning; artificial neural network
Autoencoder is an artificial neural network. It can learn representation for a set of data without any supervision. The network automatically learns by copying its input to the output; typically, the internal representation consists of smaller dimensions than the input vector. As a result, they can learn efficient ways of representing the data. Autoencoder consists of two parts; an encoder tries to fit the inputs to the internal representation, and a decoder converts the internal state to the outputs.

What do you mean by Dropout?
Key concepts: dropout; regularization; overfitting; model averaging
Dropout is a cheap regularization technique used for reducing overfitting in neural networks. We randomly drop out a set of nodes at each training step. As a result, we create a different model for each training case, and all of these models share weights. It's a form of model averaging.

What do you understand by Tensors?
Key concepts: tensors; multidimensional arrays; high dimensional data
Tensors are nothing but a de facto for representing the data in deep learning. They are just multidimensional arrays, which allows us to represent the data having higher dimensions. In general, we deal with high dimensional data sets where dimensions refer to different features present in the data set.

What is Model Capacity?
Key concepts: model capacity; underfitting; overfitting; regularization; early stopping
Capacity is the range of functions a model can represent; it grows with the number and size of layers and parameters. Too little capacity underfits; too much relative to the amount of data overfits. It is managed through architecture size, regularisation and early stopping.

Neural network fundamentals
What is the cost function?
Key concepts: cost function; weights and biases; gradient descent
A cost function describes us how well the neural network is performing with respect to its given training sample and the expected output. It may depend on variables such as weights and biases.It provides the performance of a neural network as a whole. In deep learning, our priority is to minimize the cost function. That's why we prefer to use the concept of gradient descent.

Explain gradient descent?
Key concepts: gradient descent; steepest descent; cost function; optimization algorithm
An optimization algorithm that is used to minimize some function by repeatedly moving in the direction of steepest descent as specified by the negative of the gradient is known as gradient descent. It's an iteration algorithm, in every iteration algorithm, we compute the gradient of a cost function, concerning each parameter and update the parameter of the function via theta := theta - alpha * grad J(theta), where theta is the parameter vector, α - learning rate, J(Θ) - is a cost function In machine learning, it is used to update the parameters of our model. Parameters represent the coefficients in linear regression and weights in neural networks.

Explain the following variant of Gradient Descent: Stochastic, Batch, and Mini-batch?
Key concepts: gradient descent; stochastic gradient descent; batch gradient descent; mini-batch gradient descent
Stochastic Gradient Descent Stochastic gradient descent is used to calculate the gradient and update the parameters by using only a single training example. Batch Gradient Descent Batch gradient descent is used to calculate the gradients for the whole dataset and perform just one update at each iteration. Mini-batch Gradient Descent Mini-batch gradient descent is a variation of stochastic gradient descent. Instead of a single training example, mini-batch of samples is used. Mini-batch gradient descent is one of the most popular optimization algorithms.

Initialisation and optimisation
What are the main benefits of Mini-batch Gradient Descent?
Key concepts: mini-batch; gradient variance; vectorisation; SGD; saddle points; batch size; learning rate
Mini-batch gradient descent updates the weights using the gradient over a small batch (e.g. 32-512 examples), which sits between SGD (batch of 1) and full-batch descent. Benefits: - Computational efficiency: batches are processed as vectorised matrix operations, which uses GPU/CPU hardware far better than one-example-at-a-time SGD. - Memory: only one batch has to be in memory, so datasets larger than memory or very large models can be trained. - Lower-variance gradient than SGD: the variance of the gradient estimate shrinks roughly as 1/batch size, giving more stable updates, while you still get many updates per epoch (unlike full-batch descent), which usually means faster progress per unit of compute. - Useful noise: the remaining gradient noise can help move through saddle points and shallow regions, and is often reported to act as a mild regulariser.

Neural network fundamentals
What is matrix element-wise multiplication? Explain with an example.
Key concepts: element-wise multiplication; Hadamard multiplication; matrix multiplication; NumPy
Element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication multiplies corresponding entries of two matrices of the same shape. Example: [[1,2],[3,4]] * [[5,6],[7,8]] = [[5,12],[21,32]]. In NumPy this is a * b (not a @ b, which is matrix multiplication).

Convolutional networks
What do you understand by a convolutional neural network?
Key concepts: CNN; convolutional layer; filters; feedforward neural network; dot product
A convolutional neural network, often called CNN, is a feedforward neural network. It uses convolution in at least one of its layers. The convolutional layer contains a set of filter (kernels). This filter is sliding across the entire input image, computing the dot product between the weights of the filter and the input image. As a result of training, the network automatically learns filters that can detect specific features.

What is an RNN?
Key concepts: RNN; hidden state; sequential data; backpropagation through time
An RNN is a neural network for sequential data (text, speech, time series). It processes one element at a time and carries a hidden state forward, so earlier inputs can influence later outputs; the same weights are reused at every time step. It is trained with backpropagation through time and suffers from vanishing/exploding gradients, which LSTM and GRU cells were designed to reduce.

Sequence models and transformers
What are the issues faced while training in Recurrent Networks?
Key concepts: RNN; backpropagation through time; vanishing gradient; backpropagation
Recurrent Neural Network uses backpropagation algorithm for training, but it is applied on every timestamp. It is usually known as Back-propagation Through Time (BPTT). There are two significant issues with Back-propagation, such as: Vanishing Gradient When we perform Back-propagation, the gradients tend to get smaller and smaller because we keep on moving backward in the Network. As a result, the neurons in the earlier layer learn very slowly if we compare it with the neurons in the later layers.Earlier layers are more valuable because they are responsible for learning and detecting simple patterns. They are the building blocks of the network. If they provide improper or inaccurate results, then how can we expect the next layers and complete network to perform nicely and provide accurate results. The training procedure tales long, and the prediction accuracy of the model decreases. Exploding Gradient Exploding gradients are the main problem when large error gradients accumulate. They provide result in very large updates to neural network model weights during training. Gradient Descent process works best when updates are small and controlled.

What is a perceptron?

A perceptron is similar to the actual neuron in the human brain. It receives inputs from various entities and applies functions to these inputs, which transform them to be the output. A perceptron is mainly used to perform binary classification where it sees an input, computes functions based on the weights of the input, and outputs the required transformation.
