Key concepts: PCA; LDA; maximum variance; dimensionality reduction; class labels
PCA is unsupervised: it finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance and ignores class labels. LDA is supervised: it uses class labels to find directions that maximise between-class separation relative to within-class scatter. PCA is used for general dimensionality reduction/compression; LDA for class-separating projections and as a classifier. LDA yields at most (number of classes - 1) components.

Instance-based and probabilistic classifiers
What distance metrics can be used in KNN?
Key concepts: distance metrics; KNN; Euclidean distance; Manhattan distance; cosine distance
Common distance metrics for KNN: Euclidean (default; continuous features), Manhattan, Minkowski (generalises both), Hamming (categorical/binary features), cosine distance (text, high-dimensional sparse data) and Mahalanobis (accounts for feature correlation). Features should be scaled first so no single feature dominates.

Statistics fundamentals
Which metrics can be used to measure correlation of categorical data?
Key concepts: categorical variables; chi-square test; Cramer's V; mutual information
The chi-square test of independence tests whether two categorical variables are associated; its p-value indicates evidence of association, and Cramer's V (derived from chi-square, range 0 to 1) measures the strength of the association. Mutual information is another option.

Feature engineering and data preparation
Which algorithm can be used in value imputation in both categorical and continuous categories of data?
Key concepts: imputation; KNN imputation; MICE; random forest imputation; mean imputation
Several methods work for both types. KNN imputation fills a missing value from the nearest neighbours (mean for continuous, mode for categorical). Others: MICE / iterative imputation with a suitable model per column, random forest imputation (missForest), and simple mean/median/mode imputation.

Bias-variance and regularisation
When should ridge regression be preferred over lasso?
Key concepts: ridge regression; lasso; L2 vs L1 penalty; correlated predictors; sparsity; elastic net
Prefer ridge (L2 penalty) when you believe many predictors each contribute a little, so you do not want to discard any: ridge shrinks coefficients toward zero but never exactly to zero. It is particularly better with highly correlated predictors: lasso tends to pick one of a correlated group arbitrarily and the choice is unstable across samples, whereas ridge spreads weight across them. Lasso can also select at most n variables when p > n. Ridge also has a closed-form solution and a smooth objective, which makes it easy to fit, and it usually predicts better than lasso when the true coefficients are dense. Choose lasso (L1) when you expect a sparse truth and need automatic feature selection and an interpretable model. Elastic net combines both penalties and is a good default when predictors are correlated and you still want some sparsity. Standardise predictors first, since the penalties depend on feature scale, and choose the penalty strength by cross-validation.

Feature engineering and data preparation
Which algorithms can be used for important variable selection?
Key concepts: filter methods; wrapper methods; embedded methods; permutation importance; impurity importance bias; recursive feature elimination
There are three families. Filter methods score features independently of a model: correlation or mutual information with the target, chi-square test, ANOVA F-test, variance threshold. Wrapper methods search subsets by fitting a model repeatedly: forward/backward stepwise selection and recursive feature elimination (RFE). Embedded methods select during training: lasso (L1) shrinks coefficients to zero, and tree ensembles such as random forest or XGBoost give feature importances. Caution with importance charts: impurity-based (Gini) importance in random forests is biased toward continuous and high-cardinality features and splits credit among correlated features; permutation importance on held-out data is more reliable. Do selection inside cross-validation (not on the full dataset first), or you will leak information and overestimate performance. Practical combo: remove constant and near-duplicate features, rank with a tree model plus permutation importance, then confirm by CV that dropping the lowest-ranked features does not hurt.

Decision trees and ensembles
What ensemble technique is used by Random forests?
Key concepts: random forest; bagging; ensemble technique
Bagging is the technique used by Random Forests. Random forests are a collection of trees which work on sampled data from the original dataset with the final prediction being a voted average of all trees.

Decision trees and ensembles
What ensemble technique is used by gradient boosting trees?
Key concepts: boosting; gradient boosting; pseudo-residuals; learning rate shrinkage; additive model; early stopping
Gradient boosting machines (GBM) use boosting: trees are added sequentially, each one trained to correct the errors of the current ensemble. Concretely, at each step the new tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions (the pseudo-residuals; plain residuals for squared error), and its output is added to the model scaled by a learning rate: F_m = F_{m-1} + eta * h_m. The result is a stage-wise additive model of shallow trees. Contrast with bagging (random forest), where deep trees are trained independently in parallel on bootstrap samples and averaged to reduce variance; boosting mainly reduces bias and can overfit if run too long. Control it with a small learning rate, number of trees (with early stopping on a validation set), tree depth and row/column subsampling.

Bias-variance and regularisation
If we have a high bias error what does it mean? How to treat it?
Key concepts: high bias; underfitting; model complexity; high variance; regularization
High bias means the model is too simple to capture the true pattern (underfitting): training and validation error are both high. Remedies: use a more complex model, add features or interactions, reduce regularisation, and train longer (for iterative models such as neural networks). Compare with high variance, where training error is low but validation error is high.

Validation and model selection
Which type of sampling is better for a classification model and why?
Key concepts: stratified sampling; random sampling; class balance; train and test sets
Stratified sampling is better in case of classification problems because it takes into account the balance of classes in train and test sets. The proportion of classes is maintained and hence the model performs better. In case of random sampling of data, the data is divided into two parts without taking into consideration the balance classes in the train and test sets. Hence some classes might be present only in train sets or validation sets. Hence the results of the resulting model are poor in this case.

Regression diagnostics
What is a good metric for measuring the level of multicollinearity?
Key concepts: multicollinearity; VIF; tolerance
The variance inflation factor (VIF) measures how much the variance of a coefficient is inflated by multicollinearity: VIF_j = 1 / (1 - R_j^2), where R_j^2 comes from regressing predictor j on the other predictors. Tolerance = 1 - R_j^2 = 1 / VIF. Rule of thumb: VIF = 1 means no correlation; above about 5 (some use 10) signals problematic multicollinearity.

Feature engineering and data preparation
When can a categorical value be treated as a continuous variable and what effect does it have when done so?
Key concepts: ordinal encoding; one-hot encoding; nominal vs ordinal; linearity assumption; misspecification; tree-based models
An ordinal categorical variable can be encoded as integers and treated as continuous when the order is meaningful and the gaps between levels are roughly equal, e.g. a 1-5 rating or an education level, or when it is really a count or discretised numeric (year, number of rooms). The effect: one parameter instead of k - 1 dummy variables (fewer parameters, less risk of overfitting, works with sparse data), but a linear model then assumes each step has the same effect on the target. If spacing is unequal or the relationship is non-monotonic, the model is misspecified and performance can suffer. Tree-based models are less affected, since splits only use the ordering. Nominal categories (no order, e.g. colour or city) should not be integer-coded as continuous for linear or distance-based models, since the arbitrary numbers invent an order and distances.

Linear and logistic regression
What is the role of maximum likelihood in logistic regression.
Key concepts: maximum likelihood estimation; logistic regression; log-likelihood; cross-entropy; gradient descent
Logistic regression has no closed-form solution, so coefficients are found by maximum likelihood: choose the weights that maximise the log-likelihood sum[ y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p) ], where p = sigmoid(w.x + b). Maximising this is equivalent to minimising cross-entropy loss, solved iteratively (gradient descent, Newton/IRLS).

Validation and model selection
What is a pipeline?
Key concepts: pipeline; data leakage; preprocessing; cross-validation; scikit-learn
A pipeline chains data-processing steps (imputation, scaling, encoding, feature selection) and a final estimator into a single object (e.g. scikit-learn Pipeline). It applies the same steps in order at fit and predict time, avoids data leakage during cross-validation (preprocessing is fitted only on training folds), and makes the workflow reproducible and easy to tune and deploy.

Decision trees and ensembles
What are the benefits of pruning?
Key concepts: pruning; overfitting; model complexity; bias; variance
Pruning helps in the following: - Reduces overfitting - Shortens the size of the tree - Reduces complexity of the model - Trades a small increase in bias for lower variance

Statistics fundamentals
What is normal distribution?
Key concepts: normal distribution; symmetric curve; area under the curve
The distribution having the below properties is called normal distribution. - The mean, mode and median are all equal. - The curve is symmetric at the center (i.e. around the mean, μ). - Exactly half of the values are to the left of center and exactly half the values are to the right. - The total area under the curve is 1.

Statistics fundamentals
What is the 68 per cent rule in normal distribution?
Key concepts: 68-95-99.7 rule; normal distribution; standard deviation; empirical rule
In a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two, and about 99.7% within three (the empirical or 68-95-99.7 rule).

Statistics fundamentals
What is a chi-square test?
Key concepts: chi-square test; contingency table; test statistic
A chi-square determines if a sample data matches a population. A chi-square test for independence compares two variables in a contingency table to see if they are related. A very small chi-square test statistics implies observed data fits the expected data extremely well.

Statistics fundamentals
What is a random variable?
Key concepts: random variable; random experiment; discrete vs continuous random variables
A random variable is a variable whose value is a numerical outcome of a random experiment (formally a function from outcomes to numbers). Examples: the number of heads in 10 coin tosses, or the value shown when rolling a die. It can be discrete or continuous.

Statistics fundamentals
What is the degree of freedom?
Key concepts: degrees of freedom; sample variance; chi-square test; t distribution; F distribution
Degrees of freedom is the number of values in a calculation that are free to vary. For a sample variance it is n - 1 (one degree is used up by estimating the mean); for a chi-square test of independence on an r x c table it is (r - 1)(c - 1). Degrees of freedom determine the shape of the t, chi-square and F distributions.

Recommender systems
How does item-based collaborative filtering recommend similar items?
Key concepts: item-based collaborative filtering; cosine similarity; adjusted cosine; user-item matrix; nearest neighbours; cold start; precomputed similarity
Item-based collaborative filtering computes similarity between items from users' interaction patterns, then recommends items similar to those a user has already liked or bought. Each item is represented by its column of the user-item matrix (ratings or purchases), and the similarity of two items is computed over the users who interacted with both, e.g. cosine similarity, adjusted cosine (subtracting each user's mean rating) or Pearson correlation. To score item i for user u, take a similarity-weighted average of u's ratings of the items most similar to i: score(u, i) = sum_j sim(i, j) r_uj / sum_j |sim(i, j)|, over the k nearest neighbours of i that u has rated. Rank the unseen items by this score.

Model evaluation and metrics
What is a false positive?
Key concepts: false positive; diagnostic test; presence of a condition
It is a test result which wrongly indicates that a particular condition or attribute is present. Example – “Stress testing, a routine diagnostic tool used in detecting heart disease, results in a significant number of false positives in women”

Model evaluation and metrics
What is a false negative?
Key concepts: false negative; diagnostic test; absence of a condition
A test result which wrongly indicates that a particular condition or attribute is absent. Example – “it’s possible to have a false negative—the test says you aren’t pregnant when you are”

Regression diagnostics
What is the error term composed of in regression?
Key concepts: error term; irreducible error; bias; variance
Error is a sum of bias^2 + variance + irreducible error (noise) in regression. Bias and variance error can be reduced but not the irreducible error.

Regression diagnostics
Which performance metric is better R2 or adjusted R2?
Key concepts: adjusted R2; R2; number of predictors
Adjusted R^2 is generally preferred when comparing models with different numbers of predictors. R^2 never decreases when a predictor is added, even a useless one. Adjusted R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p - 1) penalises extra predictors and only rises if the new variable improves the fit more than chance would.

What do you understand by L1 and L2 regularization?
Key concepts: L1 regularization; L2 regularization; lasso; ridge regression; sparse solutions
L1 (lasso) adds lambda * sum|w| to the loss; it produces sparse solutions (many weights exactly zero), so it also performs feature selection, and corresponds to a Laplace prior. L2 (ridge) adds lambda * sum(w^2); it shrinks all weights toward zero without making them exactly zero, handles correlated features more stably, and corresponds to a Gaussian prior.

Which one is better, Naive Bayes Algorithm or Decision Trees?

What is log likelihood in logistic regression?
Key concepts: log-likelihood; logistic regression; maximum likelihood estimation; AIC; deviance
The log-likelihood of a logistic regression is the sum over observations of y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p), where p is the predicted probability. Higher (less negative) values mean a better fit. Maximum likelihood estimation maximises it; deviance = -2 * log-likelihood is used to compare nested models (likelihood-ratio test) and AIC = 2k - 2 * log-likelihood to compare models with different numbers of parameters.

Evaluate on data the model has not seen (hold-out set or cross-validation), using several complementary tools: 1. Discrimination: ROC curve, which plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across all thresholds; AUC is the probability that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative (0.5 is chance). Threshold-based metrics: the confusion matrix at a chosen cut-off gives precision, recall, F1 and specificity. Support vector machines
What are the advantages of SVM algorithms?
Key concepts: SVM; high-dimensional spaces; margin maximization; kernel trick; support vectors
Advantages: effective in high-dimensional spaces, including when features outnumber samples; the margin-maximising objective gives good generalisation; the kernel trick allows non-linear boundaries; the decision function depends only on the support vectors, so the model is compact. Applied ML case studies
When does XGBoost tend to outperform an SVM, and when might an SVM be preferable?
Key concepts: XGBoost; gradient boosting; SVM kernels; tabular data; feature scaling; high-dimensional sparse data; cross-validation
Neither is universally better; it depends on the data, so compare with cross-validation. XGBoost (gradient-boosted trees) tends to do better on tabular data with mixed numeric and categorical-like features, non-linear interactions, and missing values (it handles missing values natively). It needs little feature scaling, is invariant to monotonic transformations of features, scales to large numbers of rows, and gives feature importances. It has many hyperparameters to tune (learning rate, depth, number of trees, regularisation) and can overfit noisy small data. SVMs can be preferable on smaller datasets, in high-dimensional sparse settings such as text (a linear SVM is a strong baseline), when the margin-based solution suits the problem, or when a suitable kernel is known for structured inputs.

Support vector machines
What is the difference between SVM Rank and SVR (Support Vector Regression)?
Key concepts: SVM Rank; SVR; ranking; regression
One is used for ranking and the other is used for regression. There is a crucial difference between regression and ranking. In regression, the absolute value is crucial. A real number is predicted. In ranking, the only thing of concern is the ordering of a set of examples. We only want to know which example has the highest rank, which one has the second-highest, and so on. From the data, we only know that example 1 should be ranked higher than example 2, which in turn should be ranked higher than example 3, and so on. We do not know by how much example 1 is ranked higher than example 2, or whether this difference is bigger than the difference between examples 2 and 3.

Support vector machines
What is the difference between hard-margin and soft-margin SVM, and what role does the kernel play?
Key concepts: hard-margin SVM; soft-margin SVM; slack variables; kernel; linearly separable data
Hard-margin SVM requires every training point to be correctly classified outside the margin, so it only works if the data are linearly separable and is sensitive to outliers. Soft-margin SVM allows some violations, penalised by slack variables and controlled by C (large C = fewer violations, higher variance; small C = wider margin, more regularisation). The kernel is a separate choice: a linear kernel keeps a linear boundary, while kernels such as RBF or polynomial map data implicitly into a higher-dimensional space to give non-linear boundaries. Soft-margin can be used with any kernel.

Support vector machines
How is linear classifier relevant to SVM?
Key concepts: linear classifier; SVM; loss function; kernels
An svm is a type of linear classifier. If you don’t mess with kernels, it’s arguably the most simple type of linear classifier. Linear classifiers (all?) learn linear functions from your data that map your input to scores like so: scores = Wx + b. Where W is a matrix of learned weights, b is a learned bias vector that shifts your scores, and x is your input data. This type of function may look familiar to you if you remember y = mx + b from high school. A typical svm loss function ( the function that tells you how good your calculated scores are in relation to the correct labels ) would be hinge loss. It takes the form: Loss = sum over all scores except the correct score of max(0, scores – scores(correct class) + 1).

Instance-based and probabilistic classifiers
What are the advantages of using a naive Bayes for classification?
Key concepts: conditional independence; Bayes' rule; Laplace smoothing; multinomial naive Bayes; probability calibration; Gaussian naive Bayes
Naive Bayes applies Bayes' rule with the assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class, so P(class|x) is proportional to P(class) * product_j P(x_j|class). Advantages: - Very simple, fast to train (mostly counting or estimating per-feature means/variances) and to predict; cost grows linearly with the number of samples and features, so it scales to large, high-dimensional data such as text. - Zero counts are handled with Laplace (additive) smoothing so an unseen feature value does not zero the whole product. - Needs relatively little training data: it estimates many low-dimensional distributions rather than a joint one. A known result (Ng and Jordan, 2001) is that it reaches its asymptotic error with fewer samples than logistic regression, although that asymptotic error is higher when the independence assumption is badly violated.

Instance-based and probabilistic classifiers
Is Gaussian Naive Bayes the same as Bernoulli Naive Bayes?
Key concepts: Gaussian Naive Bayes; Bernoulli Naive Bayes; binary features; continuous features; normal distribution
Bernoulli Naive Bayes: It assumes that all our features are binary such that they take only two values. Means 0s can represent “word does not occur in the document” and 1s as “word occurs in the document”. Gaussian Naive Bayes: Because of the assumption of the normal distribution, Gaussian Naive Bayes is used in cases when all our features are continuous. For example in Iris dataset features are sepal width, petal width, sepal length, petal length. So its features can have different values in the data set as width and length can vary. We can’t represent features in terms of their occurrences. This means data is continuous. Hence we use Gaussian Naive Bayes here.

Instance-based and probabilistic classifiers
What is the difference between the Naive Bayes Classifier and the Bayes classifier?
Key concepts: Naive Bayes; Bayes classifier; conditional independence; Bayes error; Bayesian networks
The Bayes classifier assigns x to the class with the highest posterior P(y|x); it is the theoretically optimal classifier (lowest possible error, the Bayes error) but needs the true joint distribution, which is impractical in high dimensions. Naive Bayes approximates it by assuming the features are conditionally independent given the class, so P(x|y) factorises into a product of per-feature terms that can be estimated from limited data. Bayesian networks sit in between by allowing selected dependencies.

Instance-based and probabilistic classifiers
In what real world applications is Naive Bayes classifier used?
Key concepts: Naive Bayes; spam filtering; text classification; conditional independence assumption; Laplace smoothing; probability calibration
Naive Bayes is used mostly where features are high-dimensional counts or indicators and a fast, simple, data-efficient baseline is wanted: - Spam filtering: classify an email from the words it contains. This is the classic use. - Document and topic categorisation: news articles into technology, politics, sports, and similar labels. - Sentiment analysis: positive vs negative text with bag-of-words features (a strong baseline, though often beaten by discriminative or neural models). - Real-time or large-scale classification where training (just counting) and prediction are very cheap, and incremental updates are easy. - Medical diagnosis or fault detection as a probabilistic baseline with roughly independent symptoms or tests. Why it works despite the unrealistic assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class: it only needs the correct ranking of class scores, not accurate probabilities, and with limited data its low variance is an advantage.

Instance-based and probabilistic classifiers
Is naive Bayes supervised or unsupervised?
Key concepts: Naive Bayes; supervised learning; Bayes' theorem; conditional independence; generative classifier
Naive Bayes is a supervised learning algorithm: it is trained on labelled data. It is a family of generative classifiers based on Bayes' theorem with a conditional-independence assumption, with variants such as Gaussian, Multinomial and Bernoulli Naive Bayes depending on the feature type. It handles multi-class problems naturally.

Model evaluation and metrics
What do you understand by Precision and Recall?
Key concepts: precision; recall; F1 score; sensitivity; positive predictive value
Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the items predicted positive, the fraction that are truly positive (positive predictive value). Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of the actual positives, the fraction found (sensitivity). Higher precision means fewer false alarms; higher recall means fewer misses; F1 combines them.

Bias-variance and regularisation
What are overfitting and underfitting? Why does the decision tree algorithm often suffer from overfitting?
Key concepts: overfitting; underfitting; decision tree; generalization
Overfitting occurs when a model captures noise in the data, while underfitting occurs when the model fails to capture the underlying pattern. Decision trees overfit because they may perfectly fit training data, creating overly specific branches that do not generalize well.

Decision trees and ensembles
What is OOB error and how does it occur?
Key concepts: out-of-bag error; bootstrap sampling; bagging; random forest; 1/e probability; validation without hold-out
Each tree in a bagged ensemble (e.g. a random forest) is trained on a bootstrap sample: n draws with replacement from n rows. The chance that a given row is never drawn is (1 - 1/n)^n, which tends to 1/e, about 36.8% (roughly one third); so about 63.2% of distinct rows are in each tree's sample. The rows left out of a tree are its out-of-bag (OOB) samples. OOB error is computed by predicting every training row using only the trees for which it was out-of-bag, aggregating those predictions (vote or mean) and comparing with the true label. No separate validation set is needed and it is similar in spirit to cross-validation, since each prediction comes from models that did not see that row.

Data preparation and cleaning
How do you handle outliers in the data?
Key concepts: IQR rule; z-score; winsorising; robust statistics; error versus genuine outlier; isolation forest
First investigate: is the outlier a data error (typo, sensor fault, wrong unit) or a genuine extreme value? The treatment depends on that, and sometimes the outliers are the signal (fraud, failures). Detect: boxplots and scatter plots for a visual check; the IQR rule (flag values below Q1 - 1.5*IQR or above Q3 + 1.5*IQR); z-scores (commonly |z| > 3), noting that mean and standard deviation are themselves distorted by outliers, so a median/MAD-based modified z-score is more robust; and multivariate methods such as isolation forest or Mahalanobis distance for outliers that are unusual only in combination.

Validation and model selection
List popular cross-validation techniques.
Key concepts: cross-validation; k-fold cross-validation; stratified k-fold; leave-one-out; bootstrap resampling
K-fold, stratified K-fold (preserves class proportions), leave-one-out, leave-p-out, repeated k-fold, group k-fold (keeps groups together), time-series (forward-chaining) split, and bootstrap resampling. Grid search and random search are hyperparameter-search strategies that are usually combined with cross-validation.

Advanced learning paradigms
What can you do if your dataset has no target variable but you need supervised learning?
Key concepts: active learning; weak supervision; semi-supervised learning; self-supervised learning; pseudo-labels; clustering; annotation
Supervised learning requires labels, so the real task is to obtain or approximate them. Options: - Get labels: manual annotation by domain experts or crowdsourcing; active learning to label only the most informative samples; or derive them from a business rule or an existing outcome that is a legitimate proxy for the target. - If some labels exist: semi-supervised learning or weak supervision (labelling functions, heuristics) to extend them. - Self-supervised pre-training on the unlabelled data to learn representations, which still needs a small labelled set to train the downstream task. - Reframe as unsupervised learning if the goal allows (clustering, anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction). Cluster assignments can be used as pseudo-labels, but they reflect the clustering algorithm's assumptions and not ground truth, so a model trained on them mostly reproduces the clusters.

Recommender systems
How do recommendation systems handle sparsity issues?
Key concepts: sparsity; matrix factorization; ALS; recommendation system; latent factors
Common approaches: matrix factorisation (SVD-style latent factor models, ALS) that learns dense low-dimensional user and item factors; dimensionality reduction; content-based or hybrid features so items/users with few interactions can still be scored; using implicit feedback to add signal; and regularisation. RMSE is used afterwards to evaluate prediction accuracy.

Validation and model selection
What are hyperparameters and how are they different from parameters?
Key concepts: hyperparameters; model parameters; validation set; cross-validation; random search; test-set leakage
Parameters are values the model learns from the training data by optimization, e.g. neural-network weights and biases, linear/logistic regression coefficients, or the split features and thresholds of a decision tree. Hyperparameters are configuration choices set before (or outside) the training procedure that control the model's structure or the learning process itself, e.g. learning rate, number of layers or units, batch size, regularization strength, tree depth, k in k-NN, or SVM C and gamma. The training algorithm does not update hyperparameters by gradient descent on the training loss; they are chosen by tuning: grid search, random search or Bayesian optimization, evaluated on a validation set or by cross-validation. The final test set must stay untouched, otherwise the performance estimate is optimistically biased through tuning leakage. Hyperparameters strongly affect capacity (bias-variance trade-off) and optimization behaviour.

ML foundations
What is VC Dimension?
Key concepts: VC dimension; shattering; hypothesis class capacity; generalisation bound; linear classifier capacity; XOR labelling
The VC (Vapnik-Chervonenkis) dimension of a hypothesis class H is the size of the largest set of points that H can shatter, where shattering means that for every one of the 2^h possible labellings of the points some hypothesis in H classifies them exactly. Precision matters: it is enough that there exists one set of h points that can be shattered; it does not need to work for every set of h points. If arbitrarily large sets can be shattered the VC dimension is infinite. Examples: lines (linear classifiers with a bias) in 2D have VC dimension 3: some 3 points (non-collinear) can be shattered, but no 4 points can (the XOR labelling of a square fails). In general, linear classifiers in R^d have VC dimension d + 1. The class {sign(sin(ax))} has one parameter but infinite VC dimension, so it is not simply the parameter count.

ML foundations
What are the advantages and disadvantages of neural networks?
Key concepts: neural networks; non-linear relationships; black box; overfitting; GPUs
Advantages: learn complex non-linear relationships, learn features automatically from raw data, scale well with large datasets, and parallelise well on GPUs. Disadvantages: need large amounts of data and compute, act as black boxes (hard to interpret), are sensitive to hyperparameters and prone to overfitting without regularisation.

Dimensionality reduction
Explain Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues.
Key concepts: eigenvectors; eigenvalues; PCA; covariance matrix; principal directions
For a square matrix A, an eigenvector v is a non-zero vector whose direction is unchanged by the transformation, A v = lambda v; the eigenvalue lambda is the factor by which it is stretched. In PCA the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are the principal directions and the eigenvalues give the variance along each.

Model evaluation and metrics
What performance metrics are used for linear regression?
Key concepts: MSE and RMSE; MAE; R-squared; adjusted R-squared; held-out evaluation; residual analysis
Common metrics: MSE (mean of squared errors; penalises large errors, in squared units), RMSE (its square root, in the target's units), MAE (mean absolute error; less sensitive to outliers, easy to interpret), R-squared (fraction of variance in y explained, 1 - SSE/SST) and adjusted R-squared (R-squared penalised for the number of predictors, so it does not rise automatically when useless variables are added). MAPE is sometimes used for relative error but breaks when targets are near zero. Use them on held-out data (or via cross-validation): training R-squared always increases with more predictors and can overstate quality, while test R-squared can even be negative. For comparing models with different numbers of parameters, AIC or BIC are also used. Metrics should be complemented by residual plots to check linearity and constant variance.

Hypothesis testing and A/B testing
How is p-value useful?
Key concepts: p-value; null hypothesis; alpha; effect size
The p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a result at least as extreme as the one found. A small p-value (below the chosen alpha, e.g. 0.05) is evidence against the null hypothesis. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about effect size or model quality.

Regression diagnostics
How do you deal with multicollinearity?
Key concepts: multicollinearity; variance inflation factor; ridge regression; principal component regression; partial least squares; condition number
Multicollinearity means predictors are strongly linearly related. It inflates the variance of coefficient estimates (large standard errors, unstable or sign-flipping coefficients) but does not bias them, and does not necessarily hurt prediction, so it matters mostly when you need to interpret coefficients. Detect: correlation matrix, variance inflation factor (VIF; values above roughly 5 to 10 are a common warning rule of thumb), or a high condition number of the design matrix. Remedies: drop or combine redundant variables (or pick one from each correlated group using domain knowledge); use PCA to build uncorrelated components (principal component regression) or partial least squares, which make components relevant to the target, at the cost of interpretability; use ridge regression (or elastic net), which stabilises estimates; centre variables when the collinearity comes from polynomial or interaction terms; or collect more data/more variation. If the goal is only prediction, you can often leave it alone, ideally with regularisation.

Regression diagnostics
What is heteroscedasticity?
Key concepts: heteroscedasticity; homoscedasticity; residual plot; Breusch-Pagan test; robust standard errors; weighted least squares
Heteroscedasticity means the variance of the regression errors is not constant across observations (for example, it grows with the fitted value or a predictor), violating the homoscedasticity assumption. Typical example: spending variability increases with income. Consequences for OLS: coefficient estimates remain unbiased and consistent, but the usual standard errors are wrong, so t-tests, p-values and confidence intervals are unreliable, and OLS is no longer the most efficient estimator. Detect: a residuals-vs-fitted plot showing a funnel shape, or formal tests such as Breusch-Pagan and White. Fix: use heteroscedasticity-robust (White/HC) standard errors; transform the target (log is common when variance scales with the mean); weighted least squares or GLS when the variance structure is known or modelled; or change the model family (for example a GLM).

Decision trees and ensembles
What is a voting model?
Key concepts: voting ensemble; hard voting; soft voting; model diversity; probability calibration; stacking
A voting model (voting ensemble) combines the predictions of several different base models into one prediction. In hard voting each classifier casts a class vote and the majority (plurality for more than two classes) wins. In soft voting the predicted class probabilities are averaged (optionally weighted) and the class with the highest average probability is chosen; this requires models that output reasonably calibrated probabilities and often does better than hard voting because confident models count for more. For regression the analogue is averaging the predictions. It works because, if the members make partly independent errors, the combined error is lower than the typical member's; so diversity matters (different algorithms, features or hyperparameters), and combining near-identical models gains little. It does not guarantee beating the best single model, and costs more training and inference time. Example: scikit-learn's VotingClassifier with logistic regression, a random forest and an SVM. Unlike stacking, there is no meta-learner; the combination rule is fixed.

Support vector machines
What are the hyperparameters of an SVM?
Key concepts: regularization parameter C; kernel choice; gamma (RBF); polynomial degree and coef0; support vector regression epsilon; log-scale grid search; feature scaling
The main SVM hyperparameters are: C, the regularization (penalty) parameter: small C gives a wider margin and tolerates more margin violations (more regularization, higher bias), large C penalizes violations heavily (narrower margin, risk of overfitting). The kernel (linear, polynomial, RBF, sigmoid) sets the shape of the decision boundary. Kernel parameters: gamma for RBF/polynomial/sigmoid (large gamma means each point has a narrow influence, giving a wiggly, overfit boundary; small gamma gives a smoother, more linear one), degree for polynomial, and coef0 for polynomial/sigmoid. For support vector regression there is also epsilon, the width of the insensitive tube. Other settings include class_weight for imbalance and the solver tolerance.

Dimensionality reduction
What impact does correlation have on PCA?
Key concepts: PCA; correlation; dimensionality reduction; components; standardized data
Strong correlation between variables means redundant information, so PCA can capture most of the variance with few components; it is therefore more effective at dimensionality reduction. With uncorrelated variables each component carries similar variance and little compression is possible. PCA is applied to standardised data (or the correlation matrix) so that scale differences do not dominate.

Decision trees and ensembles
Differentiate between boosting and bagging.
Key concepts: bagging; boosting; bootstrap sampling; variance reduction; bias reduction; gradient boosting; random forest
Both are ensemble methods built from many base learners, but they train and combine them differently. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains each model independently, in parallel, on a bootstrap sample of the data and averages (regression) or votes (classification). Its main effect is variance reduction, so it works best with low-bias, high-variance learners such as deep decision trees (random forest adds random feature subsets to decorrelate the trees); it is fairly robust to noisy labels and gives out-of-bag error estimates. Boosting trains models sequentially, each one focusing on what the ensemble so far gets wrong, either by reweighting misclassified examples (AdaBoost) or by fitting the negative gradient/residuals of the loss (gradient boosting), and combines them as a weighted sum. It mainly reduces bias, using weak learners such as shallow trees, but can also reduce variance.

Support vector machines
What is the significance of Gamma and Regularization in SVM?
Key concepts: RBF kernel gamma; soft-margin parameter C; margin width; overfitting and underfitting; grid search cross-validation; feature scaling
With an RBF kernel, K(x, z) = exp(-gamma ||x - z||^2). Gamma sets how far the influence of a single training example reaches (it is the inverse of the squared kernel width, gamma = 1/(2 sigma^2)). High gamma gives each point a narrow, local influence, so the boundary becomes very wiggly and can memorise the training set (overfitting). Low gamma gives each point wide influence, so the boundary is smooth and approaches a linear one (underfitting if too low). C is the soft-margin regularisation parameter: it weights the penalty for margin violations and misclassified training points against the margin width. Large C punishes errors heavily, gives a narrower margin and a more complex fit that can overfit; small C tolerates more violations, gives a wider margin and a simpler, more regularised model that can underfit.

ML foundations
Explain the terms Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning.
Key concepts: artificial intelligence; machine learning; deep learning; neural networks
Artificial Intelligence is the broad field of making machines behave intelligently. Machine Learning is a subset of AI where systems learn from data, and Deep Learning is a subset of ML that uses neural networks, especially for large and complex datasets.

ML foundations
What are the different types of learning or training models in ML?
Key concepts: supervised learning; unsupervised learning; reinforcement learning; semi-supervised learning; self-supervised learning; reward signal
Machine-learning approaches are usually grouped by the kind of feedback available during training. Supervised learning learns from labelled input-target pairs to predict the target (classification, regression). Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering, dimensionality reduction, density estimation). Reinforcement learning is different: an agent interacts with an environment and learns a policy from reward signals, not from labelled targets, so it is not defined simply by the presence or absence of a target variable. Common in-between or related categories: semi-supervised learning (a few labels plus many unlabelled examples) and self-supervised learning (labels derived from the data itself, as in masked-language-model pre-training). Also distinguished are online versus batch learning (incremental versus all-at-once updates). Example: spam detection with labelled emails is supervised; customer segmentation with k-means is unsupervised; a game-playing agent learning from win/loss reward is reinforcement learning.

ML foundations
What is the main key difference between supervised and unsupervised machine learning?
Key concepts: supervised learning; unsupervised learning; labeled data; classification
Supervised learning technique needs labeled data to train the model. For example, to solve a classification problem (a supervised learning task), you need to have label data to train the model and to classify the data into your labeled groups. Unsupervised learning does not need any labelled dataset. This is the main key difference between supervised learning and unsupervised learning.

Feature engineering and data preparation
How do you select important variables while working on a data set?
Key concepts: filter wrapper embedded methods; lasso feature selection; recursive feature elimination; mutual information; permutation importance; data leakage in feature selection; correlated features
Methods fall into three groups: - Filter methods rank features independently of any model: correlation or mutual information with the target, chi-square for categorical features, information gain; and drop one of each highly correlated pair (note that pairwise linear correlation misses non-linear or multi-feature redundancy). - Wrapper methods search subsets using a model's performance: forward, backward and stepwise selection, recursive feature elimination. They are costly and can overfit the selection. - Embedded methods select while fitting: lasso (L1) zeroes coefficients, tree ensembles give importances.

ML foundations
There are many machine learning algorithms till now. If given a data set, how can one determine which algorithm to be used for that?
Key concepts: algorithm selection; no free lunch; baseline; cross-validation; gradient boosting
No algorithm is best for all data (no free lunch). Consider the problem type (regression, classification, clustering), data size, feature types, linearity, interpretability needs, training/inference cost and available labels. Start with a simple baseline (linear/logistic regression, decision tree), then try stronger models (random forest, gradient boosting, SVM, neural networks for images/text/audio) and choose using cross-validation on a suitable metric after EDA.

Statistics fundamentals
How are covariance and correlation different from one another?
Key concepts: covariance; correlation; Pearson correlation; linear relationship; independence
Covariance, cov(X,Y) = E[(X - mu_x)(Y - mu_y)], gives the direction of the linear relationship; its magnitude depends on the units of X and Y, so it is not comparable across variables. Correlation (Pearson) = cov(X,Y) / (sigma_x * sigma_y) is the standardised version, unit-free and bounded between -1 and 1. Zero correlation means no linear relationship, not necessarily independence.

Statistics fundamentals
State the differences between causality and correlation.
Key concepts: causation; correlation; confounders; A/B testing; causal inference
Correlation means two variables move together; causation means a change in one produces a change in the other. Correlation can arise from confounders or coincidence (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer). Establishing causation needs randomised experiments (A/B tests) or careful causal inference methods that control for confounding.

Feature engineering and data preparation
Explain One-hot encoding and Label Encoding. How do they affect dimensionality?
Key concepts: one-hot encoding; label encoding; dimensionality; categorical variable; ordinal variables
One-hot encoding turns a categorical variable with k levels into k binary columns (one per level), so it increases dimensionality and implies no order. Label encoding maps each level to an integer (0, 1, 2, ...) in a single column, so dimensionality is unchanged, but it implies an artificial order, so it suits ordinal variables or tree-based models rather than linear models.

Statistics fundamentals
In a normally distributed feature, values within one standard deviation of the mean are missing. What fraction of the data remains?
Key concepts: 68-95-99.7 rule; normal distribution; z-score; truncated distribution; symmetry of the normal; tail probability
About 31.7%, assuming the feature really is normally distributed and 'remains' means the values that were not removed (those more than one standard deviation from the mean). For a normal distribution, P(|X - mu| < sigma) = P(|Z| < 1) = erf(1/sqrt(2)) which is about 0.6827 (the '68' in the 68-95-99.7 rule). The values that remain are the two tails: 1 - 0.6827 = 0.3173, roughly 15.9% in each tail. This holds for any mean and standard deviation because it is a statement about z-scores. Notes: the mean, median and mode coincide for a normal distribution, so the choice of centre does not matter here, but for a skewed feature the 68% figure would not apply and the answer would have to come from the empirical distribution.

Bias-variance and regularisation
Is a high variance in data good or bad?
Key concepts: variance of a feature; model variance; overfitting; bias-variance decomposition; irreducible noise; bagging
It depends on which variance is meant. Variance of a feature (spread of data values): not bad in itself. A feature needs some variance to carry information, and a constant feature is useless. High variance mainly matters for practical reasons: it makes features scale-sensitive in distance-based methods and PCA (so standardise), and outliers or noise inflate it. Variance in the target that the features cannot explain is irreducible noise and limits achievable accuracy. Variance of a model (how much predictions change if it is trained on a different sample): high variance is bad. It means overfitting, where the model fits noise in the training set, so training error is low but test error is high. This is the variance term in the bias-variance decomposition: expected error = bias^2 + variance + irreducible noise. Signs: a large train-test gap.

Bias-variance and regularisation
How would you reduce high variance (overfitting) in a model?
Key concepts: high variance; overfitting; regularization; bagging; dropout
Options: get more training data; reduce model complexity (shallower trees, fewer parameters); add regularisation (L1/L2, dropout, early stopping); use feature selection or dimensionality reduction; use bagging/random forests, which average many high-variance models trained on bootstrap samples; use cross-validation to tune.

Model evaluation and metrics
A fraud detection classifier achieved 98.5% accuracy. Is this a good model?
Key concepts: fraud detection; imbalanced data; accuracy; F1 score; threshold tuning
Not necessarily, because fraud datasets are usually imbalanced. Accuracy may be misleading, so metrics such as recall, precision, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and class-wise performance should be checked. Resampling, threshold tuning, class weights, or anomaly detection can help.

Data preparation and cleaning
Explain the handling of missing or corrupted values in a dataset.
Key concepts: missing data mechanisms; imputation; pandas dropna and fillna; type coercion; missingness indicator; data leakage
First diagnose: how much is missing, and why? Missing completely at random, at random (depends on other observed variables) or not at random (depends on the missing value itself) matters, because dropping or imputing can bias results when missingness is informative. Corrupted values (wrong types, impossible values such as age -4, bad encodings) are found with validation rules (type, range, allowed categories, duplicates). Options: drop rows or columns (dropna) when little is lost or a column is mostly empty; impute with a constant, mean (symmetric data), median (skewed data) or mode (categorical) using fillna; model-based imputation (kNN, regression, iterative imputation) for better accuracy; for time series, forward fill or interpolation. Add a missing-value indicator column when missingness may be informative.

Time series
What is Time series?
Key concepts: time series; trend; seasonality; forecasting; anomaly detection
A time series is a sequence of observations recorded over time, usually at regular intervals (hourly, daily, monthly). Observations are time-ordered and often dependent on earlier values. Typical components: trend, seasonality, cyclical patterns and noise. Standard tasks: forecasting, anomaly detection and decomposition.

Data preparation and cleaning
What is a Box-Cox transformation?
Key concepts: Box-Cox transformation; power transformation; Yeo-Johnson; lambda; maximum likelihood
Box-Cox is a power transformation for strictly positive data: y(lambda) = (y^lambda - 1) / lambda for lambda != 0 and y(lambda) = ln(y) for lambda = 0. Lambda is chosen by maximum likelihood to make the data as close to normal (and variance as stable) as possible. For data with zeros or negatives, use Yeo-Johnson.

Loss functions and optimisation
What is the difference between stochastic gradient descent and gradient descent?
Key concepts: gradient descent; stochastic gradient descent; mini-batch; learning rate decay; unbiased gradient estimate; convergence
Both minimise a loss by repeatedly stepping against the gradient: w <- w - lr * grad. Batch gradient descent computes the gradient over all n training samples for every update, so each step is exact and the loss decreases smoothly (for a small enough learning rate on a convex problem), but each step costs O(n) and large datasets make it slow. Stochastic gradient descent uses the gradient of a single randomly chosen sample (in practice, a small mini-batch of 32-1024 samples is used, which is also often called SGD). That gradient is a noisy but unbiased estimate of the full gradient, so updates are cheap and start making progress immediately, memory use is low and it supports online learning.

Decision trees and ensembles
Can you mention some advantages and disadvantages of decision trees?
Key concepts: decision tree interpretability; overfitting and variance; pruning; greedy splitting; axis-aligned splits; invariance to monotonic transforms; ensembles
Advantages: - Easy to interpret and visualise; a prediction is a sequence of simple if-then rules. - Little preprocessing: no feature scaling needed, and splits depend only on the ordering of a feature, so trees are invariant to monotonic transformations and not much affected by outliers in the input features (a split threshold does not care how extreme an outlier is). - Handle numeric and categorical features and capture non-linear relationships and feature interactions without manual feature engineering. - Fast prediction (depth-limited traversal). Disadvantages: - High variance: a fully grown tree overfits, and small changes in the training data can produce a very different tree. Controlled with hyperparameters such as max depth, minimum samples per leaf, minimum impurity decrease, or cost-complexity pruning. - Greedy, locally optimal splits; the resulting tree is not guaranteed globally optimal.

Decision trees and ensembles
Explain the differences between Random Forest and Gradient Boosting machines.
Key concepts: random forest; gradient boosting; bootstrap samples; variance; bias
Random forest builds many deep trees independently on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets and averages them, reducing variance; it is easy to tune and hard to overfit. Gradient boosting builds shallow trees sequentially, each fitted to the errors (negative gradient of the loss) of the ensemble so far, mainly reducing bias; it often reaches higher accuracy but needs careful tuning (learning rate, trees, depth) and is more sensitive to noisy labels and outliers.

Feature engineering and data preparation
Explain the difference between Normalization and Standardization.
Key concepts: normalization; standardization; min-max scaling; z-score; outliers
Normalisation (min-max scaling) rescales values to a fixed range, usually [0, 1]: x' = (x - min) / (max - min). Standardisation (z-score) rescales to mean 0 and standard deviation 1: z = (x - mu) / sigma. Min-max is sensitive to outliers because they set the min and max; standardisation is less affected and is preferred for algorithms that assume centred data (e.g. linear models, SVM, PCA). Fit the scaler on training data only.

Regression and classification are categorized under the same umbrella of supervised machine learning. Main assumptions: (1) linear relationship between predictors and target; (2) independent errors (no autocorrelation); (3) homoscedasticity (constant error variance); (4) approximately normal residuals, needed for confidence intervals and tests; (5) no severe multicollinearity among predictors.

How is the best-fit line determined in linear regression?
Key concepts: ordinary least squares; best-fit line; normal equations; sum of squared residuals; gradient descent
The line is chosen to minimise the sum of squared residuals (ordinary least squares). This has a closed-form solution (the normal equations) and can also be reached with gradient descent. For a given dataset, minimising squared error is equivalent to maximising R^2.

Linear and logistic regression
Why is logistic regression a classification technique despite its name, and which function does it use?
Key concepts: logistic regression; sigmoid function; log-odds; classification
Logistic regression models the probability of a class with the sigmoid (logistic) function, P(y=1|x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(w.x + b))); equivalently, it models the log-odds as a linear function of the features. Because the output is a probability that is thresholded (e.g. at 0.5) to assign a class, it is used for classification, even though it is a regression on the log-odds.

What is the process of carrying out a linear regression?
Key concepts: exploratory analysis; ordinary least squares; normal equation; regression assumptions; residual diagnostics; held-out evaluation
Steps: (1) Frame the problem and explore the data: scatter plots, correlations (the strength and direction of the linear relationships), outliers and missing values. (2) Prepare features: encode categoricals (drop one dummy level), transform skewed variables if needed, split into train and test sets. (3) Estimate the model by ordinary least squares, choosing coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals, with the solution beta = (X'X)^-1 X'y (or via numerical solvers). (4) Check assumptions through residual diagnostics: linearity, independent errors, constant variance (homoscedasticity), approximately normal residuals if you need inference, and no severe multicollinearity. (5) Evaluate: R-squared, RMSE/MAE on held-out data, and coefficient significance and confidence intervals.

NLP fundamentals
What do you understand by Natural Language Processing?
Key concepts: NLP; tokenization; POS tagging; NER; sentiment analysis
Natural Language Processing is the field of AI and linguistics concerned with enabling computers to process, understand and generate human language. Typical tasks: tokenisation, part-of-speech tagging, parsing, named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, machine translation, question answering and summarisation. Speech is handled by a speech-recognition front end that produces text.

Text preprocessing and representation
What are stop words?
Key concepts: stop words; bag of words; negations; sentiment analysis
Stop words are very common words (the, is, a, of) that carry little discriminative meaning for many tasks, so they are often removed to reduce noise and feature space in search and bag-of-words models. They should not always be removed: negations and function words matter for sentiment, and modern transformer models use them.

Text preprocessing and representation
What is TF-IDF?
Key concepts: TF-IDF; term frequency; inverse document frequency; keyword extraction; search ranking
TF-IDF weights a term by how frequent it is in a document (TF) and how rare it is across the corpus (IDF): tf-idf(t,d) = tf(t,d) * log(N / df(t)), where N is the number of documents and df(t) the number containing t (libraries add smoothing variants). Words common in one document but rare overall get high weights; words in nearly every document get low weights. Used for search ranking, keyword extraction and text-classification features.

Syntax and parsing
What is Syntactic Analysis?
Key concepts: syntactic analysis; parsing; constituency trees; dependency trees; semantic analysis
Syntactic analysis (parsing) determines the grammatical structure of a sentence - how words group into phrases and how they relate (constituency or dependency trees) - using grammar rules or statistical models. It deals with structure, not meaning, which is the job of semantic analysis.

Semantics and pragmatics
What is Semantic Analysis?
Key concepts: word sense disambiguation; semantic role labelling; relation extraction; word embeddings; polysemy; lexical vs syntactic vs semantic analysis
Semantic analysis is the NLP stage concerned with the meaning of words, phrases and sentences, as opposed to their form (lexical analysis) or grammatical structure (syntactic analysis). The goal is a representation of what a text says that a program can use. Typical tasks and techniques: - Word sense disambiguation: choose the sense of an ambiguous word from context ('bank' as a financial institution or a river bank). - Semantic role labelling: identify who did what to whom, when and where (agent, patient, instrument and so on). - Relation extraction and semantic parsing: turn text into relations or a logical/structured form. - Distributional and embedding-based representations: word and sentence vectors that place similar meanings close together, used for similarity and semantic search. - Named entity recognition and entity linking are information-extraction tasks that often serve as a supporting step.

Stemming reduces inflected or derived words to a root-like form (the stem) by stripping suffixes with heuristic rules, with no dictionary or part-of-speech information. Semantics and pragmatics
What is Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI)?
Key concepts: latent semantic indexing; SVD; information retrieval
Latent semantic indexing is a mathematical technique used to improve the accuracy of the information retrieval process. The design of LSI algorithms allows machines to detect the hidden (latent) correlation between semantics (words). To enhance information understanding, machines generate various concepts that associate with the words of a sentence. The technique used for information understanding is called singular value decomposition. It is generally used to handle static and unstructured data. The matrix obtained for singular value decomposition contains rows for words and columns for documents. This method best suits to identify components and group them according to their types. The main principle behind LSI is that words carry a similar meaning when used in a similar context. Computational LSI models are slow in comparison to other models. However, they are good at contextual awareness that helps improve the analysis and understanding of a text or a document.

Syntax and parsing
What are Regular Expressions?
Key concepts: regular expressions; tokenization; finite automata; pattern-based extraction
A regular expression (regex) is a pattern language for matching and extracting strings, e.g. r'\d+' matches digits and r'\b[A-Z][a-z]+\b' matches capitalised words. In NLP they are used for tokenisation, cleaning (removing URLs and punctuation), pattern-based extraction (emails, dates) and rule-based tagging. Formally, regular expressions describe regular languages and are equivalent to finite automata.

NLP fundamentals
What is the difference between NLP and NLU?
Key concepts: NLP; NLU; NLG; intent detection; entity extraction; semantic parsing
NLP (Natural Language Processing) is the broad field of getting computers to process human language: it covers understanding, generation (NLG), and supporting tasks such as tokenisation, tagging, parsing, translation, summarisation and speech-text interfaces. NLU (Natural Language Understanding) is the subfield focused on comprehension: extracting meaning from input, for example intent detection, entity extraction, semantic parsing, coreference and sentiment. A compact comparison: - Scope: NLP is the umbrella; NLU is a part of it (NLG is the other main part). - Direction: NLU goes from text to a machine-usable meaning representation; NLG goes from structured data or meaning to text. - Example: a tokeniser or machine translator is NLP but not really NLU; mapping 'book me a flight to Paris on Friday' to {intent: book_flight, destination: Paris, date: Friday} is NLU.

NLP fundamentals
What is the difference between NLP and a conversational interface (CI)?
Key concepts: natural language processing; conversational interface; dialogue management; intent classification; speech recognition; NLG
NLP is a field and set of techniques for processing language (parsing, entity recognition, intent classification, generation, translation and so on). A conversational interface is a kind of application: a chatbot, voice assistant or messaging interface through which a user interacts with a system in natural language, turn by turn. Differences: - Level: NLP is an enabling technology; a CI is a product or interaction style built from several components. - Components: a CI typically combines NLP/NLU for understanding input, a dialogue manager that tracks state and decides what to do next, back-end integrations (databases, APIs) and a response generator (templates or an NLG/language model). Voice interfaces add speech recognition and text-to-speech. - Dependence: NLP exists without a CI (search ranking, machine translation, document classification), whereas a CI needs some form of language processing, although a very simple one can be rule- or menu-based.

Semantics and pragmatics
What is Pragmatic Analysis?
Key concepts: pragmatics; speech acts; implicature; context dependence; deixis; discourse analysis; intent detection
Pragmatic analysis is the part of language understanding that interprets an utterance in context: who is speaking, to whom, in what situation and with what intent, going beyond the literal meaning established by syntax and semantics. Typical phenomena: speech acts ('Can you pass the salt?' is a request, not a question about ability), implicature ('Some students passed' suggests not all did), presupposition, deixis and reference ('I', 'here', 'tomorrow', 'it'), and sarcasm or politeness. Example: 'It's cold in here' is literally a statement about temperature but may be a request to close the window. In the classic textbook view of NLP stages (lexical, syntactic, semantic, then pragmatic/discourse) it comes last, because it needs world knowledge and conversational context, which makes it the hardest to formalise.

Text preprocessing and representation
What are unigrams, bigrams, trigrams, and n-grams in NLP?
Key concepts: n-gram; bigram; sliding window; n-gram language model; Markov assumption; data sparsity and smoothing; bag-of-n-grams
An n-gram is a contiguous sequence of n items (usually words, but also characters or subword tokens) taken from a text. A unigram is a single token, a bigram two consecutive tokens, a trigram three, and an n-gram is the general case. They are extracted with a sliding window that moves one token at a time, so neighbouring n-grams overlap: a sentence of L tokens yields L - n + 1 n-grams. For 'the cat sat on the mat' the bigrams are 'the cat', 'cat sat', 'sat on', 'on the', 'the mat'.

Syntax and parsing
What is Parsing in the context of NLP?
Key concepts: parsing; grammatical structure; phrase grouping; subject and object identification
Parsing in NLP refers to the understanding of a sentence and its grammatical structure by a machine. Parsing allows the machine to understand the meaning of a word in a sentence and the grouping of words, phrases, nouns, subjects, and objects in a sentence. Parsing helps analyze the text or the document to extract useful insights from it.

Text preprocessing and representation
What is Feature Extraction in NLP?
Key concepts: feature extraction; bag of words; n-grams; TF-IDF; word embeddings
Feature extraction converts raw text into numerical features a model can use: bag of words, n-grams, TF-IDF, word embeddings (word2vec, GloVe, contextual embeddings from transformers), plus linguistic features such as POS tags, named entities and sentence length.

NLP tasks and models
What is Naive Bayes algorithm, When we can use this algorithm in NLP?
Key concepts: Naive Bayes; Bayes' theorem; conditional independence assumption; Laplace smoothing; multinomial model; text classification; generative vs discriminative
Naive Bayes is a family of generative probabilistic classifiers based on Bayes' theorem plus the 'naive' assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class: P(c | d) is proportional to P(c) * prod_w P(w | c). For text, multinomial (word counts) or Bernoulli (word presence) variants are standard. Training is just counting word frequencies per class; prediction sums log-probabilities (to avoid underflow), and add-alpha (Laplace) smoothing prevents a word unseen in a class from zeroing the probability.

Syntax and parsing
Explain dependency parsing in NLP.
Key concepts: dependency parsing; head word; treebanks; Universal Dependencies; information extraction
Dependency parsing analyses the grammatical structure of a sentence as directed, labelled relations between a head word and its dependents (e.g. nsubj, dobj), producing a tree rooted at the main verb. Parsers are transition-based or graph-based and trained on treebanks (Universal Dependencies). Uses: information extraction, relation extraction, question answering and grammar checking.

NLP tasks and models
What is text Summarization?
Key concepts: text summarization; extractive summarization; abstractive summarization; ROUGE; TextRank
Text summarisation produces a shorter version of a text that keeps its key information. Extractive summarisation selects the most important sentences from the source (e.g. TextRank, TF-IDF scoring); abstractive summarisation generates new sentences, typically with sequence-to-sequence or transformer models, and can hallucinate. Evaluated with ROUGE and human judgement.

NLP fundamentals
What is NLTK? How is it different from Spacy?
Key concepts: NLTK; spaCy; pretrained pipelines; Doc object; WordNet; production vs research toolkit; dependency parsing
NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a Python library originally built for teaching and research. It provides many algorithms for tokenising, stemming, tagging, parsing and classification, along with interfaces to corpora and lexical resources such as WordNet. It mostly works on plain strings and lists of tokens and often offers several alternative implementations for the same task, which suits experimentation and learning. spaCy is geared to production use. You load a pretrained pipeline, call it on text and get a Doc object with tokens, part-of-speech tags, dependency parse, named entities, lemmas and (in models that include them) word vectors, all attached to the same object. It is implemented in Cython for speed, has a trainable pipeline architecture, supports transformer-based pipelines, and generally gives one maintained implementation per task rather than many.

NLP tasks and models
What is information extraction?
Key concepts: information extraction; NER; relation extraction; coreference resolution; knowledge graph
Information extraction automatically turns unstructured text into structured data. Main tasks: named entity recognition, relation extraction (e.g. person-works-for-company), event extraction, coreference resolution and template filling. Output is typically stored in a database or knowledge graph.

Text preprocessing and representation
What is Bag of Words?
Key concepts: bag of words; count vectorisation; TF-IDF; sparse vectors; n-grams; loss of word order
Bag of Words represents a document as a vector over a fixed vocabulary, where each entry is the count (or a binary presence flag, or a TF-IDF weight) of a word in that document. Stacking the vectors gives a document-term matrix, which is sparse because most documents contain few vocabulary words. Grammar and word order are discarded, hence 'bag'. It is a simple, strong baseline for text classification with models such as Naive Bayes or logistic regression. Weaknesses: no word order or context ('not good' and 'good' share a word; 'dog bites man' equals 'man bites dog'), no semantic similarity between words (car vs automobile), very high dimensionality and sparsity, and vocabulary that is fixed at training time (unseen words are ignored). Remedies: n-grams, TF-IDF to down-weight common words, stop-word removal, hashing, or dense embeddings. Example: ```python

Semantics and pragmatics
What is Pragmatic Ambiguity in NLP?
Key concepts: pragmatic ambiguity; speech acts; lexical ambiguity; syntactic ambiguity; context and speaker intent; sarcasm
Pragmatic ambiguity is ambiguity in what a sentence is meant to do or convey, which cannot be resolved from the words and grammar alone but depends on context, speaker intent, shared knowledge and the situation. The sentence may be perfectly clear lexically and syntactically. Examples: - 'Can you pass the salt?' is literally a question about ability but is normally a request (an indirect speech act). - 'It's cold in here' may be a statement or a request to close the window. - 'Great, another meeting' may be sincere or sarcastic. - Reference to the discourse or the world, such as 'Put it there' without knowing what 'it' and 'there' denote.

NLP tasks and models
What is Masked Language Model?
Key concepts: masked language model; BERT; pre-training; bidirectional context; fine-tuning
A masked language model hides (masks) a fraction of the input tokens (about 15% in BERT) and trains the model to predict them from the surrounding bidirectional context. This pre-training objective yields deep contextual representations that are then fine-tuned for downstream tasks.

Syntax and parsing
What is POS tagging?
Key concepts: POS tagging; grammatical tagging; parts of speech
Parts of speech tagging better known as POS tagging refers to the process of identifying specific words in a document and group them as part of speech, based on its context. POS tagging is also known as grammatical tagging since it involves understanding grammatical structures and identifying the respective component. POS tagging is a complicated process since the same word can be different parts of speech depending on the context. The same generic process used for word mapping is quite ineffective for POS tagging because of the same reason.

NLP tasks and models
What is Named Entity Recognition (NER)?
Key concepts: NER; entity chunking; proper nouns
Named entity recognition is more commonly known as NER is the process of identifying specific entities in a text document which are more informative and have a unique context. These often denote places, people, organisations, and more. Even though it seems like these entities are proper nouns, the NER process is far from identifying just the nouns. In fact, NER involves entity chunking or extraction wherein entities are segmented to categorise them under different predefined classes. This step further helps in extracting information.

Feature engineering and data preparation
What could be some issues if the distribution of the test data is significantly different than the distribution of the training data?
Key concepts: dataset shift; covariate shift; label shift; concept drift; adversarial validation; importance weighting
This is dataset shift: the joint distribution of inputs and labels differs between training and deployment, so performance measured on validation data no longer predicts real performance. The main types: covariate shift (P(x) changes while P(y|x) stays the same), prior or label shift (P(y) changes), and concept drift (P(y|x) changes, so the relationship itself changed). Consequences: accuracy drops, probabilities become miscalibrated, the model must extrapolate into regions it never saw (where it can be confidently wrong), thresholds and decision costs are off, and the offline validation score is over-optimistic. Detect: compare feature distributions (KS test, population stability index), train a classifier to distinguish train from test inputs (adversarial validation; high AUC means a shift), and monitor live performance or label rates.

Feature engineering and data preparation
What are some ways I can make my model more robust to outliers?
Key concepts: robust loss functions; Huber loss; winsorizing; robust scaling; log transformation; outlier detection; RANSAC
First investigate: decide whether outliers are errors (fix or remove), genuine rare-but-valid cases the model must handle (keep), or a different process (model separately). Then options: (1) Robust loss: Huber, MAE/quantile or Tukey-style losses instead of squared error, which squares large residuals and lets a few points dominate. (2) Robust models/estimators: tree-based models are insensitive to extreme feature values; RANSAC, Theil-Sen or Huber regression for linear models; median-based statistics. (3) Transform the target or features: log or Box-Cox/Yeo-Johnson for skewed variables, rank transforms. (4) Cap/winsorize at percentiles, and use robust scaling (median and IQR) instead of mean/std.

Loss functions and optimisation
What are some differences you would expect in a model that minimises squared error versus a model that minimises absolute error? In which cases would each error metric be appropriate?
Key concepts: squared error; absolute error; conditional mean vs median; outlier sensitivity; Huber loss; differentiability
Minimising squared error (L2) makes the model estimate the conditional mean; minimising absolute error (L1) estimates the conditional median. Differences: squared error penalises large errors quadratically, so the fit is pulled toward outliers and heavy-tailed noise; absolute error grows linearly and is more robust. Squared error is smooth and differentiable, and has a closed-form solution for linear models (OLS) and a unique minimum; absolute error has a kink at zero (needs linear programming or subgradient methods), gradients of constant size, and its minimiser may not be unique. Use squared error when large errors are disproportionately costly, noise is roughly Gaussian, and you want the mean (for example when predictions will be summed or averaged).

Model evaluation and metrics
What error metric would you use to evaluate how good a binary classifier is? What if the classes are imbalanced? What if there are more than two groups?
Key concepts: accuracy; precision and recall; F1 score; PR-AUC; ROC-AUC; macro F1; micro F1; confusion matrix
The metric should follow the cost of errors, not habit. Balanced binary data: accuracy is fine as a summary, ROC-AUC measures ranking quality independent of threshold, and log loss or Brier score assess probability quality. Imbalanced data: accuracy is misleading (predicting the majority class can score 99%), so use the confusion matrix with precision, recall and F1 (or F-beta if recall or precision matters more), and PR-AUC/average precision; ROC-AUC can look optimistic when negatives vastly outnumber positives because the false-positive rate stays small, whereas precision reacts to them. Also choose the decision threshold deliberately from the cost trade-off rather than defaulting to 0.5.
