Feature engineering and data preparation
Why might it be preferable to include fewer predictors over many?
Key concepts: overfitting; bias-variance trade-off; multicollinearity; interpretability; feature selection; curse of dimensionality; lasso
Fewer well-chosen predictors usually give a model that generalizes better and is easier to use. Reasons: (1) Lower variance and less overfitting: each extra predictor adds parameters that can fit noise, especially when the number of predictors is large relative to the number of samples. (2) Interpretability: a smaller model is easier to explain and audit. (3) Multicollinearity: correlated predictors make coefficient estimates unstable with inflated standard errors, which harms inference more than raw predictive accuracy. (4) Cost and reliability: fewer features to collect, store, monitor and keep available in production, and less exposure to data drift or missingness. (5) Speed of training and inference, and less curse-of-dimensionality pressure on distance-based methods. Condition: this holds for predictors that are noisy or redundant; dropping genuinely informative ones increases bias, so it is a bias-variance trade-off.

Applied ML case studies
Given training data on tweets and their retweets, how would you predict the number of retweets of a given tweet after seven days after only observing two days worth of data?
Key concepts: early-growth features; log-transformed target; time-based validation; data leakage; Hawkes process; prediction intervals
Treat it as supervised regression on historical tweets with at least seven days of history. Target: the retweet count at day 7 (or its log, log(1 + count), since counts are heavy-tailed). Features must use only information available at two days: cumulative retweets at several checkpoints (for example 1, 6, 12, 24, 48 hours) and their growth rate, tweet features (text, media, links, hashtags), author features (followers, past retweet performance), and posting time (hour, weekday). Strong baseline: predict the day-7 count as the day-2 count times a typical growth ratio learned from the data; this works because most retweets happen early.

Recommender systems
How would you construct a feed to show relevant content for a site that involves user interactions with items?
Key concepts: candidate generation; ranking model; collaborative filtering; cold start; re-ranking and diversity; position bias; A/B tests
Build it as a multi-stage recommender: candidate generation, ranking, then re-ranking. Candidate generation cheaply narrows millions of items to a few hundred using several sources: items from followed accounts or topics, collaborative retrieval (matrix factorisation or two-tower user/item embeddings with approximate nearest-neighbour search), content similarity, and fresh or popular items. A ranking model (often gradient-boosted trees or a neural network) then scores each candidate using user history, item features, user-item affinity, context and recency, predicting probabilities of several actions (click, like, share, long dwell, hide) that are combined into one value score. Re-ranking applies diversity, de-duplication, freshness and business or safety rules. Handle cold start with popularity, content features and exploration (e.g. bandits). Train on logged interactions, remembering that logs are biased by what was previously shown (position and selection bias).

Recommender systems
How would you design the people you may know feature on LinkedIn or Facebook?
Key concepts: link prediction; mutual connections; Adamic-Adar; candidate generation; graph embeddings; time-based evaluation; privacy
Frame it as link prediction on the social graph, in two stages. Candidate generation: take friends-of-friends (2-hop neighbours) and add other sources such as shared employer or school, imported contacts and profile views; cap or sample high-degree nodes because the 2-hop set explodes. Ranking: train a supervised model (e.g. gradient-boosted trees) where a positive is a suggested person who was connected to (invite sent and accepted) within a time window and negatives are shown-but-ignored or dismissed suggestions. Features include mutual-connection count, Adamic-Adar or Jaccard graph similarity, shared attributes (company, school, location), interaction signals (profile views, messages), recency and graph embeddings from node2vec or a GNN.

Applied ML case studies
How would you suggest to a franchise where to open a new store?
Key concepts: expected profit; catchment features; cannibalisation; spatial cross-validation; small-sample regression; prediction intervals; ROI
Treat it as predicting expected profit for each candidate site and ranking sites. First define the target, e.g. first-year or steady-state revenue or profit of existing stores. Build features per location: demographics and income in the catchment area, foot and car traffic, nearby anchors, competitor count and distance, rent and build cost, visibility and accessibility, and distance to the franchise's own stores. Train a regression model (regularised linear model or gradient-boosted trees) on existing stores; with only tens to hundreds of stores the data is small, so keep the model simple, regularise, and report prediction intervals. Validate with spatial or region-grouped cross-validation, because neighbouring stores are correlated and random splits leak. Model cannibalisation: a new store takes sales from nearby own stores, so use net incremental sales, not gross. Convert to expected profit (sales times margin minus fixed and capital costs) and payback or ROI, then rank candidates and consider risk.

Applied ML case studies
In a search engine, given partial data on what the user has typed, how would you predict the user's eventual search query?
Key concepts: autocomplete; prefix trie; P(query | prefix); learning to rank; n-gram language model; trending queries; MRR
Model it as ranking completions of a prefix. Retrieval of autocomplete candidates: index historical queries in a trie or prefix index (or a finite-state structure) with counts, so every query starting with the typed prefix is found in milliseconds. Baseline score is the estimated probability P(query | prefix), proportional to query frequency among queries sharing that prefix, usually with recency weighting so trending queries rise. Improve with a learning-to-rank model using features such as global and recent frequency, personal history, session context (previous queries), location, language, device and time. For rare or unseen prefixes use a language model (n-gram or neural) to generate or score completions, and handle typos with fuzzy or edit-distance matching. Filter unsafe, offensive or private suggestions.

Applied ML case studies
Given a database of all previous alumni donations to your university, how would you predict which recent alumni are most likely to donate?
Key concepts: donation propensity; RFM features; class imbalance; temporal split; data leakage; PR-AUC and lift; uplift modelling
Frame it as binary classification: will this alumnus donate within a fixed window (e.g. next 12 months)? Build features as of a cutoff date: giving history in RFM form (recency, frequency, monetary value), including any giving while a student, graduation year, degree and major, location, event attendance, email opens and clicks, volunteering or mentoring, and whether contact details are current. Recent graduates have little giving history, so engagement and demographic features carry more weight. Use logistic regression as an interpretable baseline and gradient-boosted trees as a stronger model. Split by time (train on earlier cutoffs, test on later) to avoid leakage, and make sure features contain nothing recorded after the cutoff. Donors are a small minority, so judge with PR-AUC and lift or precision in the top decile rather than accuracy, and check probability calibration if scores drive budgets.

Applied ML case studies
You are Uber and you want to design a heatmap to recommend to drivers where to wait for a passenger. How would you approach this?
Key concepts: demand forecasting; grid cells; Poisson regression; demand-supply ratio; driver herding; time-based backtest; smoothing
Divide the city into cells (e.g. H3 hexagons or geohash rectangles) and time buckets, then forecast pickup demand per cell and time. Use count regression (Poisson or negative binomial) or gradient-boosted trees with features such as hour, day of week, holidays, lagged demand, weather, scheduled events, and live signals like recent request rate. Demand alone is the wrong thing to show, though: if every driver heads to the hottest cell, supply swamps it. A better score estimates the expected value of waiting in a cell, e.g. forecast demand minus expected nearby supply (or the demand-to-driver ratio), the likelihood and expected wait for a pickup, and expected trip earnings, perhaps discounted by travel distance from the driver. Smooth across space and time so the map is stable and not noisy, and refresh frequently.

Applied ML case studies
You want to run a regression to predict the probability of a flight delay, but there are flights with delays of up to 12 hours that are really messing up your model. How can you address this?
Key concepts: flight delay prediction; logistic regression; robust loss; target transformation; quantile regression; winsorizing; two-part model
First note the mismatch: a probability of delay is a classification target, so the natural fix is to define a binary label (e.g. delayed by more than 15 minutes) and fit logistic regression or gradient boosting. Then the length of an extreme delay no longer matters, since a 12-hour delay is just a 1.

Product and business metrics
What would be good metrics of success for an advertising-driven consumer product? A service-driven consumer product?
Key concepts: north-star metric; guardrail metrics; ARPU / revenue per DAU; click-through rate; retention cohorts; customer lifetime value; conversion funnel; segmentation
Start with the business model: in each case the product's value comes from a different exchange, so the primary metric differs. For each, pick one north-star metric, a few supporting metrics, and guardrails. Advertising-driven product (revenue comes from advertisers, so user attention is the asset): - North star: ad revenue per daily active user (or total ad revenue), which combines reach and monetisation. - Supporting: DAU/MAU and time spent or sessions per user (attention supply); ad impressions per session and fill rate; click-through rate and, where available, conversion rate and advertiser ROI; eCPM. - Guardrails: retention and session length (heavier ad load can drive users away), ad hides/reports and complaints, page latency, advertiser churn.

Product and business metrics
What would be good metrics of success for a productivity tool? A MOOC?
Key concepts: activation rate; retention curves; north-star metric; completion rate; funnel drop-off; guardrail metrics; free-to-paid conversion; cohort analysis
Define success as users getting the job done (or learning), not just opening the product. For each: a north-star metric, supporting funnel/engagement metrics, and guardrails. Productivity tool (e.g. notes, tasks, documents): - North star: weekly active users who complete a core action (create/complete a task, edit and save a document), sometimes called 'activated and engaged' users. Raw logins overstate value. - Supporting: activation rate (new users reaching a first meaningful action in the first days), retention curves by signup cohort, frequency of use per week, depth (features used, items created), collaboration/sharing (teams adopting it), task completion rate, time to complete a task, and for paid tiers free-to-paid conversion and seat expansion. - Guardrails: error/crash and sync-failure rates, latency, support tickets, churn.

Product and business metrics
What would be good metrics of success for an e-commerce product? A subscription product? Premium subscriptions?
Key concepts: conversion funnel; average order value; customer lifetime value; churn rate; MRR; LTV/CAC; free-to-paid conversion; cohort analysis
Match metrics to how each model makes money, and pair every growth metric with a quality/cost metric. E-commerce (transactions): - North star: revenue or gross margin per visitor/session (conversion rate times average order value times margin). - Supporting: funnel conversion (visit to product view to add-to-cart to checkout to purchase) and cart abandonment, AOV, repeat purchase rate and customer lifetime value, customer acquisition cost, search-to-purchase success. - Guardrails: return/refund rate, delivery on-time rate, payment failures, page speed, customer satisfaction. Subscription product (recurring revenue): - North star: monthly recurring revenue (MRR) or retained paying subscribers.

Product and business metrics
What would be good metrics of success for a consumer product that relies heavily on engagement and interaction? A messaging product?
Key concepts: DAU/MAU stickiness; north-star metric; activation; retention cohorts; network effects; response rate; guardrail metrics; engagement quality
For engagement-driven products the risk is optimising raw activity instead of value, so choose metrics that capture meaningful interactions and pair them with health guardrails. Engagement/interaction-heavy product (social, content, community): - North star: the count of users who perform the core value action regularly, for example weekly users who post, comment, or consume content for a meaningful period. - Supporting: DAU/MAU (stickiness), sessions per user and session length, interactions per active user (likes, comments, shares), content creation vs consumption ratio, new-user activation and retention cohorts, network effects such as connections made.

Product and business metrics
What would be good metrics of success for a product that offered in-app purchases?
Key concepts: payer conversion; ARPU vs ARPPU; customer lifetime value; retention cohorts; refund rate; revenue concentration; purchase frequency
Success needs both monetisation and sustained engagement, since purchases come from a base of retained users. Monetisation metrics: - Payer conversion rate: share of active (or new) users who make at least one purchase. - ARPU (average revenue per user, including non-payers) and ARPPU (average revenue per paying user). They answer different questions: ARPU for overall monetisation, ARPPU for how much payers spend. - Purchase frequency and average transaction value; repeat-purchase rate. - LTV by acquisition cohort, compared with user acquisition cost (payback period). - Revenue concentration: share of revenue from the top payers; heavy dependence on a few big spenders is a risk. Engagement and funnel metrics: activation, day-1/day-7/day-30 retention, sessions per user, time to first purchase, store-view to checkout conversion, and checkout failure rate.

Analytical case studies
A certain metric is violating your expectations by going down or up more than you expect. How would you try to identify the cause of the change?
Key concepts: metric decomposition; segmentation; data quality check; seasonality; mix shift / Simpson's paradox; root-cause analysis; release and experiment timeline
Work from cheap, likely explanations to deeper ones, and keep a record of what you ruled out. 1. Confirm it is real: check the metric definition and the data pipeline (logging changes, delayed or missing data, duplicate events, timezone or backfill effects, dashboard filter or query changes). Compare with related metrics and other sources. Many 'changes' are measurement artefacts. 2. Quantify against what you expected: compare to the same weekday last week or the same period last year to account for seasonality, day-of-week effects and trends; check whether the move is outside normal variation (for example past the usual range of week-to-week noise). 3. Decompose the metric: split into its components (for a ratio, numerator and denominator; for revenue, users times conversion times order value) and see which moved.

Analytical case studies
Growth for total number of tweets sent has been slow this month. What data would you look at to determine the cause of the problem?
Key concepts: metric decomposition; active users; cohort retention; tweets per active user; segmentation; data quality check; seasonality
Treat total tweets as a product: tweets = active users x tweets per active user (and further by tweet type), then find which factor slowed. 1. Validate the data: confirm the logging and counting pipeline did not change and that the slowdown is not an artefact; compare with the same period in previous months to separate seasonality and holidays from a real change. 2. Decompose: - User side: daily and monthly active users, new signups, resurrected users, churned users, retention by signup cohort. Slow user growth or higher churn lowers total volume. - Per-user side: tweets per active user, share of active users who post at all versus only read, and the distribution (did heavy posters reduce activity, or did the long tail shrink?).

Analytical case studies
You are a restaurant and are approached by Groupon to run a deal. What data would you ask from them in order to determine whether or not to do the deal?
Key concepts: incremental profit; cannibalisation; redemption rate; customer lifetime value; break-even analysis; repeat visit rate; capacity constraints
Decide by estimating the deal's incremental profit, so ask for data that lets you compute it and understand the risks. Data to request: - Results from comparable deals: restaurants of similar type, price point and location; number of vouchers sold, redemption rates, and how many redeemers were new customers versus existing ones. - Expected volume: how many vouchers they expect to sell and over what period, to size capacity needs (staffing, kitchen, tables). - Deal terms: discount level, Groupon's revenue share/commission and payment timing, expiry date, and any limit on vouchers per customer. - Customer behaviour: what share of redeemers spend beyond the voucher value (average check, add-ons, drinks, tips), the repeat-visit rate after redemption, and whether redeemers return at full price.

Applied ML case studies
Say you are working on Facebook News Feed. What would be some metrics that you think are important? How would you make the news each person gets more relevant?
Key concepts: engagement metrics; retention; negative feedback guardrails; affinity; multi-objective ranking; exploration; A/B tests
Metrics: engagement (reactions, comments, shares, clicks per user or per session), time spent, and retention (DAU/MAU, return rate), which is closest to long-term value. Pair these with negative signals as guardrails: hides, unfollows, reports, and low-quality or misinformation exposure, plus survey-based measures of whether content was worthwhile. Also watch ecosystem health such as creator reach and content diversity. Be careful that per-impression CTR alone rewards clickbait. Relevance: treat ranking as a prediction problem. From a pool of candidate posts, a model predicts per-user, per-post probabilities of actions (click, like, comment, share, dwell, hide) using features for author-user affinity, past interactions, post type, post age, popularity and predicted content quality.

Hypothesis testing and A/B testing
How would you measure the impact that sponsored stories on Facebook News Feed have on user engagement? How would you determine the optimum balance between sponsored stories and organic content on a user's News Feed?
Key concepts: randomised controlled experiment; unit of randomisation; guardrail metrics; retention and long-term effects; network interference; holdout group; ad load response curve; revenue-engagement trade-off
Use a randomised experiment, because comparing users who see more ads with those who see fewer confounds exposure with user behaviour. Measuring the impact: - Randomise users (the unit should be the user, not the impression, to avoid within-user contamination) into control (current ad load) and treatment (different sponsored-story load, or none) groups, and run long enough to cover weekly cycles and to see retention effects, not just novelty. - Primary engagement metrics: time spent, sessions per day, likes/comments/shares on organic content, daily active users. Longer-term: retention and return rate after 1, 4 and more weeks.

Applied ML case studies
You are on the data science team at Uber and you are asked to start thinking about surge pricing. What would be the objectives of such a product and how would you start looking into this?
Key concepts: supply-demand balance; price elasticity; fulfilment rate; randomised price experiments; demand forecasts; switchback experiments; marketplace interference
Objective: keep the marketplace balanced in real time. A higher price in a zone should dampen marginal demand and attract more drivers there, so that riders can still get a car with a reasonable ETA and the fulfilment rate (requests that end in a trip) stays high. Secondary objectives are driver earnings and satisfaction, rider trust and fairness, regulatory compliance, and sustainable revenue. Start by defining zones and time windows and measuring imbalance: requests per available driver, ETAs, unfulfilled requests, cancellations. Then estimate how demand and supply respond to price (elasticities), ideally from randomised price multipliers or natural experiments rather than purely observational data, which is confounded because prices rise when demand is already high. Add short-horizon demand forecasts so prices act before shortages form.

Applied ML case studies
Say that you are Netflix. How would you determine what original series you should invest in and create?
Key concepts: subscriber retention; viewing behaviour; taste segments; comparable titles; confounding; portfolio risk; licensing alternative
Define the objective first: the value a series adds per dollar spent, i.e. subscriber acquisition and retention (and engagement) relative to production cost, over its lifetime. Then gather evidence. Viewing data shows which genres, themes, formats and talent attract and hold different taste segments; completion rate, repeat viewing and abandonment signal quality; search and watch-list data reveal unmet demand; performance of comparable titles (by genre, budget, cast, market) provides a baseline. Cluster members into taste communities and find segments that are large but underserved, including by country. Model expected audience and incremental retention for a proposed title, e.g. a regression or gradient-boosted model on comparable titles, reporting uncertainty because hits are high-variance. Beware confounding: viewership of existing titles depends on promotion and placement, so estimate retention impact with causal methods (matched cohorts or experiments) rather than raw correlation.

Product and business metrics
What kind of services would find churn helpful? How would you calculate churn?
Key concepts: churn rate; retention rate; subscription services
Churn is useful for subscription and recurring-use services (telecom, SaaS, streaming, banking). Churn rate = customers lost during a period / customers at the start of the period (for example 50 lost out of 1,000 gives 5% monthly churn). Retention rate = 1 - churn rate.

SQL fundamentals
What is SQL?
Key concepts: declarative language; relational database; DDL and DML; query optimizer; SQL dialects; ORDER BY
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard declarative language for defining, querying and modifying data in relational databases. Declarative means you state what result you want and the database's query optimizer decides how to compute it (which indexes, join order and algorithms). Its statements are usually grouped into: DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) for structure, DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and often SELECT) for data, DQL when SELECT is treated separately, DCL (GRANT, REVOKE) for permissions, and TCL (COMMIT, ROLLBACK) for transactions. SQL is standardised by ANSI/ISO, but each system (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, SQLite) has its own dialect and extensions, so code is only partly portable. It operates on tables made of rows and columns, and results are sets or multisets of rows, so without ORDER BY the row order is not guaranteed.

SQL fundamentals
What is a primary key?
Key concepts: primary key; uniqueness; NOT NULL; composite key; surrogate key; unique constraint; foreign key
A primary key is a column or set of columns (a composite key) whose values uniquely identify each row in a table. A table can have only one primary key; it must be unique and, by the SQL standard, cannot contain NULL, so every row can be reliably referenced. Databases enforce this with a unique index, which also makes lookups by key fast, and other tables point to it with foreign keys. Keys can be natural (a real-world attribute such as an ISO country code) or surrogate (an auto-increment integer or UUID with no business meaning); surrogate keys are stable when business data changes, while natural keys can change and be wider. Keep keys small and immutable because they are copied into foreign keys and, in some engines (e.g. InnoDB), into every secondary index. Differences from a UNIQUE constraint: a table may have many UNIQUE constraints, which usually allow NULLs, but only one primary key.

SQL fundamentals
What is a foreign key?
Key concepts: foreign key; referential integrity; ON DELETE CASCADE; parent and child table; NULL foreign key; indexing foreign keys
A foreign key is a column (or set of columns) in a child table whose values must match an existing primary key or unique key value in a parent table, or be NULL. It enforces referential integrity: you cannot insert an order for a customer that does not exist, nor delete a customer that still has orders (unless a rule says otherwise). Referential actions on delete or update define what happens to child rows: RESTRICT or NO ACTION (reject), CASCADE (propagate the change), SET NULL or SET DEFAULT. A NULL foreign key means no relationship, and the check is skipped for it; declare the column NOT NULL if the relationship is mandatory. Foreign keys also document the schema and guide joins. Costs: checks add some write overhead, and the child column usually should be indexed, because deletes or updates on the parent need to find child rows (some databases, e.g. PostgreSQL, do not create that index automatically).

SQL fundamentals
Difference between WHERE and HAVING?
Key concepts: WHERE clause; HAVING clause; GROUP BY; aggregate functions; order of evaluation; row-level vs group-level filter
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and aggregation; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation. Logical order of evaluation: FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, aggregate functions, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. Consequently WHERE cannot use aggregate functions such as SUM() or COUNT(*) (they do not exist yet), whereas HAVING can; conversely, a condition on a plain column that does not depend on aggregates is better placed in WHERE, because it discards rows early so fewer rows are grouped (optimizers may sometimes push such predicates down, but do not rely on it). Example: total paid amount per customer, counting only paid orders, keeping customers whose total exceeds 100. The status filter is row-level so it goes in WHERE; the total filter is group-level so it goes in HAVING.

Joins
What is an INNER JOIN?
Key concepts: inner join; join condition; matching rows; one-to-many duplication; NULL join keys; left join
An INNER JOIN combines rows from two tables and returns only the pairs of rows for which the join condition is true; rows with no match on either side are dropped. Conceptually it is the cross product filtered by the ON condition. Points to know: on a one-to-many relationship each parent row is repeated once per matching child row, so aggregates over the parent's columns can be inflated; NULL never equals NULL, so rows whose join key is NULL do not match; for an inner join, a filter in ON or in WHERE gives the same result (unlike outer joins). Use a LEFT JOIN when you need to keep unmatched rows. Example: list each order with its customer name; customers with no orders and orders with no customer do not appear. ```sql SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.amount FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY o.id; ```

Joins
What is a LEFT JOIN?
Key concepts: left join; NULL-extended rows; anti-join; ON vs WHERE; COUNT(column) vs COUNT(*); outer join
A LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN) returns every row from the left table, together with the matching rows from the right table; where there is no match the right table's columns are NULL. If a left row matches several right rows it appears once per match. It is used when you must keep all entities, e.g. all customers including those with no orders, and for anti-joins (find left rows with no match by testing a right-side non-null column IS NULL). Common pitfalls: a WHERE condition on a right-table column (such as o.status = 'paid') discards the NULL-extended rows and silently turns the query into an inner join, so put right-table filters in the ON clause when you want to keep unmatched left rows; and use COUNT(o.id), not COUNT(*), to count matches, because COUNT(*) counts the NULL-extended row as 1. SQL fundamentals
What is GROUP BY?
Key concepts: GROUP BY; HAVING; aggregate functions; WHERE vs HAVING; NULL group; logical query order
GROUP BY collapses rows that share the same values in the listed columns into one output row per group, so that aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) are computed per group. Logical order: FROM/JOIN, WHERE (filters rows before grouping), GROUP BY, HAVING (filters groups, can use aggregates), SELECT, ORDER BY. Every selected column must be either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate (standard SQL; some databases such as SQLite and older MySQL are lenient and return an arbitrary row's value, which is a bug source). NULLs form a single group. Without GROUP BY, an aggregate treats the whole table as one group. Example: number of employees and average salary per department, keeping departments with more than one employee; the two employees with no department form a single NULL group. ```sql SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY dept; ```

SQL fundamentals
What is DISTINCT?
Key concepts: DISTINCT; duplicate rows; COUNT(DISTINCT); NULL handling; GROUP BY alternative; performance cost
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from a query result. It applies to the entire combination of selected columns, not to just the first one: SELECT DISTINCT city, country returns unique (city, country) pairs. For this purpose NULLs are treated as equal, so multiple NULLs collapse into one row. It is evaluated after the select list is formed, usually via sorting or hashing, which can be expensive on large results. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values (NULLs are ignored), whereas COUNT(*) counts rows and COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values. Pitfalls: using DISTINCT to hide duplicates caused by a bad join usually masks a logic error and hurts performance; fix the join or aggregate instead. GROUP BY can produce the same unique list. In the example, COUNT(DISTINCT city) is 2 (NULL ignored) while SELECT DISTINCT city returns 3 rows (NULL kept as one): ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows, COUNT(city) AS non_null, COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS distinct_non_null,

What is a NULL value?
Key concepts: NULL; three-valued logic; IS NULL; NOT IN trap; COALESCE; aggregates ignore NULL
NULL is a marker meaning a value is missing or unknown (or not applicable); it is not zero and not an empty string. SQL uses three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN): any comparison with NULL, including NULL = NULL and NULL <> 1, yields UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE. So test with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, not = NULL. Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL. Aggregates (SUM, AVG, COUNT(col), MIN, MAX) ignore NULLs, but COUNT(*) counts rows. GROUP BY and DISTINCT treat NULLs as one group. The classic trap is NOT IN: x NOT IN (1, NULL) can never be TRUE, so a subquery returning a NULL makes NOT IN return no rows; use NOT EXISTS or filter out NULLs. SQL fundamentals
What are aggregate functions?
Key concepts: aggregate functions; COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column); NULL handling; HAVING; empty set behaviour; GROUP BY
Aggregate functions compute a single value from a set of rows: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX are the standard ones (databases add others such as string and statistical aggregates). Used with GROUP BY they produce one value per group; without it the whole result is one group and returns one row. Key rules: except COUNT(*), they ignore NULL inputs; COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values, COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values; on an empty input COUNT returns 0 but SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX return NULL (and SUM of only NULLs is NULL). AVG divides by the number of non-NULL values, not by the row count. Aggregates cannot appear in WHERE because WHERE runs before grouping; use HAVING for conditions on aggregates. Subqueries and CTEs
What is a subquery?
Key concepts: subquery; correlated subquery; derived table; EXISTS vs IN; scalar subquery; NOT IN with NULL
A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another statement, in parentheses. It can appear in WHERE or HAVING (with IN, EXISTS, ANY/ALL or a comparison), in FROM as a derived table (needs an alias), or in the SELECT list as a scalar subquery that must return one row and one column. An uncorrelated subquery does not reference the outer query and can be evaluated independently; a correlated subquery refers to outer columns, so it is logically re-evaluated per outer row, although optimizers often rewrite it into a join. Pitfalls: a scalar subquery returning more than one row is an error (or arbitrary in lenient engines); NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL returns nothing, so prefer NOT EXISTS; EXISTS only checks for existence and is often clearer than IN or a join that creates duplicates. Many subqueries can be rewritten as joins or CTEs for readability or speed.

Subqueries and CTEs
What is a CTE?
Key concepts: common table expression; WITH clause; recursive CTE; readability; materialisation; chained CTEs
A Common Table Expression is a named temporary result set defined with WITH at the start of a statement and usable in that statement only (it is not stored). It makes complex queries readable by splitting them into named steps, lets you reference the same sub-result several times, and chains: later CTEs can use earlier ones. WITH RECURSIVE supports hierarchical or graph traversal (org charts, bill of materials) via an anchor query UNION ALL a recursive step, which stops when the step returns no new rows; guard against cycles. A CTE is not necessarily materialised or faster than an equivalent subquery: whether it is computed once or inlined depends on the engine and version (e.g. PostgreSQL and SQLite offer MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED hints), so check the plan. Example: department averages in a CTE, then employees above their department average. ```sql WITH dept_avg AS ( SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM emp GROUP BY dept )

Database design
What is normalization?
Key concepts: normalization; normal forms; update anomalies; transitive dependency; 3NF and BCNF; redundancy; foreign key
Normalization is organising a schema so each fact is stored once, which removes redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies. It proceeds through normal forms: 1NF (atomic values, no repeating groups, a key), 2NF (1NF plus no non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key), 3NF (2NF plus no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, i.e. no transitive dependency; informally, every attribute depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key), and BCNF (every determinant is a candidate key). Example: an orders table that repeats customer name and address on every order breaks 3NF; if the address changes you must update many rows and can leave them inconsistent. Split into customers and orders linked by a foreign key. The benefits are consistency, smaller storage and simpler updates; the cost is more tables and joins on reads.

Database design
What is denormalization?
Key concepts: denormalization; redundancy; precomputed aggregates; materialized views; read vs write trade-off; data consistency; star schema
Denormalization deliberately introduces redundancy into a normalised schema to make reads faster or simpler, typically by avoiding joins or repeated aggregation. Common forms: copying a column into another table (e.g. customer name on the order row), storing precomputed aggregates or counters (order_total, comment_count), summary or reporting tables, and materialized views. Star and snowflake schemas in data warehouses are denormalised by design. The trade-offs: reads become cheaper, but writes get more expensive and complex because every copy must be updated, there is more storage, and the risk of inconsistency rises unless you keep copies in sync with triggers, transactions, application logic or scheduled refreshes. Rule of thumb: normalise first, measure, and denormalise only for a proven bottleneck on a read-heavy path where slight staleness or the extra write work is acceptable. Indexing, caching or query tuning are often cheaper alternatives to try first.

Indexing and performance
What is an index?
Key concepts: B-tree index; composite index; leftmost prefix; covering index; write overhead; selectivity; sargable predicates
An index is a separate data structure, most commonly a B-tree, that stores the values of one or more columns in sorted order with a pointer to the row, letting the database find rows without scanning the whole table: lookup is roughly O(log n) instead of O(n). It speeds up WHERE filters, joins, ORDER BY and GROUP BY on the indexed columns, and enforces UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY constraints. Costs: extra storage, and every INSERT, UPDATE of an indexed column and DELETE must also maintain the index, so over-indexing slows writes.

Database design
What is a view?
Key concepts: view; virtual table; materialized view; access control; updatable views
A view is a stored, named SELECT query that you query like a table. A normal view stores no data: the database substitutes its definition into the outer query each time, so results are always current and performance is that of the underlying query. Uses: hide complexity (pre-written joins), present a stable interface when the schema changes, and restrict access by exposing only some columns or rows, with permissions granted on the view rather than on the base tables. Limitations: views can be stacked, which hides expensive queries; many engines allow INSERT/UPDATE through a view only when it maps cleanly to one base table (no aggregates, DISTINCT etc.), and SQLite views are read-only. A materialized view (PostgreSQL, Oracle and others; not SQLite) physically stores the result and must be refreshed, trading freshness for speed. Example: ```sql CREATE VIEW active_customers AS SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE active = 1; ``` ```sql SELECT * FROM active_customers ORDER BY id; ```

Transactions and concurrency
What is a transaction?
Key concepts: transaction; ACID; commit and rollback; isolation levels; atomicity; write-ahead log; MVCC
A transaction is a group of statements executed as one logical unit of work: either all take effect (COMMIT) or none do (ROLLBACK). Relational databases aim to give ACID guarantees: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work, to a degree set by the isolation level) and Durability (committed data survives crashes, usually via a write-ahead log). Classic example: a bank transfer debits one account and credits another; if the second update fails the first must be undone. Isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE) trade concurrency against anomalies such as dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms; engines implement them with locking or MVCC. Keep transactions short to reduce lock contention and deadlocks. Most databases run in autocommit mode unless you open a transaction explicitly. Example showing rollback: ```sql BEGIN;

Transactions and concurrency
Explain ACID properties.
Key concepts: ACID properties; atomicity; consistency; isolation; durability
Atomicity: a transaction is all-or-nothing - if any step fails, every change is rolled back. Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's uncommitted changes (controlled by isolation levels). Durability: once committed, changes survive crashes (via write-ahead logging).

Joins
What is a self join?
Key concepts: self join; table alias; hierarchical data; left join; pair comparison; recursive CTE
A self join joins a table to itself, using two different aliases so the database can tell the two roles apart. It is not a separate join type: any join type (INNER, LEFT) can be a self join. Typical uses: hierarchies stored with a parent column (employee to manager), comparing rows within the same table (employees earning more than their manager, products in the same category), and finding pairs such as duplicates or related rows. To avoid pairing a row with itself and listing each pair twice, add a condition like a.id < b.id. Use LEFT JOIN when rows without a partner (e.g. the CEO with no manager) must be kept. A self join only goes one level up or down; for arbitrary depth use a recursive CTE. Make sure the join column is indexed on large tables. Example: employees with their manager's name. ```sql SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM emp e LEFT JOIN emp m ON m.id = e.manager_id

Database design
What is a stored procedure?
Key concepts: stored procedure; parameters; round trips; permissions; SQL injection; function vs procedure; portability
A stored procedure is a named, parameterised block of SQL and procedural code (T-SQL, PL/SQL, PL/pgSQL and similar) that is stored in the database and executed on the server with CALL or EXEC. Benefits: encapsulates business logic in one place, cuts network round trips because many statements run in one call, can be granted EXECUTE permission without exposing the underlying tables, and passing parameters (instead of concatenating strings) helps prevent SQL injection. Some engines can reuse the compiled plan. It can hold multiple statements, control flow, transactions and error handling, and may return result sets or output parameters, whereas a function is meant to return a value and be used inside queries (exact rules differ by database). Drawbacks: logic is split between application and database, version control, testing and debugging are harder, the code is not portable across dialects, and heavy logic loads the database server. SQLite has no stored procedures.

Window functions
What is a window function?
Key concepts: window function; PARTITION BY; ROW_NUMBER vs RANK; running total; window frame; LAG and LEAD; top N per group
A window function computes a value for each row using a set of related rows (its window) defined by OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame), but unlike GROUP BY it does not collapse the rows, so you keep detail and add aggregates, ranks or neighbours alongside. Families: ranking (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE), value (LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE), and aggregates used as windows (SUM, AVG, COUNT) for running totals and moving averages. PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups; ORDER BY orders within the partition; the frame (ROWS or RANGE BETWEEN ...) limits which rows are used, and with ORDER BY the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, where ties count as peers. Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so you cannot filter on them directly; wrap the query in a subquery or CTE (the usual 'top N per group' pattern).

Window functions
Difference between ROW_NUMBER and RANK?
Key concepts: ROW_NUMBER; RANK; DENSE_RANK; ties; partition
ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequential number to each row in the partition, breaking ties arbitrarily (or by the ORDER BY). RANK gives tied rows the same number and then skips numbers (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same number without gaps (1, 2, 2, 3).

Partitioning and scaling
What is partitioning?
Key concepts: table partitioning; range and hash partitioning; partition pruning; partition key; vertical vs horizontal; sharding
Partitioning splits one large logical table (or index) into smaller physical pieces, partitions, inside the same database, while queries still see a single table. Horizontal partitioning divides rows by a partition key: range (e.g. by month), list (by region) or hash (even spread). Vertical partitioning splits columns, for example moving rarely used or large columns to another table. Benefits: partition pruning, where a query filtering on the partition key reads only the relevant partitions; cheap maintenance such as dropping or archiving an old partition instead of a huge DELETE; smaller indexes and per-partition operations; and sometimes parallelism. Costs: queries that do not filter on the partition key touch all partitions; a poor key creates skew or hot partitions; extra operational complexity; and in some systems (e.g. PostgreSQL) unique and primary keys must include the partition key. It differs from sharding, where pieces live on different servers.

Indexing and performance
What is a clustered index?
Key concepts: clustered index; one per table; leaf level holds rows; page splits; range scans; InnoDB primary key; heap
A clustered index defines how the table's rows themselves are organised: the leaf level of the index is the data, with rows kept in the order of the clustering key (physically approximately, as linked pages). Because the rows can be in only one order, a table has at most one clustered index. It makes range scans and ORDER BY on the key fast, and lookups by key need no extra step. Trade-offs: inserting keys out of order (random UUIDs) causes page splits and fragmentation, while an ever-increasing key appends efficiently; updating the key moves the row; and the clustering key is carried in every non-clustered index, so a wide key bloats them.

Indexing and performance
What is a non-clustered index?
Key concepts: non-clustered index; row locator; key lookup; covering index; INCLUDE columns; write cost
A non-clustered (secondary) index is a separate structure, usually a B-tree, holding the indexed key columns in sorted order plus a row locator that points back to the table row. The locator is a row id (RID) when the table is a heap, or the clustering key when the table has a clustered index (as in SQL Server and InnoDB). A table can have many of them. A lookup finds the key in the index, then performs a lookup (key lookup / bookmark lookup) into the table to fetch other columns; this extra step is why the optimizer may ignore a non-clustered index when many rows match and a scan is cheaper. A covering index avoids the lookup by containing all columns the query needs, e.g. with INCLUDE columns in SQL Server or PostgreSQL. Trade-offs: each index costs storage and slows INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, so index the columns used in filters, joins and sorts, not everything.

Transactions and concurrency
What is a deadlock?
Key concepts: deadlock; lock cycle; wait-for graph; victim rollback; consistent lock ordering; retry logic; blocking vs deadlock
A deadlock is a cycle of transactions in which each holds a lock another needs and waits for it, so none can proceed. Example: T1 locks row A then requests row B, while T2 locks B then requests A. Unlike ordinary blocking, which ends when the holder commits, a deadlock cannot resolve itself. Databases detect it (typically with a wait-for graph, or via lock timeouts) and abort one transaction, the victim, with an error; its work is rolled back and the application must catch that error and retry. So they are not 'indefinite' in practice, but they cost latency and failed requests. Prevention and mitigation: access tables and rows in a consistent order, keep transactions short, avoid user interaction inside a transaction, acquire needed locks early (e.g. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), use appropriate indexes so fewer rows are locked, use a lower isolation level where acceptable, and implement retry with backoff. Deadlock logs or graphs show which statements collided.

Partitioning and scaling
What is sharding?
Key concepts: sharding; shard key; consistent hashing; cross-shard queries; hotspots; replication; horizontal scaling
Sharding is horizontal partitioning of data across multiple independent database servers (shards), each holding a subset of the rows, so storage and read/write load scale out beyond one machine. A shard key decides placement: range-based (simple, supports range queries, but can create hot shards), hash-based (even spread, poor range queries) or directory/lookup-based (flexible, extra lookup layer). Consistent hashing reduces data movement when shards are added. Trade-offs: queries must include the shard key to hit one shard, otherwise they fan out; cross-shard joins and transactions are hard or need distributed commit; rebalancing and resharding are operationally difficult; skewed keys create hotspots; and global unique ids and schema changes need coordination. It differs from replication (copies of the same data for availability and read scaling) and from partitioning within a single server.

Indexing and performance
How do you improve a slow query?
Key concepts: execution plan; index design; sargable predicates; statistics; keyset pagination; N+1 queries; materialized view
Measure before changing anything. Capture the slow statement (slow query log or monitoring) and read its execution plan with actual row counts (EXPLAIN ANALYZE or equivalent) to see where time goes. Then work through the usual causes. Full scans on large tables: add or fix an index matching the filter, join and sort columns, with composite column order chosen for the query, and consider a covering index. Non-sargable predicates that cannot use an index: functions or casts on the indexed column, implicit type conversion, leading-wildcard LIKE; rewrite them (e.g. a date range instead of wrapping the column in a function). Doing too much work: select only needed columns, filter early, avoid SELECT *, avoid correlated subqueries that run per row if a join works, and replace deep OFFSET pagination with keyset pagination. Bad estimates: update statistics so the optimizer picks good join order and join type. Application patterns: remove N+1 queries and batch.

What is quicksort and how would you implement it in Python?
Key concepts: quicksort; pivot; divide-and-conquer; partition; worst case
Quicksort is a divide-and-conquer sort: choose a pivot, partition the items into smaller, equal and larger groups, and recursively sort the outer groups. Average time is O(n log n); the worst case is O(n^2) (for example consistently bad pivots), and the in-place version uses O(log n) extra stack space on average. The version below favours clarity (it allocates new lists): ```python def quicksort(arr): if len(arr) <= 1: return arr pivot = arr[len(arr) // 2] left = [x for x in arr if x < pivot] mid = [x for x in arr if x == pivot] right = [x for x in arr if x > pivot] return quicksort(left) + mid + quicksort(right) ```

Key concepts: async/await; asyncio; coroutine; event loop; I/O-bound work
async def defines a coroutine; await suspends it until an awaitable finishes, letting the event loop run other tasks. asyncio.gather (or tasks created with asyncio.create_task) runs coroutines concurrently, which helps I/O-bound work but not CPU-bound work. Write out Adam's update rule and explain what m and v each track and why bias correction is needed. Implement one Adam step in numpy and test it against a hand-computed first step. Then say when SGD with momentum might still be a better choice.
Key concepts: Adam update rule; first moment (m); second moment (v); bias correction; per-parameter adaptive step; SGD with momentum; AdamW decoupled weight decay
Adam keeps two exponential moving averages per parameter: m = beta1*m + (1-beta1)*g (a smoothed gradient direction) and v = beta2*v + (1-beta2)*g^2 (a smoothed gradient scale). Both start at zero, so early on they are biased toward zero. Bias correction divides by (1 - beta^t): m_hat = m/(1-beta1^t), v_hat = v/(1-beta2^t). The update is theta -= lr * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps).

Normalisation
You move a model from a CNN with batch norm to a transformer and someone asks why the transformer uses layer norm. Over which axes does each compute its statistics, how does each behave at training versus inference, and what goes wrong with batch norm for small batches or variable-length sequences?
Key concepts: batch normalisation; layer normalisation; normalisation axes; running mean and variance; train/inference discrepancy; small-batch noise; group normalisation
For an activation tensor, batch norm computes mean and variance per feature/channel across the batch (and spatial positions for a conv layer, i.e. over N, H, W for each channel). Layer norm computes them per sample across the feature dimension (for a transformer, over d_model of each token independently). Both then apply a learned scale and shift. Training vs inference: batch norm normalises with the current mini-batch statistics during training while updating exponential moving averages of mean and variance; at inference it uses those running estimates so a prediction does not depend on the other examples in the batch. Layer norm uses the same computation in both modes, with no batch dependence and no running statistics.

Architectures
Very deep plain convolutional networks were observed to get worse training error than shallower ones. How do residual (skip) connections address this, what is the gradient argument, and what do you do when the input and output of a residual block have different shapes?
Key concepts: residual connection; identity mapping; degradation problem; gradient path; projection shortcut (1x1 conv); y = x + F(x)
That observation is the degradation problem: deeper plain networks can show higher training error than shallower ones, so it is an optimisation difficulty rather than overfitting. A residual block computes y = x + F(x). If an identity mapping is optimal, the layers only need to drive F towards zero, which is easier than making a stack of nonlinear layers approximate the identity. Gradient argument: dy/dx = I + dF/dx, so the backward signal has a direct additive identity path from later layers to earlier ones instead of only a product of many layer Jacobians. This helps gradients reach early layers and eases optimisation. The identity path is exact in pre-activation blocks; the original ResNet applies a ReLU after the addition.

Your team's dashboards mention 'covariate drift', 'label drift' and 'concept drift' as if they were the same thing. Define each, give one example each for a credit-risk model, and say which of the three you can detect without waiting for ground-truth labels.
Key concepts: covariate shift; prior probability (label) shift; concept drift; P(y|X); PSI; KS test; drift detection without labels
Covariate drift: the input distribution P(X) changes while P(y|X) stays the same. Credit example: marketing shifts toward younger applicants, but a given profile is as risky as before. Label (prior) drift: P(y) changes, with P(X|y) assumed stable. Example: a recession lifts the default rate from 3% to 6%; this is pure label drift only if defaulters still look like past defaulters, which rarely holds exactly, so real cases are often a mix of label and concept drift. Concept drift: P(y|X) itself changes. Example: new fraud tactics or regulation mean applicants with the same features now default at a different rate.

Key concepts: right-skewed distribution; mean vs median; robustness to outliers; percentiles; revenue = mean x orders
Report the median as the 'typical order' and show the mean alongside it, because the two answer different questions and the gap tells you the data is right-skewed. Order values are bounded at zero but have a long upper tail (a few very large baskets). The mean is pulled up by that tail, so a mean of 84 against a median of 41 says half of orders are under 41 while a minority of big orders lifts the average. The mean is still the right number when you care about totals: revenue equals the mean times the number of orders, so forecasting revenue or comparing revenue per order across periods needs the mean. The median is robust to extreme values and describes the typical customer, but it ignores how big the tail is and cannot be summed.

A customer survey has 30 percent of income answers missing. Explain how you would decide whether the missingness is MCAR, MAR or MNAR using business examples, what happens if you just drop those rows versus impute, and what you can actually test.
Key concepts: MCAR; MAR; MNAR; complete-case analysis; multiple imputation; missing-indicator; sensitivity analysis
MCAR (missing completely at random): the chance a value is missing is unrelated to anything, observed or not. Example: a survey tool bug that randomly loses 5 percent of responses. MAR (missing at random): missingness depends on observed variables but not on the missing value itself once those are accounted for. Example: younger respondents skip the income question more often, and age is recorded. MNAR (missing not at random): missingness depends on the unobserved value itself. Example: very high earners decline to state income. Consequences. Dropping rows (complete-case analysis) is unbiased under MCAR, only losing power, but can be biased under MAR and MNAR because the remaining sample is not representative; with 30 percent missing you may also lose much data when several columns have gaps.

A teammate says 'the 95 percent confidence interval for the mean delivery time is 31 to 35 minutes, so there is a 95 percent chance the true mean is between 31 and 35.' Is that right? What does the interval mean and what makes it wider or narrower?
Key concepts: confidence interval; coverage of a procedure; standard error; sample size effect on width; confidence level; credible interval vs confidence interval
Strictly, no. In the frequentist framework the true mean is a fixed (unknown) number, so after you compute the interval it either contains it or it does not. The 95 percent describes the procedure: if you repeated the sampling and interval construction many times under the same conditions, about 95 percent of the intervals produced would contain the true mean. This particular interval 31 to 35 is one draw from that process. Common misreadings to avoid: that 95 percent of individual deliveries fall between 31 and 35 (the interval is about the mean, not individual values, which spread much more); that a repeat sample's mean has a 95 percent chance of landing inside it; and that values inside the interval are all equally plausible.

Direction: satisfaction is typically overstated, since dissatisfied customers are more likely to have churned. Average tenure of current customers is also not what it appears: it describes how long today's survivors have been around, which is a different quantity from how long a newly acquired customer stays. Distance concentration (a 'curse of dimensionality' effect): for points with many independent, similarly distributed coordinates, the distance from a query to every point concentrates around a common value, so the relative gap between the nearest and farthest points, (d_max - d_min) / d_min, shrinks as the dimension rises. In the limit, ranking by distance is dominated by small fluctuations. This is a statement about specific data distributions (broadly: high intrinsic dimension and little structure), not about every vector set with many coordinates. Recall@10 counts gold chunks in 10 positions, but the generator sees 5. Candidate explanations: 1. The gain sits at ranks 6-10. Recall@5 may not have moved at all. Always report recall at the k actually passed to the generator (and the rank distribution of the gold chunk). 2. The generator is the bottleneck.

RAG evaluation (recall@k, MRR, nDCG, faithfulness, golden sets, LLM judges)
Your retrieval golden set was built by annotators who judged only the top 10 results of the existing BM25 system for each query. You now evaluate a new dense retriever against it: its recall@10 and nDCG@10 come out lower than BM25's, yet when you read its results for 20 queries by hand, they look as good or better. Why can the metrics say this, and how would you fix the evaluation?
Key concepts: pooling; unjudged documents; incomplete relevance labels; judged fraction at k; condensed lists; candidate pool diversity
Recall, precision and nDCG all treat a document as relevant only if it appears in the judged-relevant set; unjudged documents count as non-relevant. When the labelled set came from the top 10 of BM25 only, relevant documents that BM25 cannot find were never shown to annotators, so they have no label.

Some of your RAG questions need several pieces of evidence (for example a policy rule plus its exception), and for each piece there may be several acceptable chunks because the corpus contains near-duplicates. Averaging plain recall@k over queries hides whether the generator actually receives everything it needs.

Implement evidence_coverage(ranked, groups, k), where groups is a list of sets of chunk ids and a group counts as covered if any of its chunks is in the top k, returning (fraction of groups covered, whether all groups are covered), and aggregate(runs, k) returning (mean coverage, full-coverage rate). Here runs is a list of (ranked, groups) pairs. Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
A 20M-chunk collection sits in an HNSW index. Queries always carry a metadata filter. For a filter such as department='legal' AND year=2019, only about 0.5% of vectors match (roughly 100,000 chunks). With ef_search=100 and top_k=10, the service often returns only 0 to 2 results, though the same query unfiltered returns 10 sensible hits and an exact scan with the filter returns 10 good ones.

Explain why this happens with post-filtering, what in-graph (filtered) traversal and pre-filtering change, and how you would choose a strategy by selectivity.
Key concepts: post-filtering; pre-filtering; filter selectivity; ef_search; graph connectivity under filters; query planner / fallback to exact scan
Post-filtering: the index returns the ef_search nearest candidates ignoring the filter, then the engine discards non-matching ones.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
You must serve 50 million chunks, 768-d float32 embeddings, from an in-memory HNSW index with M=16, with 3 replicas for availability and throughput. Each node has about 100 GB usable for the index. Estimate memory for the base design, work out how many nodes it needs, and compare it with int8 scalar quantisation and product quantisation with 96-byte codes. Which would you choose and what would you verify before deciding?
Key concepts: vector memory arithmetic; HNSW link overhead; scalar quantisation; product quantisation; sharding vs replication; re-ranking with full vectors
Assumptions (state them in the interview; real engines differ): decimal GB; layer 0 stores up to 2M = 32 neighbour ids of 4 bytes per node; upper layers add roughly n/(M-1) node-layer entries with up to M links each; per-node headers, ids, allocator overhead and metadata are ignored and typically add more. Base design: vectors = 50e6 x 768 x 4 B = 153.6 GB.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
A RAG service re-ingests documents weekly; each document is split into chunks and upserted into an HNSW-based vector store, and deleted documents are removed with a 'delete by chunk id' call. Six months in, you see: memory and disk keep growing though the corpus is stable, p95 latency is creeping up, recall on a fixed monitoring set has dropped a little, and legal reports that a withdrawn document still appears in answers.

Explain the likely mechanisms and design the update and delete path properly.
Key concepts: tombstone deletes; index compaction / rebuild; stable chunk ids; orphaned chunks; alias swap; query-time validity filter
Likely mechanisms: 1. Soft deletes. Many ANN implementations mark deleted vectors (tombstones) and filter them from results but leave them in the graph and storage until a compaction or rebuild. Memory and disk do not shrink; searches can still traverse deleted nodes, which may consume part of the ef budget (implementation-dependent; Qdrant documents graph disconnection with many soft-deleted points); and repeatedly inserting into a graph around deleted nodes can reduce graph quality.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
Users of a news-assistant RAG product expect a newly published article to be answerable within about 30 seconds. Today the vector index is rebuilt every night, ingestion runs at roughly 200 new chunks per second at peak, and queries must stay under 200 ms at p95.

Design how new documents become searchable quickly without rebuilding the whole index, say where the 30 seconds actually go, and discuss the consistency and cost trade-offs.
Key concepts: fresh segment; brute-force scan of a small segment; segment merge / compaction; refresh interval; embedding pipeline latency; read-your-writes
Architecture: a main index (ANN, large, rebuilt or compacted in the background) and a delta/fresh segment that accepts writes. Ingestion path: document arrives, is queued, chunked, embedded (often a batched model call), written to a durable log, then added to the fresh segment.

Candidate designs: (a) one shared index with a tenant_id filter, (b) a separate index per tenant, (c) a hybrid. Customers require that one tenant can never retrieve another's data, and that deleting a tenant removes all its vectors.

Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
A hybrid search service runs BM25 and dense retrieval across 8 shards. Each shard computes BM25 with its own local statistics, returns its top 20, and the coordinator merges the lists by raw score and then fuses with the dense list. After the corpus was resharded unevenly, queries with rare terms started returning odd rankings, and the hybrid scores seem on a different scale than the dense ones.

Why does this happen, and how should the merging and fusion work?
Key concepts: shard-local IDF; global statistics; scatter-gather top-k; reciprocal rank fusion; score scale mismatch; candidate depth
Why raw merging fails: BM25 weights terms by IDF, computed from document frequency and collection size. Using the common Lucene-style form idf = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)), a term that appears in 5 of 250,000 documents on one shard has idf of about 10.72, while on another shard where it appears in 40 of 250,000 it has about 8.73.

RAG failure diagnosis
A RAG assistant answers 'What is the notice period for terminating the Enterprise plan?' with '30 days', but the policy says 60 days. Logging shows the correct policy chunk was retrieved at rank 2 and is in the prompt. Lay out a step-by-step triage to find out why the answer is wrong, with the experiment that separates each cause.
Key concepts: triage ladder; context ablation; conflicting evidence; parametric override; gold-chunk-only test; chunk position; quote-then-answer; faithfulness conditional on retrieval
Retrieval recall is not the problem if the correct chunk is truly in the prompt (retrieval precision may still be), so the question is why the generator did not use it correctly. Candidate causes and the discriminating checks: 1. A conflicting chunk is also in the prompt (for example an older policy or a different plan saying 30 days). Check: read the whole prompt, not just rank 2. If another chunk says 30 days, this is a retrieval/versioning problem after all (stale or wrong-plan chunk), and the fix is filtering by version or plan. 2.

RAG failure diagnosis
Answers are fluent and confident, but spot checks show many sentences are not in any retrieved chunk. Some are true, some are wrong. How do you determine whether the model is drawing on its own training knowledge, over-generalising from the chunks, or being fed irrelevant context, and what does each finding imply for the fix?
Key concepts: atomic claims; faithfulness; closed-book test; parametric knowledge; over-generalisation; abstention; context recall; verifier step
'Unsupported' is a property of claim versus context; the causes differ in where the claim came from, so the first step is to measure support at claim level, then run tests that vary the context. Step 1: split answers into atomic claims and label each as supported, contradicted or not found in the provided context (human labels on a sample, or a calibrated entailment judge). This gives the unsupported-claim rate, and shows whether unsupported claims are mostly true (suggesting parametric knowledge or sensible inference) or mostly wrong (confabulation or over-generalisation). Step 2: closed-book test. Ask the same questions with no retrieved context.

RAG failure diagnosis
Offline, your RAG system scores recall@5 of 0.92 and faithfulness 0.95 on the golden set, yet thumbs-down feedback is high, and users say answers are 'not what I asked' or 'outdated'. List the plausible reasons offline metrics and user feedback disagree and the analysis you would run to find which applies.
Key concepts: distribution shift; golden set coverage; stale evaluation; user feedback bias; faithfulness versus usefulness; failure classification; production query sampling; multi-turn queries
The two signals measure different things, so the mismatch is informative. Possible causes: 1. Query distribution shift. Golden queries are often written by the team, clean and well-formed; real users write short, vague, typo-laden, multi-part or follow-up queries ('what about for contractors?') that need conversation context. Retrieval and answers on those can be much worse. 2. Stale evaluation. The golden set labelled last quarter's corpus; new or changed documents are not represented, and 'outdated' complaints reflect freshness failures that offline sets cannot see. 3. Metric blind spots.

RAG failure diagnosis
Users of an internal assistant complain that questions containing acronyms and IDs ('What does SLA-7 cover?', 'Status of ticket INC-48213?', 'Is DPA required?') get wrong or irrelevant answers, while natural-language questions work well. The system uses dense retrieval only. Explain why, how you would confirm the diagnosis with measurements, and the fixes in order of cost.
Key concepts: exact-match retrieval; subword tokenisation; BM25; hybrid retrieval; reciprocal rank fusion; acronym expansion; query routing; identifier lookup
Why: a dense embedding encodes semantic similarity of text pieces learned from training data. Rare strings such as 'INC-48213' or a company-specific acronym are tokenised into subword fragments with little meaning, so their embeddings are plausibly weakly informative and may sit close to many other IDs (dense retrievers are documented to underperform sparse methods on entity-centric questions); 'SLA-7' may be close to 'SLA-8' or generic SLA text.

A schema or constrained decoder only guarantees syntax and types: the value is valid JSON of the right shape, not a true statement about the document. Schema-constrained decoding (the strict structured-output modes some providers offer) restricts which token sequences can be produced, so the result parses and has the declared types and enum values.

Prompting and structured output (few-shot, CoT caveats, schemas, determinism)
A 5-class ticket-routing prompt uses 10 fixed few-shot examples and scores 81% on a 300-item dev set. A colleague merely reorders the same 10 examples and gets 76%. How do you interpret these numbers, and how would you test for ordering and example-selection effects before shipping?
Key concepts: example ordering sensitivity; recency bias; label balance in demonstrations; similarity-based example retrieval; permutation testing; paired comparison; near-duplicate leakage
Reading the numbers. On 300 items at about 80% accuracy the binomial standard error is sqrt(0.8*0.2/300), roughly 2.3 points, and treating the two scores as independent the standard error of a 5-point difference is about 3.3 points (1.5 standard errors). Function calling gives the model a list of tool names, descriptions and argument schemas, and it picks by matching the request to that text. lookup_order and get_order overlap, 'query' is free text so a bare order number looks acceptable, and nothing tells the model that get_order wants a specific id format.

Tool use and agents (function calling, loops, failure modes, action guardrails)
A research agent sometimes runs 40+ steps, repeating essentially the same web_search with slightly reworded queries. Each tool result adds about 1,500 tokens and the full history is resent at every step. Explain what is going wrong in cost and quality terms, and which guards you would add to the loop.

Two problems compound. 1. Loop without progress. The model has no built-in notion of 'I already tried this'. If results do not satisfy it, rewording the query is a locally reasonable next action. Tool use and agents (function calling, loops, failure modes, action guardrails)
A refund agent calls issue_refund(order_id, amount). Last week a tool call timed out at the payment service although the refund had actually gone through; the agent retried, and the customer was refunded twice. The orchestrator (not the model) generates an idempotency key per intended action, for example derived from the conversation id, order id and refund intent, and passes it with the call.

LLM evaluation (benchmarks, contamination, LLM-as-judge bias, regression suites)
You have a 200-case regression suite for a support-answer prompt. The old prompt passes 168 cases; the new prompt passes 174. Looking case by case, the new prompt fixes 15 cases and breaks 9. Is the new prompt better? Explain how to analyse this properly, how sampling variance and flaky cases change the picture, and how many cases you would want for a regression gate.
Key concepts: paired comparison; discordant pairs; exact sign test; sampling variance; flaky cases; bootstrap over cases; tiered regression gate
The headline +6 (84.0% to 87.0%) is a difference between two numbers computed on the same 200 cases, so it should be analysed as a paired comparison. Only the discordant cases carry information about which prompt is better: cases both pass or both fail do not. Here 15 cases favour the new prompt and 9 favour the old one.

LLM evaluation (benchmarks, contamination, LLM-as-judge bias, regression suites)
You must compare four candidate answer styles for a help-centre assistant using an LLM judge. Should the judge score each answer on an absolute 1-5 scale or compare pairs? How would you treat ties and judge inconsistency, and what are the cost implications?
Key concepts: pointwise vs pairwise judging; order swap; position bias; tie handling; Bradley-Terry aggregation; length bias; pair-count growth
Absolute (pointwise) scoring gives each answer a score against a rubric. It scales linearly with the number of answers, can be tracked over time and supports thresholds ('must score at least 4'). Weaknesses: scores often cluster (most answers get 4), different judge prompts or judge versions shift the scale, and small quality differences between candidates vanish. Pairwise comparison asks which of two answers is better. Relative judgments are often easier and more discriminating for close candidates, but give no absolute quality level, scale with the number of pairs (4 candidates need 6 pairs, 20 need 190), and need aggregation.

LLM evaluation (benchmarks, contamination, LLM-as-judge bias, regression suites)
You want to use an LLM judge to label support answers as 'acceptable' or 'not acceptable'. On 150 answers that a human reviewer also labelled, the counts are: both acceptable 120, judge acceptable but human not 10, judge not acceptable but human acceptable 5, both not acceptable 15. The vendor says '90% agreement, so it's good enough'. Evaluate that claim, state how you would calibrate the judge, and say how to treat the two kinds of labels honestly.
Key concepts: Cohen's kappa; class imbalance and raw agreement; judge false-accept rate; human-human agreement ceiling; stratified calibration sample; disagreement analysis; AI label vs human label
Raw agreement is 135/150 = 90%, but it is a weak summary here because the classes are imbalanced: the judge accepts 130 of 150 answers and the human accepts 125. A judge that always said 'acceptable' would agree with this human 125/150, about 83%, so 90% is less impressive than it sounds.

LLM evaluation (benchmarks, contamination, LLM-as-judge bias, regression suites)
Over six weeks a team iterated its assistant prompt against a fixed 300-item dev set scored by an LLM judge. The judge score rose from 3.1 to 4.2 out of 5, but thumbs-up rate in production is flat and the average answer length is up 40%. What happened, and how do you change the evaluation process so improvements are real?
Key concepts: Goodhart's law; dev set overfitting; locked test set; judge verbosity bias; length-controlled comparison; guardrail metrics; online validation
This looks like Goodhart's law: optimising a proxy until it stops tracking the goal. Goodhart's law says that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure. Three mechanisms probably combine here. 1. Overfitting to the dev set: with dozens of prompt edits evaluated on the same 300 items, each edit that happens to help those items is kept. The final score is a biased estimate, like tuning hyperparameters on the test set. Part of the 3.1 to 4.2 rise can be adaptation to those items. 2.

Implement in Python (standard library only) a function wilson_interval(successes, n, z=1.96) with input validation, compare it with the naive normal-approximation interval on this data, and explain what the interval does and does not tell you at n=30, and how many cases you would need for a +/-3 point interval at about 90%.
