A pass rate on n cases is an estimate from a sample, so it should be reported with an interval. For 27/30 the point estimate is 0.90, but the 95% Wilson score interval is about 74.4% to 96.5%: the true pass rate on the underlying distribution could plausibly be well below the point estimate.

Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting (LoRA/QLoRA, SFT, forgetting, data needs)
A 40-agent helpdesk wants every internal ticket summary in one fixed five-section layout (Issue, Impact, Steps tried, Current status, Next action). A developer proposes fine-tuning a model on 300 past summaries. Today, a plain zero-shot prompt produces the layout correctly in about 60% of cases, and the content is usually accurate. A manager asks if fine-tuning is the right first move. What do you recommend, and what result would change your mind?
Key concepts: format adherence; few-shot examples; output validator with retry; prompt baseline; SFT data curation; operational cost of fine-tuning; plateau criterion
Start with prompting. The observed problem is format adherence, not missing knowledge: content is usually right and only the layout is wrong 40% of the time. That kind of gap is often closed by cheaper levers: explicit section instructions, two or three representative examples, and a deterministic validator that checks the five headings appear in order and triggers one retry with the error message.

Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting (LoRA/QLoRA, SFT, forgetting, data needs)
A product team lists three needs for a single assistant: (A) answer HR questions from policy documents that are edited every week, (B) always reply in a warm, concise brand voice with a fixed sign-off, and (C) pull 12 fields from scanned expense reports into a strict schema with at least 98% field accuracy. Someone says 'just fine-tune one model for all three'. How would you map each need to prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning, and which of your choices is the weakest?
Key concepts: new knowledge vs style; retrieval freshness; few-shot style transfer; SFT for skills; schema validation; evaluation per need
Treat the three needs as three different kinds of gap. (A) is a knowledge need with a short shelf life. Fine-tuning stores information in weights, which makes updates slow and unverifiable, and in published comparisons of knowledge injection, retrieval often beat unsupervised fine-tuning, which struggled to absorb new facts (Ovadia et al.; results are setup-dependent).

Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting (LoRA/QLoRA, SFT, forgetting, data needs)
After LoRA supervised fine-tuning, your support-intent classifier scores 80% on a 400-item held-out set. Your best hand-tuned prompt on the untuned model scored 74% on the same 400 items. The team wants to declare that fine-tuning beat prompting. What would you check before accepting this, and how would you decide whether a 6-point gap is real?
Key concepts: fair baseline; test-set leakage; paired comparison; McNemar exact test; discordant pairs; prompt-effort parity; confidence interval
A 6-point gap on 400 items is neither obviously real nor obviously noise; several things must hold before you accept it. Fairness of the baseline. The prompt should have received comparable effort: clear label definitions, a few representative examples chosen from training data, the same output format constraint. If the fine-tune had weeks of tuning and the prompt had an afternoon, the comparison measures effort, not method. Also compare at matched deployment conditions (same output parsing, same decoding settings). Leakage and selection.

Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting (LoRA/QLoRA, SFT, forgetting, data needs)
A team ran full-parameter supervised fine-tuning for 3 epochs on 6,000 internal ticket-classification examples. The classifier meets its target. During release testing, though, the model ignores formatting rules in the system prompt, answers unrelated general questions more tersely, and declines clearly out-of-scope requests less often than before. What probably happened, what checks should have caught it, and how would you change the training pipeline?
Key concepts: catastrophic forgetting; narrow-distribution SFT; regression suite on base capabilities; replay or data mixing; adapter-based tuning; lower learning rate and early stopping; safety behaviour regression
Likely cause. Three epochs of full-parameter training on a narrow, single-format dataset pushes the weights toward one input-output pattern (short label outputs). The model's behaviour on prompts unlike the training data can drift: terse answers, weaker adherence to system-prompt style rules and shifted refusal behaviour are all plausible consequences, because instruction-following and safety behaviour were themselves learned in earlier stages and nothing in your loss preserves them.

Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting (LoRA/QLoRA, SFT, forgetting, data needs)
Your team can LoRA fine-tune a mid-sized decoder on two GPUs, but only one is available this quarter, and someone suggests QLoRA. Describe what QLoRA changes relative to plain LoRA, what you give up, and what you would verify before shipping an adapter trained that way.
Key concepts: frozen 4-bit base weights; dequantise on the fly; higher-precision adapters; activation memory; step-time overhead; merging adapters into a different-precision base; evaluate the deployed artefact
Plain LoRA freezes the base weights, usually held in 16-bit, and trains low-rank adapter matrices, so optimiser state and gradients exist only for the small adapters.

Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting (LoRA/QLoRA, SFT, forgetting, data needs)
A team has 200 high-quality human-written support replies and plans to prompt a larger model to generate 20,000 more, then run supervised fine-tuning on all 20,200 to improve a smaller deployed model. What are the main risks, which controls would you add, and how would you decide whether the synthetic expansion actually helped?
Key concepts: model-generated training data; diversity collapse; error propagation; near-duplicate filtering; human-only evaluation set; mixing ratio ablation; data licence and terms review
Why 20,200 is not obviously better than 200. The 200 human examples carry the target behaviour and real phrasing; the 20,000 generated ones carry whatever the generator tends to produce. Fine-tuning on a modest set often mostly shifts style and format, and some work (for example LIMA) argues a small, carefully curated set can be enough for that, so the marginal value of volume can be low while the marginal risk is not. Main risks.

Safety, security and privacy (prompt injection, PII, jailbreaks, red teaming)
An email-triage assistant summarises a user's inbox and can draft replies. A security reviewer shows that a message from an external sender can steer the assistant's behaviour even though the user never typed anything unusual. The team's first fix is a filter that blocks emails containing phrases such as 'ignore previous instructions'. Explain the distinction between direct and indirect prompt injection here, and why that filter is a weak defence.
Key concepts: direct injection; indirect injection; untrusted data in context; blocklist limits; no instruction/data separation; defence in depth
Direct injection comes from the person interacting with the application, who types text intended to override the developer's instructions. Indirect injection is delivered through data the application ingests: an email body, a web page, a document in a vector index, a tool result. The attacker never talks to the assistant. The victim's own session carries the attacker's text into the prompt, which is why this is dangerous in an assistant with the user's mailbox privileges.

Safety, security and privacy (prompt injection, PII, jailbreaks, red teaming)
You are asked to ship an assistant that can read a user's email and calendar, search the web, and (when asked) send email and create events. Design a layered defence against prompt injection from external content. For each layer say what it stops and what it cannot stop, and be explicit about the residual risk.
Key concepts: least privilege; human-in-the-loop confirmation; separating trusted and untrusted content; output validation; egress restrictions; audit logging; residual risk
Assume injected text will sometimes influence the model. Design so that influence cannot cause irreversible harm. 1. Least privilege. Separate read tools from write tools; scope each to the minimum (read mail from one mailbox, send only from the user's address, create events only on the user's own calendar). This stops a hijacked model from using powers it never had. It does not stop misuse of powers it does have. 2. Human confirmation for side effects.

Safety, security and privacy (prompt injection, PII, jailbreaks, red teaming)
A chat assistant renders model output as markdown, including images. A security test shows that after the assistant summarised a shared document, the user's browser made an outbound request to an unfamiliar domain, and the request contained fragments of the user's earlier conversation. No tool call was involved. Walk through how this can happen, why it is hard to notice, and what you would change. Describe the mechanism and fixes, not attack text.
Key concepts: markdown image fetch; indirect injection; URL as data channel; image proxy or allowlist; content security policy; link display; no automatic rendering of external URLs
The mechanism has three parts. First, an injection: the shared document (untrusted data) contains text that the model treats as an instruction. Second, the model's output is attacker-influenced: it can include a markdown image or hyperlink whose URL includes text copied from the conversation. Third, the client behaviour: the UI renders markdown to HTML, and an image tag causes the browser to issue a GET request to that URL as soon as the message is displayed.

Safety, security and privacy (prompt injection, PII, jailbreaks, red teaming)
A support-copilot stores full prompts, retrieved chunks and model responses in application logs for 90 days. Retrieved chunks come from past tickets that contain names, emails, order numbers and sometimes health information. All tenants share one vector index with a tenant_id filter. Design the privacy controls for this system across prompts, logs, retrieval and deletion requests, and say where each control is weakest.
Key concepts: PII redaction; data minimisation; retention limits; access control at retrieval time; tenant isolation; deletion from index and backups; embedding leakage
Treat PII as data that flows through four places: the index, the prompt, the model output and the logs, plus the model provider's own retention and training terms if the model is hosted. Each needs its own control, enforced by code outside the model. For the prompt itself, send the model only the fields the task needs (for example a masked order reference rather than a full email address) and use a provider no-retention setting where one is offered (you can contract for, but not verify, provider deletion).

Safety, security and privacy (prompt injection, PII, jailbreaks, red teaming)
You must red-team a customer-facing assistant that has read access to internal knowledge and one write tool, before launch. Describe a red-team plan, how you would define and measure attack success rate (ASR), and what you would conclude if 200 attack attempts all fail. Include how to treat adaptive attackers and what the plan cannot prove.
Key concepts: threat model; attack categories; success criteria; attack success rate; upper confidence bound on zero failures; adaptive attacks; regression test set
Plan. Start with a threat model: who attacks (a user, an outside content author), what they want (read other tenants' data, trigger the write tool, make the bot say something harmful or off-brand), and through which channels (chat, retrieved documents, uploaded files). From that, enumerate categories and build scenarios per category with a written success criterion. Use a mix of people and tooling, include testers outside the build team, and give them the real system, including its tools and retrieval content, because many failures are about the system, not the model alone. Defining success.

Safety, security and privacy (prompt injection, PII, jailbreaks, red teaming)
In a security review a colleague says 'jailbreaks and prompt injection are the same thing, so one safety classifier covers both'. Give a precise distinction between the two, say who the attacker and the victim are in each case, and explain why the mitigations only partly overlap.
Key concepts: jailbreak; prompt injection; threat model; safety training bypass; trust boundary; tool permissions; content classifier
The cleanest distinction is the trust boundary being attacked. Jailbreak: the person talking to the model tries to get content or behaviour that the model's safety training or provider policy is meant to prevent. The attacker is the user; they have chosen to send adversarial input to the service. The 'victim' is the policy (and potentially people harmed by the output). There may be no tool, document or third party involved. Prompt injection: text that the application does not trust, or that the user did not write, ends up in the model's context and is followed as if it were an instruction from the developer or user.

A team hosting a decoder-only model wants a small capacity-planning helper. Write two functions.

kv_cache_bytes(n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1, bytes_per_elem=2) returns the bytes needed to cache keys and values for `batch` sequences of `seq_len` tokens.

max_concurrent_sequences(total_bytes, weight_bytes, reserve_bytes, n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, bytes_per_elem=2) returns how many full-length sequences fit after subtracting the weights and a fixed reserve (activations, runtime overhead) from the device memory. Then, for a hypothetical 32-layer model with head_dim 128, 4,096-token sequences, an fp16 cache, an 80 GiB device, 14e9 bytes of weights and a 6 GiB reserve, report how many sequences fit with 32 KV heads versus 8 KV heads, and what that tells you about the design of the attention layer.
Key concepts: KV cache size; n_kv_heads vs attention heads; grouped-query attention; bytes per element; capacity planning; input validation

On a hypothetical accelerator with 300 TFLOP/s of usable fp16 compute and 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth, you serve a 7B-parameter fp16 model (14 GB of weights) with 32 layers, 32 KV heads and head_dim 128. A colleague says: "Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound, so just keep growing the decode batch until the GPU is saturated." Using a back-of-envelope roofline, show why batch-1 decode is bandwidth-bound, how far batching really helps with 2,000-token contexts, and what the numbers say about prefill.
Key concepts: arithmetic intensity; roofline ridge point; prefill vs decode; weight reads amortised over batch; KV-cache bandwidth; time to first token
Ridge point: 300e12 FLOP/s / 2e12 B/s = 150 FLOP per byte. A kernel below that intensity is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.

Serving, latency and cost (KV cache, batching, quantisation, caching, token budgets)
Write a small simulator that compares static and continuous batching. All requests arrive at time 0 and are served in FIFO order; request i needs lengths[i] decode steps; one decode step costs one time unit regardless of batch size, and prefill is ignored.

static_batching(lengths, max_batch): requests are taken in groups of max_batch; a group runs until its longest member finishes, and every member is returned when the group ends.
continuous_batching(lengths, max_batch): at every step boundary free slots are filled from the queue in FIFO order, and a request leaves after exactly its own number of steps.

Both return {"total_steps": int, "completion": [finish time of each request, in input order]} and raise ValueError for a non-positive max_batch or a non-positive or non-int length. Run them on lengths = [2, 10, 3, 9] with max_batch = 2, and say what this model leaves out that matters for a real serving system.
Key concepts: static vs continuous batching; iteration-level scheduling; slot utilisation; idle slots in static batches; mean completion time; simulation limits

A chat feature sends about 3,000-token prompts and gets about 400-token answers. Your support assistant has a response cache keyed on embedding similarity: if a new query has cosine similarity of at least 0.92 to a cached query, the cached answer is returned and the model is skipped. It serves 30% of 1,000,000 daily queries; a human reviews a random sample of 500 cache hits and finds 10 wrong answers. (a) Estimate daily wrong answers with a rough 95% interval. A serving stack reserves a contiguous KV-cache region for the maximum 4,096-token length for every request at admission. The model has 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, an fp16 cache, and 60 GiB is available for cache. In your traffic a typical request ends at about 700 tokens (prompt plus output). (a) How many concurrent requests fit, and what fraction of the reserved memory is actually used? (b) A paged scheme allocates 16-token blocks on demand: roughly how many requests fit and how much is wasted per request? (c) Why will the real throughput gain be smaller than the capacity ratio, and what else does block-level allocation enable?
Key concepts: contiguous reservation; internal fragmentation; block allocation; KV memory per token; copy-on-write sharing; capacity vs throughput
Per token the cache is 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes = 128 KiB. (a) Reserving 4,096 tokens costs 512 MiB per request, so 60 GiB / 512 MiB = 120 concurrent requests.

Hallucination, grounding and long context
A model asked for references on a niche topic returns three plausible-looking papers with authors, titles, venues and years; two of them do not exist. A colleague asks: "It clearly knows how to say 'I don't know' in other chats, so why did training leave it guessing here?" Describe how the pretraining objective and the way answers are typically scored encourage confident guessing, why facts seen once or never are especially at risk, and which part of the problem retrieval can and cannot fix.
Key concepts: next-token likelihood; rare facts; no-abstention incentive; accuracy-only scoring; guessing vs abstaining; retrieval limits
A pretrained language model is trained to put high probability on the next token of text, not to verify truth. When the training data supports a pattern strongly (the format of a citation: authors, a venue, a year), it learns to generate that pattern fluently.

Hallucination, grounding and long context
A policy Q&A assistant outputs an answer and a confidence score. On 1,000 held-out questions the confidence bands look like this (hypothetical): at least 0.9: 400 questions, 380 correct; 0.7 to 0.9: 300 questions, 210 correct; 0.5 to 0.7: 200 questions, 90 correct; below 0.5: 100 questions, 20 correct. When the bot abstains the user is routed to a human, at a cost of 1 unit; a wrong answer costs 10 units. Where should the abstention threshold sit, what changes if a wrong answer costs only 3, and what must you verify before trusting these numbers?
Key concepts: coverage vs accuracy; cost-ratio break-even rule; calibration; answered-only accuracy; confidence intervals per band; human handoff cost
Decision rule: answering a question whose chance of being correct is a costs (1 - a) x C_wrong in expectation; abstaining costs C_abstain. Answer when a > 1 - C_abstain / C_wrong.

Hallucination, grounding and long context
Your company has a 300,000-token body of product manuals, updated weekly, and about 50,000 questions a day from customers with different entitlements. A manager says a hypothetical 400,000-token context model makes RAG unnecessary: "just paste all the manuals into every prompt." Assume prefill runs at 10,000 tokens/s per GPU, a typical RAG prompt is 6,000 tokens, and the KV cache costs 128 KiB per token. Compare the two designs on latency, compute, memory, freshness and access control, and say when long context is the right choice.
Key concepts: prefill cost; KV memory of a cached prefix; attention dilution; freshness; access control; hybrid design
Latency and compute: pasting 300,000 tokens means a prefill of 300,000 / 10,000 = 30 s before the first token, versus 6,000 / 10,000 = 0.6 s for a RAG prompt, and 50,000 x 300,000 = 1.5e10 tokens processed per day versus 3e8, a 50x difference.

Hallucination, grounding and long context
To catch hallucinations cheaply, a team proposes two signals: (1) flag any answer whose average token log-probability falls below a threshold; (2) sample the model 5 times at a non-zero temperature and flag the answer when fewer than 4 of the samples agree. Where would each signal be informative, where would it fail, and how would you decide whether to deploy either?
Key concepts: token log-probability; paraphrase probability spreading; sample agreement; consistent errors; semantic clustering; calibration evaluation
Token probabilities. They carry some information: in controlled settings with the right prompt format, larger models' confidence on multiple-choice and true/false questions has been found reasonably reliable, and models can also be asked to rate the probability that their own answer is correct, which works fairly well (Kadavath et al.), though models trained to predict whether they know an answer struggled with calibration on new tasks.

Hallucination, grounding and long context
You build a hallucination detector for a RAG assistant: split each answer into sentences, run an NLI-style entailment model of (retrieved passages, sentence), and flag sentences that are not entailed. On 10,000 production sentences, 3% are truly unsupported by the retrieved context (hypothetical). The detector has 80% recall and a 5% false-positive rate. (a) What share of flags are real problems, and what does that imply for how you use the detector? (b) Beyond the threshold, what systematic error modes does this approach have? (c) How would you validate and improve it?
Key concepts: precision at low prevalence; entailment checking; claim decomposition; multi-passage evidence; numbers and negation; true but unsupported claims
(a) Out of 10,000 sentences, 300 are unsupported. Recall 80% gives 240 true positives and 60 misses. A 5% false-positive rate on the 9,700 supported sentences gives 485 false positives. Flags total 725, so precision = 240 / 725 = 33.1%.

Hallucination, grounding and long context
A product team wants to show a green "Verified by sources" badge whenever an assistant answer includes at least one citation. A hypothetical audit of 500 badged answers found that in 430 the cited passage supports the claim, in 45 it supports only part of the claim, and in 25 it does not support it at all. What is wrong with the badge, how would you change the UI and wording to reduce over-trust, and how would you test that the change works?
Key concepts: citation presence vs support; claim-level citations; highlighted evidence span; abstention in the UI; calibrated wording; over-trust measurement
The badge asserts verification, but the audit shows 70 of 500 badged answers (14%) are only partly supported (45, 9%) or unsupported (25, 5%). A binary badge based on citation presence measures the wrong thing: the model can cite a real document that does not contain the claim, or support one clause while an adjacent clause is invented. It also invites over-trust: users who see an authoritative marker may check less (automation bias is plausible here, and worth measuring rather than assuming). Changes.

GenAI product scenarios (support bot, document QA)
A retailer's support team handles about 12,000 conversations a month. The ten most common intents (order status, returns, delivery changes and so on) make up roughly 45% of volume. Leadership wants an LLM support bot live in 8 weeks and quotes 'containment rate' as the success target. Design the launch: scope, escalation, rollout, metrics beyond containment, how to handle wrong answers and legal risk, and a measurable go/no-go gate.
Key concepts: containment vs resolution; scope limiting; human handoff; shadow mode; re-contact within 7 days; Wilson lower bound; rollback
Scope. Roughly 45% of volume sits in ten intents, which is where to start. Pick intents with stable policies and low harm if wrong (order status, standard return window). Keep money-moving, legal, safety and complaint-escalation topics out of the first release, and route anything off-scope or low-confidence to a human with the conversation summary attached so customers do not repeat themselves. Make the human route visible at any point; hiding it inflates containment and damages trust. Metrics.

GenAI product scenarios (support bot, document QA)
A legal-tech team is building a contract question-answering product. Lawyers upload their own contracts, ask things like 'what is the notice period for termination?' and expect answers with exact clause references. Say what you would and would not promise users, how you would present answers and citations, how access control must work, and what evaluation results you would require before launch.
Key concepts: clause-level citation; abstention on missing information; per-document access control; quote verification; scope of promise; evaluation set from real contracts; human review for high stakes
What to promise. Position the product as an assistant that finds and summarises relevant text with traceable references, not as legal advice. Promise things the system can show: here is the clause, here is the quoted text, here is a plain-language reading. Do not promise that it catches every relevant clause, or that its interpretation is correct. State that lawyers remain responsible for conclusions, and make that visible in the interface. Answers and citations. Each claim should link to a specific passage (document, page, clause number) and show the quoted text beside the answer.

GenAI product scenarios (support bot, document QA)
An A/B test of a support bot ran on 10,000 conversations, 5,000 per arm. The bot arm resolves 39% of conversations without a human versus 31% for the control (which has a simple FAQ widget). However, among conversations marked 'resolved without a human', 21% of the bot arm contacted support again within 7 days about the same issue versus 12% in the control. Customer satisfaction scores are 0.1 points lower in the bot arm on a 5-point scale, from a survey answered by about 8% of users. Should you ship? Argue with the numbers.
Key concepts: containment; true resolution; re-contact within 7 days; guardrail metrics; survey non-response; two-proportion test; segment analysis
Headline versus net. Containment rose by 8 points (31% to 39%), but a contained conversation that comes back is not resolved. Computing net resolution: control 31% x (1 - 0.12) = 27.3%; bot 39% x (1 - 0.21) = 30.8%.

A teammate hands you a notebook that reported 0.87 F1 on the validation set and says 'just rerun it to get the same number'. Which pieces of information must have been recorded for the run so that someone else can re-create that result, and which of them are most often forgotten?
Key concepts: run record; code commit hash; dataset snapshot identity; split rule; random seed; environment lockfile; fitted preprocessing artifacts
A reproducible run record has to pin down every input that influences the number, not just the model code. At minimum: 1. Code identity: the commit hash, plus a note (or saved diff) if the working tree had uncommitted changes. A notebook with out-of-order cells is a classic way to lose this. 2. Data identity: which dataset snapshot or content hash was read, and exactly how the train/validation split was made (rule, key and seed). 'The latest table' is not an identity. 3.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
Why does 'it works on my machine' cause more trouble in machine-learning projects than in ordinary application code?
Key concepts: silent failure; unpinned dependencies; container image; data version; hardware nondeterminism; run-to-run variance
Because an ML result depends on more than the code, and many of the extra dependencies fail silently. In ordinary software a missing library or wrong version usually crashes or fails a test. In ML the program still runs and simply returns a slightly different number or a slightly different model. Typical sources of 'my machine vs yours' differences: - Data: your laptop has a sample or an older extract; the pipeline reads a table that has since been refreshed. - Library versions: an unpinned dependency can resolve to a newer release with changed defaults, a different tokeniser, a different numerical kernel or changed random-number behaviour. - Hardware and drivers: CPU versus GPU, different GPU generations, or different driver/runtime libraries can change floating-point results and which algorithm is chosen.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
Three weeks ago a run on branch main reported 0.842 AUC on a fixed validation set. Today, the same script on main gives 0.829, and nobody changed the code on purpose. Give an ordered checklist for finding out why, and say how you would decide whether 0.829 is a real regression at all.
Key concepts: run-to-run variance; bisecting one factor at a time; data snapshot hash; lockfile; moving image tag; moved validation set; run manifest
Work from the cheapest and most likely explanations to the most expensive, and change one factor at a time. 0. Check the comparison itself. Is it the same evaluation set (same rows, same ordering of any sampling), the same metric code and the same threshold/averaging convention? A moved validation set explains many 'regressions'. 1. Measure the noise first. Re-run the old configuration with several seeds.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
You fix every random seed in a training script, yet two runs on the same GPU box differ in the third decimal of validation loss, and a colleague's run on a different machine differs more. Why is setting the seed necessary but not sufficient, and what else would you control or accept?
Key concepts: floating-point non-associativity; parallel reduction order; cuDNN algorithm selection; DataLoader worker seeding; SeedSequence.spawn; deterministic algorithms mode; seed variance
A seed only initialises pseudo-random generators. It does not make the rest of the computation identical. 1. Floating-point order. Floating-point addition is not associative, so summing the same numbers in a different order can give a different result. Parallel reductions, tiled matrix multiplies and, in some GPU kernels, accumulation whose order depends on scheduling can change the order from run to run. Differences are tiny per operation but can compound over many training steps. 2. Algorithm selection. Libraries may auto-tune and pick different convolution or matmul algorithms.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
Your team logs every training run to an experiment tracker and also keeps a model registry. A new hire asks why one of them is not enough. What belongs in each, and how would you answer 'which code, data and run produced the model that is serving traffic right now?'
Key concepts: experiment tracker; model registry; immutable model version; alias or stage pointer; lineage; data snapshot hash; serving-time version logging
Different jobs, different lifecycles. Experiment tracker: high volume, mostly disposable. For each run it stores parameters, metrics over time, tags, evaluation plots and output artifacts, plus the identity of the inputs (code commit, data snapshot id, config, seeds, environment). MLflow Tracking, for instance, describes logging parameters, code versions, metrics and output files, with a run holding metadata and artifacts. Use it to compare, filter and debug experiments; runs that never get promoted are still valuable evidence of what was tried. Model registry: low volume, governed.

ML lifecycle and reproducibility (data/model versioning, experiment tracking, environments)
Your training set is 400 GB of images plus a labels file. About 2% of the files are added or relabelled each week, and models from the last year must stay reproducible. Compare keeping a dated full copy of the dataset every week with content-hash versioning using small pointer files, say what each training run records, and name what can still go wrong.
Key concepts: content-addressable storage; manifest hash; pointer file in Git; immutable snapshot; deduplication; garbage collection and retention; split rule
Full dated copies are simple but scale linearly with the number of versions and give no cheap way to answer 'what changed'. Content-addressed versioning stores each distinct file once, keyed by a hash of its bytes, and a small manifest or pointer file maps names to hashes. The pointer file is what lives in version control, so a Git commit pins an exact dataset state.

Two training configurations, A and B, are each run with 5 seeds on the same data split. Validation accuracy for A is 0.912, 0.905, 0.918, 0.909, 0.915 and for B is 0.917, 0.908, 0.921, 0.913, 0.919 (seed i uses the same initial weights and data order in both). A teammate wants to ship B because 'it won in every seed'. How would you compare the two fairly, and how strong is the evidence?
Key concepts: seed variance; paired comparison; standard error of a difference; best-of-n selection bias; sign test limits; minimum worthwhile effect
Principles for comparing runs: use the same data split and evaluation set for both; run several seeds because a single run mixes real differences with seed noise; report mean and spread (standard deviation), not the best run; and never pick the best of many runs for one configuration and compare it with a single run of the other, which builds in selection bias.

A pull-request check trains a small model on a 200-row fixture and asserts validation accuracy >= 0.75. It fails in roughly one build in seven even when no relevant code changed, and engineers have started re-running it until it is green. Diagnose the problem and redesign the check, saying what a PR-level test can and cannot establish about a model.
Key concepts: flaky test; seed variance; smoke test floor; overfit-a-tiny-batch test; small fixtures; PR check vs post-merge evaluation; quarantining flaky tests
The test asserts a statistical outcome of a stochastic process against a threshold that sits inside the process's own noise, so it is flaky by construction. Re-running until green trains the team to ignore the check, which is arguably worse than having none.

CI/CD for ML (data and model tests, gating, rollback) - includes data and model validation
A newly promoted model passes every offline gate and goes to full traffic at 14:00. At 14:40 the endpoint's error rate is normal but the business metric 'orders per 1,000 sessions' looks 6% lower than the same hour last week. Define the rollback criteria you would have agreed in advance, and what has to be true for the rollback to be quick and safe.
Key concepts: rollback criteria; hard vs soft signals; canary before full traffic; concurrent control; previous artifact retention; expand-contract schema change; model version in logs
Rollback criteria should be written, with thresholds, before the promotion, because deciding during an incident is when people rationalise. Hard signals, automatic: error and timeout rate above a limit for N minutes; p95 or p99 latency breaching the SLO; prediction health checks such as a share of NaN, constant or out-of-range outputs; a sudden shift in the output score distribution against the previous model on the same traffic. These are cheap to evaluate and rarely ambiguous.

A registry turns 'a file somewhere' into a managed, addressable model with history. The folder gives you bytes with a naming convention; a registry typically adds: 1. Version identity. Each registration under a model name gets a new, immutable version number (MLflow's registry documents the incrementing version number; treating a version as immutable is the intended usage rather than something that page spells out), so 'model X v12' means one specific artifact. 2. Lineage. Each version links back to what produced it: the training run, code commit, data snapshot and config, so you can answer 'how was the model in production built?' 3. Metadata.

Model registry and packaging (containers, ONNX, signatures, dependency pinning)
Your team stores scikit-learn pipelines as joblib files in a shared bucket that several teams, and one external partner, can write to. The serving image loads whichever file is newest at startup. After a base-image refresh the service starts logging version warnings and a handful of predictions change; separately, the security team flags the loading step. Explain both problems and what you would change in the loading path.
Key concepts: pickle deserialization; arbitrary code execution on load; library version coupling; joblib; artifact integrity (hash/signature); environment pinning; fail-fast version check
Two different problems share one loading step. Compatibility. A pickle records instance state plus references to classes by import path; it does not embed the class code (the Python docs say only instance data is pickled). Loading therefore needs a compatible version of the library that defined the classes. scikit-learn's persistence guide says loading a model trained with a different scikit-learn version is not supported, may emit an inconsistent-version warning, and can give different results or crash.

A fraud model (a scikit-learn pipeline: one-hot encoding, scaling, then gradient-boosted trees) is exported to ONNX so it can be served without a Python environment. In a shadow comparison, 0.8% of rows get a different predicted class from the original pipeline, and the ops lead asks whether ONNX 'guarantees identical behaviour'. What does an exchange format like this actually fix, what can still make outputs differ, and how would you test the export before it ships?
Key concepts: ONNX computation graph; operator set (opset); custom operators; preprocessing outside the graph; float32 vs float64 precision; decision threshold flips; parity testing
What it fixes. ONNX specifies a portable, serialized computation graph plus named operator sets (the IR specification). The serving side needs a runtime that implements those operators, not the training Python environment, and loading a model does not unpickle Python objects. scikit-learn's guide lists these as advantages and also notes that arbitrary computation can be expressed in ONNX, so untrusted models should still run in a sandbox.

Choose batch, online (request/response) or streaming inference for each case and justify it on latency, freshness, cost and failure handling: (a) re-ranking 3 million product pages once a week for a newsletter; (b) a card-payment risk score that must return in about 100 ms at checkout and should reflect the cardholder's last 10 minutes of activity; (c) 50,000 sensor readings per second where an alert must fire within a few seconds of a pattern. (a) Batch. Nobody waits on an individual prediction, the entity set is known in advance, and staleness of a week is acceptable. Run it as a scheduled job that is partitioned and retried per partition, with idempotent writes (overwrite by partition or upsert by key) so a rerun cannot duplicate.

Serving patterns (batch, online, streaming, REST/gRPC, autoscaling, batching) - includes monitoring fundamentals for serving
Implement a deterministic simulator for dynamic request batching on a single worker, plus a percentile helper.

simulate_microbatch(arrivals, max_batch, max_wait, overhead, per_item) -> (latencies, batch_sizes)

arrivals is a sorted list of arrival times in ms (ValueError if unsorted; ValueError if max_batch < 1 or max_wait < 0). Requests are served FIFO. A batch is dispatched at the first moment the worker is free AND (max_batch requests are waiting OR the oldest waiting request has waited max_wait ms). It contains the waiting requests up to max_batch (a request arriving exactly at the dispatch instant counts as waiting). Service time is overhead + per_item * batch_size, and the worker is busy for that time. Latency of a request is its finish time minus its arrival time. Also write percentile(values, p) using the nearest-rank definition. Then use it to explain, with an arrival every 1 ms (1000 requests/s) and every 20 ms, why max_batch and max_wait must be chosen from the load, using overhead=10 ms and per_item=0.5 ms.
Key concepts: dynamic batching; max batch size and max wait; fixed overhead vs per-item cost; queueing delay; throughput capacity; p95 latency; head-of-line wait

A model endpoint scales out when average CPU passes 70%. Each replica serves about 4 requests at a time at roughly 120 ms each and takes about 90 s to become useful (image pull, model load, warm-up). Normally 3 replicas handle 50 requests/s. At 09:00 traffic ramps to 200 requests/s within two minutes. p99 goes to timeouts for several minutes even though CPU graphs look unremarkable (the work happens on an accelerator). Key concepts: autoscaling signal; Little's law (concurrency = rate x latency); saturation; cold start and warm-up; readiness gating; scale-up lag; bounded queue and load shedding
Diagnosis. Capacity per replica is about 4 in flight / 0.12 s = 33 requests/s. Three replicas give about 100 requests/s, which is fine for 50 requests/s (50% busy) but not for 200. The excess is about 100 requests/s.

During a deploy, a prediction service's p99 rises from 200 ms to 1.5 s. Its callers use a 1 s timeout and retry up to 3 times immediately. Within minutes the service, which normally runs at about 80% of capacity, is completely down. Explain the mechanism and describe the client and server changes (timeouts, retries, idempotency, fallbacks) that would have contained it.
Key concepts: retry storm; timeouts and deadlines; retry budget; exponential backoff with jitter; idempotency; load shedding; fallback prediction; circuit breaker
Mechanism. The slow deploy pushes some requests past the 1 s client timeout. Each timeout triggers an immediate retry, so offered load grows. If a fraction f of attempts fail, a client with up to 3 retries sends about 1 + f + f^2 + f^3 attempts per original request; at f = 0.5 that is 1.875x.

Serving patterns (batch, online, streaming, REST/gRPC, autoscaling, batching) - includes monitoring fundamentals for serving
Your scoring API has a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, where a request is 'good' only if it returns a valid score within 300 ms. In the last hour 1.5% of requests were bad; in the last 5 minutes 0.4% were bad. How fast is the error budget burning, how much of the monthly budget did that hour use (assume uniform traffic), would a multiwindow policy that pages at a 14.4x burn rate over 1 hour and 5 minutes fire, and how should responses served by a fallback model be counted?
Key concepts: error budget; burn rate; multiwindow alert; SLI definition (valid and within 300 ms); fallback accounting; long and short window
The error budget is the allowed bad fraction: 100% - 99.9% = 0.1%. Burn rate is observed bad ratio divided by that: over the last hour 1.5% / 0.1% = 15x; over the last 5 minutes 0.4% / 0.1% = 4x.

Deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, rollback)
How does a canary release of a new model differ from a blue-green deployment, and what does each one cost you?
Key concepts: canary release; blue-green deployment; traffic shifting; control group; instant rollback; duplicate capacity; blast radius
Canary. Google's SRE workbook defines canarying as a partial, time-limited deployment of a change and its evaluation, with the rest of the service acting as control. For a model: route, say, 5% of requests to the new version, compare error rate, latency and behavioural metrics against the concurrent baseline, and increase the share in stages. Benefits: small blast radius, real-traffic evidence, gradual capacity growth. Costs: you need weighted routing and a way to compare the two groups; the canary must be large and long enough to be representative (the workbook says so), and a small slice can be too small to detect rare or slow-to-appear problems. Blue-green.

Deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, rollback)
A team replacing a ranking model proposes: 'We will shadow the new model for two weeks. If its offline metrics on the logged shadow outputs and its latency look good, we go straight to 100%.' What can shadow deployment tell you, what can it not, and how would you sequence shadow, canary and A/B testing instead?
Key concepts: shadow deployment; canary release; A/B test; feedback effects; selection bias in logged data; guardrail metrics; staged rollout
Shadow deployment sends copies of live requests to the new model while only the old model's output is used. What it can tell you: whether the new model runs reliably on real inputs (errors, malformed outputs), how latency and resource use behave under real traffic, how its output distribution compares with the old model's, and how often the two agree. If you log the shadow outputs you can also compute offline metrics once outcomes arrive, with care. What it cannot tell you: 1. User response. Shadow outputs are never shown, so clicks, purchases or complaints about them never happen.

Deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, rollback)
Your service handles 2 million requests per day. A new model is canaried at 1% of traffic for one day. The guardrail is the complaint rate, baseline 0.20%, and you do not want it to rise by more than 30% relative (to 0.26%). At the end of the day the canary shows 50 complaints in 20,000 requests (0.25%). One colleague says 'not statistically significant, so it is safe'; another says 'close enough to the limit, ship'. Evaluate both, and say how you would design the check. Complaints are only reliably known after a week.
Key concepts: canary statistical power; non-inferiority margin; confidence bound; event counts; delayed labels; proxy metrics; traffic share vs duration
Neither colleague is right. Expected complaints at baseline in 20,000 requests are 0.20% x 20,000 = 40, so 50 observed is within ordinary noise of 40 (Poisson standard deviation about 6.3).

A marketplace tests a new ranking model with a 50/50 split. One engineer wants to randomise each request; another wants to hash the user ID. The 'recommended for you' carousel shows a +6% click lift in week 1 that decays to +1.5% by week 3. Compare the two ways of splitting traffic for consistency and interference, explain the decay, and say what you would put in place.
Key concepts: split unit (request vs user); sticky assignment by hashing; experiment-specific salt; interference between arms; novelty effect; switchback test; sample ratio check
Per-request randomisation gives many independent assignments and the highest statistical power for request-level outcomes (for example, 'was this impression clicked'), but each user sees both models. The experience is inconsistent, and outcomes that accumulate over a user (retention, repeat purchase, trust) are blended across arms, so they cannot be attributed to either model. It suits stateless, memoryless situations such as a latency or error comparison.

A teammate's Dockerfile for a model-serving API is: a slim Python base image, WORKDIR /app, COPY . ., RUN pip install -r requirements.txt, then CMD to start the server. Docker builds an image as a stack of layers and caches each instruction's result. Per Docker's build-cache documentation, when a layer changes every layer after it must be rebuilt. In the original file, COPY . . comes before the install step, and that copy includes the application source.

Its Deployment has a liveness probe on /health with initialDelaySeconds 20, periodSeconds 10 and failureThreshold 3, and no readiness or startup probe. Pods enter CrashLoopBackOff and never serve. Explain what is happening and design the probe configuration, including what each endpoint should check and one way your design could still go wrong.
Key concepts: liveness probe; readiness probe; startup probe; CrashLoopBackOff; failureThreshold; model warm-up; dependency checks in probes; Service endpoints
What happens: Kubernetes documents that a failed liveness check makes the kubelet kill the container and restart it. With these settings the first check starts about 20 s after start-up, and three consecutive failures at 10 s intervals take it to roughly 40 to 50 s. The model needs up to 150 s, so the container is killed before it is ever ready, restarts, repeats, and eventually backs off.

Your GPU inference Deployment has 4 replicas, each requesting 1 GPU, on a node pool that currently has exactly 4 GPUs in total, all occupied by those replicas. A model release is rolled out with maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0, and the rollout never completes. A new pod sits in Pending while the 4 old pods keep serving. Why, what are your options, and what does each cost? Assume a pod needs about 90 s to load the model.
Key concepts: maxSurge; maxUnavailable; Pending pod; GPU capacity; rolling update; minReadySeconds; revision history; rollback
With maxSurge 1 the Deployment is allowed to create one pod above the desired 4, and maxUnavailable 0 forbids taking any old pod down until a new one is available. The surge pod needs a free GPU, but all 4 are held by old pods, so the scheduler cannot place it; Kubernetes documents that a pod stays Pending as long as its resource request cannot be satisfied.

Feature stores and training-serving skew
What is training-serving skew, and how is it different from data drift? Use a small concrete example, and say how you would tell which one you are looking at.
Key concepts: training-serving skew; data drift; feature computation paths; unit mismatch; default value handling; distribution comparison; replay of raw events
Training-serving skew is a difference between the data a model sees during training and the data it sees when serving, caused by how the data is produced, not by the world changing. A typical case is a feature computed by different code in each path: a price stored in cents in the training table but sent in dollars by the live service, or a missing value filled with -1 offline and 0 online. The same real-world event yields different feature values in the two places, so the model's learned relationships no longer apply. Data drift is a change over time in the distribution of inputs (or labels) in the real world, for example customer behaviour shifting after a price change. The pipelines may be perfectly consistent; the population simply moved away from the training window. The tools for them overlap, which is why people confuse them.

A lender's credit model approves applicants scoring above a threshold (about 40% of 50,000 monthly applications). The two dependencies have different roles, so they need different designs. Registry (start-up dependency).

Reliability, incident response, rollback/recovery, performance and cost (SLOs, scaling, GPU utilisation, spend)
Your pricing model's API has availability and latency SLOs and an error budget policy that halts releases when the budget is exhausted. Last quarter the service met 99.95% availability while a stale feature quietly degraded pricing quality for nine days. Labels (realised outcomes) arrive about three weeks late. How would you extend SLIs, SLOs and the budget policy to cover model quality, and what should the policy say when the quality budget is burning?
Key concepts: quality SLI; good event definition; delayed-label SLI; error budget policy; burn rate; feature freshness; proxy SLIs; release freeze
Availability and latency SLIs describe whether the service answered, not whether the answer was good, so a model service needs SLIs on the quality of what it returns. The SRE material frames the error budget as the allowed unreliability that decides whether releases continue; the same mechanism works for quality if quality is turned into countable good and bad events. Fast proxy SLIs (available in minutes, no labels).

MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
A recommender model passes a 5% canary and a 2-week A/B test (click-through +4%, no latency or error regressions) and goes to 100%. Six weeks later, repeat purchases per active user are down 2% against the pre-launch trend while click-through is still up. List the plausible mechanisms, say what evidence would separate them, and explain what release practice would have caught this earlier or made it cheaper to resolve.
Key concepts: proxy metric; long-term holdback; novelty effect; outcome horizon; difference-in-differences; seasonality confound; exposure narrowing
Likely mechanisms, which can overlap: (1) Proxy mismatch. The test optimised click-through, but the goal is repeat purchase. Google's Rules of Machine Learning note that metrics measurable in A/B tests are proxies for longer-term goals, and that launch decisions need several metrics. A model that attracts clicks with narrower or more clickable items can raise clicks and lower later satisfaction. (2) Horizon.

MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
A new fraud-scoring model ran in shadow for three weeks: the shadow logged scores for all mirrored requests, 99.9% of them agreed with the expected output computed offline, and the shadow call's p99 latency was 70 ms. After promotion, p99 for the live decision is 400 ms, customers get duplicate 'transaction held' notifications, and live scores for similar customers are noticeably lower than what the shadow had logged. Which properties of the shadow setup could have produced a clean pass that did not predict this, and what would you change in the next shadow?
Key concepts: shadow deployment; critical-path latency; side effects; idempotency key; feature freshness; serving-time feature logging; recording stubs
The shadow comparison measured whether the model's output agreed with an expectation, not whether the system around it would behave the same once it is the live path. Four properties of a typical shadow setup explain the gap: 1. Latency off the critical path.

MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
An A/B test of a new ranking model (planned 50/50 by user hash) reports +3.1% conversion for treatment. A reviewer notices that assignment counts are 51,000 vs 49,000 users out of 100,000, and that the serving stack has (a) a result cache keyed by (query, locale) with a 10-minute TTL and (b) an online-learning component that updates one shared set of item-popularity weights from clicks in both arms. Explain what each of these can do to the experiment, how you would test for them, and how you would fix the setup.
Key concepts: sample ratio mismatch; chi-square test; cache key contamination; shared online learner; interference (SUTVA); A/A test; served versus assigned variant
Two separate problems show up in the description. 1. Sample ratio mismatch (SRM). With 100,000 users and a 50/50 plan, you expect 50,000 per arm.

MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
A product-search ranker trained on click logs raises offline AUC from 0.78 to 0.81 on a held-out week of logged impressions, but the online A/B test shows conversion of 3.10% vs 3.09% (not significant, with enough traffic that a 1% relative change would have been detectable). Give the explanations specific to logged-data evaluation that you would investigate, in the order you would check them, and how you would change the offline evaluation so it predicts the online result better.
Key concepts: position bias; selection bias; logged propensities; inverse-propensity weighting; direct feedback loop; nDCG at top ranks; objective mismatch
Offline AUC measures how well the model separates clicked from non-clicked impressions in logged data. That is not the same as improving what users do when the new model controls the page, and several mechanisms can open that gap. 1. Logged data come from the old policy. Items shown high up got more attention, so click labels mix item relevance with position and exposure.
